papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) deliver high-fidelity image and video generation, but inference requires many sequential model evaluations. Two acceleration strategies are increasingly important: model compression makes each evaluation cheaper, while adaptive inference avoids selected teacher computation through reuse, forecasting, or speculative execution. Their combination, however, is brittle: directly applying the evaluated adaptive methods to a compressed student can degrade quality, an observed failure mode we call the \textbf{Combination Gap}. We link this gap to a mismatch between pointwise distillation and short-horizon execution: a student trained at teacher states need not remain reliable when its own predictions are chained. We propose \textbf{TamedFlow}, which trains a compressed DiT for this deployed role through cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision. At inference, a lightweight Learnable Trajectory Estimator routes completed drafts: accepted drafts bypass the teacher, while rejected drafts roll back and receive one teacher rescue step. Distilling DiT-XL/2 into DiT-B/2, TamedFlow reaches FID $2.58$ at $2.25\times$ measured speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet $256\times256$. Ablations support trajectory supervision, and routing controls favor LTE over random decisions at nearly matched latency. Evaluations on ImageNet $512\times512$, MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics extend the empirical scope.
bullets: The work addresses quality degradation when adaptive inference methods are applied to compressed diffusion students.
It combines cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision.
A Learnable Trajectory Estimator accepts completed drafts or triggers rollback with one teacher rescue step.
For DiT-XL/2 distilled to DiT-B/2, it reports FID 2.58 and a 2.25× measured speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet 256×256.
Additional evaluations cover higher-resolution ImageNet, MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics; ablations support trajectory supervision and learned routing.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a trajectory-aware distillation method directly applicable to accelerating video diffusion models.
papers.title: TamedFlow: Trajectory-Aware Distillation for Teacher-Assisted Diffusion Sampling
papers.tldr: TamedFlow closes the compression–adaptive-inference combination gap by training diffusion students for reliable multi-step rollouts and routing drafts to reduce teacher evaluations.

papers.abstract: Camera-controlled video generation re-renders a video along a target camera trajectory, yet moving the camera around an object, the most natural way to change the viewpoint of an object-centric scene, remains difficult. Existing methods condition either on camera parameters, which are scale-ambiguous in monocular video, or on explicit geometry such as warped point clouds or depth, which breaks down under large viewpoint changes. We present AnyCam, a method that represents the camera with an anchor object in the scene: we reconstruct it in 3D and render it along the target trajectory, a camera signal that is scale-aware, view-complete and easy to specify relative to the object. A video diffusion model transfers the content and dynamics of the source video to the new viewpoint. Its H-Concat layout aligns source and target frames in time, so the model can be distilled into AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control. Both models are trained on paired videos with pixel-aligned anchor renderings from multi-camera videos and static-scene captures. Experiments on diverse datasets and trajectories show that AnyCam performs favorably against camera-controlled video generation and 3D reconstruction methods in camera control and visual quality.
authors: Weijie Lyu, Zhixin Shu, Yuntian Ke, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of changing viewpoints around objects, where camera parameters are scale-ambiguous and explicit geometry can fail under large viewpoint changes.
Reconstructs an anchor object in 3D and renders it along a target trajectory to represent the camera relative to the scene.
Uses a video diffusion model with H-Concat temporal alignment to transfer source-video content and dynamics to the new viewpoint.
Introduces AnyCam-AR, a streaming few-step generator for on-the-fly camera control.
Experiments across diverse datasets and trajectories show favorable camera control and visual quality compared with existing camera-controlled generation and 3D reconstruction methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of AnyCam. (a) The user selects an anchor object in the source video. SAM 2 [37] tracks it to give the source camera representation (the anchor cut-out), and SAM 3D [8] reconstructs it; the reconstruction is aligned to the source cameras and rendered along the target trajectory to give the target camera representation. The noisy target latent and the source latent are concatenated along the height (H-Concat), each half receives its camera representation through channel concatenation, and the diffusion transformer denoises the target half, which the VAE decodes into the target video. (b) The numbers under the tokens are their RoPE positions (t, h), with the role ID as a third entry in the fourth layout. The grids mark which source frames each target frame attends to. Frame concatenation [1, 7, 28] places the whole source after the target, so the first target frame needs the complete source video and therefore the generation cannot stream. Channel concatenation [15] merges the two frames into one token, which loses information and lowers fidelity to the source video [1]. Frame interleaving [52] doubles the length of the temporal axis. A shared position with a role phase [49] needs an additional positional encoding to tell the two streams apart. Our H-Concat keeps the source and target as separate tokens at the same temporal index and offsets the source in height, so the base model is used without new parameters or a custom attention mask.

Figure 10. Video-to-video comparison on CO3D. Each case takes two rows with the source frame (Input), the ground-truth frame and the frame of every method at the same time. 3DGS [20] is optimized per scene on the 81 source frames. AnyCam-AR, HY-WorldPlay [41] and InSpatio-World [40] are autoregressive models. On the sides of the objects that the source video does not show, AnyCam and AnyCam-AR match the ground truth, while 3DGS and DepthDirector [7] break down and most other baselines show the object from a wrong angle or lose it. For the television (bottom), ReDirector [30] and DepthDirector show only the floor and HY-WorldPlay shows its back.

Figure 6. Visual comparison on DAVIS. AnyCam follows every trajectory and keeps the scene intact, since the anchor rendering fixes the scale of the motion relative to the anchor and covers it from every side. Methods that warp estimated geometry show holes and stretched content at new viewpoints: TrajectoryCrafter [56] tears the airplane apart during rotation (rows 1 and 2), GEN3C [39] leaves stripes (row 2), and DepthDirector [7] breaks down under zoom-in and rise (rows 3 to 6). Methods conditioned on camera parameters guess the scale of the motion: ReCamMaster [1] loses the airplane after the orbit (row 2), Wan-Fun-Cam [44] zooms far past the train into the tree (row 4), ReDirector [30] and Wan-Fun-Cam collapse into noise under large orbit and rise (rows 2 and 6).

Figure 11. Single-image comparison on CO3D. Each block shows one case with the input image (Input), the ground-truth frame and the frame generated by each method of Tab. 3 from the same target camera. The 3D reconstruction methods render only the object and often distort its shape, e.g., LGM [42] for three of the four objects and TRELLIS [48] for the handbag and the bench. Most video generation baselines move to an incorrect viewpoint. GEN3C [39], TrajectoryCrafter [56], ReDirector [30] and Wan-Fun-Cam [44] lose the banana (top right). GEN3C, TrajectoryCrafter, DepthDirector [7], ReCamMaster [1] and ReDirector shift the sandwich (bottom right) to the right. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR match the viewpoint and the appearance of the ground truth.
Figure 21. Anchor selection prompt. System prompt given to Qwen3-VL-32B together with 8 frames of the video.

Figure 8. Long-video comparison on CO3D (left) and RealEstate10K (right). The anchor rendering gives every chunk a reference to the object, so AnyCam-AR stays registered to the scene over hundreds of frames. The baselines drift as their errors accumulate over the chunks: both lose the cellphone (left, rows 5, 6), and both turn away from the house (right, rows 1, 2) and the deck (right, rows 5, 6).

Figure 7. Single-image to video comparison on Mip-NeRF 360. Since the anchor rendering is object-relative and view-complete, AnyCam always reaches the target viewpoints. Wan-Fun-Cam [44] and ReCamMaster [1] are conditioned on camera parameters, whose scale a single photo cannot determine, and barely move away from the input view (rows 1 to 3). GEN3C [39], TrajectoryCrafter [56] and DepthDirector [7] warp a depth map that covers only the visible surface, which leaves distorted or missing content (rows 1 to 3).

Figure 4. Anchor rendering as a camera signal only. The anchor (center console) is poorly reconstructed with no texture (column 3), compared with its cut-out in the source video (column 2). AnyCam still recovers the appearance of the console and the cabin from the source video and controls the camera movement correctly, showing that the rendering only provides a camera signal and the model is robust to poor reconstructions.

Figure 12. Additional visual comparison on DAVIS (same layout as Fig. 6). The camera zooms out from the swing (rows 1 and 2) and rises by 60◦ over the display shelf, the skate bowl and the railway crossing (rows 3 to 8). AnyCam shows the whole swing frame after the zoom-out and looks down on the other three scenes. DepthDirector [7] breaks apart on the swing (rows 1 and 2) and the crossing (rows 7 and 8) and turns toward the sky above the skate bowl (rows 5 and 6). Wan-Fun-Cam [44] moves closer to the swing instead of away from it (rows 1 and 2), stays at the height of the input at the shelf (rows 3 and 4) and turns into noise on the skate bowl and the crossing (rows 6 and 8).

Figure 13. Comparison with the Plücker-ray models. Wan-Fun-Cam† and Wan-Fun-Cam-AR† are trained on our data with our recipe and receive the camera as Plücker rays instead of the anchor rendering. Top: DAVIS [32, 34] with a 60◦ rise, AnyCam and Wan-Fun-Cam†; the numbers on the input frames give the frame index. Middle: a 333-frame CO3D [38] video (166 frames out and back) generated from an 81-frame source video; bottom: a 165-frame RealEstate10K [63] video generated from a single image; AnyCam-AR and Wan-Fun-CamAR†; the labels on the ground-truth frames give the frame index and the video length. Wan-Fun-Cam† distorts the street in the last frames of the rise. Wan-Fun-Cam-AR† drifts off the bench, which the frame border cuts off from frame 94 on. On RealEstate10K, it moves into the armchair instead of toward the coffee table. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR follow the target views.

Figure 15. Failure case: small anchors. When the anchor covers only about 1% of the frame, its rendering gives little information about the rotation of the camera. For the agave plant (row 1, 0.7% of the frame), the output camera barely moves, and for the garden stool (row 2, 1.2%) it turns much less than the target orbit. Both rows show AnyCam.

Figure 2. Camera representations. Yellow represents the input camera. (a) Camera parameters are scale-ambiguous: a small object near the input camera and a large object farther away give the same input image, but the same target camera parameters (blue and red camera) see them at a different size, position and angle (blue and red boxes), so the target view is not determined. (b) A point cloud or depth warp of the input image only covers the surface seen from the input camera. Under a large viewpoint change, views are often heavily distorted (red box). The points in the target view sometimes come from the inside of the object or from the back of the image (blue box). The renderings are wrong and mislead the subsequent video generation. (c) Our anchor rendering uses the complete reconstructed object, so target cameras at any angle (green) see the whole anchor with the correct size and pose.
Figure 5. Training samples. Top: MultiCamVideo [1], a dynamic scene captured by two synchronized cameras. Bottom: DL3DV [24], two clips of a static capture.

Figure 9. CO3D target trajectories of the three difficulty levels for one sequence (hydrant), seen from above. Positions are normalized by the median radius of the source cameras. The target camera moves from source frame 0 to the first real target camera (dotted) and then follows real CO3D cameras, with ground truth at the dots.

Figure 14. Moving and deforming anchors. The anchor need not be static or rigid: a swimming swan (DAVIS [32, 34], row 1), a walking dinosaur (row 2), and a person from the DyCheck dataset [9] (bottom left: holding a teddy bear; bottom right: sitting in a chair). The condition renders the anchor reconstructed from one frame, while the generated video keeps the motion of the source, e.g., the swimming swan, the walking legs, and the moving hands and arms. Row 2 shows AnyCam-AR; all other examples show AnyCam.

Figure 16. Different anchors in the same video. For each source video, the user picks two or three objects as anchors and a target trajectory around each of them. The tags above each example name the anchors and their trajectories. Each anchor has its own trajectory, so the rows show camera control through different objects of one video, not one camera applied to several anchors. Each condition renders only its anchor. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index. All outputs are from AnyCam. In the first video, the camera pushes in toward the mirrorless camera or the instant camera on the table, or pulls back and rises over the armchair. In the second video, it orbits around the food truck toward its front or pushes in to the sandwich board.

Figure 17. Different anchors in the same video (continued). Same setting as Fig. 16. All outputs are from AnyCam. In the gaming room, the output orbits around the gaming chair or moves toward the PC tower. In the second video, it orbits around the carved armchair or rises over the side table.

Figure 18. Different anchors in the same video (continued). Same setting as Fig. 16. All outputs are from AnyCam. The output moves toward the telephone or the perfume bottle while the person keeps moving as in the source. In the studio, it rises over the writing desk or turns toward the stool.

Figure 19. The anchor leaves the frame. The camera moves past anchor A until A leaves the view; starting at the switch frame, the condition renders anchor B, a second object reconstructed from the first source frame, and the camera continues toward it. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index; tags A and B mark the anchor in the condition. All rows show AnyCam. The output keeps moving after A has left and approaches anchor B (the sports car, the red car, the white SUV and the PC tower in rows 1 to 4).

Figure 20. Switching the anchor during a video. The target camera follows one continuous trajectory. The condition renders anchor A up to frame 32 and anchor B from frame 33 (tags A and B), and both anchors are reconstructed from the first source frame. The numbers on the source frames give the frame index. Rows 1 to 3 show AnyCam, row 4 shows AnyCam-AR. After the switch, the output moves toward the side table, the perfume bottle, the bentwood chair and the PC tower.

Table 3. Single-image comparison on CO3D. oPSNR, oSSIM and oLPIPS are computed inside the object mask. AnyCam achieves better reconstruction quality than 3D reconstruction methods (top) and video generation methods (bottom).

Table 6. Video-to-video comparison on CO3D by target difficulty. Easy targets have an arc center within 45◦ of the nearest source camera; medium targets have an arc center at least 90◦ away; and hard targets sweep 150◦ to 200◦ across the unobserved side of the object (34 cases each). IoU compares the anchor tracked in the generated video with the CO3D object mask.
Table 5. Long-video comparison on RealEstate10K. AnyCamAR’s rotation error is less than half that of InSpatio-World [40].

Table 1. Video-to-video comparison on CO3D. IoU compares the anchor tracked in the generated video with the CO3D object mask. AnyCam and AnyCam-AR generate videos more similar to the ground truth and with better visual quality and object consistency. FPS is measured on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU.

Table 2. Video-to-video comparison on DAVIS. AnyCam has the lowest translation error and the best visual quality and consistency; although GEN3C [39] and ReDirector [30] achieve better rotation accuracy, their visual quality suffers.
Table 4. Single-image comparison on Mip-NeRF 360. AnyCam is best on all ground-truth metrics and FID.

Table 8. Long videos on CO3D, all metrics. 30 sequences; the source is an 81-frame clip played forward and backward to the target length, and the target follows the real CO3D cameras around the object for 165 or 249 frames, or for 166 frames and back (333 frames). PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS compare each generated frame with the ground-truth frame of the same camera, and oPSNR, oSSIM and oLPIPS do so inside the object mask. Unseen views are the ground-truth frames whose camera is at least 45◦ in azimuth away from the arc covered by the source clip, i.e. sides of the object the input never shows; the way back is the second half of the 333-frame videos. Anchor IoU compares the anchor tracked in the generated video with the object mask, and Lost is the fraction of frames where the track is lost. Best in bold, second underlined, ranked within each group.

Table 7. Attention fine-tuning versus LoRA. LoRA [16] of rank 32 on the attention and feed-forward layers, trained with a learning rate of 10−4, versus fine-tuning the self-attention layers and the patch embedding with a learning rate of 5 × 10−5. Both are trained on the same data for 10K steps with a batch size of 32. The attention fine-tuning row is AnyCam; the cases and metrics are those of its DAVIS and CO3D comparisons (Tabs. 1 and 2). Better in bold.
Table 9. Streaming cost of AnyCam-AR on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q GPUs, median of 4 DAVIS [32, 34] videos at 832× 480.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for camera-controlled video generation using 3D reconstruction of an anchor object, fitting Video Diffusion and 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: AnyCam: Anything Can Represent Camera for Video Generation
papers.tldr: AnyCam enables camera-controlled video generation by using a reconstructed 3D anchor object to specify scale-aware, view-complete camera motion.

papers.abstract: A general-purpose Vision-Language Model (VLM) has surpassed expert vision models in many domains such as object detection and video recognition. However, point correspondence is known to be challenging for VLMs since it goes beyond object-level recognition: it requires pixel-level localization of the same physical surface point across observations, even when appearance changes or the point disappears and later reappears. In this paper, we introduce AgenTAP, a VLM-based agent that directly predicts point coordinates and visibility and actively reasons over videos. Starting from its own estimate, the agent autonomously chooses what to inspect and uses the resulting evidence to verify point identity and refine its predictions. With GPT-6 Astra, it surpasses expert vision models in both point localization and visibility prediction, without correspondence-specific fine-tuning. We further use AgenTAP to re-identify physical points after disappearance and reconnect fragmented tracks, constructing EgoTAP-4D, a dataset of 3D point trajectories in long real-world egocentric videos. On sampled reappearing points, its predictions approach human agreement, and adding EgoTAP-4D to D4RT training improves average 3D tracking performance.
authors: Xuweiyi Chen, Jin Yao, Linzhan Mou, Lei Gong, Di Liu, Cheng Zhang, Ziqiao Ma, Sihan Xu, Adam W. Harley, Shengyi Qian, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Addresses VLM difficulty with pixel-level point correspondence under appearance changes and occlusions.
Predicts point coordinates and visibility, then actively selects video evidence to verify identity and refine estimates.
Outperforms expert vision models on localization and visibility without correspondence-specific fine-tuning.
Uses re-identified points to build EgoTAP-4D, a dataset of 3D trajectories from long egocentric videos.
Its reappearing-point predictions approach human agreement, and EgoTAP-4D improves D4RT’s average 3D tracking performance when used for training.

figures.caption: Figure 6 EgoTAP-4D annotation pipeline. From a stereo egocentric video with camera poses and hand motion capture, we recover metric depth and camera poses, label each region as static (blue), moving (orange), or hand (green), and build 2D trajectories from the fused scene geometry, AllTracker, and MANO. When an object returns after leaving the view, AGENTAP with GPT-6 Astra locates its query points again (Fig. 9, first row). All trajectories are then lifted to 3D in one world frame.

Figure 4 Analysis of VLM correspondence. Direct prediction improves with model size (a), transfers to held-out videos (b), and trails trackers on synthetic videos (e). AGENTAP’s lead over trackers grows with frame gap (c), its improvement over direct prediction is largest at strict thresholds (d), and its verification is robust (f). Agent results use GPT-6 Astra. Red: linear fit. Shading: 95% CIs. †: video input.

Figure 3 AgenTAP. (1) Initial prediction: the VLM agent inspects both views and records its own prediction. (2) Optional expert consultation: expert vision models propose candidate locations. (3) Iterative visual verification: the agent selects visual tools to test its hypothesis, revises the point’s location and visibility, and re-checks as needed.

Figure 8 EgoTAP-4D trajectories. Each panel shows one recording. The main view shows 3D trajectories in world coordinates together with the reconstructed scene, and the inset shows the corresponding video frame with the 2D trajectories. The same color marks the same track in both views. The white frustum shows the current camera pose, and the dashed white line shows the camera trajectory.

Figure 9 Point reconnection after reappearance. Two Xperience-10M sequences in which an object or a person exits the field of view and later re-enters it. From left to right, the columns show the query points, their tracks shortly before the exit, a frame in which they are out of view (dimmed), and the predictions of AGENTAP and AllTracker after the return. Colors denote point identity. Points predicted invisible are omitted, and each prediction panel reports how many of the ten query points are predicted visible. The arrow gives the time between exit and re-entry. Supplementary Fig. S14 shows two more sequences.

Figure 7 AgenTAP and AllTracker on DAVIS. Trails show each point from frame 0 to the shown frame. Each answer uses only that frame and frame 0, and AGENTAP also receives the RoMa v2 and AllTracker answers. A point predicted invisible has no dot.
Figure 5 Visibility and localization. In direct prediction, VLMs that localize better also judge visibility better. †: video input.
Figure 1 Tracking Any Point with Agentic Visual Reasoning.

Table 1 Main results on TrackingBench. Direct prediction, AGENTAP, and expert vision models answer the same 2,000 queries. Overall columns evaluate all queries together rather than averaging the six domains, and domain columns omit EPE. Higher is better except for EPE. HR: high resolution. Subscripts give each agent’s change from the same VLM’s two-image direct prediction, which is also the reference
Table 2 Agentic inference ablation. Tool use helps even without expert proposals. Proposals and intermediate frames add further improvements, most for the weaker backbone.
Table 3 Comparison of 3D point tracking datasets. EGOTAP4D has the longest average video duration among the compared real-video datasets. Duration is the total video length.

Table 4 Training D4RT with EgoTAP-4D. Adding EGOTAP-4D improves average 3D localization and visibility. Overall is the unweighted mean across the four datasets, with improvements in green. † denotes our D4RT reproduction.

papers.abstract: Image editing models can follow a wide range of instructions, but video editing models still lag behind, limited in part by the difficulty of collecting paired source and edited videos. Is it possible to transfer advanced image editing capabilities to video editors without new paired videos? We introduce Image-to-Video Transfer (I2VT), which improves pretrained video editors and expands them to new editing tasks using an image editor. It enables efficient post-training with no architectural changes and no new videos, using only individual images. Our key idea is to let the video editor role-play as an image editor: it edits an image as a one-frame video, with the image editor guiding the video editor's predictions at each denoising step. Although the video editor sees only single images during training, at test time it applies the improved and expanded capabilities to whole video clips while preserving temporal consistency. To push the boundaries of video editing, we introduce OpenVE++, an extension of OpenVE-Bench that adds four new editing tasks useful for video production, including action changes, expression changes, body movements, and scene relighting. Our experiments across three different video editors show that I2VT improves existing editing capabilities and expands them to new tasks, and our models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.
authors: Ji Xie, Yanhao Jia, Xiangpeng Yang, Martin Q. Ma, Sihan Xu, Erik Cambria, Louis-Philippe Morency
bullets: Addresses the lack of paired source–edited videos for training video editors.
Uses an image editor to guide a video editor’s frame-level predictions during denoising, with no architectural changes or new videos.
Applies the resulting capabilities to full video clips at test time while maintaining temporal consistency.
Introduces OpenVE++, extending OpenVE-Bench with action, expression, body-movement, and scene-relighting edits.
Experiments across three video editors report improved existing capabilities, broader task coverage, and SOTA performance on OpenVE-Bench and OpenVE++.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Qualitative results. Top and middle rows show new and basic edits, comparing the source, base editor, and I2VT. The bottom row compares I2VT-1.3B with other editors on OpenVE++ action and expression edits. Each video shows two frames at matched times.

Figure 3. I2VT and the offline distillation baseline. Left: offline distillation fine-tunes on teacher-edited images. Middle: I2VT supervises the student along its own rollout. The cross marks stop-gradient. Right: at inference, the student edits whole video clips.

Figure 5. Offline versus online distillation with I2VT. Bernini-R-1.3B on a basic edit from OpenVE-Bench (left) and a body-movement edit from OpenVE++ (right), showing three frames sampled from each video.

Figure 2. Motivation and intuition. Left: image editors handle complex edits such as actions and relighting on single frames, whereas video editors lack the paired data to learn them. Our goal is a video editor that makes these edits while keeping the video temporally consistent. Middle: can a video editor learn to edit images by treating each image as a one-frame video? Right: video editing ability improves while temporal quality remains comparable.

Table 3. One I2VT model handles both basic edits and new editing tasks. All scores are reported without prompt enhancement. We cite OpenVE-Bench baselines from previous work except those marked ⋆, and run all OpenVE++ evaluations ourselves.
Table 2. New editing abilities after distillation. All three students improve on their base editors.
Table 1. Basic edits after distillation. I2VT raises the basic-edit score of all three video editors.
Table 5. Ablation on guidance scales. On OpenVE-Bench, the default ωR = ωS = ωT = 1 scores highest overall.
Table 8. Temporal quality remains comparable after finetuning. We report VBench metrics on edited OpenVE++ videos from the base editors and I2VT.
Table 9. IVEBench results. I2VT raises the overall score and instruction compliance of all three editors, and temporal quality stays on par with the base editors. Short-video subset, scores ×100.
Table 7. Ablation on matching losses. We compare velocity (v) and clean-latent (x) targets using mean squared error (mse) or cosine distance (cos). All four improve on Base.

papers.abstract: We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.
authors: Yipengjing Sun, Chenyang Wang, Boyao Zhou, Jiapeng Zhu, Ka Leong Cheng, Shengping Zhang
bullets: Factorizes synthesis into an animatable 3D proxy for geometry and reflectance and a neural shader for complex facial light transport.
Renders view- and motion-consistent physically based buffers from deformed Gaussians to condition relighting.
Uses a two-step causal autoregressive shader distilled from a multi-step bidirectional video-diffusion teacher for low-latency streaming.
Fine-tunes on a hybrid relighting dataset designed to capture realistic facial dynamics and physically grounded lighting.
Experiments report improved visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy over prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LuxAvatar. Driven by target FLAME and camera parameters, the canonical Gaussians are deformed and rasterized into 4D-consistent PBR buffers {Ct}. (b) Causal Neural Shader: Conditioned on {Ct}, the reference image, and target scene illumination, our distilled causal neural shader autoregressively streams photorealistic relit video chunks in just two denoising steps, while reusing KV caches across chunks to maintain temporal coherence.

papers.abstract: Real-time autoregressive video generators stream minutes of video and accept new prompts on the fly, but struggle to keep people, objects, and places consistent over a long interactive story. Agent systems provide such memory for offline multi-shot generation, yet they read the whole script in advance, plan each shot before generating it, and regenerate failed shots, which a live stream does not allow. We present Agentic LongLive, an asynchronous agentic memory for long video generation. A memory agent on separate GPUs reads only the prompts revealed so far, never the generated video, and keeps a text state and evolving images for every person, object, and scene. From this entity memory it composes a global image and a per-shot memory image, which an auxiliary GPU prefills into the generator's attention sink before the next shot starts, and writes entity cards for the prompts that name them, so the video never waits for memory and video errors are not written back. A small language model, trained with reinforcement learning and an image reward calibrated using downstream video outcomes, decides what to remember before the next prompt is known. On LongStory-Online, a new benchmark of 25 stories (857 shots) revealed one shot at a time, Agentic LongLive improves persistent-state accuracy of LongLive-2.0, its base generator, by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4, at about 1% extra generation time on H100. The full system streams faster than real time on one 8xB200 node with the generator in BF16 (34.3 FPS), keeps image quality stable over 14-minute stories, and improves identity on two MiniMax-H3 generators, one of which, LongLive-H3, also runs in real time with it. To our knowledge, it is the first real-time video generator with text and image memory kept by an LLM agent.
authors: Shaoteng Liu, Shuai Yang, Wei Huang, Luozhou Wang, Song Han, Yukang Chen
bullets: Targets identity and scene consistency in interactive, multi-minute video where future prompts and generated video are unavailable in advance.
A memory agent processes only revealed prompts, maintains entity and scene state, and prepares global and per-shot memory images before generation.
An RL-trained language model selects what to remember using an image reward calibrated to downstream video quality.
On LongStory-Online, it improves persistent-state accuracy by 26.3 points, protagonist identity by 44.9, and revisited-place consistency by 40.4.
Adds about 1% generation time, supports real-time streaming, and maintains image quality over 14-minute stories.

papers.abstract: Processing long videos with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is prohibitively expensive, making informative frame selection essential for accurate video understanding. The default uniform sampling often misses task-relevant keyframes, while recent training-free selectors instead pick frames by how well each one matches the question under an image-text alignment (ITA) score. However, we show that ITA signals correspond poorly with the MLLM's true needs: their rankings correlate weakly with downstream accuracy and are even negatively correlated on over 40% of questions, whereas the MLLM's internal yes/no judgment yields a much stronger signal. We present ProbFaS, a training- and label-free probabilistic pipeline that fuses both signals for key frame selection. ProbFaS treats dense ITA scores as cheap, biased measurements and sparse MLLM judgments as accurate, costly ones, unifying them via co-kriging, a multi-fidelity Gaussian process, to calibrate relevance across all frames. A temporal determinantal point process then selects frames capturing relevance peaks while preserving temporal coverage. Across Video-MME, MLVU and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS is the most accurate among fourteen state-of-the-art training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings (8-128 frames), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 3.1 percentage points. On MLVU and LongVideoBench, 32 ProbFaS frames match or surpass the top baseline at 128 frames and uniform sampling with up to 768 frames.
authors: Tianru Zhang, Mayank Nautiyal, Hugo Eidmann, Prashant Singh, Ekta Vats
bullets: Uniform sampling can miss keyframes, while image-text alignment rankings often poorly reflect the MLLM’s actual needs.
The training- and label-free method fuses dense ITA scores with sparse, more accurate MLLM yes/no judgments using co-kriging.
A temporal determinantal point process selects relevance peaks while maintaining temporal coverage.
Across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, ProbFaS leads training-free selectors and uniform sampling in 13 of 15 settings.
Using 32 frames, it matches or surpasses top-baseline performance obtained with 128 frames on MLVU and LongVideoBench.

figures.caption: Figure 4. ProbFaS pipeline. An image–text alignment model first scores every frame of a one-frame-per-second candidate grid against the question, and then the answering MLLM judges m of these frames with a label-free yes/no question. Co-kriging calibrates the low-fidelity alignment scores to these judgments on every frame, and a temporal DPP selects the k frames that the MLLM answers from.

Figure 2. Frames chosen by uniform sampling, GIFT and ProbFaS (k = 8) for a Video-MME question, and the answers of Qwen3-VL-8B. Uniform sampling shows no price, and GIFT only the full price before the code is applied (8:43); without the discount in view, the model answers 4,950 rubles, as it does with no frame at all.

Figure 3. Usefulness, alignment scores and the MLLM probe on Video-MME. Left: results on question 254-1, each curve scaled to [0, 1]. Right: per-question mean usefulness u(t) of each score’s top-10% frames, over all questions.

Figure 1. ProbFaS against state-of-the-art training-free selectors on MLVU dev [75]: official score against the number of selected frames (left) and accuracy on the seven tasks at 64 frames (right; dotted line on the left).

Figure 6. Video-MME, action reasoning, 70-s video from a language-learning channel, k = 8. Figure 7. Video-MME, temporal reasoning, 31-min animated explainer, k = 8. Options A and B list the same weapons except the “weapons that spawn non-detectable fragments”. ProbFaS selects the title card of that section (27:35–27:37). Uniform sampling, WFS-SB and GIFT miss it and choose B, as does every other selector except A.I.R. and OTFS.

The answer is read from overlays: a name card at 4:41 (“Luvo Manyonga 8.61m, Shanghai 2017”) and the scoreboard at 5:15, which ProbFaS selects. papers.abstract: How an object deforms when it hits the ground reveals what it is made of. From a single real video of a drop, we estimate a deformable object's density-normalized stiffness $E/\rho$, and its yield stress $\sigma_Y/\rho$ when the impact causes plastic deformation, with a feed-forward predictor trained only in simulation. Real videos carry no material labels, so such predictors are developed and validated on synthetic data alone. We show that synthetic validation ranks their geometric inputs in the wrong order. Material acts through 3D deformation, and tracklets lifted to 3D with estimated depth are indeed the most accurate input in simulation. However, on real drops they are the least accurate, and better depth does not repair them: the failure persists with simulator depth in training, LiDAR depth at test time, and exact depth on rendered replays of the real drops. Short 2D optical-flow tracklets do the opposite: they improve nothing in simulation, yet they transfer best. Material is therefore better read from what perception measures consistently in both domains than from what is most informative in simulation. Our predictor, PhysReader, reads the video and 2D tracklets and learns the lift to 3D in simulation by matching a teacher that sees exact 3D deformation. To measure transfer, we introduce PhysReader-Real: 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, with reference materials fit jointly to each object's drops and checked against tensile tests. On PhysReader-Real, PhysReader is closer to the reference materials than every other input and baseline. The one exception is a per-scene optimizer started from PhysReader's prediction, which ends slightly closer but takes 49 minutes per video instead of 12 seconds.
authors: Ziyue Peng, Yanxi Hu, Junyoung Kim, Andrew Chen, Jin Yang, Chandrajit L. Bajaj, Etienne Vouga, William T. Freeman, Qixing Huang, Brandon Y. Feng
bullets: The task is to estimate density-normalized stiffness and, for plastic impacts, yield stress from how an object deforms when dropped.
Synthetic experiments misleadingly favor 3D tracklets, while real-world transfer favors short 2D optical-flow tracklets.
PhysReader learns to infer 3D deformation from video and 2D tracks by matching a teacher trained with exact simulated 3D deformation.
On 16 everyday objects dropped five times each, PhysReader was closer to reference materials than other inputs and baselines.
A scene optimizer improved accuracy slightly but required 49 minutes per video versus 12 seconds for PhysReader.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PhysReader. Training in simulation (left): ❶ a teacher encodes exact 3D deformation, available only in simulation, into a feature fT , from which material heads predict E/ρ and σY /ρ (loss ℓ against the GT material). ❷ PhysReader sees only inputs that real video also provides: the RGB clip (V-JEPA 2 with LoRA), 2D optical-flow tracklets, and temporal and scale context. It maps them to f̂T and is trained to match fT (loss d) and the material through a frozen copy of the teacher’s heads (ℓ; Eq. 4). Inference in real (right): PhysReader alone predicts the material, without depth. For evaluation, the prediction re-simulates the drop with density ρ and Poisson’s ratio ν, and we report the replay loss and the parameter distance to the plausible region of reference materials (Sec. 4).

Figure 4. Simulation ranks the inputs backwards: stiffness error on synthetic validation and on real drops. Left: arrows connect each model with 2D flow tracklets to the same model with tracklets lifted to 3D (tracklets only, RGB + tracklets, and the two students). Every arrow leads to a lower error in simulation and a higher error on real videos. The feed-forward baselines (gray) are less accurate than PhysReader in both. Right: lifted tracklets, under each geometry condition of Table S7, beat 2D flow tracklets in simulation and lose to them on real videos.

Figure 3. PhysReader-Real. Left: the 16 objects, each dropped five times in different orientations. Right: for the 8 objects we cut specimens from, the reference stiffness fit jointly to the five drops (dot) and its plausible region (blue) against the measured stiffness of tensile specimens (gray).

Table 1. Inputs in simulation and on real drops. Every model uses the same RGB branch, training data, and protocol, except the “tracklets only” rows. Syn.: zE error on synthetic validation (dex). Real: distance to the plausible region, relative increases in total and deformation replay loss, and direct simulation difference (Sec. 4).

Table 3. Error budget for log10(E/ρ) (MAE, dex). Each row is one step from the row above. Synthetic rows use the 10,202 validation videos on which every row is defined; real rows use the 80 PhysReader-Real drops, scored against the reference materials. Exact geometry comes from the simulator; flow tracks from WAFT [76]; estimated depth from 4RC [51].

Table 4. Same drops, three domains: zE error (dex) of epoch-5 predictors on synthetic validation, on rendered replays of the real drops, and on real videos. The second column names the training depth and its alignment (one scale per clip or frame). “Rendered” and “LiDAR” replace the estimated depth at evaluation. Dashes: not applicable.

papers.selection_reason: Estimates material properties from video deformation dynamics; fits video understanding of physical dynamics.
papers.title: What a Drop Reveals: Sim-to-Real Material Estimation for Deformable Objects from Video
papers.tldr: PhysReader estimates deformable-object material properties from a single real drop video using simulation-trained learning and transfers better with 2D motion cues than with explicit 3D tracks.

papers.abstract: Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv
bullets: Addresses object loss in long videos when uniform token merging accidentally coarsens fast-moving targets.
Uses velocity-shifted and block-matched mask unions, camera-compensated surprise checks, uncertainty delegation, and an all-objects-lost fallback.
On LVOS V2, improves J&F over ALGM by 2.76 points at ViT-S and 3.89 points at ViT-B, with 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs at ViT-S.
Remains close to dense-encoder accuracy on DAVIS 2017 validation, within 0.19 J&F points at ViT-S.
Reduced counted encoder FLOPs did not translate into lower startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time; latency depends on implementation and regime.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Tiers and predictions on three held-out LVOS videos (head R31c). Rows 1 and 2: the method keeps a fast-moving target that ALGM 0.98 has lost (ALGM predicts no mask in these frames). Row 3: the video where the method does worst against ALGM; ALGM keeps the target (a child), the method has lost it. These frames already run the fallback (ALGM’s own merging), so the loss happened earlier and persists through the memory. Red: high tier; orange: middle tier; white outline: the method’s predicted mask; dashed blue: ALGM 0.98’s. Frames are annotated frames where one of the two predicts no mask, whichever is more frequent in that video. Tiers replayed from the run’s own predictions through the reference implementation, whose decisions the timed run equals.

Figure 2: J&F against encoder FLOPs. (a) LVOS V2 valid, mean over three ViT-S heads; the paired difference against ALGM 0.98 with its 95% interval is given as text. (b) Short clips (the Table 5 baseline grid at ViT-S); the line marks dense.

Figure 1: The focus map. Before the encoder runs on frame t, for each tracked object we take the union of its velocity-shifted and block-matched masks on frame t (high tier). A surprise check compares frame t with frame t−1 shifted by the camera motion and promotes patches that changed without explanation. Rings sized by each object’s speed and search regions around lost objects form the middle tier, merged by the compared merger’s own rules; the rest is merged aggressively. Every decision is made before the first block, on the patch grid.
Table 4: Share of an object’s ground truth inside each region (mean over object-frames; in brackets the share of frames below 0.9). Development split, 34 videos, the method at ViT-S.

Table 2: Held-out LVOS V2 valid (140 videos, 239 objects; 42 in videos over 600 frames), three ViT-S heads, reference implementation (FLOPs frame-weighted across videos as everywhere; Table 1 is the timed-implementation run, whose method row is 0.385). Schedule: every 20th frame written to Cutie’s permanent memory. τ is the surprise threshold (0.06 in the method).

papers.selection_reason: Training-free focus-map token merging for efficient long-video object segmentation.

papers.abstract: Spike cameras capture high-speed motion through an integrate-and-fire mechanism, providing fine-grained temporal observations without exposure blur. However, their binary streams encode accumulated illumination rather than instantaneous intensity, making reliable motion estimation challenging. Existing spike-based methods exploit temporal aggregation to construct motion representations, but this process may weaken fine-grained firing patterns. Meanwhile, correlation-based estimators often rely on learned matching features without explicitly characterizing the spatial distribution and ambiguity of candidate displacements. To address these challenges, we propose TIDE-Flow, a spike-based optical flow estimation framework that jointly exploits Temporal Integration Evidence (TIE) and Displacement Evidence Encoding (DEE). TIE combines raw spike patterns, multi-scale firing statistics, temporal moments, and boundary-aware interval cues, preserving complementary temporal information before spatial feature compression. DEE further integrates structured candidate-grid features with explicit displacement statistics to characterize matching geometry and competing correspondences. Both components are incorporated into a difference-correlation recurrent refinement framework, enabling effective temporal motion modeling and correspondence estimation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of TIDE-Flow, with controlled ablations validating the contributions of temporal and displacement evidence modeling.
authors: Hanwen Liang, Wenxuan Liu, Wenxin Huang, Jingling Yuan, Zhaofei Yu, Xian Zhong, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Spike cameras provide blur-free temporal observations, but binary accumulated-illumination streams make motion estimation difficult.
Temporal Integration Evidence (TIE) combines raw spikes, multi-scale firing statistics, temporal moments, and boundary-aware interval cues.
Displacement Evidence Encoding (DEE) models candidate-grid structure, displacement statistics, and correspondence ambiguity.
Both components are integrated into a difference-correlation recurrent refinement framework for temporal motion modeling and flow estimation.
Experiments and controlled ablations demonstrate the effectiveness of the temporal and displacement evidence designs.

papers.abstract: Underexposure weakens object details, and overexposure obscures boundaries. Spike cameras encode light into high-frequency binary streams. Long-window spike counts give stable appearance cues, while short observations reveal changes in firing rates from sparse measurements. We propose SPIRE, a sensor-grounded semantic-spiking framework for illumination-robust object detection from a single spike stream. SPIRE builds an appearance view from the full packet through detection-oriented illumination adaptation and constructs a sequence of cumulative views from progressively longer prefixes. Each prefix supplies a rate map, an edge map, and a rate difference that tracks changes as spikes accumulate. At selected scales, ANN features and spike-derived initialization jointly set the initial membrane potentials and firing thresholds, allowing semantic cues to shape the responses during temporal encoding. Local spike-count contrasts supervise both branches during training. The residual between measured and ANN-predicted contrasts combines with the spiking features to produce a bounded correction to the fused feature pyramid. On simulated VOC and COCO, SPIRE-D outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.00-5.50 AP50 points across the four under- and overexposure settings. On real PKU-Vidar-DVS recordings, it achieves 67.07 AP50 and 40.10 AP75. SPIRE-D also uses 50.4% fewer MACs than SPFD.
authors: Hanwen Liang, Wenxuan Liu, Wenxin Huang, Jingling Yuan, Zhaofei Yu, Xian Zhong, Tiejun Huang
bullets: Addresses object-detail loss under underexposure and boundary loss under overexposure.
Builds an appearance view plus progressively accumulated views containing rate, edge, and rate-difference maps.
Uses ANN features and spike-derived signals to initialize membrane potentials and firing thresholds during temporal encoding.
Applies contrast supervision and a residual correction to refine the fused feature pyramid.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.00–5.50 AP50 points in simulated settings, reaches 67.07 AP50 and 40.10 AP75 on real recordings, and uses 50.4% fewer MACs than SPFD.

papers.abstract: Guidance repels the prediction of a diffusion model away from a weaker reference prediction. It substantially improves sample quality, but its mechanism remains poorly understood. We first find that, at the scales used in practice, guidance does not improve the prediction of the posterior mean (the model's training target); it makes the prediction worse, while samples improve. Second, posterior-mean predictions have less variance than the data, and we find that guidance restores it. We introduce variance-matched guidance: a closed-form rule that picks the guidance scale by matching the variance of the guided predictions to that of the data. Without tuning, it recovers the hand-picked scales of eleven widely used models across image, video, audio, motion, and world generation; to our knowledge, no previous explanation of guidance predicts them. Applied per noise level, it yields a schedule without tuned hyperparameters that users prefer to hand-crafted ones on SD 3.5 Medium. Third, we offer an interpretation of the mechanism behind guidance: each model makes a random error in predicting the posterior mean, and guidance rescales the difference of these errors into a sample with the posterior's covariance, which improves sampling. This view also suggests two new hypotheses that our experiments support: guidance can work with negative scales, and guiding a model with its own checkpoint needs a larger scale than guiding it with an independently trained model.
authors: Ali Backour, Artem Lukoianov, Frank Permenter, Tommi Jaakkola, Justin Solomon, Vincent Sitzmann
bullets: Guidance can worsen posterior-mean prediction even as it improves generated samples.
Variance-matched guidance selects scales by matching guided-prediction variance to the data variance.
The rule recovers hand-tuned scales across image, video, audio, motion, and world-generation models.
Applied across noise levels, it produces an untuned schedule preferred over handcrafted schedules on SD 3.5 Medium.
The error-based interpretation supports guidance with negative scales and explains why self-guidance needs larger scales.

papers.abstract: Poetry-to-video generation requires more than translating text into visual scenes. Poetic language is highly compressed, often depends on historical and cultural knowledge, and frequently conveys meaning through metaphor, imagery, and other non-literal expressions. We introduce PoVi, a benchmark and agentic framework for grounded poetry-to-video generation, evaluating semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization. PoVi reconstructs poem semantics into an evidence-bounded representation and progressively transforms them into narration, interpretation, character assets, and shot-level visual plans, followed by narration-aligned video generation. Across three planning backbones and four video generators, PoVi consistently improves over single-call generation, with the largest gains on implicit background knowledge and metaphorical relations. PoVi provides a testbed for studying knowledge-grounded, long-horizon multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.
authors: Yuxia Zhu, Shiying Zhang, Lingzhuang Sun, Song Yang, Siheng Wu, Xinglong Xu, Sizhe Qiu, Hao Liang, Cheng Tan, Asher Qin, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Targets the challenges of compressed poetic language, implicit background knowledge, and figurative meaning in poetry-to-video generation.
Builds an evidence-bounded semantic representation, then progressively creates narration, interpretations, character assets, and shot-level plans.
Generates videos aligned with narration and evaluates semantic grounding, discourse coherence, and audiovisual realization.
Across three planning backbones and four video generators, consistently outperforms single-call generation, especially for implicit knowledge and metaphorical relations.
Provides a testbed for long-horizon, knowledge-grounded multimodal generation beyond direct text-to-video synthesis.

papers.abstract: Generative video models are becoming powerful renderers, yet lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional systems such as HTML/CSS engines or Blender. Their capabilities emerge implicitly from training, making it difficult to determine what they can reliably execute. We present Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which automatically probes frozen video models to construct model-specific capability manuals describing which semantic requirements they can reliably satisfy. NeurCo represents user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, then compiles it into model-specific execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while unreliable ones are selectively rewritten or compiled into alternative execution strategies. We introduce VComBench, a benchmark of 380 compositional, multi-requirement tasks spanning text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation. NeurCo improves requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on Wan and from 66.5% to 69.3% on Minimax H3, and achieves further gains when combined with prompt enhancers, including on Seedance 2.5. Our analysis reveals model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism, highlighting capability-guided compilation as a promising approach to programmable generative video rendering.
authors: Yuxia Zhu, Xinglong Xu, Hao Liang, Linzhuang Sun, Caijun Jia, Qifeng Cai, Jincen Luo, Lei Li, Alden Cai, Asher Qin, Wentao Zhang, Cheng Tan
bullets: Addresses the lack of reliable control interfaces in generative video models.
Represents intent using objects, constraints, events, and cameras in a model-agnostic intermediate representation.
Automatically builds capability manuals, preserving reliable requirements while rewriting or recompiling unreliable ones.
Introduces VComBench, a 380-task benchmark covering text-, image-, and reference-to-video generation.
Improves requirement satisfaction on Wan and Minimax H3, with additional gains when combined with prompt enhancers; results expose controllability–photorealism trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Counting how many times something happens is among the simplest questions about a video and among the hardest for video-language models, autoregressive and diffusion alike. The difficulty lies between the frames: a model samples only a few of them, while each repetition unfolds as movement in between. Video codecs already record this movement densely as block displacements, and codec-based video models use it to shape their visual input. We are the first to show that this motion provides direct evidence for the count: a candidate count is a testable motion hypothesis, and unwinding the cycles it implies measures how strongly the observed directions support it. We present CoDiCount, a unified training-free framework that turns this test into a count potential and applies it while a frozen diffusion vision-language model (dVLM) denoises its answer. At every denoising step, structured count messages map each option letter, or each grammar-valid edit of an open integer, to the count it expresses and reweight the model's own probabilities within that set. Consistent gains over the official decoders on MotionBench, TOMATO, and SVCBench demonstrate the broad generalization of CoDiCount across diffusion models, datasets, and diverse counting tasks. With CoDiCount, a 7B dVLM outperforms GPT-5.1 and Gemini-2.5-Pro on MotionBench, surpasses GPT-4o and much larger open models on TOMATO, and matches GPT-5.4 on SVCBench.
authors: Zhuoqin Li, Jiayu Ding, Ge Li
bullets: Video counting is difficult because sparse frames miss repetitions occurring between them.
Codec motion vectors provide dense evidence about the direction and cycles of movement.
CoDiCount is a training-free framework that converts motion consistency into a count potential during diffusion denoising.
Structured count messages reweight probabilities for multiple-choice options or grammar-valid edits of open-ended integer answers.
It consistently improves official decoders across MotionBench, TOMATO, and SVCBench, with reported comparisons to leading proprietary and open models.

papers.abstract: We introduce a new model for real-time streaming captioning on a single GPU. YoloMT is a 449.8M-parameter streaming captioner that provides Pareto-frontier performance among generative vision models in its class. Distilled from a 27B teacher by SFT and GRPO, it leads every model under 1B parameters on OVO-Bench, MVBench, StreamingBench and Video-MME, answered from its captions, and beats LFM2.5-VL-1.6B and SmolVLM2-2.2B. YoloMT is designed to read more frames cheaply and make them informative, encoding each frame once and caching it as 16 tokens. This allows the model to incorporate and infer from past frames without additional vision passes, making it efficient and effective. We also provide a detailed recipe for training YoloMT, with its stages and data, as well as ablations that demonstrate the contribution of each component.
authors: Nessim Ben Abbes, Duc Han Le, Sabri Mtibaa, Van-Tam Nguyen
bullets: Targets efficient real-time streaming captioning with a single GPU.
Encodes each frame once and caches it as 16 tokens, enabling inference over past frames without repeated vision passes.
Distilled from a 27B teacher using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO.
Leads sub-1B-parameter models on OVO-Bench, MVBench, StreamingBench, and Video-MME when evaluated from captions.
Provides a training recipe and ablations covering its stages, data, and components.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, yet existing video question answering (VQA) benchmarks mainly evaluate models in offline settings. Real-world streaming scenarios instead require models to answer context-dependent queries by retrieving and reasoning over evidence distributed across the video history. We introduce StreamRecall, a benchmark for context-aware Multi evidence reasoning in streaming video QA. StreamRecall requires models to retrieve, associate, and reason over temporally scattered evidence to answer queries at the appropriate moment. It contains 4,983 questions over 462 videos, with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations. We further propose the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose model reasoning through evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation. To enable efficient long-term streaming reasoning, we present EviStream, a training-free causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget. Experiments reveal substantial gaps between current VLMs and realistic streaming requirements, establishing StreamRecall as a foundation for developing evidence-aware streaming video intelligence.
authors: Cui Yakun, Tiantian Geng, Huixiang Kong, Xingqun Qi, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Targets the gap between offline video QA evaluation and real-time, context-dependent streaming scenarios.
Introduces 4,983 questions across 462 videos with context-aligned query times and fine-grained temporal evidence annotations.
Uses the Evidence Utilization Cascade to diagnose evidence localization, grounding, chain completion, and answer derivation.
Presents EviStream, a causal visual memory mechanism that preserves reasoning-critical evidence under a fixed KV budget.
Experiments show current VLMs remain substantially short of realistic streaming video reasoning requirements.

papers.title: Recalling the Past to Answer the Present: Context-Aware Multi-Evidence Reasoning for Streaming Video Question Answering

papers.abstract: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.
authors: Yuyao Sun, Daiqi Shi, Shuang Li, Liao Zhang, Yang Cai, Deqing Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of sampling frames for queries requiring either holistic video understanding or fine-grained local evidence.
Uses a Determinantal Point Process to select relevant, non-redundant backbone frames spanning key moments.
Infers query needs from the backbone’s temporal distribution and allocates remaining budget to local or global context.
Local enrichment captures short-range dynamics and causal relations, while global enrichment connects isolated evidence across the video.
Shows consistently superior performance when integrated with three leading MLLMs on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU.

papers.abstract: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.

papers.abstract: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.

papers.abstract: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models aim to predict future interactions that are both visually realistic and physically consistent. Yet explicit 3D motion prediction alone does not guarantee that object structure and contact relationships are preserved. Beyond motion prediction, 3D representations provide an explicit state space for imposing structural and physical constraints. Building on this insight, we introduce RehearsalWorld, an editable robot world model driven by 3D Interaction Rehearsal (3DIR). Given an initial RGB-D observation and robot actions, Interaction-Consistent Rehearsal (ICR) uses a pretrained 3D point-flow model as a motion prior. It refines the predicted trajectories through response-aware object grouping, persistent grasp memory, and contact structure refiner, preserving scene stability, object structure, and grasp attachments. Rehearsal-Aligned Video Generation (RAVG) then uses geometric projections of the rehearsal as temporal conditioning. We fine-tune a video generator on projection-video pairs to synthesize realistic interaction videos. Thanks to the decoupling of physical response from visual synthesis, RehearsalWorld also supports independent editing of material properties and camera viewpoints. Compared with PointWorld on real DROID grasping sequences, RehearsalWorld reduces gripper-relative offset by approximately 79% to 84% across deformable, articulated, and rigid objects and lowers reference motion error. For video prediction, it achieves a PSNR of 23.92 dB and an FVD of 149.

papers.abstract: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised video representation learning has achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale unlabeled video data. Recent methods commonly extend Masked Image Modeling (MIM) to Masked Video Modeling (MVM), where video representations are learned by capturing semantic information from temporal contexts during masked content recovery. Unlike static images, videos exhibit inherent temporal variation, as visual objects continuously change their positions, appearances, and motion states across frames. Therefore, MVM needs to preserve semantic consistency while capturing temporal changes of corresponding regions, which raises two central challenges: 1) how to establish reliable temporal correspondence across frames, and 2) how to formulate an appropriate representation learning objective for modeling both semantic consistency and temporal variation. To address these challenges, we propose Variation-aware Temporal Correspondence for video Representation learning (VT-CoRe) framework. For challenge 1), VT-CoRe introduces a sandwich sampling strategy to construct two-sided temporal references and a Patch Registration Module (PRM) to establish reliable patch-level correspondence. For challenge 2), VT-CoRe imposes latent-space semantic alignment on registered representations through a self-distillation architecture and further proposes temporal variation modeling to constrain representation trajectories over time. Experiments on 8 downstream tasks across 16 benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of VT-CoRe across pixel-level, frame-level, video-level, and vision-based robotic learning scenarios. Complementary representation analysis shows that VT-CoRe learns a more structured latent space for variation-aware temporal correspondence learning.

Representation analysis indicates that the method learns a more structured latent space for variation-aware correspondence.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: The architecture of the proposed framework. Given a training video, we introduce a sandwich sampling strategy to select past, current, and future frames, with the past and future frames providing two-sided temporal references via the auxiliary branch. We propose the Patch Registration Module to align the past and future representations with the current one, thereby establishing reliable correspondence for latent-space reconstruction. We further project the registered representations into a separate space for variation-aware temporal modeling, where we use a second-order Taylor approximation to construct local representation trajectories with multiple parameter groups to adaptively fit different patterns.

VT-CoRe addresses these challenges by introducing sandwich sampling and patch registration to construct reliable temporal triplets, and further combines latent-space semantic alignment with variation-aware temporal modeling.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) are designed to represent the temporal structure of audio and video, yet it remains unclear how effectively they use this temporal information to relate sounds to visual events. To examine this, we probe an AV-LLM on an audio-visual synchronization task by shifting the audio so that the queried sound overlaps a different visual event. We observe that the model still favors the originally aligned event over the newly aligned one, indicating limited sensitivity to changes in audio-visual temporal alignment. To address this, we propose Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding (MSCD), a training-free decoding method that emphasizes audio-visual temporal alignment in model predictions. MSCD contrasts logits under preserved and disrupted temporal alignment to favor predictions supported by aligned audio and video. We disrupt this alignment by temporally shifting either the audio or the video, while keeping the other modality fixed. Extensive evaluations with two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MSCD for temporally grounded audio-visual understanding. In particular, MSCD improves accuracy over the base models on Daily-Omni by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively, suggesting that emphasizing temporal alignment can also benefit broader audio-visual understanding.
authors: Minyeong Jeong, Yeonju Kim, Yong Man Ro
bullets: AV-LLMs may favor originally associated visual events even when audio is shifted to overlap a different event, revealing limited temporal-alignment sensitivity.
MSCD is a training-free decoding method that compares logits under preserved versus disrupted audio-visual alignment.
Alignment is disrupted by shifting either the audio or video while keeping the other modality fixed.
Evaluations on two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks show improved temporally grounded understanding.
On Daily-Omni, accuracy increases by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding (MSCD). MSCD swaps the two temporal halves of encoded features within each window to construct audio-shifted, video-shifted, and audio–video-shifted inputs. Logits from the original and shifted inputs are contrasted to emphasize audio–visual temporal alignment during decoding.
