papers.abstract: Two-frame video frame interpolation commonly resamples endpoint optical flow by the query time, which selects a constant-velocity straight-line path even though the same endpoint displacement is compatible with many intermediate trajectories. We present HermiteVFI, which replaces independent query-time motion prediction with one explicit continuous trajectory per pixel. The measured endpoint displacement fixes the two trajectory positions, while two latent endpoint derivatives learned from the frame pair control the interior path. A cubic Hermite curve is the minimum-degree polynomial that can independently satisfy these two position and two derivative boundary quantities. Its residual form contains linear motion exactly, structurally preserves the measured displacement endpoints for any network output, and has coefficients that are predicted once per frame pair and evaluated in closed form at arbitrary t. We further show that one interior query time gives a rank-deficient constraint on the two free trajectory coefficients, whereas any two distinct interior times are full rank at the representation level, motivating multi-time supervision. Appearance-derived directional cues help infer the latent derivatives that endpoint displacement alone cannot identify. On X4K1000FPS, SNU-FILM, and Vimeo90K-Septuplet, the largest gains occur for difficult non-uniform motion and high interpolation ratios. The amortization applies to trajectory-coefficient prediction; downstream reversal, refinement, and synthesis remain query dependent.
authors: Md Rifat Ur Rahman, Md Abtahi Majeed Chowdhury, Md Sakib Hossain Shovon, Jaesik Choi, Mohammad Ali Moni
bullets: Addresses the limitation of constant-velocity, straight-line motion assumed by common two-frame interpolation methods.
Predicts two latent endpoint derivatives from the frame pair and combines them with measured endpoint positions in a cubic Hermite curve.
The residual formulation exactly includes linear motion and preserves measured endpoints regardless of network outputs.
Multi-time supervision is motivated because two distinct interior times identify the trajectory coefficients, unlike a single time.
Evaluations on X4K1000FPS, SNU-FILM, and Vimeo90K-Septuplet show the largest gains for difficult non-uniform motion and high interpolation ratios.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of HermiteVFI. A frozen flow estimator measures bidirectional flow and auxiliary maps from the two keyframes. A shared head then predicts a velocity residual at each keyframe, which fixes the coefficients of a cubic Hermite curve. The curve is evaluated in closed form at each query time, splatted onto the target grid, refined, and rendered by warping and blending. The head does not take t as input and runs once per frame pair; only the last three stages repeat.

Table 3. Runtime (ms) versus number of interpolated frames, 720× 1280 input on a single NVIDIA V100. Motion is the trajectory model alone. Total additionally includes flow reversal, synthesis, and each method’s front-end feature extraction, a fixed cost that does not scale with K. Ours uses RAFT and reuses its internal features rather than running a second extraction pass, which is why our fixed cost is the lowest here.

papers.tldr: HermiteVFI models each pixel’s motion as a continuous cubic trajectory, improving interpolation for non-uniform motion while preserving endpoint displacement.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce EiT by exploring the key design factors of pixel-space diffusion from three perspectives: model architecture, representation, and frequency domain. Inspired by Denoising Autoencoders (DAE) which perform denoising through a bottleneck, we construct a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer that performs explicit compression along the channel dimension. In terms of representation, we find that both pixel and latent diffusion transformers exhibit a three-stage representation dynamics across layers and timesteps: denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection. Moreover, earlier denoising and a longer basis lift-up stage are associated with better generation, which EiT naturally achieves through its channel bottleneck and increased network depth. From the frequency perspective, we establish the equivalence between pixel-space and frequency-space diffusion when keeping the network operating in pixel space. On ImageNet $256\times256$ and $512\times512$, EiT consistently outperforms JiT (Just image Transformers) in generation quality. Specifically, our EiT achieves better FID than JiT: 1.61 vs. 1.85 at $256\times256$, and 1.73 vs. 1.99 at $512\times512$. Remarkably, EiT can be seamlessly applied to video pixel diffusion by simply extending the patch size to temporal dimension and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD evaluated on Kinetics-600 (resolution 256), under comparable total network parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/forever208/EiT
authors: Mang Ning, Le Zhang, Albert Ali Salah, Itir Onal Ertugrul, Jintao Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Pixel-space diffusion design involves interacting architectural, representation, and frequency-domain factors.
Method: EiT uses a U-shaped pixel diffusion transformer with explicit channel-wise compression inspired by denoising autoencoders.

Finding: Diffusion representations progress through denoising/local feature expansion, basis lift-up, and posterior projection; earlier denoising and longer basis lift-up correlate with better generation.
Result: EiT achieves lower FID than JiT on ImageNet at 256×256 and 512×512, and outperforms video latent diffusion in FVD on Kinetics-600 under comparable parameter counts.
Scope: The same approach extends to video by enlarging patch size along the temporal dimension.

PixelU constructs a spatial bottleneck by merging and splitting tokens. papers.abstract: We present SPARC, a geometry-guided attention pruning framework that turns the native self-attention of pretrained video diffusion transformers into a unified mechanism for camera control and persistent scene memory. Our key insight is that attention connectivity can simultaneously serve as geometric conditioning for camera control and spatial addressing for historical memory retrieval. Motivated by the asymmetric contextual requirements of reconstructing observed content and synthesizing novel regions, SPARC restricts observed tokens to geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context, while preserving dense attention for unobserved regions. Correspondence-aware attention biasing and order-invariant historical positioning further enable stable retrieval across long temporal gaps. Without introducing additional learnable control or memory modules, SPARC achieves precise camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation while substantially reducing attention computation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of aggressive attention pruning in improving camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity, with an inference speedup of over 50x when combined with four-step distillation. Project page is available at https://zju3dv.github.io/SPARC.
authors: Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Liyuan Cui, Yuan Li, Jiaxin Huang, Lutao Jiang, Runze Zhang, Yingda Yin, Xiaoyang Huang, Kai Yan, Keyang Luo, Xin Wang, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses camera adherence and faithful scene revisitation in long-horizon camera-controlled video generation.
Uses geometric correspondences to guide attention and retrieve relevant historical scene content.
Restricts observed regions to matching historical tokens plus local context, while retaining dense attention for novel regions.
Adds correspondence-aware attention biases and order-invariant historical positioning for stable retrieval across long temporal gaps.
Reports improved camera adherence, revisit consistency, and visual fidelity while substantially reducing attention computation.

figures.caption: Figure 3. System Overview. For each target chunk, SPARC establishes token-level correspondences with historical observations through local geometric projection, and then prunes the backbone’s native self-attention to focus on geometrically corresponding historical tokens and local spatiotemporal context for previously observed regions, while newly revealed regions retain dense attention for flexible content synthesis. Historical RoPE re-indexing is employed to eliminate artificial temporal ordering biases among retrieved historical observations. The generated observations are subsequently appended to the history bank for continuous rollout.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on DL3DV-Eval. Given the same input image and camera trajectory, we show frames generated with different methods along the roaming time. Explicit-3D baselines drift from the target trajectory or accumulate geometric distortions, and implicit baselines fail to follow the prescribed camera path, whereas SPARC preserves scene appearance and accurate camera control throughout the rollout. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 6. Qualitative comparison of revisitation on WorldScore-Static. Each scene follows a closed-loop camera trajectory (top view), and frames are sampled along the roaming time. Baselines either distort the scene or fail to recover the originally observed content upon revisiting, whereas our SPARC faithfully restores the scene at both revisits. See Supp. for additional scenes and video comparisons.

Figure 9. Additional long-horizon generation results. Without any degradation-aware augmentation, SPARC generates high-fidelity, minute-long videos with precise camera adherence and persistent scene consistency.

Figure 7. Ablation on attention pruning and historical RoPE indexing. Progressively incorporating geometric correspondence, local window attention, and correspondence bias improves camera adherence and reconstruction fidelity. The bottom rows visualize the pixel-wise difference |∆| between outputs generated using the original and shuffled history orders: sequential history RoPE yields discrepancies that grow along the trajectory, whereas our shared indexing remains invariant.

Figure 2. Redundancy of dense full self-attention. Most target regions have been observed in historical frames and require only sparse geometric correspondences for faithful reconstruction, while newly revealed regions benefit from broader contextual interactions.
Figure 8. Attention weight visualization. Given target queries, dense attention with the camera adapter exhibits attention peaks that deviate from geometrically corresponding historical regions.
Figure 5. Camera alignment. SPARC achieves the best camera alignment on DL3DV-Evaluation.

Figure 10. Training-free dynamic scene generation. We segment the foreground object and shift its correspondence locations along a prescribed motion trajectory, allowing SPARC to synthesize natural object motion consistent with the specified trajectory.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison on DL3DV-Evaluation and WorldScore-Static. CLIP-IQA and CLIP-Aesthetic jointly measure subjective quality; Style Cons. is reported in units of 10−3. Revisit metrics are reported as first / second revisit. SPARC (DMD) denotes our four-step distilled student. The best and second-best results are highlighted in bold and underline, respectively.

Table 2. Ablation on attention pruning. Geometric correspondence attention, local window attention, and correspondence bias provide complementary improvements in reconstruction fidelity, while shared historical RoPE further enhances generation quality.
Table 4. Computational efficiency. By combining attention pruning with 4-step distillation, SPARC achieves a 50× inference speedup over the original dense backbone.

Table 3. Robustness to historical frame ordering. Compared with sequential RoPE, our shared historical RoPE reduces output variations under shuffled history order. Results are reported as mean ± standard deviation.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces geometry-guided attention pruning for camera-controlled video generation, effectively combining video diffusion, efficient attention mechanisms, and interactive world modeling.
papers.title: SPARC: Geometry-Guided Attention Pruning for Long-Horizon Camera-Controlled Video Generation
papers.tldr: SPARC prunes video-transformer attention using scene geometry to enable precise camera control and long-term scene memory with over 50× faster inference when paired with four-step distillation.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence concerns both scene structure and its temporal evolution. Yet a semantically correct description can conceal a quantitative error: recognizing that objects are approaching does not determine their closing speed or whether they will meet. Such errors are critical in collision avoidance, trajectory tracking, and reactive grasping, where actions depend on motion magnitude, timing, and relative geometry. We study quantitative kinematic understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): resolving motion magnitude, rate, reference-frame dependence, and future spatial evolution from visual evidence. We introduce the Quantitative Kinematics Benchmark (QK-Bench), comprising 2,341 multiple-choice QA pairs from 379 videos and 17 tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera Ego-Motion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations. Hidden geometric and temporal signals support trajectory construction and filtering, while fixed kinematic rules map physical quantities to verifiable answers, including categorical labels. Trajectory and question validation ensure target reliability and sufficient visual support in the sampled frames. All models receive a unified monocular RGB input. Evaluations of proprietary, open-source, and spatial MLLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest model achieves only 41.2\% overall accuracy, and spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage. These findings indicate that current advances in spatial intelligence do not reliably transfer to quantitative kinematic understanding.
authors: Lennox Wei, Jiaqi Yao, Shixin Sun, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jianhua Han, Meng Tian, Shaohui Liu, Wangmeng Zuo
bullets: Introduces 2,341 multiple-choice questions from 379 videos across 17 quantitative kinematics tasks.
Covers object motion, camera ego-motion, and multi-object kinematic relations using monocular RGB input.
Uses validated trajectories, hidden geometric/temporal signals, and fixed kinematic rules to produce verifiable answers.
The best evaluated model reaches only 41.2% overall accuracy, while spatial MLLMs show no consistent advantage.
Shows that general spatial intelligence does not reliably transfer to quantitative understanding of dynamic scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the QK-Bench construction pipeline. Stage I integrates geometric and temporal signals into a hidden kinematic cache, and Stage II derives deterministic quantitative targets and generates validated QA pairs through controlled option construction, reliability filtering, and balancing. Only monocular RGB frames, timestamps, and multiple-choice questions are exposed during evaluation.

Fig. 4. QK-Bench failure cases in Speed Change, Object Turning, Camera–Object Relative Distance Change, and Closest-Approach Prediction: plausible motion interpretations with incorrect quantitative judgments.

Fig. 1. Task-wise performance of representative MLLMs on QK-Bench from monocular video inputs. The radar chart reports accuracy on 17 quantitative kinematic tasks spanning Object-Centric Kinematics, Camera EgoMotion Kinematics, and Multi-Object Kinematic Relations, highlighting substantial capability differences across fine-grained task types.

Fig. 2. Similar image motion can conceal different underlying kinematics. The leftward image change arises from object motion in Clip A and primarily from camera ego-motion in Clip B. A correct qualitative description does not establish the object’s displacement or speed in the relevant reference frame.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks quantitative kinematic understanding in MLLMs, touching spatial intelligence and video understanding.
papers.title: QK-Bench: Benchmarking Quantitative Kinematic Understanding for Dynamic Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: QK-Bench evaluates whether multimodal language models can quantitatively infer motion, timing, and spatial relationships from video, revealing major remaining weaknesses.

papers.abstract: Latent video generators are trained on clips of a few seconds, and much of this limit lies in their tokenizers, which spend as many tokens on a static frame as on a moving one and need future frames that do not exist during generation. We introduce DeltaRAE, a causal representation autoencoder for video. Its derivative tokenization encodes periodic anchor frames in full and all remaining frames with a few tokens each, and its causal encoder and decoder read a frozen pretrained image encoder. On UCF-101 and Kinetics-600, a standard diffusion transformer trained on DeltaRAE latents is competitive with state-of-the-art video tokenizers. DeltaRAE halves the tokenizer GFLOPs on 16-frame clips relative to keeping the same number of patch tokens for every frame, and it represents a minute of video with 18.8x fewer tokens. The tokenizer trains end to end on one-minute videos, and in video prediction a generator on its latents produces a full minute of video. The same generator collapses within 15 seconds in most videos when the tokenizer has the same token budget but no pretrained encoder.
authors: Mingzhuo Yu, Shengcao Cao, Chengzhi Mao, Yong Cheng, Di Jiang, Lijun Yu
bullets: Targets video tokenizers that waste equal tokens on static and moving frames and require unavailable future frames.
Uses derivative tokenization with full anchor-frame representations and a few tokens for remaining frames.
A causal encoder–decoder leverages a frozen pretrained image encoder.
Matches competitive video-tokenizer performance on UCF-101 and Kinetics-600 while halving tokenizer GFLOPs on 16-frame clips.
Represents one minute of video with 18.8× fewer tokens and supports minute-long video prediction; removing the pretrained encoder causes collapse within 15 seconds in most videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture of DeltaRAE. (a) Causal representation autoencoder. A causal encoder updates learnable registers from frozen semantic features augmented by a pixel-residual stem. The updated registers are projected and normalized into latent tokens for causal decoding. (b) Derivative tokenization. To exploit shared content over time, periodic anchor groups receive a full set of primitive tokens, while the remaining groups use fewer derivative tokens with earlier groups as context. (c) Streaming generation. A DiT generates successive chunks, reusing each chunk’s tail latents as the next input prefix. The assembled latent sequence is decoded into a 60-second video.

Figure 3. Generation quality against token count. gFVD against tokens per 16 frames, with the numbers of Tab. 1. UCF-101 shows the 736-token model. TATS, OmniTokenizer, MAGVIT and AdapTok lie outside the plotted range, and ViTok (external training data) is not plotted.

Figure 6. One-minute continuation from a 1.67-second prefix on a held-out Ego4D video, one frame every 2 seconds. Each block covers 20 seconds with the ground truth (GT), DeltaRAE, and DeltaRAE without the pretrained encoder with the same 19,584 tokens per minute and generator recipe. The framed frame is the prefix. Figs. S4 and S5 show more videos and a 20-second prefix.

Figure 5. Reconstruction of one-minute videos over time. PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS of the one-minute DeltaRAE tokenizer over 1,440 frames, averaged over each 10-second segment, on held-out Ego4D videos and, zero-shot, on YouCook2 videos not seen in training. Quality is stable over the minute on both.

Figure 4. Reconstruction of difficult 16-frame clips with 736 tokens. Input and reconstruction by DeltaRAE on two held-out clips, with frame indices on top. Every frame after the first has 32 derivative tokens, including the frames after the shot change. Fig. S7 shows more clips.

Table 1. Comparison with prior tokenizers on 16-frame benchmarks. UCF-101: rFVD on 50,000 clips and class-conditional gFVD with 10,000 samples against the training split. DeltaRAE operates at 2242, and its outputs are evaluated at 1282 and at 2562 to match the methods of each block. K600: frame-prediction gFVD at 642 on 50,000 clips. ∗Uses extra training data.

Table 4. Pixel-residual stem and token budget on K600. Reconstruction of fully causal tokenizers with and without the stem, and of the bidirectional-decoder reference. All rows use the ablation setup; see Tab. 1 for the final system.

Table 3. One minute of video, 1,440 frames, under different tokenizers. The published tokenizers (top) are an image RAE applied to every frame, tokenizers that compress each 16-frame clip into one token sequence, and 3D-convolutional VAEs with a uniform latent grid. They need several times more tokens per minute than DeltaRAE and are not trained at this length. With the same 19,584 tokens and the same generator recipe (bottom), 60-second rollouts stay coherent with the frozen DINOv2 encoder and collapse in nearly all videos without it; a rollout counts as coherent if its scene does not break down into distorted textures.

Table 2. Compute for 16 frames, DeltaRAE with 736 tokens compared with 4,096 dense per-frame tokens, measured from compiled graphs. Tokenizer cost covers encoder and decoder, with latency on CPU. DiT GFLOPs are for one forward pass, and DiT latency is for one sample with 250 steps.

papers.selection_reason: Causal video tokenizer enabling long video generation with drastically fewer tokens.
papers.title: DeltaRAE: Derivative Tokenization for Long Video Generation
papers.tldr: DeltaRAE enables causal, token-efficient long-video generation by fully encoding periodic anchor frames and sparsely encoding frame changes.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual understanding requires perceptual grounding, temporal understanding, and semantic inference. Multi-teacher distillation can consolidate these capabilities, but direct probability matching does not explicitly capture teacher prediction changes across audio-visual conditions. We introduce OmniMeld, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method that integrates domain expertise through modality-response-guided distribution matching. We train four teachers covering grounding and correspondence, temporal dynamics and event structure, causal and inferential reasoning, and contextual and holistic understanding. Each sample is routed to its corresponding teacher for supervision conditioned on student-generated answer prefixes. We derive transport costs from teacher prediction changes over shared candidate tokens across audio-visual conditions, using optimal transport to match student predictions to those of the teacher under complete audio-visual input. We also construct OmniMeld-20K for domain-specialized teacher training. The dataset spans four capability domains, with responses structured into evidence, reasoning, and answer sections and verified through consistency checks and media-based review. Experiments on audio-visual and general video understanding benchmarks demonstrate competitive teacher performance among similarly sized open-source models. The student improves over its base model across all evaluated benchmarks and surpasses the teachers' base model on several benchmarks.
authors: Daili Hua, Yifan Dai, Bohan Zeng, Yuran Wang, Zihao Wu, Chengzhuo Tong, Guoqing Jiang, Liwei Chen, Zhiheng Qin, Xuanping Li, Wentao Zhang
bullets: Targets perceptual grounding, temporal understanding, semantic inference, and the limits of direct probability matching.
Uses four domain-specialized teachers and routes each sample to the relevant teacher based on capability.
Conditions supervision on student-generated answer prefixes and applies optimal transport to align predictions across audio-visual conditions.
Introduces OmniMeld-20K, covering four domains with evidence-, reasoning-, and answer-structured responses verified for consistency and media grounding.
The distilled student improves over its base model across evaluated benchmarks and exceeds the teachers’ base model on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) requires reasoning about event progression, interactions, and the contextual conditions that distinguish abnormal behavior from common activity across diverse scenes. Although video agents enable multi-round analysis, the predefined analytical operations may not adequately satisfy these diverse reasoning demands. In this paper, we present EvoVAU, a framework that evolves a reusable tool library for a frozen video solver. Guided by task outcomes and execution trajectories, an external proposer identifies potential limitations in the library and refines it, retaining task experience as analytical operations that can be reused across questions. Specifically, Cross-Version Contrastive Feedback guides tool refinement by combining current errors with paired execution trajectories from historical corrections and regressions. Adoption-Aware Selection accepts a candidate library only when overall development-set accuracy improves and corrections outnumber regressions among questions on which the solver invokes new or modified tools. Using a small development set, EvoVAU alternates tool refinement with candidate evaluation and selection. At test time, the evolved library remains fixed, with no further involvement from the proposer. Experiments on several VAU benchmarks demonstrate strong performance and the flexibility of the evolved library across anomaly domains.
authors: Benfeng Wang, Chao Huang, Yudong Cheng, Chengliang Liu, Wei Wang, Wenqi Ren
bullets: Targets VAU’s need to reason about event progression, interactions, and contextual abnormality across diverse scenes.
An external proposer identifies tool limitations and refines the library based on task outcomes and execution trajectories.
Cross-Version Contrastive Feedback uses current errors alongside historical correction and regression trajectories.
Adoption-Aware Selection keeps candidate libraries only when development accuracy improves and corrections exceed regressions for affected questions.
Experiments across several VAU benchmarks show strong performance and flexibility across anomaly domains; the abstract provides no quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models for game interaction and control have increased the demand for large-scale gameplay videos paired with camera trajectories. However, capturing synchronized camera trajectories often requires game-specific pipelines, limiting scalability. We therefore propose GameWeaver, a unified diffusion framework that automatically produces paired video--camera data through three complementary tasks: camera pose estimation from observed video, video generation along a prescribed camera trajectory, and joint video--camera generation from a reference image and text. First, each tipxel stores the normalized 3D coordinates of a pixel ray's endpoint in a reference coordinate frame. The resulting three-channel tipxel fields and RGB frames share the pretrained video model's VAE. Next, a fully trainable dual-stream Transformer exchanges appearance and geometry features through bidirectional gated attention and conditions both streams on shared text features. Finally, deterministic fitting recovers camera intrinsics and normalized trajectories from generated tipxel fields. In our evaluation tasks, GameWeaver achieves a normalized translation MSE of 0.0029 for camera control; for joint generation, it scores 85.48 out of 100 on instruction adherence versus 64.71 for the best cascade on that metric, validating the feasibility of the proposed approach.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yifan Huang, Jixuan Zhang, Peifeng Wang, Yuying Ma, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses the scalability challenge of collecting synchronized gameplay videos and camera trajectories with game-specific pipelines.
Represents geometry using three-channel tipxel fields sharing a pretrained video model’s VAE with RGB frames.
Uses a dual-stream Transformer with bidirectional gated attention and shared text conditioning.
Supports camera-pose estimation, trajectory-conditioned video generation, and joint video–camera generation from an image and text.
Reports 0.0029 normalized translation MSE for camera control and 85.48/100 instruction adherence for joint generation, compared with 64.71 for the best cascade.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained ego-vehicle action recognition turns large-scale driving video into structured, searchable driving scenarios, providing a foundation for discovering critical maneuvers and systematically developing and evaluating autonomous driving models. However, large-scale driving videos often lack explicit ego-action labels, and existing datasets vary in action definitions, annotation granularity, and available supervision. We introduce EgoManeuver, a unified benchmark of 16 lateral and 6 longitudinal actions constructed from seven public driving datasets. Our multi-source labeling system leverages existing annotations and complementary evidence available in each source dataset, including vehicle signals, ego poses, HD-map topology, and captions, to assign labels under a unified fine-grained action taxonomy. We further standardize temporal action boundaries across datasets and validate the resulting labels through kinematic consistency checks and targeted human review. The resulting benchmark contains 86.6K segments spanning 190.8 h across 26 countries and provides a long-tail-aware evaluation protocol. We also introduce DenseEgo, a video-based baseline that combines spatially aware representations with dense per-step action supervision. On the EgoManeuver, DenseEgo achieves 82.7 lateral and 83.5 longitudinal mAP, outperforming the strongest existing video model by 1.5 and 5.0 points, respectively. Finally, we demonstrate one way to integrate DenseEgo with a language-model agent for retrieving driving videos that match user-specified actions and scenarios. All code, datasets, and model weights will be publicly released.
authors: Zhipeng Bao, Wenjie Zhao, Qianwen Li
bullets: Introduces a taxonomy of 16 lateral and 6 longitudinal ego-vehicle actions.
Constructs 86.6K segments covering 190.8 hours across 26 countries using multi-source evidence and standardized temporal boundaries.
Validates labels with kinematic consistency checks and targeted human review, and provides a long-tail-aware evaluation protocol.
Presents DenseEgo, a spatially aware video model with dense per-step supervision, achieving 82.7 lateral and 83.5 longitudinal mAP.
Demonstrates language-model-assisted retrieval of driving videos by user-specified actions and scenarios; code, data, and weights are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked which of two actions in a video happened first, given only a few sampled frames. Such frames can show that both actions occurred without showing which came first, so a reliable model should state an order only when the frames establish it. Forced-choice temporal benchmarks treat every input as answerable and reward lucky guesses, while answerability benchmarks do not separate frames that miss an action from frames that show both actions but not their order. We introduce EvOrderBench, a real-video benchmark of 579 event families. Each family fixes an episode and a question and varies only the frames: of two four-frame inputs, only one establishes the order, and two six-frame inputs extend the other one with either the frames that resolve the order or frames that do not. Every input is labeled for whether its frames establish each action and their order. Across sixteen open-weight configurations and three closed-source references, the best open models order nearly as accurately as the references when the frames establish the order, but withhold correctly on at most 83% of the inputs where they do not, against at least 90% for every reference; forced-choice accuracy cannot reveal this gap. Open models withhold mainly when the frames show neither action; once the frames show one or both, most of them commit to an order. Thinking narrows the gap, even when it is switched on within a single checkpoint, mainly by separating sufficient from insufficient evidence rather than by making models more cautious overall. Accurate ordering thus does not imply knowing when the frames fall short, and benchmarks should reward withholding alongside ordering.
authors: Xiaoqin Feng, Yuqi Li, Xinyuan Li, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Kuiye Ding, Yingli Tian
bullets: Introduces a real-video benchmark spanning 579 event families with frame sets that vary in whether they establish event order.
Labels whether each sampled input shows each action and whether it establishes which happened first.
Open models approach reference-model accuracy when order is visually established, but withhold less reliably on insufficient evidence.
Models most often withhold when neither action is shown; seeing one or both actions commonly triggers unjustified ordering.
Reasoning improves evidence sufficiency judgments, highlighting the need to reward correct withholding alongside temporal ordering.

papers.abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) specialize in offline video understanding; in contrast, their post-trained versions, streaming VLMs, can perform live interactions. We investigate whether streaming VLMs can replace their offline parent models on offline tasks. Such replacement could reduce deployment costs and improve efficiency. We propose Streaming Tax to systematically evaluate streaming VLMs on offline tasks. Our exploration spans three core dimensions: understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization across 15 benchmarks. Our findings reveal a critical gap between offline capability preservation and practical replaceability. This gap emerges at two stages: streaming adaptation can alter trustworthy behavior even when offline understanding is largely preserved, while the native streaming protocol can introduce further performance losses. Our analyses show that some of these losses arise from restricted access to historical visual evidence and failures to deliver usable responses. Importantly, regarding safety, streaming models often leave both harmful and legitimate requests unanswered rather than genuinely refusing unsafe ones. We then propose Stream++, a training-free plugin to improve streaming VLMs on offline tasks.
authors: Zhi Yang, Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang
bullets: Evaluates streaming VLMs on offline tasks across understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization using 15 benchmarks.
Finds two sources of performance loss: streaming adaptation can change trustworthy behavior, and the native streaming protocol can limit visual history and response usability.
Shows that safety behavior often manifests as unanswered requests—including legitimate ones—rather than appropriate refusal of harmful requests.
Introduces Stream++, a training-free plugin designed to improve streaming VLM performance on offline tasks.

papers.abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.
bullets: The work proposes a fixed-length (K=16) Audio-Visual Query Transformer built on a 2.7B-parameter LLM.
Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training with entropy regularization stabilizes reinforcement-learning optimization.
The authors hypothesize “temporal alignment friction”: global audio features can disrupt visual chronology and hurt visually focused metrics.
Removing audio yields 63.0 CIDEr, below Qwen2.5-VL’s 67.4 but providing a strong sub-3B baseline.
The results suggest CIDEr on datasets such as MSR-VTT may undervalue multimodal semantic richness.

papers.abstract: A developer who reproduces a video model's error on a short clip can replay that clip after an update. How often does a correct clip answer mean the original test now passes? On 960 prespecified CG-Bench questions, we updated from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Accuracy on a 64-frame sample spanning the full video rose from 27.9% to 33.3%. Before scoring the newer model, we froze 388 clips on which the older model reproduced its exact reference error. The updated model passed the reference on 51 of 116 clip passes (44.0%, 95% Wilson interval 35.3-53.0%) and on 16 of 272 clip failures (5.9%). Closing cases on a clip pass would have declared 65 unresolved reference failures fixed. Requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of the 67 reference fixes (23.9%). In a separate 1,028-video study with different checkpoints and direct option scoring, only 15 clips passed, and the 16-frame reference confirmed one. For the generated-answer update, the short replay identified cases worth checking, while the original input remained necessary to verify individual fixes.
bullets: On 960 CG-Bench questions, accuracy rose from 27.9% to 33.3% after updating from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct.
Among 388 clips reproducing the older model’s exact error, a clip pass matched a reference pass 44.0% of the time, while a clip failure still contained a reference fix 5.9% of the time.
Using clip passes to close cases would have falsely marked 65 unresolved failures as fixed; requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of 67 actual fixes.
A separate study found only one confirmed fix among 15 clip passes, reinforcing that the original input is needed for individual verification.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion and world models generate plausible videos but do not reliably match the requested camera direction and travel distance. We present DreamTour, a training-free framework that generates camera tours from a single image with more accurate control over camera motion. DreamTour first uses a frozen image inpainting prior to extend the photograph beyond its original field of view while preserving the input pixels. Depth-based rendering of this extended scene along the requested camera path produces approximate target views that serve as spatial guidance. We introduce Layout Steering, which aligns early video latents with these views through decaying low-frequency corrections, leaving later denoising to refine appearance and dynamics. For longer tours, we autoregressively generate the video segments, repeating guidance construction from each segment's final frame to maintain camera control across the full trajectory. DreamTour improves directional accuracy and travel calibration on VBench while maintaining competitive video quality. On WorldScore, it strengthens camera control and scene consistency across chained movements. Together, these results demonstrate that training-free spatial guidance enables more accurate and consistent camera control in pretrained video diffusion and world models.
authors: Srikumar Sastry, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Chenqi Li, Sarosij Bose, Mellon Zhang, Allen Tu, Ziyang Long, Yen-Liang Lin, Alexander Schwing, Nathan Jacobs
bullets: Extends the input image beyond its field of view using a frozen inpainting prior while preserving original pixels.
Renders depth-based views along the desired camera path to provide spatial guidance.
Uses Layout Steering to apply decaying low-frequency corrections early in denoising, then lets later steps refine video appearance and dynamics.
Autoregressively chains segments for longer tours, rebuilding guidance from each segment’s final frame.
Improves directional accuracy, travel calibration, camera control, and scene consistency on VBench and WorldScore while maintaining competitive video quality.

We render views along Π using depth from π3X [34] and encode them as the guide latent. papers.abstract: Understanding ultra-long videos requires retrieving sparse, query-relevant evidence from extensive video histories. Existing similarity-based retrieval methods are efficient, but they encode the question and the video content independently and thus often miss evidence whose relevance requires reasoning over both. Generative large language models (LLMs) can perform such reasoning, but they typically generate text over multiple rounds of search, which makes each query slow and costly. In this work, we introduce DeLoVi (Decision Models for Long Video), a framework that leverages pretrained decision models to retrieve evidence from ultra-long videos. Like an LLM, a decision model reads the question together with the candidate evidence, so it can reason over both. Unlike an LLM, it directly outputs a relevance score without generating text, which makes it fast and inexpensive. We first present DeLoVi-S, a simple method that generates captions for short video clips and uses a decision model to rank those captions by their relevance to a question. A generative LLM then answers the question using the top-ranked captions. Despite its simplicity, DeLoVi-S achieves state-of-the-art performance on three ultra-long video understanding benchmarks, EgoLifeQA, EgoMemReason, and MM-Lifelong, and generalizes effectively to long-video understanding benchmarks, VideoMME-L and LVBench. However, DeLoVi-S scores every caption for every question, so its cost grows linearly with video length. To reduce this cost, we propose an automated policy evolution framework that iteratively refines the memory construction and retrieval policies around a fixed pretrained decision model. The resulting method, DeLoVi-E, maintains comparable performance while reducing input tokens by 34x on average compared with DeLoVi-S. It also runs over 3x faster than the best prior method on EgoLifeQA while achieving higher accuracy.
authors: Ce Zhang, Baiqi Li, Seongsu Ha, Gedas Bertasius
bullets: Addresses the failure of independent similarity retrieval to find evidence requiring joint reasoning over queries and video content.
DeLoVi-S ranks captions of short clips with a decision model, then uses a generative LLM to answer from the top-ranked evidence.
DeLoVi-S achieves state-of-the-art results on three ultra-long video benchmarks and generalizes to additional long-video benchmarks.
DeLoVi-E evolves memory and retrieval policies to reduce input tokens by 34× on average while maintaining comparable performance.
On EgoLifeQA, DeLoVi-E runs over 3× faster than the best prior method while achieving higher accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DeLoVi. (a) DeLoVi-S divides the video into short clips of 10 to 30 seconds and captions every clip. A decision model scores the relevance of every clip caption to the question, and an LLM answers the question from the top-K clip captions. (b) DeLoVi-E answers the question in three steps. In Step 1, the decision model searches over a memory tree and selects the most relevant 3-minute window. The clip captions of this window are the first input of Step 3. In Step 2, keyword matching (BM25 [39]) shortlists the clip captions that share words with the question, and the decision model ranks the shortlisted captions by their relevance. Each top-ranked clip is passed to Step 3 together with its neighboring clips. In Step 3, the LLM answers the question from the clips of Step 1 and reports its confidence. If the LLM is not confident, the ranked clips of Step 2 are added in order and the LLM answers again, until it is confident.

Figure 8. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-S. The question asks for the color of the power bank that the camera wearer used last time and is asked on Day 6 of EgoLife, after 41 hours of video. The decision model assigns a relevance score to the memory entry of every clip, and the 100 clips with the highest scores are given to the LLM. We show the three top-ranked clips with their frames and memory entries. All three clips show the camera wearer handling a power bank on Day 6. The top-ranked clip is from the morning of Day 6 and does not show the power bank used last time, and the annotated evidence is ranked second. The LLM reads the retrieved memory entries in temporal order with their timestamps and answers correctly.

Figure 7. Requests to the decision model. (a) In a score request, the decision model receives the question and one memory entry and outputs a probability for each of the four levels. The relevance score is the expected level, normalized to [0, 1]. We show the instruction for EgoLifeQA, and its description of the video is adapted to each benchmark. (b) In a ranking request, the decision model receives the input fields, the instruction, and the candidates, and outputs a selection probability for each candidate.

Figure 1. Accuracy and runtime on EgoLifeQA. All methods use GPT-6 Luna as the LLM, and runtime is measured per question. DeLoVi-S achieves the highest accuracy, and DeLoVi-E is the fastest method while achieving the second-highest accuracy. Compared with MERIT [9], the strongest prior method, DeLoViE is 3.8× faster with 1.0% higher accuracy.

Figure 3. Accuracy gain of DeLoVi-S over MERIT at different time scales on MM-Lifelong. To answer a question, each method has to search an entire video, and the average video duration is 23.6, 51.9, and 105.6 hours on the day, week, and month splits, respectively. Both methods use the same LLM (GPT-6 Luna). MERIT is more accurate on the shortest video, whereas DeLoVi-S outperforms it on the longer videos.

Figure 9. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-E: answering from the first evidence window. The question asks what should be arranged in Alice’s room and is asked on Day 6, after 37 hours of video. In Step 1, the decision model selects Day 2, then the hour from 22:00 to 22:58, and lastly the 3-minute window from 22:48 to 22:51 (green), based on the summaries of these nodes. The clips of this window form the first evidence window, in which Alice describes the plans for the room. Each numbered box shows the frames and the memory entries of one evidence window. The LLM answers from this evidence window with a confidence of 0.97, so the search stops after a single LLM call.

Figure 6. Prompts for memory construction. (a) Prompt of the captioner. (b) Prompt of the free-text summaries of the initial policy and of DeLoVi-E. (c) One line of the timeline of an hour in DeLoVi-E, written from the summary of one 3-minute window. (d) One line of the index of a day in DeLoVi-E, written from the summary of one hour.

Figure 10. Qualitative example of DeLoVi-E: clip re-ranking after an answer that is not confident. The question asks which drinks the camera wearer usually does not buy at the supermarket. In Step 1, the decision model selects the hour of the supermarket visit and one of its 3-minute windows, and the LLM is not confident in its answer from this evidence window (confidence 0.62). In Step 2, BM25 shortlists 50 of the 763 clips, and the decision model re-ranks them. We show the ten top-ranked clips. Each of the first three forms a further evidence window together with its neighboring clips (boxes 2 to 4). The third and fourth evidence windows contain two statements of the camera wearer about not drinking coffee. The LLM answers after the 1st, 2nd, and 4th evidence windows, and its confidence reaches 0.91 after the 4th, so the search stops after three LLM calls.

Figure 5. Evolution dynamics on the validation set. Each point is the policy of one iteration, and darker points are later iterations. The input tokens per question (log scale) decrease throughout the evolution, while the accuracy stays close to that of the initial policy. DeLoVi-E (star) uses 6.5× fewer tokens than the initial policy with 1.9% higher accuracy. It also achieves similar accuracy to DeLoVi-S (square) with 34× fewer tokens.

We report DeLoVi with three LLMs, so that it can be compared with each baseline under the same LLM. DeLoVi-E uses 34× fewer input tokens than DeLoVi-S on average. Best results are in bold and second best are underlined.

papers.abstract: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.
bullets: Targets cases where models identify the correct video moment but express its timestamp incorrectly.
LLM sessions inspect weights and activations to localize the source of errors, such as an MLP layer or separator token.
Edits improve grounding across TimeLens-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B, including larger gains on long videos.
Improving edits outperform same-sized random edits, and edited models run at the original speed.
Scope is limited to the reported timestamp-error cases and evaluated model/session settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The TWS editor diagnoses failures and writes weight updates through two tools. In the shaded editing loop, the editor calls the GPU forward-pass tool, which runs practice batches by generation or teacher forcing, reads the scores and activations, writes code in the CPU Python kernel and saves complete edited tensors W ′, which the next call loads. The shown architecture is shared by Qwen3-VL-8B and TimeLens-8B. Orange and purple mark the independent Qwen query and value/output edits. Teal marks the three TimeLens MLP edits. The bottom note marks Qwen3.5-0.8B’s repetition edit. The 1,215 test questions stay hidden from the editor. Supplementary Fig. S1 gives diagnostic details.

Figure 7. Timestamp repair moves the answer to the event. Each example shows the query, frames at the centres of the base and edited answers, and the intervals (blue true, grey base, teal TWS query edit). Answers keep the model’s formatting; the parser reads 8:45 as minutes and seconds whatever unit follows. These are the four largest IoU gains among held-out practice answers that changed from seconds to m:ss.

Figure 4. TWS gains most over all TimeLens-8B test videos, and repairs long ones without harming short ones. Test mIoU overall and by video length, from the answers of Fig. 3. The arrow marks the gain of TWS (run 17) on videos of 30 minutes or more, +18.51 [+15.06,+22.24]; under 10 minutes it is level with the base model (+0.30, NS). papers.abstract: Attention over long sequences is a major computational bottleneck in video generation, which can be alleviated through sparsity and low-bit quantization. We propose JetDiffusion, a video generation system built on trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention (VSQA), with custom inference kernels that combine native NVFP4 computation and kernel fusion. At 90% sparsity, VSQA accelerates attention by 8-29x compared with FlashAttention on different hardwares. To further accelerate video generation, we combine VSQA with NVFP4 linear quantization and step distillation. Although each technique can individually preserve generation quality, jointly adapting to all three remains challenging, particularly under aggressive NVFP4 quantization. Through empirical studies, we develop an effective staged training recipe that enables stable adaptation to quantization, sparsity, and few-step denoising. On Wan2.1-14B, the resulting model achieves 273x end-to-end video generation speedup on the RTX 5090 while maintaining comparable video quality.
authors: Yulun Wu, Zihan Min, Minshen Zhang, Kaiqin Kong, Ji Xie, Will Lin, Junda Chen, Wenxuan Tan, Aryan Kumar, Loay Rashid, Qingyu Yin, Hao Zhang
bullets: Targets attention’s long-sequence computational bottleneck in video generation.
Introduces trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention with fused native NVFP4 inference kernels.
At 90% sparsity, attention is accelerated 8–29× over FlashAttention across hardware.
Uses staged training to jointly adapt sparsity, quantization, and few-step denoising.
Reports 273× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.1-14B using an RTX 5090 with comparable video quality.

papers.abstract: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, outperforming frontier VLM judges by 4.4%-12.8% while achieving at least 90% recall for both human approvals and rejections. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 5.0% to 68.0%. Across 15 models at their highest reasoning effort, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We fine-tune Qwen3.8-27B with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) using our verification programs as rewards, improving pass@1 from 30.31% to 52.19% on held-out instances. Our project page is at https://motion-graphics-bench.github.io/.
bullets: Introduces an expert-curated benchmark of 100 static-SVG motion-editing instances derived from real-world Lottie designs.
Verification programs support multiple valid implementations and achieve 93.3% agreement with human judgments, outperforming VLM judges by 4.4–12.8 percentage points.
Across 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 5.0% to 68.0%; common failures involve poses, motion trajectories, and event coordination.
Using verification programs as GRPO rewards improves Qwen3.8-27B pass@1 from 30.31% to 52.19% on held-out instances.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate sequences by progressively unmasking tokens, but errors introduced during decoding are typically irreversible. Recent work has shown that iterative correction can improve sample quality, yet existing theory fails to explain this given a learned, imperfect denoiser model. We re-formulate MDM inference as a Markov chain on the clean sequence space, defined by a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-introduces masks and then denoises. This helps us analyze the actual denoising trajectory towards the data distribution. The analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R$^2$D) inference, a purely test-time, finetuning-free, reward-free procedure. To further improve performance, we propose Trajectory Correction Training (TCT), a denoiser-training procedure that exposes the model to its own errors along the generation trajectory. On logical tasks, our approach exhibits a striking near-log-linear test-time scaling, achieving over 97% accuracy on hard Sudoku puzzles and over 99% accuracy on 3-SAT. Our approach also applies to pretrained models on actual language tasks, beating iterative correction baselines and the official Q-mode accuracy of LLaDA2.1-mini on HumanEval+.
bullets: Masked diffusion decoding errors are usually irreversible, limiting generation quality.
The paper models inference as a Markov chain using a remask-denoise kernel that randomly re-masks tokens before denoising.
This analysis motivates Random Remask-Denoise (R²D), a finetuning-free, reward-free, test-time method.
Trajectory Correction Training (TCT) trains denoisers on errors encountered during their own generation trajectories.
On logical tasks, the approach achieves over 97% Sudoku accuracy and over 99% 3-SAT accuracy, and improves pretrained-model results on language tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generative models have enabled flexible conditional generation and editing pipelines, such as text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-guided synthesis. However, these workflows are inherently one-directional, mapping conditions to videos without providing a mechanism to invert this process. In complex media production settings, the ability to recover controllable textual conditions from a given video is highly desirable, yet remains underexplored. While inverse prompting has been studied for image generation, directly extending these approaches to video is challenging due to the need to capture temporal dynamics beyond static appearance, as well as the substantial computational cost of per-video optimization. In this work, we propose the first practical framework for efficient video inverse prompting. Specifically, we formulate inverse prompting as a meta-learning problem and introduce Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized over temporal dimensions to enable fast and effective prompt inference. Our approach amortizes the inversion process, eliminating the need for costly iterative optimization at test time. Experimental results demonstrate that MVIP recovers higher-quality inverse prompts with significantly improved reconstruction fidelity compared to image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines, while achieving substantial gains in efficiency. Code and video results are available at https://ueriniuno.github.io/mvip-page/.
bullets: Addresses the lack of methods for inverting video-generation pipelines to recover controllable text conditions.
Introduces Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized across temporal dimensions.
Amortizes inversion, eliminating iterative per-video optimization at inference time.
Reports higher-quality inverse prompts, better reconstruction fidelity, and improved efficiency than image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines.
Focuses on capturing video temporal dynamics beyond static appearance.

papers.abstract: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
authors: Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman, Shuo Yang, Ratheesh Kalarot, Yingyan Celine Lin, Mingze Xu
bullets: Addresses the tight coupling between utterance timing and audiovisual diarization in video captioning.
Uses a two-stage approach: synthetic-caption training on 225K clips, followed by reinforcement learning from 2.9K human-corrected clips.
Generates transcripts, utterance timestamps, speaker grouping, and visual descriptions for each utterance.
On DiaDemBench, achieves strong diarization and substantially better timestamp accuracy than Gemini 4 Argon (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME).
Maintains performance on multilingual and minute-long videos and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Qualitative comparison with similar-looking speakers. Each track shows one model’s predicted utterances over time, colored by the ground-truth speaker that its description depicts, with wrong speakers outlined in dark red.

Figure 11. A one-word turn right before another speaker (Mandarin). The young man answers with a single syllable lasting 0.3s (first frame), and the man in the gray suit continues immediately (second frame). DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E keep the short turn as a separate line with the correct speaker. Gemini 4 Argon and DiaDem merge it into the next speaker’s line, so turn A is lost. Gemini’s timestamps also miss every boundary (TIME 0), and DiaDem predicts none. This example shows that accurate timestamps and diarization are tightly coupled, as a model without precise turn boundaries tends to absorb a short turn into a longer neighboring one.

Figure 2. Overview of DiaCap. A speech recognizer Ψ transcribes the audio, and an audiovisual LLM Θ takes the transcript T together with the video and audio to predict the timestamps and speaker of every utterance. DiaCap-E2E predicts Y directly without a recognizer.

Figure 7. Failure case: off-screen speaker merged with the on-screen one. In a handheld phone video, a girl (A) asks her mother where she is going, and the mother (B) answers from off-screen. DiaCap describes a single speaker, gives the mother’s reply (“I’ll go wherever I want”) to the girl, and drops the mother’s cut-off last words. Since only the girl is ever on screen, the model does not infer that a second person is speaking.

Figure 9. Off-screen speakers in a multi-shot scene. The first and last turns are spoken while the camera shows someone else. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and describe these speakers as off-screen voices. Gemini 4 Argon gives the woman’s “Uh, Nal-what?” to the man in the blue lab coat and truncates it. DiaDem describes both men only as “man in a lab coat”, so the second man’s two turns go to the first man.

Figure 8. One speaker who goes off-screen. In this typical shot/reverse-shot conversation, a single woman speaks both lines. During the second line, the camera cuts to the listener and the speaker is off-screen. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute both lines to the same speaker. Gemini 4 Argon gives the second line to the visible listener (short reddish-brown hair). DiaDem’s description (“woman with shoulder-length brown hair”) is too generic to identify the speaker, so neither of its lines is credited.

Figure 10. A speaker seen only from behind. The last line is spoken by the man with his back to the camera. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute it to him. Gemini 4 Argon gives it to the man in the gray suit and DiaDem to the man with the mustache, the two people whose faces are visible.

Figure 12. A short interjection from a third speaker. DiaCap and DiaCap-E2E attribute all four turns correctly and place every boundary within the collar. Gemini 4 Argon merges the woman’s two turns into one line, so when scoring Gemini, we merge consecutive groundtruth utterances from the same speaker, which leaves three ground-truth turns. Gemini’s timestamps miss most boundaries (TIME 33). DiaDem describes the speaker of the final interjection only as “man’s voice”, which depicts none of the people in the scene.

Figure 13. Four speakers in one room. DiaCap, DiaCap-E2E, and Gemini 4 Argon attribute all five turns correctly. DiaDem gets three of the five turns wrong. It gives “Are you serious?” (C) and “Me too.” (D) to the young woman, and gives her own “I’m okay with that.” to a young man. Gemini’s timestamps drift by about 0.7s on the last three turns (TIME 40), whereas both DiaCap variants place every boundary within the collar (TIME 100).

Figure 3. Training data curation and annotation. (1) Audio, audiovisual, and visual experts tag each clip. We remove clips with unrelated or out-of-sync audio, deduplicate and resample the rest to balance language, speaker count, and visual scenes, and add no-speech clips with empty targets. (2) An audiovisual LLM annotates who says what, and a speech aligner timestamps each utterance. (3) Human annotators correct hard clips mined from the SFT corpus, plus fewer single-speaker clips, to form the RL corpus.

papers.abstract: Creating a dialogue scene typically requires cutting between multiple views (e.g., close-ups, medium shots, and over-the-shoulder shots) of the actors. Yet capturing such coverage is costly and in many settings unavailable. We study dialogue re-cinematography: synthesizing additional shots from a single wide-angle dialogue video. Existing video generators can synthesize new shots, but rely on visual cues alone, so when the source video barely shows the lips, the generated lip motion fails to match the speech. Our key observation is that the speech audio is view-invariant: it constrains lip motion in any target view. Building on this insight, we adapt a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model to generate the new shot from a target frame that specifies the view, a source video that contains the performance, and the speech audio that drives lip motion. In multi-person scenes, however, pretrained audio-visual models drive every visible face with the same speech, causing speech leakage, where silent listeners mouth the speaker's words. We therefore introduce speaker-aware audio gating, a training-free module that lets the audio drive only the faces that speak in the target shot. On a cinematic paired-view benchmark spanning diverse viewpoints and framings, our method lowers perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% relative to the strongest baseline, Wan 3.0. Our method also remains robust on in-the-wild scenes, highlighting its potential for film post-production.
authors: Anthony Chen, Naomi Ken Korem, Matan Ben-Yosef, Tavi Halperin, Urska Jelercic, Ofir Bibi, Daniel Cohen-Or, Or Patashnik, Maneesh Agrawala
bullets: Addresses the costly or unavailable multi-camera coverage needed for dialogue scenes.
Adapts a pretrained audio-visual diffusion model using a target frame for composition, source video for performance, and speech audio for lip motion.
Introduces training-free speaker-aware audio gating to prevent speech leakage onto silent listeners.
On a paired-view cinematic benchmark, reduces perceptual error by 59%, landmark error by 56%, and speech leakage by 97% versus Wan 3.0.
Also shows robustness on in-the-wild scenes, supporting potential film post-production use.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Method overview. From a source video with its speech audio, a target frame of the desired shot, and its shot prompt, our audio-visual diffusion model generates the synchronized target-view video. Right: speaker-aware audio gating. To prevent silent listeners from mouthing the speaker’s words (speech leakage), an active-speaker detector labels each face in the source as speaking or silent. Cross-view attention correspondence matches each source face to the target frame, cross-frame correspondence tracks it through the generated frames, and the gate𝐺 suppresses audio-to-video updates on silent faces.

papers.abstract: Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. We also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric combining event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity. Across all datasets, EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of SOTA methods and demonstrates robustness across different cameras at any resolution.
authors: Karthik Sundar Senthilkumar, Christopher Thirgood, Simon Hadfield
bullets: Sparse RGB frames cannot uniquely recover the intervening events’ activity, polarity, and timing.
Event Activity Diffusion models discrete event counts, Event Spatial Allocation assigns them to pixels, and Event Timing Diffusion predicts continuous timestamps.

The method reportedly achieves twice the accuracy of prior state-of-the-art methods and remains robust across cameras and resolutions.

papers.abstract: Despite strong performance on standard benchmarks, video reasoning models remain vulnerable to visual degradation, raising concerns about their reliability in safety-critical scenarios. Existing benchmarks address this concern in part by simulating visual degradation or probing model reasoning with challenging questions, leaving open how well models handle naturally degraded video and whether they can make the simpler judgments that matter for safe driving. To this end, we introduce GRAPE-Bench, which jointly evaluates video reasoning across visual degradation conditions and question difficulty. It combines a synthetic set spanning twelve corruption types across daily-life and driving videos with real-world footage of driving at night or in rain, snow, or fog. Each video is paired with three progressively challenging questions, from fundamental judgments with potential safety implications to demanding reasoning stress tests. Across open-weight and frontier models, we observe ranking reversals between synthetic and real-world conditions and level-specific weaknesses obscured by overall accuracy. Synthetic-data fine-tuning improves Qwen3.5-9B's real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%, while clean-privileged on-policy distillation reaches 80.4% in a separate reasoning-enabled setting. Through preference steering, we further demonstrate continuous control over a frozen model's trade-off between safety-relevant judgments and challenging reasoning, with little change in overall accuracy. Together, GRAPE-Bench provides a unified testbed for evaluating, improving, and controlling video reasoning under degraded visual conditions.

papers.abstract: RGB-based video object segmentation (VOS) remains brittle under fast motion and adverse illumination. Event cameras preserve signal under blur and challenging exposure, but provide little evidence when motion slows. Interaction can restore object state for subsequent propagation, yet promptable event methods merely address single windows. We formalize event-based Promptable Video Segmentation (ePVS), where prompts at arbitrary windows initialize, correct, or introduce objects and predictions. We present Event Memory-As-Prompt Segmentation (E-MAPS), which transfers a pretrained promptable segmenter to event streams and learns propagation and correction. Event-to-Token (E2T) aligns recurrent event features with pretrained representations while preserving prompt-conditioning priors. Memory-Aware Prompting (MAP) converts object-conditioned history into sparse prompts, allowing memory and user inputs to share one decoder pathway efficiently. We construct Event-View Masklets (EViM) from 206K aligned RGB-event pairs and 620K masks for two-stage representation transfer and native event-video learning, and establish three training-disjoint benchmarks. E-MAPS leads prompt-once and interactive ePVS across all three benchmarks while being more efficient. It further demonstrates strong performance on zero-shot object tracking benchmarks. Trains with Event-View Masklets from 206K aligned RGB-event pairs and 620K masks, evaluated on three training-disjoint benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multi-frame video frame interpolation (VFI) aims to reconstruct dense video from sparse keyframes, requiring accurate intermediate motion and faithful appearance. As temporal gaps grow, flow-based methods can retain observed textures but misplace them under ambiguous motion, whereas iterative latent-diffusion models can synthesize plausible content but incur substantial sampling costs and may alter details during reconstruction with a variational autoencoder (VAE). We present RePix-VFI, named for Re-rendering observed Pixels, a multi-frame VFI framework that couples draft-conditioned one-step video diffusion with reconstruction from observed keyframes. A pretrained video diffusion model refines a flow-rendered draft of the whole window in a single forward pass. For each target frame, our generative readback matches its two bounding keyframes to the generated prediction using an optical-flow estimator. The resulting correspondences guide re-rendering of original keyframe RGB pixels outside the VAE. A lightweight appearance fusion head combines these renderings with generated appearance. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction and perceptual quality. On SNU-FILM at $\times$8 and $\times$16, RePix-VFI achieves the highest PSNR and the lowest LPIPS, FloLPIPS, and tOF among the compared methods, exceeding the best evaluated diffusion-based baseline by 1.71 and 1.48dB in PSNR, respectively. It also runs 32--42$\times$ faster than the state-of-the-art multi-frame VFI diffusion model.

On SNU-FILM at ×8 and ×16, achieves the best reported PSNR and perceptual metrics among compared methods, while running 32–42× faster than a leading multi-frame VFI diffusion model.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video question answering enables blind and low-vision (BLV) users to query their immediate surroundings through natural language. However, existing benchmarks and models primarily optimize for semantic agreement with reference answers, reducing visual assistance to a purely factual matching task. In real-world scenarios, a factually correct response remains practically unhelpful if it lacks the spatial orientation, actionable detail, or conciseness required by the immediate task of the user. Drawing upon real BLV egocentric videos and authentic user queries from EgoBlind, we construct the PA-EgoQA, a preference-aligned dataset that reconstructs reference answers according to empirical BLV communication criteria. Based on this dataset, we introduce Preference-Aligned Visual Egocentric Learning (PAVE), a unified learning and inference framework that couples structured answer-policy fine-tuning with deterministic question-conditioned routing to adapt response formulation directly to the surface form of the query at inference time. We further align the model via Filter-GRPO, which pairs a hierarchical correctness-quality reward with contrast-based candidate-group filtering to extract learning signals from both factual accuracy contrasts and fine-grained quality variations among correct answers. Extensive experiments across three vision-language backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in factual accuracy alongside substantial gains in assistive response quality. These results establish a concrete paradigm for translating human-centered response requirements into egocentric supervision, generation policies, and post-training objectives. Code will be provided at https://github.com/shawnliang420/PAVE.
