papers.abstract: In text-to-video retrieval, MLLM-based embedding models do well when the text describes the scene (general retrieval), but poorly when it describes actions and their direction (time-sensitive retrieval). TARA, a pioneering work, fine-tunes such a model on text triplets with temporal hard negatives; it improves time-sensitive retrieval but lowers general retrieval (mean R@1 over six benchmarks in our rerun on Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B: 58.4->44.8), and its released model keeps general retrieval only when ensembled with Qwen3-VL-Embedding. Our goal is strong general and time-sensitive retrieval with one model and one vector per clip. Three findings lead to three simple components. Keep loss: general retrieval follows how far the output embeddings drift from the base model, not how far the weights move; we therefore keep them near the base model, which keeps most general retrieval even without general-domain data. Pair loss: the text embeddings of an action description and its reversed-direction version are well separated, but the video embeddings of a clip and its reversed copy are close; we therefore widen the gap between the video embeddings of each clip and its reversed copy, in the direction of the difference between their two text embeddings. Middle-layer LoRA: frames are combined in the middle layers, and temporal information peaks in or just after them; we therefore train LoRA only on these layers, which nearly matches training all weights on most time-sensitive benchmarks with 0.15% of the parameters and keeps general retrieval better. General R@1 stays at 58.4, while R@1 with each clip's reversed copy in the gallery rises from 55.5 to 63.2; the gains carry over to unseen benchmarks and InternVL2-8B-RA. The keep loss is also a remedy for the TARA recipe (general R@1: 44.8->57.8), and ensembling TARA with Ours gives the highest scores on RTime and unseen CiA among the compared models.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in harness-based recursive self-improvement (RSI) have improved video understanding by evolving executable agent workflows without updating foundation model parameters. However, extending this paradigm to omnimodal understanding remains challenging, as the heterogeneous and interdependent nature of multimodal perception and reasoning creates a complex evolution space, making targeted harness optimization difficult. To address these challenges, we propose OmniHarness-RSI, a modality-aware framework for evolving agent harnesses. Specifically, we factorize the evolution space into three capability dimensions: modality routing and collaboration, modality-aware evidence localization, and modality-specific perception. Based on this factorization, we construct a Factorized-Harness Agent integrating specialized perception experts and audio-video retrieval tools. We further introduce modality-guided harness evolution, which identifies deficiencies through structured modality-capability attribution and refines corresponding harness strategies through interactive code revisions and execution feedback. Validation-guided selection and held-out evaluation assess generalization within and across datasets. Experiments on WorldSense, Daily-Omni, and OmniVideoBench demonstrate test accuracy improvements of 8.86, 8.13, and 6.23 percentage points, respectively, consistently outperforming modality-agnostic RSI. The evolved harnesses also demonstrate cross-dataset transfer without adaptation, while reducing planner calls and viewed frames.
authors: Shilin Ma, Xingming Shui, Jinglin Chen, Zetong Zhao, Jingqi Tian, Deyi Zhu, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of optimizing harnesses for heterogeneous, interdependent modalities.
Factorizes evolution into modality routing/collaboration, evidence localization, and modality-specific perception.
Uses specialized perception experts, audio-video retrieval tools, and interactive code revisions guided by modality-capability attribution.
Improves test accuracy by 8.86, 8.13, and 6.23 percentage points on WorldSense, Daily-Omni, and OmniVideoBench, respectively, over modality-agnostic RSI.
Shows cross-dataset transfer without adaptation while reducing planner calls and viewed frames.

papers.abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
authors: Ayush Barik, Fan Lai, Francis Y. Yan
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of selecting and compressing video evidence without modeling the value of additional tokens.
Formulates video retrieval-augmented generation as token allocation over frames and subtitles under a shared budget.
Uses an iterative water-filling algorithm with a provable convergence guarantee to optimize allocation.
Reuses tokens and VLM attention across multi-turn conversations without extra processing cost.
Improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points at comparable compute, and by up to 1.5 points with 1.7–17.3× fewer TFLOPs in multi-turn understanding.

papers.abstract: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy
authors: Divya Joshi, Ruize Yang, Colleen Peyton, R. James Cotton
bullets: Addresses the time and expertise required for observational assessments such as GMA and BabyOSCAR.
BB3D estimates 3D joint-angle trajectories from single-camera infant video rather than relying on 2D keypoint motion.
A transformer trained on BB3D trajectories predicted BabyOSCAR items and totals on held-out recordings.
The predicted BabyOSCAR total separated infants with and without cerebral palsy better than a replicated 2D-feature classifier, but worse than expert ratings.
Predictions also reflected functional ability and body distribution, though less strongly than clinician scores.

papers.abstract: Video generative models synthesize realistic scenes, yet their interactions often violate physics. A ball dropped onto sand should displace grains and settle into a crater, whereas a generated video may show it passing through the surface or leaving the sand flat. Post-hoc methods typically score generated videos with a vision-language model (VLM), but such scores offer limited guidance on which object or parameter to modify, and each correction costs another synthesis. Simulation-based pipelines instead run fixed stages before synthesis, so simulation errors reach the video. To address these limitations, we present PhysMend, a training-free framework for verification-guided program refinement. PhysMend describes the target event as an editable physical program of grounded objects, events, and required relations, paired with tunable execution parameters. Our key insight is to verify and repair the event on its simulated rollout and on the depth video that conditions the generator (depth control) rather than on generated videos, enabling quantitative violation measurement, targeted editing, and fast re-verification before synthesis. A hybrid verifier evaluates semantic event consistency, physical plausibility, solver stability, and visibility in the depth control. VLM judgments are confined to event semantics and cannot override failed physical measurements, which limits the impact of VLM hallucinations. Each failed check localizes the program fields eligible for repair, and its measured violation scales a bounded update of their parameters. Only accepted depth control reaches the generator, which runs once per input. Experiments on the commonly used benchmarks Physics-IQ, PhyGenBench, and VBench-2.0 demonstrate substantial gains across different generator backbones; for example, PhysMend raises the overall Physics-IQ score of Wan-VACE from 27.33 to 39.40.
authors: Meilong Xu, Ziyi Zhao, Bhagyashree Puranik, Shayda Moezzi, Yixiao Zhang, Kushan Thakkar
bullets: Targets physics violations in generated video interactions, such as objects passing through surfaces or failing to deform them.
Represents events as grounded objects, relations, execution parameters, and editable program fields.
Uses hybrid checks for semantic consistency, physical plausibility, solver stability, and depth-control visibility.
Localizes failed checks and applies bounded, violation-scaled parameter updates; only accepted depth control is synthesized.
Improves Physics-IQ for Wan-VACE from 27.33 to 39.40 and gains across Physics-IQ, PhyGenBench, and VBench-2.0.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of PhysMend. Masks, depth, and the VLM turn the input into an editable physical program Π, compiled with parameters θ and executed in Genesis [3]. For the ball released onto sand, Π lists the grabber, ball, sand, and table, and it chains release, fall, and collision, where the collision must contact and deform the sand. Its parameters θ include the release time, initial motion, and sand material. Inside the shaded loop, checks examine the rollout and its depth control. Accepted depth control conditions a frozen generator once, whereas a failed check’s record Rj routes the loop (dashed) to replan Π or repair θ. Frame indices are local to each sequence.

Each panel shows the input image, an expanded-prompt excerpt, and five chronological frames per method. Ellipses indicate omitted prompt text. PhysMend occupies the first row. Frames keep their original aspect ratios.

For PhysMend, it is the recorded pipeline time with inference on a single 80 GB H100 GPU; for NEWTON, it is a generation-only estimate, 3.4 calls times the measured time of one generation call. Figure 3. Quantified verification and repair on one representative example from Physics-IQ [43]. Each rollout is simulated, and the VLM and the physical measurements check every event. At k = 0, the simulation is numerically unstable, so no other check is evaluated, and parameter repair raises the solver substeps. At k = 1, the program treats the hanging block as a static fixture. The VLM and the physical measurements fail on the block’s events, and replanning makes the block a moving object. At k = 2, every check passes, and the frozen generator runs once.

Figure 5. From check record to bounded repair. A failed check reports its decision, residual, evidence, affected objects, checked interval, and editable fields. Measured violations scale bounded edits of the reported parameters, structural errors trigger replanning, and construction failures return to their stage. Every revision is re-executed against all required checks and is accepted, retained as a new starting point, or rolled back.

papers.abstract: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.
authors: NaHyeon Park, Kyeong-Hwan Moon, Youjin Jeon, Hyunjung Shim
bullets: Streaming models exhibit context inertia: previous video chunks can overpower newly changed prompts.
Discarding or editing cached context risks breaking visual continuity, even when only the previous chunk is retained.
RG measures a cache-free residual by denoising the re-noised previous chunk under the new prompt, then applies it early in generation of the next chunk.
The training-free method improves prompt switching across single- and multi-switch settings while largely preserving visual quality.
It adds one forward pass per chunk and requires no per-model tuning, enabling integration into existing pipelines.

papers.abstract: High-resolution video matting requires accurate recovery of continuous alpha values, including fine hair, soft boundaries, and motion blur, yet dense alpha supervision remains scarce. Pretrained text-to-video diffusion transformers (DiTs) offer rich spatio-temporal priors, whereas existing generative video matting approaches typically route alpha predictions through RGB-trained VAE latents, which can attenuate fine details and introduce additional decoding overhead. We present TokenMatte, which adapts a pretrained video DiT into a single-pass, auxiliary-free RGB-to-alpha predictor with a pixel-native output interface. At its core is a single shared linear readout that maps each spatio-temporal token directly to its corresponding ($t \times p \times p$) block of alpha pixels, predicting spatial details and temporal variations within the same local video block. Tiling these blocks produces the full-resolution alpha sequence without a convolutional decoder or learned upsampling. The predicted alpha is supervised directly in pixel space, while the ground-truth alpha never enters the VAE, eliminating target-side alpha encoding and output-side VAE decoding. Leveraging the pretrained video prior, TokenMatte is trained using only existing public matting datasets, without additional data curation or auxiliary inputs at inference. Compared with a matched latent-output baseline, our pixel-native interface improves matting accuracy while achieving a 1.51$\times$ inference speedup. TokenMatte establishes a new auxiliary-free state of the art on VideoMatte, YouTubeMatte, and V-HIM60.
authors: Zanyi Wang, Dengyang Jiang, Fengfei Yu, Shilong Liu
bullets: Addresses scarce dense alpha supervision and detail loss from routing predictions through RGB-trained VAE latents.
Uses one shared linear readout to map each spatio-temporal token directly to a local block of alpha pixels.
Supervises alpha directly in pixel space, avoiding alpha VAE encoding, convolutional decoding, and learned upsampling.
Outperforms a matched latent-output baseline in accuracy and achieves a 1.51× inference speedup.
Reports auxiliary-free state-of-the-art results on VideoMatte, YouTubeMatte, and V-HIM60.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method Overview. From an RGB video, a frozen VAE encoder produces latent tokens and a pretrained T2V backbone runs one deterministic pass (τ = τ0, ϵ=0) to yield a spatio-temporal token field (Sec. 3.1). A shared linear head unfolds each token into its local block of alpha pixels (Sec. 3.2), supervised in pixel space with no alpha encoding or VAE decoding (Sec. 3.3).

Figure 5. Qualitative comparison with auxiliary-free and mask-guided methods. We compare TokenMatte with auxiliary-free RVM and GVM, and with mask-guided MatAnyone2 and VideoMaMa using SAM2 guidance. The SAM2 mask sequence is shown for reference, and colored boxes indicate the magnified regions on the right. While all methods recover the main foreground, RVM produces diffuse hair boundaries and the other baselines tend to smooth some thin strands. TokenMatte preserves finer and more separated hair structures without auxiliary mask guidance.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison with auxiliary-free methods. We compare TokenMatte with RVM and latent-based GVM across three video frames. The blue and orange boxes indicate regions magnified on the right. RVM produces diffuse alpha boundaries, while GVM exhibits over-smoothed predictions that blur fine structures and merge neighboring details. In contrast, TokenMatte preserves sharper boundaries and finer, more separated alpha structures without auxiliary inputs.

Figure 1. Latent-based vs. our native pixel-based training. (a) Latent supervision encodes the GT matte through a frozen VAE and supervises in latent space; the alpha target must survive a VAE round-trip, and the pixel objective only reaches the model through the decoder. (b) We never encode the alpha target: a readout module unfolds each token directly into pixels, supervised in pixel space. (c) Quality bottleneck—the GT matte incurs reconstruction error after a VAE round-trip, revealing an empirical ceiling for alpha reconstruction, especially on detail-heavy data (VideoMatte 3.50, V-HIM60 1.22, YouTubeMatte 0.54, MAD). (d) Speed bottleneck—removing the VAE-decode stage cuts per-clip latency from 576ms to 382ms, a 1.51× saving at equal depth.

papers.abstract: Sol-Attn (Sparsifying online attention) combines sparse exact computation with low-cost representative approximation to accelerate training-free inference in diffusion video models. However, intra-block attention can focus on only a few tokens. While preserving these key interactions exactly, the block-level decision incurs the cost of evaluating many low-response members. We propose Sol$^{3}$, a training-free hierarchical sparse attention method that further refines how exact computations are allocated. First, we introduce Gaussian-guided hierarchical routing, which determines the scope of exact computation step by step, from blocks to tokens, using statistical thresholds at each level. Only a subset of members within Mixed blocks that require refinement is selected for exact computation, while representative terms approximate the remaining members. We further design heterogeneous routing statistics that combine block-center correlations with variations in Key and Value within blocks to identify blocks that are difficult to approximate. Among these Mixed blocks, we uniformly compare raw token relevance to select members requiring exact computation. Experiments on video generation, audio-video co-generation, and world simulation tasks demonstrate that Sol$^{3}$ achieves 86% attention sparsity and delivers a $3.07\times$ attention speedup while preserving quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/FofGofx/sol3.
authors: Guoxin Fan, Weilun Feng, Chuanguang Yang, Mingqiang Wu, Xiaokun Liu, Jitao Lu, Zhulin An, Libo Huang, Boyu Diao, Di Gao, Yongjun Xu
bullets: Motivation: block-level sparse attention can waste computation on low-response tokens even when only a few intra-block interactions matter.
Method: Gaussian-guided hierarchical routing narrows exact computation from blocks to selected tokens, while representative approximations handle the rest.
Routing uses block-center correlations plus Key/Value variation to identify blocks that are difficult to approximate.
Experiments across video generation, audio-video co-generation, and world simulation report 86% attention sparsity and a 3.07× attention speedup while preserving quality.
Scope: the method is training-free and targets attention computation in diffusion video models.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the Sol3 framework. (Bottom) Gaussian-Guided Hierarchical Routing (GHR) selects Full blocks in sequence and filters Mixed blocks using scores at each level and statistical thresholds; it then selects tokens from the Mixed blocks for exact computation while approximating the remaining interactions with representative items.

papers.abstract: Real-world generative problems in biology, medical imaging, or robotics, rarely come with perfectly paired source and target distributions. While unbalanced Optimal Transport (uOT) provides a robust framework to bridge unpaired datasets via minimum-length paths in probability space, existing formulations based on the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry introduce a structural bias toward high density regions, often triggering mode collapse. We introduce Contact unbalanced Optimal Transport (CuOT), a novel uOT formulation grounded in contact geometry that decouples density transport direction from mass growth to eliminate structural bias. This allows CuOT to adapt sampling steps to the local data structure, naturally reducing step sizes in high-density regions to prevent overshooting and ensuring stable convergence. The result is a stable, scalable path-length minimization solver that consistently outperforms WFR-based methods on biological dynamics reconstruction, unpaired image-to-image translation, and video generation.
authors: Andrea Testa, S{\o}ren Hauberg, Andras Gabor Kupcsik, Tamim Asfour, Leonel Rozo
bullets: Targets unpaired source and target distributions in biology, medical imaging, robotics, and related generative tasks.
Decouples transport direction from mass growth, avoiding the high-density bias of WFR-based formulations.
Adapts sampling steps to local data structure, using smaller steps in dense regions to prevent overshooting.
Provides a stable, scalable path-length minimization solver.
Reportedly outperforms WFR-based methods on biological dynamics reconstruction, unpaired image translation, and video generation.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.
authors: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu, Shengfeng He
bullets: Addresses the mutation or disappearance of moving objects after they leave and re-enter the camera view.
Couples perspective video generation with low-frame-rate panoramic evolution without auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs.
Uses Geometric Anchoring for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation for temporal aggregation.
Supports both latent-level and attention-level camera conditioning architectures.
Experiments on a new dynamic benchmark show gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the OmniPersist framework. Tokens from the dense perspective stream and the temporally sparse panoramic stream are jointly processed by a shared, frozen Diffusion Transformer (DiT) block adapted via LoRA. The two streams coordinate across space and time via dedicated learned feature projections to exchange complementary context. papers.abstract: Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time communication and live captioning. However, powerful pretrained offline models cannot be directly deployed in this setting, while existing online methods typically retrain the entire model on simulated streaming prefixes constructed from offline videos, incurring high costs. To address this challenge, we propose Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (BCP), a unified lightweight framework that converts pretrained offline methods into online counterparts for sign-to-gloss (S2G), sign-to-text (S2T), and sign-to-gloss-to-text (S2G2T). Specifically, BCP freezes the pretrained model and introduces a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained SLR model, without any human annotation. At inference, a Boundary-Controlled Wait-K Output Policy then decides what to commit via prefix voting, yielding adaptive burst commits while preserving the output progress of the base Wait-K schedule. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily across four offline methods show that BCP, with less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per offline method, achieves a strong quality-latency trade-off on S2T and remains competitive on S2G and S2G2T.
authors: Xiao Ma, Lin Li, Shiqing Wu, Wang Gao, Chuanbo Liu, Jianquan Liu
bullets: Targets real-time sign-to-gloss, sign-to-text, and sign-to-gloss-to-text streaming tasks.
Freezes the pretrained offline model and trains a boundary adapter supervised by CTC alignments, avoiding human boundary annotations.
Uses prefix voting with an adaptive Wait-K output policy to control when outputs are committed.
Evaluated across four offline methods on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily.
Adds less than 0.1% trainable parameters per offline method and achieves a strong quality–latency trade-off for S2T, while remaining competitive on S2G and S2G2T.

papers.abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).
authors: Joonghyuk Shin, Alex Trevithick, Katar\'ina T\'othov\'a, Liyuan Zhu, Shengyu Huang, Jaesik Park, Shalini De Mello, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Riccardo de Lutio, Haithem Turki
bullets: Video world models often lose long-term visual consistency, while explicit 3D worlds lack photorealistic appearance.
M2R stores rendered features on mesh surfaces in each object’s coordinate frame and retrieves them by rasterizing visible surfaces.
This makes appearance move with objects, persist across revisits, and remain shared among observing agents, with memory tied to surfaces rather than frames.
Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and coding-agent-authored worlds.
It more than doubles object permanence, nearly doubles cross-agent consistency, and renders 720p video at 40 FPS.

With a one-chunk window, it must render each revisit from the memory it wrote, supervised by a frozen teacher that sees the full past (b).

papers.abstract: Long-horizon panoramic video wandering aims to continuously synthesize scene-consistent $360^\circ$ observations along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial equirectangular projection (ERP) panorama. Existing panoramic video models have achieved promising results in camera-controlled generation, while recent 3D-guided approaches further provide geometric guidance for improving scene consistency. However, stable long-horizon wandering remains challenging due to diverse motion--orientation relationships and imperfect memory guidance induced by accumulated generation artifacts and depth inaccuracies. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PVWander}, a 3D-memory-guided framework that accumulates generated observations into an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide subsequent generation, with two complementary designs: \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} for motion--orientation alignment and \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} for adaptive memory guidance. \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} exploits the horizontal cyclic symmetry of ERP panoramas to uniformly align each clip's ERP orientation with its principal translation direction, yielding more consistent, forward-like relative motions while preserving the prescribed camera path. \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} exploits the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion denoising to adaptively regulate reprojected memory guidance through timestep-dependent channel-wise gates, preserving its structural benefits while mitigating visual artifacts from imperfect projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVWander achieves improved long-horizon generation quality, while ablations validate the effectiveness of both designs.
authors: Chuanxin Song, Xiaodong Wang, Shijie Chen, Junliang Xie, Zhanmi Zhong, Suiying Wu, Peixi Peng
bullets: Targets scene-consistent panoramic video synthesis along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial ERP panorama.
Accumulates generated observations in an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide future frames.
Path-Facing canonicalization aligns ERP orientation with the principal translation direction while preserving the camera path.
Timestep-aware gating adaptively controls memory guidance during diffusion denoising to reduce artifacts from imperfect projections.
Experiments and ablations report improved long-horizon generation quality and validate both design components.

papers.abstract: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.
authors: Chenrui Fan, Qiyang Hu, Luca Scharr, Paolo Favaro
bullets: Generated videos often contain subtle deformations and sliding that undermine 3D reconstruction and are difficult to label manually.
The method pairs real clips with keyframe-conditioned re-creations, then measures each pixel’s deviation from rigid-scene behavior along the generated camera path.
The released dataset contains 871 real-generated video twins, with construction code and an official benchmark test split.
NRG-PD predicts per-pixel rigidity-violation angles from RGB alone and achieves 0.85 AUROC, outperforming seven existing consistency or motion-segmentation methods.
Its predictions improve 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction for videos containing generated content.

papers.abstract: Temporal localization in long videos is challenging because brief, question-relevant events are dispersed among extensive redundant content. Limited visual budgets increase the risk of omitting these events or their temporal context, undermining reliable reasoning. Existing frame selection methods emphasize semantic relevance or temporal coverage, often overlooking the complementary evidence needed to locate related events and establish their temporal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TESS, a training-free framework for query-guided temporal event-structured frame selection. TESS selects frames that jointly show the reference event and the event asked about, in the required temporal order. Leveraging frozen vision-language representations, TESS integrates soft temporal gating, role-aware budget allocation, and within-role redundancy suppression to preserve complementary event evidence. Extensive experiments across four long-video understanding benchmarks and three multimodal backbones demonstrate that TESS consistently outperforms the strongest compared baseline by 4.0-5.5 percentage points under a fixed frame budget. Further analyses reveal greater improvements on longer videos and robust performance under tighter visual budgets, while independent evidence annotations confirm enhanced event and temporal-relation coverage. These findings establish explicit temporal evidence organization as an effective training-free strategy for preserving event relationships and supporting efficient temporal reasoning over long videos. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TESS_code.
authors: Qi Lu, Shiyan Tong, Shujie Li, Sen Li, Likun shi, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Yao Hu
bullets: Targets the omission of brief, related events and their temporal context in long videos.

Shows larger gains on longer videos and under tighter frame budgets, with improved event and temporal-relation coverage.

papers.abstract: Automatic visual story generation using diffusion-based models has become an increasingly important research direction in generative artificial intelligence. However, maintaining character identity consistency across consecutive frames remains an open challenge, as existing models often produce significant variations in facial traits, clothing, visual style, or anatomical proportions. This paper proposes a modular pipeline to improve character identity consistency in multi-frame visual story generation using Stable Diffusion XL alongside additional conditioning and automatic selection mechanisms. The proposed system integrates LoRA fine-tuning for character personalization, ControlNet for pose-based structural control, and IP-Adapter for visual identity transfer. Furthermore, a reranking mechanism based on Best-of-K candidate selection and persistent identity memory is introduced to automatically select the most visually consistent generated images. The work also includes integrating and extending the StoryDiffusion framework into a reproducible local workflow, along with improvements for generated frame selection. Performance evaluation uses automatic metrics such as CLIP image similarity, DINO similarity, and CLIP text-image alignment. Experimental evaluation was conducted on a custom benchmark of multiple characters and visual stories organized into difficulty levels (easy, medium, and difficult). Both progressive variants of the proposed pipeline and extended versions of StoryDiffusion were evaluated, including SDXL baseline, Best-of-K, Identity Memory, and the Full Pipeline. Results show that reranking, identity memory, and visual conditioning reduce identity drift across frames and improve the overall coherence and stability of generated visual stories.
bullets: Addresses identity drift in facial features, clothing, style, and anatomy across consecutive generated frames.

Uses Best-of-K reranking and persistent identity memory to select more consistent frames automatically.
Evaluates progressive pipeline variants and StoryDiffusion extensions on a custom benchmark spanning easy, medium, and difficult stories.
CLIP, DINO, and text-image alignment results indicate improved identity consistency and story coherence, though the evaluation is limited to the custom benchmark and tested configurations.

papers.abstract: In streaming video understanding, the evidence needed to answer a question may have already left the recent-frame window. Keeping all frames does not scale with video length, while dropping older frames limits the model's ability to reason about the past. We propose Visual-State Graph (VSG), a training-free memory that stores the state of a stream rather than the raw sequence of frames. VSG represents the stream as a graph of objects and their relations, together with a log of events; similar to a dynamically evolving scene graph. An object observed repeatedly is represented by one persistent node, with a timestamped history of how its state changes. To determine whether a newly mentioned object already exists in the graph, we compare the relations it takes part in with those of stored objects. We build this memory as the video arrives, before the questions are known. When a question arrives, we retrieve relevant objects and events alongside recent frames under a fixed input budget. Our evaluation spans four streaming-video benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models ranging from 7B to 32B parameters. Under matched input budgets, VSG improves reasoning about the past while preserving real-time understanding.
authors: Ailar Mahdizadeh, Pritam Sarkar, Xiangteng He, Leonid Sigal
bullets: Addresses the loss of long-term evidence when streaming systems retain only recent frames.
Builds a dynamically updated graph of persistent objects, their relations, and timestamped state histories, plus an event log.
Matches newly observed objects to existing graph nodes using their relational context.
Constructs memory online before questions are known, then retrieves relevant objects and events with recent frames.
Evaluated on four streaming-video benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models; improves past reasoning while preserving real-time understanding under matched budgets.

papers.abstract: In fitness and sports training, timely action quality assessment (AQA) is essential for learners to identify and correct technical errors during movement execution. However, most AQA methods assess completed performances, limiting their ability to provide timely feedback. Streaming methods alleviate this latency, but limited reasoning hinders their use of subtle movement cues and sport-specific knowledge. Moreover, their fragmented feedback focuses on one body part at a time, overlooking movement details of other body parts and transitions between action phases. To address these limitations, we propose StreamCoach, a streaming AQA framework under the OnCueCoaching paradigm that couples continuous chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with proactive, evidence-gated coaching. Technique-Aware Reasoning tracks body-part movements and action-phase transitions against sport-specific criteria, while Holistic Coaching integrates accumulated evidence to deliver timely, comprehensive feedback on strengths and technical errors. To support training and benchmarking, we construct EE4D-Stream from 1,213 sports video sequences in Ego-Exo4D through LLM-assisted reannotation and manual review of selected claims, pairing dense CoT annotations with evidence-gated speech content. Building on this dataset, we train StreamCoach using Temporal-Semantic Alignment Reinforcement Learning to jointly optimize feedback timing and content. We benchmark 11 offline and streaming baselines on EE4D-Stream, including three proprietary models. StreamCoach achieves state-of-the-art results across intervention timing, action assessment, and coaching quality, surpassing both GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5.
authors: Xiaoye Liang, Yiming Huang, Jialu Wu, Yushe Cao, Ruxiang Duan, Yi Sun, Tie Liu, Lai Jiang, Mai Xu, Shikun Feng, Yiheng Zhu

Introduces EE4D-Stream, a dataset of 1,213 sports video sequences with dense reasoning annotations and evidence-gated coaching content.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across intervention timing, action assessment, and coaching quality against 11 baselines, including proprietary models.

papers.abstract: Video recasting aims to transform the entities and environments of existing videos into new visual worlds while preserving their essential actions and interactions. However, achieving coherent transformations remains challenging, as coordinated edits can disrupt the original event structure. In this paper, we introduce RecastAgent, an experience-guided agentic framework for source-conditioned video recasting that operates under frozen model weights. Our framework employs an Experience-Guided Planner to choose edit prompts and input video states under qualitative visual critique, allowing the agent to build upon partial progress or backtrack to preserve source structure. Across tasks, an Experience Accumulation module distills completed trajectories into conditional, evidence-linked principles that record both an editing strategy and its scope of validity. We additionally construct a benchmark of 67 source videos with 134 paired-specification tasks across six creative categories for evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that RecastAgent outperforms single-pass and agentic rewriting baselines across Bernini and Ditto. Furthermore, accumulated experience improves performance on held-out test videos and transfers zero-shot to external benchmarks like FiVE-Bench and VE-Bench.
authors: Shiying Zhang, Yuxia Zhu, Huaze Xue, Shengqi Dang, Yizhen Wu, Yijie Li
bullets: Addresses incoherent transformations caused by coordinated edits that disrupt source event structure.

papers.abstract: Existing clip-based soccer commentary models often produce delayed, repeated, or poorly synchronized narration on untrimmed full-match videos. Recent streaming video-language models make low-latency full-match narration feasible, but they often favor general descriptions rather than professional, event-grounded soccer commentary. They may describe nearby actions while failing to mention key events such as goals, cards, substitutions, and offsides correctly and on time. In this paper, we present SoccerNarrate to bridge low-latency streaming narration with event-grounded professional soccer commentary across data, training, and evaluation. First, we construct SoccerNarrate-Data, a large-scale time-anchored dataset with word-level ASR alignment, quality filtering, and entity calibration. Second, we perform macro-window preference alignment (MWPA), which aligns the model with complete event-level commentary semantics by comparing causal multi-step rollouts from the same streaming prefix while keeping second-level inference unchanged. We further use event-mismatched human commentaries as counterfactual negatives to emphasize event semantics over commentary style. Third, we introduce SoccerNarrate-Eval, an event-centric benchmark based on temporally constrained event entailment. Full-match experiments show that SoccerNarrate improves event coverage and event-aligned precision over strong offline and streaming baselines. Code and models are released at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/SoccerNarrate.
authors: Zihan Jia, Zhilin Dai, Zhengming Zhang, Min Yang, Zhenpeng Huang, Jiaqi Li, Caixia Sun, Xi Chen, Liang Li, Junlan Feng, Gangshan Wu, Limin Wang
bullets: Targets delayed, repetitive, poorly synchronized, and overly generic commentary in existing systems.
Introduces SoccerNarrate-Data with time-anchored annotations, word-level ASR alignment, quality filtering, and entity calibration.
Uses macro-window preference alignment to compare multi-step streaming rollouts and emphasize complete event-level semantics.
Adds event-mismatched human commentaries as counterfactual negatives and proposes the event-centric SoccerNarrate-Eval benchmark.
Full-match experiments show improved event coverage and event-aligned precision over strong offline and streaming baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 4: SoccerNarrate-Data curation pipeline. The output is a clean, time-anchored, and entity-grounded text stream for streaming SFT, macro-window preference construction, and event-centric evaluation. The bottom example shows how a commentary sentence is converted into timestamped word tokens.

The Noisy Text (top) contains multiple error types highlighted in red, including phonetic entity errors (e.g., "Daicha"), word fragmentation (e.g., "coa- ch"), token repetition, and irregular punctuation. The Corrected Text (bottom) displays the final output with all restored and normalized segments highlighted in green, verifying the model’s robustness in simultaneously performing de-duplication, de-fragmentation, and entity correction.

Figure 5: Overview of Macro-window Preference Alignment (MWPA) and counterfactual hard-negative construction. Given the same streaming prefix and video window, MWPA compares two human commentary trajectories from the same match. The preferred trajectory Y + k matches the target event, while the rejected trajectory Y − k is sampled from a type-mismatched event as a counterfactual hard negative. This provides event-level preference supervision while preserving micro-step streaming inference.

Figure 2: Issues in existing soccer commentary models. Left: Offline models react late to real events and may also produce hallucinated commentary on non-events. One-second fragments rarely contain explicit event mentions, while longer windows provide a more reliable unit for event-level preference construction and evaluation.

papers.abstract: In embedding-based video anomaly detection (VAD), normal clips can have high similarity to anomalous descriptions, an anomaly bias that leads to false positives. Methods such as PRISM mitigate this bias by measuring deviations from a normality reference along anomaly directions. Both the normality reference and the anomaly directions are derived from text and shared across videos, although normal activity and the appearance of anomalies vary across scenes. The resulting scores are also sensitive to prompt selection. To address these limitations, we propose Visual Intrinsic Distribution Estimation (VIDE), a training-free framework that adapts text-derived scoring to each test video using frozen clip embeddings. VIDE estimates normal scene content from clips with low initial anomaly scores and uses this estimate to partially correct the textual reference. It then rescales category responses, penalizes clips with strong responses across categories, and refines the anomaly directions using high-scoring clips. VIDE averages scores across prompt views to reduce sensitivity to prompt selection and fuses scores from two frozen encoders. With both encoders, VIDE improves AUC over the best PRISM result by $1.5$, $1.9$, and $3.5$ points on UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, respectively, and AP by $6.5$ points on XD-Violence and $9.3$ points on MSAD. VIDE yields the highest AUC among the compared training-free methods on all three benchmarks and the highest reported AUC among all compared methods on XD-Violence and MSAD. Our code is included in the supplementary material and will be made publicly available.
authors: Kevin D. Nguetche, Atif Belal, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli

Averages scores across prompt views and fuses two frozen encoders for greater robustness.
Improves over PRISM across UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, achieving the best reported AUC among compared methods on XD-Violence and MSAD.

papers.abstract: Switching scenes while preserving the original subject in streaming video generation exposes a conflict: cached history helps maintain the subject but also sustains old-scene objects that should disappear. Through controlled interventions on text conditioning, denoising steps, the local window, and the attention sink, we identify how cached visual history keeps this obsolete content. When the original frames remain in the cache, KV flush and sink recomputation still leave old-scene objects in the generated videos. Replacing this history with target-scene history largely removes those objects, but also changes the subject, reducing face similarity to the pre-switch subject. We then propose Molt Forcing, a training-free method that rebuilds scene history from a cold-start target scene while selectively retaining subject tokens from the original cache. Across 16 scene families, Molt Forcing removes old-scene objects at least as reliably as an Echo-Forcing hard cut while keeping the subject much closer to its pre-switch appearance.
authors: Hao Zhou, Ziyang Xu, Chenhan Jin, Hao Qin, Shengze Xu, Tieyong Zeng
bullets: Cached visual history preserves old-scene objects even after KV flushing and attention-sink recomputation.
Replacing the cache with target-scene history removes stale objects but alters the subject.
Molt Forcing rebuilds history from a cold-start target scene while selectively retaining subject tokens.
Across 16 scene families, it matches or exceeds Echo-Forcing’s old-object removal while better preserving subject similarity.

(2)); the boundary ring and the background are resynthesized under pcold, giving the bridge block. papers.abstract: Promptable video trackers such as SAM2 achieve accurate and robust performance through strong temporal consistency, making them important foundations for downstream video understanding and tracking applications. As their use continues to expand, understanding their robustness to adversarial perturbations becomes increasingly important. Existing attacks on SAM2 largely focus on local mask degradation and short-term temporal feature disruption, leaving its longer-term dynamics and competing object interferences (Distractors) insufficiently explored. We observe that SAM2 itself exposes useful distractor cues when tracking becomes uncertain. Based on these observations, we propose DistractAttack, a white-box attack that uses background distractors to disrupt target tracking persistently. Its core procedure, Counterfactual Distractor Search (CDS), propagates clean and attacked trajectories in parallel to discover plausible competing regions and identify those that become increasingly effective under perturbation. The discovered evidence is accumulated over time to weaken target support and promote recurrent alternatives or disappearance predictions. Extensive experiments under video-level and one-shot perturbations across Visual Object Tracking and Video Object Segmentation demonstrate strong attack effectiveness, raising DRE to $4.4\times$ and NRE to $7.3\times$ their nearest baselines under video perturbation, while transferring effectively across model scales and tracker variants in black-box settings. authors: Adonay Demewez Gebremedhin, Mohamad Alansari, Wessam Shehieb, Muzammal Naseer

Across tracking and segmentation tasks, reaches up to 4.4× higher DRE and 7.3× higher NRE than nearest baselines under video perturbations.
Transfers effectively across model scales and tracker variants in black-box settings.

papers.abstract: Generating videos with physically plausible dynamics remains challenging despite advances in visual quality. Latent world models offer predictive signals for evaluating physical plausibility, but higher agreement between predicted and observed features may reflect easier-to-predict scene content rather than more plausible dynamics. We propose \textbf{S}elf-Referenced \textbf{P}hysical \textbf{A}lignment \textbf{R}ewards (\textbf{SPAR}), a framework that uses world-model predictions for inference-time physical alignment. SPAR compares each video's prediction error with that of static clips constructed by repeating its own frames, providing a content-matched reference for evaluating generated dynamics. To account for the uneven spatial and temporal distribution of physical interactions, we introduce a unified \textbf{spatiotemporal reward refinement} strategy. \textbf{Spatial refinement} emphasizes localized prediction discrepancies, while \textbf{temporal refinement} moderates brief error peaks and supplements prediction errors with agreement between predicted and observed feature changes. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SPAR improves the physical plausibility of both \textbf{text-to-video generation} and \textbf{image-to-video continuation}, bringing generated dynamics into closer alignment with the physical regularities governing real-world events. Additional results and resources are available at https://gavin-jy.github.io/spar-page/
authors: Junyi Zhang, Qichao Wang, Wenzhe Qian, Yuanchuan Wang, Min Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that world-model prediction agreement can reflect predictable content rather than physically plausible dynamics.
Compares a video's prediction error with static, frame-repeated clips from the same video to create a content-matched reference.
Uses spatial refinement to focus on localized interactions and temporal refinement to reduce sensitivity to brief error spikes.
Adds agreement between predicted and observed feature changes to complement prediction-error signals.
Evaluations across multiple benchmarks show improved physical plausibility for both text-to-video and image-to-video generation.

papers.abstract: Advancing surgical automation requires a comprehensive spatio-temporal understanding of how instruments act on tissue throughout an action. Existing surgical benchmarks, however, largely define supervision through task-specific targets, leaving the relationships between action semantics, instrument motion, and tissue interaction incompletely specified. To address this limitation, we introduce TACTUS (Tool, Action, Contact and Trajectory Understanding in Surgery), a new dataset and benchmark that establishes a unified annotation framework for complete surgical actions. The framework jointly specifies tool and action identities, nested action and interaction windows, instrument-specific landmark trajectories, and tissue-region tracks. To construct these annotations at scale, we develop a two-tier pipeline combining human annotation, point tracking, and model-generated spatial prompts. Using this pipeline, we re-annotate 141 videos from five public sources, producing 22,995 action clips spanning 2.9 million frames. The dataset comprises 15,668 Gold clips with human spatial prompts followed by review and re-checking, and 7,327 Silver clips combining human semantic and temporal annotations with model-generated spatial prompts. We further introduce TactusNet, the companion reference network, to benchmark semantic, temporal, and spatial prediction from shared video features. Across TactusNet and 13 published baselines, tool-action accuracy reaches 95.8% with per-head encoder fine-tuning, while the best temporal recall and contact Dice reach 46.6% at temporal IoU 0.7 and 0.351, respectively. Moreover, adding Silver improves the default TactusNet's pair accuracy from 93.8% to 95.5%. Together, these contributions establish a foundation for learning and evaluating the instrument-tissue interactions underlying future surgical automation.
authors: Lurui Wang, Hao Ding, Chenhao Yu, Chenyan Jing, Jiru Xu, Ruoqi Zuo, Liwei Mei, Chang Liu, Lalithkumar Seenivasan, Mathias Unberath
bullets: Introduces a unified framework for complete surgical actions, linking tools, actions, interaction windows, trajectories, and tissue-region tracks.
Uses a two-tier annotation pipeline combining human labeling, point tracking, and model-generated spatial prompts.

Provides TactusNet and 13 baselines for semantic, temporal, and spatial prediction; reported tool-action accuracy reaches 95.8%.
Establishes a foundation for modeling and evaluating instrument–tissue interactions in surgical automation.

papers.abstract: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.

papers.abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
authors: Jian Yang, Zhizhuo Kou, Qiyuan Zhu, Han Chen, Sirui Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Persistent clean-KV updates can dominate runtime once denoising is accelerated, while stale-cache reuse increases later denoising work.
SAMR combines motion-aligned historical KV with in-flight KV, using calibrated affine correction and selective true $t=0$ refreshes.
Tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels implement the reconstruction efficiently without retraining the frozen video DiT.
On LongLive-1.3B, it cuts DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7%, while improving final-quarter PSNR over token reuse.
It transfers to Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B, reducing reuse-induced step inflation and improving late-stage PSNR, with calibration further recovering diagnostic quality.

papers.abstract: Training capable omni video agents requires more than diverse question-answer pairs: agents must learn to reliably find, connect, and correct task-relevant evidence in omni-setting. However, we argue that existing data pipelines provide limited control over task-relevant evidence and weak supervision for these capabilities. In this work, we present Open OmniCoach, a new framework for evidence-seeking omni video agents. It contains a high-quality dataset, OmniCoach-240K, and a new agentic reinforcement learning (RL) method, Step-Level Evidence-Guided Policy Optimization (SEPO). For the former, OmniCoach-240K comprises 248.2K interaction trajectories, including 230.7K multi-span trajectories and 17.4K reflection trajectories. We design a three-stage data pipeline by leveraging both fine-grained omni-evidence and the agent's own errors. Meanwhile, compared with other RL baselines, SEPO provides turn-level credit based on improvements in evidence coverage and temporal localization. Applying both trajectory data and the SEPO method, we obtain Open OmniAgent models. The resulting models outperform the baselines across multiple video and audio-visual understanding tasks by significant margins, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Open OmniCoach framework. In particular, Open OmniAgent-30B improves average accuracy over Qwen3-Omni by 6.3 percentage points across nine benchmarks, with gains of 12.2 and 13.3 points on LVOmniBench and LVBench, respectively.

papers.abstract: Video understanding depends not only on how models reason about visual evidence, but also on which evidence they observe. Fixed observation policies determine this evidence in advance; agentic harnesses allow models to seek further observations as their understanding develops. This shift creates an opportunity to realize capabilities that fixed inputs leave untapped, yet the ability to request observations does not ensure their effective use. We investigate when and why video harnesses improve understanding, examining how task demands and models' capacity for interaction jointly shape their benefits. Using Video-Relook as an experimental framework, we let models adapt their temporal and spatial observations from a common default configuration, and analyze performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks. Adaptive observation yields substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2. Even under the same observation interface, gains differ substantially across models; interaction traces reveal corresponding differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision. The benefits also vary across tasks for the same model, ranging from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions. Together, these findings support an account in which harness effectiveness depends on the alignment between opportunities for informative observation and the model's ability to turn interaction into reliable revisions. They motivate video harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning, matching observational autonomy to task demands and model capabilities.

papers.abstract: As live video streams grow longer, repeatedly encoding and processing their full histories becomes increasingly costly. Answering questions as they arrive therefore calls for visual memory built in one pass before future questions are known. Existing methods mainly keep tokens that differ from earlier ones or match surrogate queries fixed in advance. Without modeling world dynamics, these criteria struggle to tell subtle surprising details from expected change. We introduce Dreamcatcher, a training-free framework and, to our knowledge, the first to use predictive signals from an independently pretrained, frozen video world model for online memory formation in streaming video question answering. Conditioned on recent history, the world model predicts incoming features using learned world priors. Its normalized prediction errors yield temporal and spatial surprisal signals that guide online segmentation and the retention of a frozen Video-LLM's native visual tokens, balancing surprising details with broad visual coverage under budgets that decay with segment age. At query time, an evidence gate admits a segment from a similarity-based shortlist only when the Video-LLM judges that it adds evidence for the question beyond the current view. We evaluate Dreamcatcher on three streaming and three offline long-video benchmarks. On OVO-Bench, Dreamcatcher achieves the highest overall accuracy among the compared training-free methods for each of four frozen Video-LLMs, reaching 78.9% with Qwen3.8-27B. With the three Qwen Video-LLMs, it also reduces average input tokens for answer generation by more than 80% relative to their base models at 1 fps.
authors: Jinxi He, Ce Zhang, Wenhe Liu, Jianshu Zhang, Katia P. Sycara, Yaqi Xie
bullets: Addresses the cost of repeatedly processing full histories in long, streaming videos.
Uses a frozen video world model to derive temporal and spatial surprisal signals for online memory formation.
Retains frozen Video-LLM visual tokens through adaptive segmentation and age-decayed memory budgets.
Uses an evidence gate to admit shortlisted segments only when they add question-relevant evidence.
Achieves the best accuracy among compared training-free methods on OVO-Bench and cuts answer-generation input tokens by over 80% for three Qwen Video-LLMs.

(c) The Evidence Gate shortlists segments by PE-Core [6] similarity to the question. The reader scores each candidate for evidence beyond the current view in a separate pass, reusing the cached anchor Wt as a shared prefix. papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation requires predicting how robot-object interactions evolve over time, encompassing both visual appearance and scene geometry. In multi-camera settings, such predictions need to capture the evolving 3D scene consistently across viewpoints, while supporting controllable generation under different robot actions and camera configurations. Existing video generation models provide strong priors for visual appearance and motion but typically lack explicit geometric modeling. Meanwhile, recent advances in geometry-aware and multi-view generation have explored joint appearance-geometry modeling and cross-view consistency, yet generating temporally coherent appearance and geometry across multiple viewpoints under robotic manipulation conditions remains challenging. In this work, we propose GeoMVGen, a framework for joint multi-view RGB and pointmap video generation in robotic manipulation. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework employs modality-specific adaptation modules to capture the distinct characteristics of appearance and geometry, while using cross-modal residual connections to facilitate information exchange between the two modalities. To establish geometric correspondences across viewpoints, we further introduce a cross-view projection mechanism with complementary geometric supervisions, combining pointmap consistency with geometry foundation model-guided feature alignment. These designs enable controllable generation of temporally evolving multi-view observations with coherent appearance and geometrically consistent scene structures. Extensive experiments on 4D video generation dataset comprising simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios demonstrate that GeoMVGen outperforms state-of-the-art methods in video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency.
authors: Qiaoqiao Jia, Guile Wu, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting evolving 3D robot–object interactions consistently across viewpoints and under controllable actions and camera configurations.

Evaluations on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation scenarios report improved video quality, geometric accuracy, and cross-view consistency over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/
authors: Shaina Raza, Mohamed Hafez, Ahmed Y. Radwan, Khalid Elgazzar, Kathryn Hume
bullets: Provides four matched real/fake audio-video combinations per source clip, enabling direct measurement of modality reliance.
Covers face swaps, whole-frame video diffusion, and voice conversion across four tasks: authenticity, manipulation type, identity verification, and explanation.
Evaluates multimodal LLMs, trained detectors, and LoRA-fine-tuned MLLMs.
MLLMs perform poorly on four-way authenticity and detect video-only fakes much more reliably than voice-only fakes; trained detectors perform strongly in-distribution.
Held-out-generator testing shows reduced detector performance, while LoRA improves explanation scores; generalization and explanation remain open challenges.

papers.abstract: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.
authors: Chen Wang, Jiahui Huang, Riccardo de Lutio, Alex Trevithick, Bryan Chu, Jiawei Ren, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Shengyu Huang, Lingjie Liu, Haithem Turki
bullets: Addresses camera drift and scene inconsistency when generating beyond the captured view.
Uses persistent point-cloud memory for observed or generated regions and a vision-language model to create layouts for unseen areas.
Represents each object with a coarse labeled 3D box that is both user-editable and usable by the video generator.
Produces walkthroughs exceeding three minutes and 50 meters from one photo, including unseen rooms beyond doorways.
On minute-long round trips across four datasets, reduces camera error by 3.8× and improves return consistency by 22% on average.

The memory video preserves what has been seen, while the layout video specifies what appears where beyond it and anchors the camera to its path. To remain consistent upon return, we reconstruct each generated chunk and write it into the memory.

papers.abstract: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.
authors: Boyang Wang, Kevin Blackburn-Matzen, Oindrila Saha, Matheus Gadelha, Zezhou Cheng
bullets: Condition tokens from modalities such as identity, scribbles, depth, and motion videos create substantial computation and memory costs.
A codec-based pruning method removes redundant spatiotemporal conditioning tokens.
On-policy self-distillation trains a DiT adapter to reproduce the codec’s pruning pattern without degrading quality.
Scaled to 16 conditioning modalities, it prunes 66% of condition tokens on average, makes denoising 2× faster, and reduces KV-cache memory by up to 73%.
Benefits extend to pretrained image and video generators and increase with more conditions, longer videos, and higher resolution.
