papers.abstract: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.
authors: Atakan Topcu, Mohammadhossein Momeni, Alfredo De Goyeneche, Michael Lustig
bullets: Addresses the high latency and memory costs of video priors for medical image reconstruction.
Uses a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior with a global low-resolution encoder and a shallow decoder that shifts from low-resolution views to full-resolution space-time tiles.
Introduces ReTile, which uses randomized grid shifting and re-noising to replace overlapping tile evaluations with one network pass per sampling step.
Achieves about one 256×256 frame per second and reports 20–367× speedups over patch and latent video priors.
Matches or exceeds the best generative baseline across cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT while using less GPU time.

Figure 2. TesseraFlow and ReTile. One sampling step: a coarse step (t < ts, top, purple) or a fine step (t ≥ ts, middle, teal), and the schedule of steps (bottom). At every step, the encoder Eθ reads a low-resolution version of every frame, the size of a tile. In a coarse step, the shallow decoder Lθ predicts the velocity of this low-resolution video from all encoder features Gt. In a fine step, it predicts the velocity of each space-time tile from the tile and the features at its location, and the tile predictions are placed side by side. ReTile refines the predicted clean video against the measurements, re-noises it, and moves the tiles to a new random offset for the next step.

papers.abstract: We present XShot, a framework for cross-shot video object insertion, which adds objects to a shot by watching another shot of the same scene. Video productions show a scene through many shots, and objects added to one shot must appear consistently in the others. Most video editors take the appearance of new objects from reference images and their location from a text prompt, a mask or an edited keyframe, leaving this consistency to the user. XShot reads both from a reference video of another shot, which need not be aligned with the target, and needs no mask, box or camera pose. We build on a video Diffusion Transformer and formulate the task as in-context generation over the reference video, a few images of the objects and the target video. A geometry-aware cross-shot attention estimates the epipolar geometry between the two shots from the model's own correspondences and uses it to guide where the target reads the reference and the exemplars. We train XShot with an erase-and-restore data engine: objects are erased from one shot of a film or a multi-camera recording and restored from another shot of the scene. Experiments show that XShot places objects more accurately and renders them more faithfully than open-source and commercial video editors, while leaving the rest of the shot intact.
bullets: Addresses cross-shot object consistency, reducing manual placement and appearance specification by editors.
Uses in-context generation with a video Diffusion Transformer, reference video, object images, and target video.
Geometry-aware cross-shot attention estimates epipolar relationships from learned correspondences to guide reference information.
Trains via an erase-and-restore pipeline using shots from films or multi-camera recordings.
Experiments report more accurate placement, more faithful rendering, and preservation of the unchanged scene compared with open-source and commercial editors.

(b) Positions of the reference and exemplar tokens. (c) Epipolar geometry estimated from the model’s own matching points guides the attention to the reference and the exemplars.

papers.title: XShot: Cross-Shot Video Object Insertion from a Reference Video
papers.tldr: XShot inserts objects into a target video shot by using another, potentially unaligned shot of the same scene, without requiring masks, boxes, or camera poses.

papers.abstract: Purpose: Analyzing clinicians' visual attention from exocentric camera views can support surgical scene understanding without requiring wearable eye trackers. However, existing gaze-following research in the operating room (OR) estimates only 2D gaze locations without identifying attended scene entities or localizing gaze targets in 3D space. In this work, we investigate gaze graphs as a scene-level representation of visual attention that connects clinicians to attended scene entities, and evaluate their utility for fine-grained surgical action recognition and semantic scene graph (SSG) generation. Methods: We extend the public EgoExOR dataset with gaze annotations to create EgoExOR-Gaze, the first benchmark for multi-view gaze graph generation in the OR. We propose a novel architecture that jointly estimates 3D gaze targets and predicts attended entities using only exocentric camera views. Specifically, our approach exploits 3D gaze geometry to sample local visual features across multiple views for attended entity prediction. We further utilize predicted gaze graphs for fine-grained surgical action recognition and SSG generation. Results: For gaze graph generation, our model outperforms both exocentric-only and combined exocentric-egocentric baselines. For surgical action recognition, our model incorporating predicted gaze graphs outperforms both exocentric and egocentric baselines across all evaluated metrics, with particularly strong gains in temporal metrics. For SSG generation, incorporating gaze graphs improves macro-F1 from 0.42 to 0.52 compared to exocentric inputs alone, although performance remains below that achieved with egocentric inputs. Conclusion: Our results demonstrate the value of gaze graphs for surgical action recognition and SSG generation, highlighting the importance of explicitly modeling scene-level visual attention even when egocentric views are unavailable.
authors: S\'eraphin Baributsa, Keqi Chen, Vinkle Srivastav, Nicolas Padoy
bullets: Introduces EgoExOR-Gaze, a multi-view operating-room benchmark with gaze annotations.
Proposes a model that jointly predicts 3D gaze targets and attended entities using multi-view exocentric features.
Predicted gaze graphs outperform exocentric-only and combined exocentric–egocentric baselines for gaze graph generation and action recognition.
Gaze graphs improve semantic scene graph macro-F1 from 0.42 to 0.52 over exocentric inputs alone.
Semantic scene graph performance remains below that achieved using egocentric inputs.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the gaze graph generation architecture. A frozen DINOv3 backbone extracts raw and text-aligned visual features. The initial 3D gaze point is computed from the estimated gaze direction and depth. The role prediction module estimates each clinician’s role, and the corresponding role embedding is added to the initial appearance query. Decoder layers iteratively refine the 3D gaze point and appearance query through projective attention. Finally, the appearance query is compared with ‘dino.txt’ vocabulary embeddings using cosine similarity to identify attended entities.

Fig. 1: An example of dataset annotations. On the left, we show the annotated head bounding box, clinical role, and corresponding gaze point of each person. On the right, we show the annotated gaze graph where arrows denote “looking” relations pointing from clinical roles to one or multiple entities within the attended regions.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.
bullets: Targets suboptimal sample fidelity and text alignment in diffusion and flow-based models.
Perturbs attention logits in a single block against the reward gradient, then extrapolates away from the perturbed reference.
Theoretically shown to increase the clean estimate’s reward to first order.
Achieves the highest target reward across reported FLUX.2-klein settings with 30–65% less time than gradient- and candidate-based baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an efficient inference-time alignment method for diffusion models using reward-attentive guidance, reducing computational cost while improving alignment.
papers.title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: RadAG efficiently improves diffusion-model alignment by using reward-adversarial attention perturbations to guide inference without backpropagating through the full generator.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models can render convincing frames while failing to produce the requested action. Increasing classifier-free guidance (CFG) can strengthen motion, but also saturates and shifts colors. Scalar CFG assigns the same coefficient to the averaged and frame-varying components of its prediction difference, limiting independent control of temporal variation. THAW, Temporal Harmonic Amplification during Warm-up, retains stock CFG and adds a separately weighted residual during an initial denoising window. Its dose specifies the added norm relative to the current CFG difference, giving the extra guidance a consistent relative budget across sampling steps. THAW is training-free and reuses CFG's two model predictions with an unchanged network evaluation count. It improves cost-matched motion over scalar and scheduled CFG on five video models, with positive point estimates against existing guidance methods on three of them. On VBench, THAW raises dynamic degree by about 14 to 15 points over stock CFG while increasing total scores on a different set of three models.
authors: Xuanhua Yin, Boyu Wei, Chengkun Yue, Shunqi Mao, Chuanzhi Xu, Wei Guo, Weidong Cai
bullets: Scalar CFG can strengthen motion but may saturate and shift colors because it controls averaged and frame-varying components together.
THAW adds a separately weighted residual during an initial denoising window while retaining standard CFG.
Its dose is normalized to the current CFG difference, providing a consistent relative guidance budget across sampling steps.
The training-free method improves cost-matched motion across five video models and shows positive point estimates against existing guidance methods on three.
On VBench, THAW increases dynamic degree by about 14–15 points over stock CFG, while total-score gains occur on a different set of three models.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have enabled the synthesis of high-fidelity, visually compelling videos. However, despite being trained on internet-scale video data, understanding underlying physical laws and generating physically plausible dynamics remain challenging. To mitigate this, conditioning video generators on explicit physical reasoning has emerged as a promising direction. Nevertheless, existing conditioning approaches often fail to incorporate detailed physical guidance into generation, resulting in physically implausible motion or visual artifacts. We propose PSC-Gen, a training-free framework that employs an agentic approach to synthesize visual conditions and inject their core dynamics via low-frequency filtering. By iteratively planning physical states and verifying generated keyframes, our Physics Agent constructs visually and physically consistent keyframe sequences. We then interpolate these keyframes into a continuous physical sequence and inject only its low-frequency components, steering the video model to preserve physical dynamics while synthesizing fine visual details. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations across physics-informed and robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that PSC-Gen faithfully follows instructions and generates physically plausible videos.
authors: Wonsik Shin, Jinju Jang, Junhoo Lee, Yeonjin Chang, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses physically implausible motion and artifacts in video diffusion models despite large-scale video training.
Uses a training-free Physics Agent to iteratively plan physical states and verify generated keyframes.
Interpolates verified keyframes into continuous physical sequences and injects their low-frequency components into the video generator.
Evaluations on physics-informed and robotic manipulation benchmarks show improved instruction following and physically plausible videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method Overview. PSC-Gen generates physically plausible videos through (a) Agentic Visual Planning and (b) Physical Sequence Conditioning. A vision-language model (VLM) acts as a Physics Agent to plan physical states and iteratively generate and verify keyframes. These keyframes are interpolated into a physical sequence, which guides diffusion sampling through low-frequency velocity injection. This design effectively transfers physical dynamics while allowing the diffusion model to synthesize fine visual details.

Figure 5. Ablation Study on Physical Sequence Conditioning. The top row shows the variant without Physical Sequence Conditioning, and the bottom row shows our full pipeline. While the ablated variant simply reconstructs and interpolates the static keyframes, our full pipeline achieves more natural, physically plausible motion guided by the physical sequence.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free physical-sequence conditioning improves physical plausibility of video diffusion, relevant to video generation and world-model-style dynamics.
papers.title: PSC-Gen: Physical Sequence Conditioning for Video Generation via Agentic Visual Planning
papers.tldr: PSC-Gen improves physical plausibility in video generation by planning, verifying, and injecting physically consistent visual sequences without training the generator.

papers.abstract: Learning-based optical flow estimation approaches generally rely on both inter-frame correspondence evidence and intra-frame contextual guidance, yet features from general-purpose image encoders may not fully support these roles. Strongly activated but weakly discriminative channels can outweigh more informative ones when computing inter-frame feature similarity, while context feature affinities can be low within motion-coherent regions yet high across motion boundaries. To address these mismatches, this study proposes TO-Flow, a task-oriented feature adaptation framework that aligns matching and context features with their respective requirements through dedicated channel modulation and spatial reorganization approaches. An affinity-based soft partition distinguishes motion-region interiors from boundary-adjacent regions to guide both processes. Channel modulation uses simulated flow refinement to assess whether each channel assigns higher similarity to estimated correspondences than to nearby competing candidates. The resulting similarity differences are aggregated within each region type and averaged across iterations to derive channel weights that emphasize informative channels and suppress ambiguous ones. Spatial reorganization combines affinity-guided feature attraction and repulsion from coarse to fine to simultaneously improve consistency within motion-coherent regions and distinctiveness across motion boundaries, with feature resampling mitigating boundary blurring during cross-scale fusion. Extensive experiments on the MPI Sintel, KITTI 2015, Spring, and LayeredFlow datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and general applicability of TO-Flow across diverse iterative refinement architectures as well as supervised and unsupervised training paradigms. The source code will be publicly available at https://mias.group/TO-Flow upon publication.
authors: Mengtan Zhang, Dazhong Wang, Haoran Zhang, Hongbo Zhao, Yuhang Ming, Weihao Yuan, Wei Ye, Hanli Wang, Rui Fan
bullets: General-purpose features can overemphasize weak channels and confuse motion interiors with boundaries.
An affinity-based soft partition separates motion-region interiors from boundary-adjacent regions.
Channel modulation reinforces features that distinguish estimated correspondences from competing matches.
Coarse-to-fine spatial reorganization improves within-region consistency and cross-boundary distinctiveness while reducing boundary blur.
Experiments on MPI Sintel, KITTI 2015, Spring, and LayeredFlow show effectiveness across iterative, supervised, and unsupervised flow systems.

papers.abstract: Event cameras capture brightness changes with high temporal resolution and dynamic range, but converting event streams into videos remains fundamentally ill-posed due to the lack of absolute intensity information. Resolving this ambiguity calls for a brightness reference that complements the intensity changes recorded by events. Inspired by the complementary spatial and temporal processing of the parvocellular and magnocellular pathways in human vision, we propose EvDualDiff, a dual-stream framework that combines a brightness reference from temporal-mapping events with motion-event cues for video reconstruction. Conditioned on both streams, our video diffusion model autoregressively reconstructs long sequences from a single temporal map. Photometric constraints and finetuning on self-generated rollouts reduce accumulated drift. At the hardware level, our approach requires only a minimal light-modulation mechanism on the lens of an event camera. We build this setup and collect a dataset comprising temporal-mapping events, motion events and synchronised ground-truth RGB frames. Experiments on a public benchmark and on our collected EvDual dataset demonstrate that EvDualDiff outperforms existing event-to-video reconstruction methods in fidelity, perceptual quality and video-level realism. The code and dataset will be released.
authors: Lei Sun, Zhendong Li, Chenxin Shao, Weilun Li, Ruibo Ming, Kaiwei Wang, Jinjin Gu, Danda Pani Paudel, Luc Van Gool
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed nature of event-to-video reconstruction caused by missing absolute intensity information.
Uses temporal-mapping events as a brightness reference alongside motion events, inspired by complementary visual pathways.
Autoregressively reconstructs long sequences with photometric constraints and rollout finetuning to reduce drift.
Requires only a minimal lens-based light-modulation mechanism and introduces the EvDual dataset with synchronized RGB frames.
Outperforms existing methods on a public benchmark and EvDual in fidelity, perceptual quality, and video-level realism.

papers.abstract: Long video question answering requires finding relevant evidence before reasoning over it. With a limited frame budget, single-pass frame selection can miss critical evidence, while adaptive search often relies on repeated text generation to decide where to look. We introduce LoopSeek, a framework that decouples evidence search from answer generation through a division of labor between a non-thinking System I and a generative System II. Our key insight is that search can be expressed as a sequence of small, typed decisions, allowing System I to find the evidence that System II needs. Four System I role agents navigate a tree of video windows and coordinate through probability outputs to select frames, assess evidence, and revise the search without generating text. To align search with System II, System I learns from annotated evidence on questions that System II answers correctly only from that evidence, and the verifier's evidence estimates steer the search without calling System II, which stays frozen and answers once from the selected frames. On five long-video benchmarks, with a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B reading 32 frames, LoopSeek improves average accuracy from 53.5 to 63.9 over the uniform baseline and takes 32--80\% less GPU time per question than agentic methods.
authors: Chengzhong Wang, Lang Lin, Xinyang Liu, YueQin Yin, Mingyuan Zhou, Shengwei An
bullets: Addresses missed evidence under limited frame budgets and the cost of repeated text-based search.
Uses four non-generative System I agents to navigate video-window trees, select frames, assess evidence, and revise searches.
Trains search using annotated evidence from questions that a frozen System II answers correctly from that evidence.
On five long-video benchmarks, accuracy rises from 53.5 to 63.9 with 32 frames, while using 32–80% less GPU time than agentic methods.

papers.abstract: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We construct X-AQA-40K, a training corpus comprising 40,163 samples from 22 data sources across four domains: competitive sports, fitness exercises, rehabilitation, and general skills. We convert heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format, incorporating dataset-specific annotation guidelines and official scoring rules when available. Using this corpus, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to develop a single MLLM capable of handling diverse AQA tasks. We further establish X-AQA-Bench, which evaluates both in-distribution (ID) performance on datasets represented during training and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on four held-out datasets. The resulting model outperforms all evaluated open-source MLLMs on X-AQA-Bench and achieves competitive performance relative to proprietary MLLMs. Ablation studies further demonstrate that multi-domain joint training and explicitly providing assessment criteria in prompts both improve OOD generalization. X-AQA establishes a unified foundation for advancing general-purpose AQA across diverse real-world domains. Data and models are released at \hyperlink{https://huggingface.co/collections/Kelly0510/x-aqa}{here}.
authors: Kaili Zheng, Wei Ding, Yuchen Ding, Kaiwen Wang, Xun Zhu, Chenyi Guo, Yudong Zhang, Ji Wu
bullets: Addresses fragmented AQA methods that use dataset-specific task formulations and scoring criteria.
Introduces X-AQA-40K, with 40,163 samples from 22 sources spanning sports, fitness, rehabilitation, and general skills.
Converts heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format while preserving assessment guidelines and scoring rules.
Fine-tunes Qwen3.5-9B and evaluates it with X-AQA-Bench on in-distribution and four held-out out-of-distribution datasets.
Reports stronger performance than evaluated open-source MLLMs, competitive performance with proprietary MLLMs, and improved OOD generalization from joint training and explicit criteria prompts.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of AI-generated content (AIGC) video generation and editing technologies has raised growing societal concerns about the authenticity and reliability of digital videos. Existing video detection methods primarily exploit temporal inconsistencies through holistic frame-level representations, whereas manipulation localization methods focus on artifacts within individual spatial regions. However, holistic representations may obscure localized artifacts through global feature aggregation, while region-centric approaches may overlook disagreements between individual regions and their surrounding spatiotemporal context. To address these limitations, we propose VIdeo Contextual Agreement (VICA), a unified framework that masks individual video regions and leverages a frozen V-JEPA model to predict their representations from the surrounding spatiotemporal context. Complementary masking ensures complete regional coverage, while context-conditioned predictions establish references for assessing regional agreement with the broader video context. By comparing predicted and observed representations, VICA derives spatial residuals that characterize intra-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals that capture inconsistencies across preceding and subsequent frames. These residuals characterize contextual disagreements, providing a shared forensic representation for both tasks and shifting the focus from identifying isolated manipulation artifacts to assessing regional agreement with expectations inferred from the broader video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VICA achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks across multiple benchmarks, with strong generalization to unseen video generators and editing methods.
authors: Runheng Lin, Jialiang Shen, Jiyang Zheng, Ruiqi Liu, Zonglin He, Yu Yao, Huajie Chen, Chris Russell, Runqi Lin
bullets: Addresses limitations of frame-level holistic features and isolated region-artifact analysis.
Masks video regions and uses a frozen V-JEPA model to predict each region from surrounding context.
Computes spatial residuals for within-frame discrepancies and bidirectional temporal residuals for cross-frame inconsistencies.
Provides a shared forensic representation for both AIGC video detection and manipulation localization.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks with strong generalization to unseen generators and editing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of VICA. Given an input video clip, the frozen V-JEPA 2.1 target encoder extracts observed features Y , while the frozen context encoder and predictor generate context-conditioned predictions from two complementary masked views. The resulting predictions are combined into P̂ , providing a predicted representation for every spatiotemporal token. Spatial residuals S are computed between predicted and observed features at the same time step, whereas bidirectional temporal residuals F and B capture discrepancies across paired time steps. Finally, a shared readout integrates [S, F,B] to support both video-level detection and region-level localization.

Figure 2. The video is generated by Vidu and sourced from AIGVDBench, which does not provide localization annotations. P̂t and Yt denote the predicted and observed regional features at temporal step t, respectively. The three rows show the spatial residual P̂1 − Y1 and the bidirectional temporal residuals P̂2 − Y1 and P̂1 − Y2. The columns display the input frame, channel-wise signed residual sums, and ℓ2 norms, with and without overlays on the input frame. The right boxer’s glove appears malformed, while the spatial residual P̂1 − Y1 produces a localized response around the fist. In comparison, the bidirectional temporal residuals P̂2−Y1 and P̂1−Y2 exhibit stronger and more extensive ℓ2 responses along the moving arms and gloves, highlighting motion-dependent discrepancies that are less apparent in the spatial residual. This visualization illustrates how spatial and bidirectional temporal residuals reveal complementary patterns of contextual disagreement in AI-generated videos.

Figure 3. Localization results on authentic videos. Each row presents an input frame (left) and its corresponding per-region edit-probability overlay (right). Sparse false-positive responses occur primarily in featureless background regions rather than on foreground subjects.

Table 3. Backbone comparison. All variants use frozen backbones with identical task heads, training objectives, and data. VJEPA 2.1-based models extract features from four selected layers, whereas other backbones use only the final layer. Baselines operate on features extracted from unmasked videos, while VICA uses context-conditioned prediction residuals from V-JEPA 2.1. We report video-level AUROC and AP for detection on AIGVDBench and token-level IoU and F1 for localization on AINPAINT, averaged across generators and editing methods, respectively.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion streams a video chunk by chunk, but large AR models are too slow for real-time use. We ask where in an AR rollout a large model is actually needed. Pairing Krea-Realtime-14B with Self-Forcing-1.3B, which share their latent space and denoising schedule, we find that the order of the two models matters: when the 14B model generates only the first chunk and the 1.3B model continues, the rollout keeps 95\% of the 14B model's semantic advantage, whereas the reverse allocation keeps 16\% at about ten times the cost. The large model decides what the video shows; the small model only has to carry it forward. We turn this into BigSmall, a training-free planner--renderer sampler. The 14B model plans the opening chunk and sketches the chunks in which content changes, which preserves motion, and the 1.3B model renders the rest; a faster variant, BigSmall, plans only the opening chunk. A cross-model KV cache that is approximate, windowed and lazy lets the planner leave and re-enter the rollout at low cost. On VBench, BigSmall is $3.02\times$ faster than the 14B model at an unchanged semantic score and motion, and $1.55\times$ faster than SDVG, which lets the small model draft first; BigSmall reaches $3.77\times$ at the same semantic score, trading away 10\% of the motion. On minute-long videos (LoCoT2V-Bench), where the 14B model degrades when it reads its own long history, BigSmall is $3.14\times$ faster than the 14B model and scores higher ($+1.78$).`
bullets: Large-model computation is most valuable at the rollout’s beginning and when video content changes; reversing the model order largely loses the semantic benefit.
BigSmall is a training-free planner–renderer sampler: the 14B model plans the opening and selected transition chunks, while the 1.3B model renders the rest.
An approximate, windowed, lazy cross-model KV cache enables the large planner to leave and re-enter generation efficiently.
On VBench, BigSmall is 3.02× faster than the 14B model with unchanged semantic score and motion; a faster variant reaches 3.77× speedup with a 10% motion trade-off.
On minute-long videos, BigSmall is 3.14× faster and scores 1.78 points higher than the 14B model.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of BIGSMALL on a real rollout (“a teddy bear and a frisbee”). Top: a zero-cost change score decides, chunk by chunk, whether the 14B planner is called. The planner generates the plan chunk c0 with all four denoising steps and only the first step t1 of each sketch chunk; the 1.3B renderer takes all other steps (squares: denoising steps t1–t4; orange: 14B, blue: 1.3B). Bottom: each model reads its own KV cache; dashed arrows write a finished chunk into a cache, solid arrows read from it. The renderer’s cache is exact: every chunk is written. The planner’s cache is windowed: a planner call reads only the sink c0 and the previous chunk. It is lazy: that previous chunk is written only when the planner needs it (c1 when c2 is sketched, c4 when c5 is sketched), and other chunks are never written. It is approximate: a chunk is re-encoded sparsely, only its moving tokens, while the others copy K/V from the previous frame with re-rotated RoPE; it is re-encoded densely if the chunk before it was never written, as for c4. Right: inside sketch chunk c5, the planner’s first step from noise already fixes the layout (x̂(1) 0 ); it is re-noised to σ2, keeping 6% of the signal, and the renderer completes the chunk from its own cache.

papers.title: Plan Big, Paint Small: Semantic-Aware Computation Allocation for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editors are trained on millions of edit pairs and follow instructions far more reliably than current video editors. We show that this ability can be transferred to video editing without any training. Our key observation is that a growing number of image editors and video generators share the same latent space. Their velocity fields can therefore be combined at sampling time: the difference between the editor's velocity under the instruction and under a neutral prompt, which we call the \emph{edit velocity}, can be added to the sampler of a video model. Added naively, however, it blurs the video, alters the background and flickers. An analysis of the edit velocity explains why. It is small and reliable only at coarse scales and high noise levels, not concentrated on the edited object, and uncorrelated across frames. From these properties, we derive a simple guidance operator that amplifies the edit velocity and restricts it in noise level, space, and time. The video model then turns the incoherent per-frame signal into a temporally coherent edit. Our method, TOGO, combines Qwen-Image-Edit with the Wan2.1 video model without training or fine-tuning. On FiVE-Bench, it raises the edit success rate from 47.0\% (the same video model without the editor) to 65.6\%, above the best published method (59.2\%). At the same time, it maintains the background PSNR and obtains the best LPIPS and SSIM of all methods. Because the video editor is assembled at inference time, it can be upgraded to any newer image editor that shares the latent space with no cost.
authors: Yixuan Luo, Jose Caballero, Yanjing Li
bullets: Addresses unreliable instruction following and artifacts in current video editors.
Combines image-editor and video-model velocity fields through an edit-velocity guidance operator.
Restricts guidance by noise level, spatial region, and time to reduce blur, background changes, and flicker.
Combines Qwen-Image-Edit with Wan2.1 without training or fine-tuning.
On FiVE-Bench, improves edit success from 47.0% to 65.6% while maintaining background PSNR and achieving the best reported LPIPS and SSIM.

papers.abstract: Video verifiers judge whether a candidate answer or trajectory agrees with a video, and are themselves chosen by a score. We show that this score depends on two choices in the test, the type of negative and the judgment interface, strongly enough to reverse conclusions about what a model can do and which verifier to deploy. We separate the two with controlled constructions that have exact truth conditions: endpoint-matched negatives, wrong only in their internal states, and a truth-switch test, in which the same two candidates swap correctness between two videos. Under direct judgment, where the verdict is read from answer scores, models that reject a visibly wrong start fall to near chance against endpoint-matched negatives. When the frames disclose each event, writing out reasoning before the answer lifts three of four models from under 10% to 70-100% on the truth-switch test, and staged inputs trace the direct failure to one step, composing events into states. But when the event must first be found, on human-validated natural video, the same change brings no significant gain under a protocol common to all models and can lower accuracy if one candidate denies that the event occurs. The negative type also changes which verifier is selected: one chosen on event-denial negatives is 8.9 points less accurate against negatives that keep the event and change a detail, the errors a generator mostly makes, and recovers about half as much accuracy when it reranks that generator's answers. A verifier should be evaluated on the errors it will face, and neither a low direct score nor a gain from reasoning should be read as a property of the model alone.
bullets: Endpoint-matched negatives expose failures in composing event-level evidence into internal states, even when the start appears visibly wrong.
Writing reasoning before answering raises performance substantially when all events are disclosed, but not when the event must first be found in natural video.
Verifier rankings change with the negative examples used for evaluation; event-denial negatives may not reflect generator-like detail errors.
Verifier evaluation should match the errors it will encounter in deployment.
Low direct scores and reasoning gains should not be interpreted as intrinsic model properties without controlling the test protocol.

papers.title: When Video Verifier Scores Mislead: Capability Assessment and Verifier Selection

papers.abstract: Surgical triplet recognition requires identifying which instrument performs which action on which anatomical target, and following these interactions as they unfold over time. The task is challenging because several triplets can occur at once, their components span very different durations, and the evidence for an interaction is rarely complete in a single frame. We introduce STRIDE, a post-hoc temporal readout that adds temporal context to any trained recogniser. It averages the recogniser's features and logits over a few fixed temporal windows and combines them with the current frame through ridge regression, solved in closed form on a CPU. Applied as a plug-and-play readout to nine existing methods, STRIDE improves $AP_{IVT}$ in 24 of 27 method-dataset pairs, by up to 7.4 points. Moreover, we propose a simple pipeline consisting of an adapted foundation vision encoder with a linear classifier and STRIDE. Across thirteen encoders, STRIDE improves 37 of 39 encoder-dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points. STRIDE reduces false alarms by 41%, at the cost of a slower response at interaction boundaries. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Lemar Abdi, Amaan Valiuddin, Fida Mohammad Thoker, Karen Sanchez, Bernard Ghanem, Fons van der Sommen
bullets: Addresses overlapping surgical interactions whose instrument, action, and target components unfold over different durations.
Averages features and logits over fixed temporal windows, then combines them with the current frame using CPU-solvable ridge regression.
Improves $AP_{IVT}$ in 24 of 27 method–dataset pairs by up to 7.4 points when added to nine existing recognisers.
With a foundation vision encoder and linear classifier, improves 37 of 39 encoder–dataset pairs by up to 7.2 points.
Reduces false alarms by 41%, but responds more slowly at interaction boundaries.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent videos as thousands of visual tokens, creating a large key-value cache whose memory grows with video length. At the same time, small VLMs that fit on limited hardware understand video far worse than large models. Existing compression methods shorten visual tokens into a brief prompt to save memory, yet the small model still processes them through fixed weights and cannot close this capability gap. To address both challenges, we introduce Video-as-Weights (VaW), which compiles a video once without seeing any question into the parametric and token memory of a frozen interpreter VLM. Specifically, a compiler VLM watches the video, and a single weight decoder jointly generates the interpreter's LoRA weights and optional prefix tokens from every compiler layer, enabling both same-model compilation and strong-to-weak transfer across model sizes and depths. Across six video QA benchmarks, a 0.8B interpreter beats full in-context reading by 1.7 points when compiled by itself and by 4.3 points with a 9B compiler, reducing context from up to 8,192 visual tokens to 64 prefix tokens while using 5.5x less memory than the video's key-value cache. Generated weights add 3.9 points over token compression alone, and all-layer decoding outperforms layer-wise generation by 2.9 points. Mechanistic analysis shows that with prefix tokens, the weights mainly alter attention queries and MLP down projections to guide retrieval and store a baseline summary, whereas without tokens, they shift to attention output projections to write video content directly into the residual stream.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Ian Miao, Chen Qu, Bill Bi, Donna Schut, Yuntian Deng, Yale Song
bullets: Addresses video VLMs’ growing key-value memory and the capability gap of small models.

papers.abstract: Answering questions over days or weeks of video requires searching for scattered clues across long timelines. Existing video agents rely on complex memory graphs and fixed retrieval pipelines, which restrict how the agent can search. We propose VideoJSON, a minimal harness for ultra-long video understanding that keeps the memory simple and lets a coding agent write its own search programs. During indexing, a vision-language model turns each minute of video into a single JSON record containing a dense caption and structured fields such as events, entities, places, and speech transcripts. At query time, the agent writes Python or Bash programs in a sandboxed container to filter, link, and read these records over multiple steps, without task-specific training or raw video access. On four ultra-long video benchmarks, VideoJSON with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outperforms MAGIC-Video by 7.0, 20.0, and 24.75 points on EgoLifeQA, Ego-R1-Bench, and MM-Lifelong Week, and beats the best prior EgoMemReason score by 12.6 points. Across four policy models of increasing capability, VideoJSON's average score rises by up to 11.58 points over the weakest model, compared with at most 5.50 points for MAGIC-Video. Ablations show that both agentic code search and the structured JSON records drive these gains, while adding hourly summaries, extra tools, or video access changes the average score by less than 1.5 points. In addition, fine-tuning Qwen-3.5-Flash on 64 VideoJSON trajectories from an unrelated 100-hour livestream improves its MM-Lifelong scores by up to 8.25 points. Code will be open-sourced after publication.
authors: Wenqi Marshall Guo, Kuan-Hao Huang, Junda Chen, Hao Zhang
bullets: Targets questions requiring scattered evidence across days or weeks of video.

Ablations attribute gains mainly to agentic code search and structured records; fine-tuning on 64 unrelated trajectories further improves one benchmark by up to 8.25 points.

papers.abstract: Interactive long-video generation lets users build a story through successive prompts and reuse earlier characters and settings under new instructions. Existing memory methods retain past content, yet they often fail at precise selective recall, returning the wrong appearance of a person, mixing different people, or keeping an unrequested background. Based on our analysis of memory form and retrieval, we introduce an object-aware key--value (KV) memory framework for a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator. It keeps the original KV of tracked object regions, selects background KV outside them by attention-scores, and links each memory with a readable record of its source scene and observed appearance. An LLM selects the requested records, and a memory integrator supplies their KV for generation under the current prompt. We also introduce a six-scene evaluation that tests selective attribute modification, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition, in which each person's requested past appearance changes across requests. Experiments show that our framework more reliably preserves each person's identity while reproducing their requested past appearance than existing memory methods, under both explicit scene references and natural-language cues.
authors: Hyunwook Kang, Junoh Park, Hyunggyu Lim, Taesup Kim
bullets: Targets failures in existing memory methods, including wrong appearances, identity mixing, and unrequested background retention.
Stores tracked-object KV features, selectively retains background KV using attention scores, and attaches readable scene/appearance records.
Uses an LLM to select requested memories, then integrates their KV into a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator.
Introduces a six-scene evaluation covering selective attribute edits, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition.
More reliably preserves identities and requested past appearances under explicit references and natural-language cues than existing memory methods.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon image animation must keep the scene fixed while natural material (e.g., water, smoke, or fire) continues to move. Autoregressive video generators read recent frames for temporal continuity, but this history also carries accumulated appearance errors, and sparsifying it disrupts motion. We introduce SceneTether, a training-free attention-read policy that keeps where attention reads recent memory but changes what appearance that memory returns. SceneTether keeps every key of the newest latent, blends its low-activity values toward co-located source-image values, and leaves high-activity values untouched so motion can evolve; an activity map estimated from the first generated latents and then frozen decides where to blend. It adds no denoising evaluations and leaves the cache-update rule unchanged. On a Causal Forcing++ generator, SceneTether raises source-support PSNR by 5.15 dB over its framewise Echo host across two seeds with 1.5x its late activity, and by 7.31 dB over spatial Echo-Forcing on a preselected four-minute subset. At equal recent-memory coverage, value anchoring alone adds 8.14 dB. A post-hoc pixel composite with the same map matches static fidelity but retains nearly twice the moving-region color drift, and viewers in a small blinded study preferred SceneTether for its natural scene and motion preservation. Project page: https://minar09.github.io/scenetether/
authors: Matiur Rahman Minar, Seunghun Oh, Ganghyeon Jeong, Unsang Park
bullets: Targets accumulated appearance drift in static scene regions without disrupting evolving materials such as water, smoke, or fire.

Freezes an activity map estimated from early generated latents; adds no denoising evaluations and does not alter cache updates.
Improves source-support PSNR over framewise and spatial Echo baselines, with additional gains from value anchoring alone.
A small blinded study favored SceneTether for preserving natural scene appearance and motion; evaluation covers two seeds and a preselected four-minute subset.

papers.abstract: A cross-modal routing module can improve over its backbone while its transport plan accounts for no demonstrable part of that improvement. In ABVnet with DFEW, Sinkhorn cross-modal routing (SCR) exceeds the retrained baseline by 0.87 unweighted average recall (UAR) points, a resolved difference, yet sits 0.17 points above an individually trained, parameter-matched pooled variant, an unresolved difference that establishes no equivalence; under the development protocol the comparison with the baseline reverses. Separating the two needs comparisons a module-against-backbone test cannot supply: parameter-matched variants changing only the plan rule, and interventions replacing the plan without retraining. The evaluation covers MMA-DFER and ABVnet on DFEW and MAFW, and MMA-DFER on CREMA-D, with a single training run per configuration and paired fold intervals. ABVnet with DFEW motivated the follow-up after the broader results were available. Replacing the plan everywhere with a uniform one reduces UAR by 0.72, whereas permuting its rows gives an unresolved difference of -0.20 UAR points; permutation is less damaging by 0.51 UAR points, a resolved contrast. Replacing the plan with the product of its own marginals, preserving both marginals and removing only frame-specific mixtures, reduces UAR by 0.70. These reductions concern reliance at inference; attribution of the module gain to the transport plan remains unestablished. Under the 1.5 fold-dependence widening, the baseline gain remains resolved, whereas the replacement reductions and the paired contrast are unresolved.
authors: Vu Nhat Minh Pham, Cong Khanh Nguyen, Minh Tuan Le, Van Thong Huynh
bullets: SCR improves over the retrained backbone by 0.87 UAR points in ABVnet on DFEW under one protocol, but this gain reverses under the development protocol.
A parameter-matched pooled comparison and plan-replacement interventions are needed to separate module effects from transport-plan effects.
Replacing the learned plan with a uniform plan or its marginal-product approximation reduces UAR, indicating inference-time reliance on frame-specific routing.
Row permutation is less damaging than uniform replacement, but the corresponding comparisons are unresolved under wider fold-dependence intervals.
Results cover MMA-DFER and ABVnet across DFEW, MAFW, and CREMA-D, with one training run per configuration.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers (vDiTs) have become the main backbone for video generation. The quadratic cost of self-attention limits their efficiency at high resolutions and long durations. Existing sparse attention methods often rely on preserving high attention weights. However, these criteria do not fully capture the fidelity of the final value-weighted output, whose error depends jointly on changes to the attention numerator and the softmax denominator. We propose NOVA, a coarse-to-fine sparse attention framework that first approximates the full normalized output using size-weighted key/value centroids. Building on this estimate, we construct a residual proxy that accounts for coupled numerator-denominator errors by centering value contributions around the estimated output. This proxy guides the selection of query-key blocks for refinement under a predefined block budget for each query cluster. Selected blocks are evaluated through exact token-level computation, while the remaining blocks contribute through their centroids under a shared softmax normalization. On five vDiTs, NOVA achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among sparse attention methods, improving PSNR by up to 1.55\,dB over the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 1.82$\times$ end-to-end speedup on an H100 GPU.
authors: Wenxuan Miao, Haosong Liu, Aiyue Chen, Yiwu Yao, Zihan Liu, Anbang Wu, Yiming Gan, Jingwen Leng, Minyi Guo, Yu Feng
bullets: Targets the quadratic self-attention cost of high-resolution and long-duration video generation.
Uses size-weighted key/value centroids to estimate full normalized attention outputs coarsely.
Builds a residual proxy that captures coupled softmax numerator and denominator errors.
Refines selected query-key blocks exactly while approximating the rest with centroids under shared normalization.
Across five vDiTs, reports the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among compared sparse-attention methods, with up to 1.55 dB PSNR improvement.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains video agents to locate sparse evidence for long-video question answering through structured memory retrieval and temporal re-observation. This training, however, faces a long-tail modality distribution in the data. In our source pool, text-heavy questions account for 58% of samples, compared with 15% graph-heavy, 17% visual-heavy, and 10% time-range questions. Fixed-distribution RL therefore allocates fewer rollouts to underperforming question types. Reweighting these types could increase their sampling frequency but repeatedly reuses the same finite banks of original questions. To solve this problem, we introduce VideoGym, a curriculum-based RL environment that jointly constructs video-grounded training tasks and allocates rollouts among them. Within the environment, a memory-augmented VideoAgent is trained to coordinate retrieval from text, graph, and visual memories with temporal re-observation. Across episodes, VideoGym adapts VideoAgent's training distribution online: it casts per-period sample selection as an adversarial bandit over (modality, mode) arms and applies the EXP3 update to shift sampling toward arms with low answer accuracy. To supply the augmented-mode arms, a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline produces harder variants of existing questions that remain answerable within the same video. Across five long-video benchmarks, VideoGym lifts RL accuracy from 60.4% to 64.8% on average and by up to 10.5 pp on underrepresented graph-heavy questions with 3.3x sample efficiency. Together, these results show that task expansion and adaptive allocation can improve video agent learning from limited, imbalanced training data.
authors: Jing Wang, Yi Ke Yun, Yifeng Yao, Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao, Tao Wang
bullets: Addresses imbalanced training data, where text-heavy questions dominate and graph-, visual-, and time-range questions are less frequent.
Uses a curriculum-based RL environment with a memory-augmented VideoAgent for text, graph, and visual retrieval plus temporal re-observation.
Models task selection as an adversarial bandit over modality and task-mode arms, using EXP3 to favor low-accuracy areas.
Generates harder but answerable question variants through a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline.
Across five benchmarks, average RL accuracy rises from 60.4% to 64.8%; graph-heavy questions improve by up to 10.5 percentage points with 3.3× sample efficiency.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video generators differ by two orders of magnitude in price, and a cheap configuration of a strong model is often good enough for a prompt. Routing prompts across such arms (model x sampling configuration) should buy quality at fixed budget, but no dataset supports studying it: public video-preference sets contain only closed models, one configuration each. We release VidRouteBench: 16 arms from 7 open families spanning 121x in measured cost ($0.0025-$0.298 per clip), 27,110 clips (1,421 A800-hours) over 1,625 grouped prompts, a quality score frozen after calibration against human preferences (68.7% CV accuracy vs 66.2% for the best single scorer), per-clip scores on 9 identifiable quality dimensions, repeated seeds, an encrypted test split, and a sealed newest family for cold start. The evaluator compares a router against the best prompt-agnostic mixture of arms, not the best single arm. Per-prompt specialisation here is real and predictable (oracle gap 0.642, 47% reproducible across seeds, prompt-arm interaction F=4.47 at p=1.6e-63), unlike LLM-routing arms, where the same pipeline finds none. We then propose OPMU (one probe, many utilities): label a new arm on K probe prompts, predict its 9 dimensions once, and serve any scenario utility by scalarising afterwards. Over 215 utility directions OPMU Pareto-dominates the prompt-agnostic baseline for 94% of directions versus 90% for per-scenario routers, with no per-scenario retraining. Three baselines fail instructively: bag-of-words features lose almost all routing gain in the low-data regime (0.009 vs 0.168); crediting a new arm with its probe average is harmful (-3.32 recovery) although it is the strong baseline on RewardBench-style arms (0.786); Chebyshev scalarisation does not help, our cost-utility front being convex.
bullets: Introduces 16 arms from 7 open model families, spanning 121× in measured generation cost and 27,110 clips across 1,625 grouped prompts.
Provides calibrated quality evaluation across 9 dimensions, repeated seeds, encrypted testing, and a sealed newest family for cold-start evaluation.
Shows prompt-specific arm selection is substantial and reproducible, motivating comparison with the best prompt-agnostic mixture rather than the best single arm.
Proposes OPMU: probe a new arm once, predict its quality dimensions, then scalarise for different utility scenarios without retraining.

papers.abstract: Two centuries ago, an early cinema-like theater called the Diorama could already control its scenes at will. Today's video generation models produce videos of near-cinematic quality, yet they still lack this controllability. This limitation stems from the inherent semantic gap between text and pixels, since a prompt can describe a video only coarsely and leaves its details and relations beyond control. We bring this ability to video generation with Causal Dioramas, modules that decompose a video into a concept graph of variables that can be intervened on individually. Each instruction is translated into an intervention on the concept graph, modifying the specified concepts and their dependents. A connector then conveys this intervention to the video generator, which reuses the original noise to produce a counterfactual video while preserving all other content. Building on Causal Dioramas, we develop a unified framework for controllable generation, counterfactual revision of generated videos and editing of real videos. We outperform both open-source and commercial models in controllability on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench and OpenVE-Bench.
authors: Yifan Shen, Xinyi Yang, Peiyuan Zhu, Yichang Jian, Jinyuan Hu, Xilin He, Fengming Zhu, Guangyi Chen, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited detail and relational control of text-to-video prompts caused by the semantic gap between text and pixels.
Decomposes videos into concept graphs whose variables can be individually intervened on, including their dependents.
Translates instructions into graph interventions and uses a connector to guide the video generator with reused noise for counterfactual outputs.
Supports unified text-to-video generation, revision of generated videos, and editing of real videos.
Reports better controllability than open-source and commercial models on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench, and OpenVE-Bench.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. None of them requires that the label be unrecoverable from the frames once their order is discarded, so a model can fit such data from static cues without learning to use frame order. We propose ORDO, a framework that builds this requirement into the training data. We define order-necessary supervision as data in which the unordered set of frames has the same distribution under competing labels, and we realise it for motion attributes with three constructions, time-reversal pairing, matched spatial extent and uniform interval coverage. A procedural curriculum of six motion primitives instantiates these constructions, and low-rank adapters of the language model are trained on it with an answer-level objective and self-distillation replay on real videos. With 4,000 synthetic clips, ORDO raises the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks by +7.6, +4.9 and +5.1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Molmo2-8B, while the same training with shuffled frames changes it by less than one point. Code and generator will be made publicly available.
authors: Jiaye Luan, Chaoning Zhang, Pengcheng Zheng, Dongshen Han, Sheng Zheng, Ping Guo, Caiyan Qin, Yang Du, Yang Yang
bullets: Targets failures on motion attributes such as speeding up or slowing down, which models may otherwise solve using static visual cues.
Constructs order-necessary supervision through time-reversal pairs, matched spatial extent, and uniform interval coverage.
Uses six procedural motion primitives, low-rank adaptation, answer-level training, and self-distillation replay on real videos.
Training on 4,000 synthetic clips improves mean accuracy across four motion benchmarks by 7.6, 4.9, and 5.1 points for three video LLMs.
Shuffled-frame training yields less than one point of change, supporting the importance of order-dependent supervision.

papers.abstract: Long videos spanning tens of minutes to hours far exceed the context window of today's vision-language models, and the standard remedy of sparse uniform frame sampling discards exactly the fine-grained evidence that specific questions depend on. Existing video agents explore on demand but re-explore from scratch for every question and discard their exploration state once an answer is produced, so per-question cost scales with video length. Hierarchical-memory methods instead fix the scope of each depth in advance and deepen along a pre-committed pyramid rather than toward the question. We observe that a video's coarse structure (where its scenes and topics begin and end) is question-independent, whereas which part a question must zoom into, and how deep, is question-dependent. We propose VTree, which builds a coarse hierarchical memory tree over a video once and then, for each question, grows branches only where that question needs depth. The growth is globally routed so any part of the timeline is reachable, sufficiency-gated so drilling stops when the evidence suffices, and query-conditioned so a branch unfolds into the sub-intervals that answer \emph{this} question. Crucially, every expansion is written back into the video memory, allowing later questions to reuse previously discovered structure and evidence without repeating the corresponding expansion process. Across five long-video understanding benchmarks, VTree consistently improves the accuracy of diverse vision-language backbones while substantially reducing the context length and execution time required for each question.
authors: Xiaoyu Ma, Lianyu Hu, Zixuan Hu, Zhizhen Wu, Zeqin Liao, Shengqian Qin, Yang Liu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling and agents that re-explore long videos independently for every question.
Separates question-independent coarse video structure from question-dependent evidence and required zoom depth.
Uses globally routed, sufficiency-gated, query-conditioned branch growth to locate relevant fine-grained content.
Writes each expansion back to memory so later questions can reuse discovered structure and evidence.
Improves accuracy across five long-video benchmarks while reducing per-question context length and execution time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VTree. (1) Build phase: a question-independent level-1 event skeleton is constructed once per video. (2) Growth phase: for each question, the controller routes over the updated level-1 nodes, reuses stored descendants, and expands an unexplored leaf only when finer evidence is needed. Newly acquired information is propagated bottom-up. (3) Persistent memory: the refined hierarchy is retained across questions for subsequent reuse.
Figure 3: Qualitative examples of the Route–Check–Expand process. VTree routes to a relevant branch, checks evidence sufficiency, and expands the branch only when finer detail is required.

Figure 1: VTree raises accuracy while sharply cutting perquestion cost. papers.abstract: Multimodal Egocentric Human Activity Recognition (Ego-HAR) leverages complementary cues from first-person vision (V) and inertial sensor data (S) to recognize daily activities, where video mainly captures appearance and object-related context while inertial signals capture motion cues that video may miss. However, existing pre-training methods typically supervise the fused representation with a single joint objective, which may underemphasize the complementarity between the two modalities and limit the model's ability to learn from distinct modality-oriented signals. To address this issue, we propose Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction (MDR2), a teacher-guided pre-training framework in which frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers each provide dense, modality-specific targets to a multimodal student trained on temporally sparse inputs. On the EvIs-Kitchen dataset, MDR2 improves noun/verb F1-macro over the supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at K=4 video key frames and by 1.21/1.82 points at K=32. These results show that MDR2 consistently achieves higher mean recognition performance across the evaluated video-observation settings under the unified backbone setting, with more pronounced gains under sparse inputs.
authors: Yuzhe Hao, Ikuro Sato, Rei Kawakami, Koichi Shinoda
bullets: Targets the limitation of single-objective pre-training, which can underuse differences between video and inertial modalities.
Uses frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers to provide dense modality-specific targets.
Trains a multimodal student from temporally sparse inputs through dual representation reconstruction.
On EvIs-Kitchen, improves noun/verb F1-macro over supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at 4 frames and 1.21/1.82 points at 32 frames.
Reports larger gains under sparse video observation settings within the evaluated unified-backbone setup.

papers.abstract: Violence in films and streaming media remains a concern for audience protection and creates substantial workload for manual content classification. Existing violence-detection methods often rely on limited modalities or short video clips, making it difficult to capture complementary evidence and localise violent events in long, untrimmed videos. In this study, we develop a framework for multimodal video understanding that classifies violence severity, predicts multiple violence types, and locates violent events in time. We combine temporally aligned visual and audio features extracted using pretrained encoders through attention-based adaptive fusion, followed by Transformer-based temporal modelling. Our framework supports three complementary tasks: video-level violence-severity classification, multi-label violence-type prediction, and temporal localisation of violent events. We evaluate the framework on the XD-Violence benchmark and examine its cross-domain performance using AIRTLab. On XD-Violence, our multimodal model achieves 93.27\% severity-classification accuracy and a micro-F1 score of 88.60\% for multi-label violence-type prediction, outperforming the corresponding unimodal configurations. We achieve a mean temporal intersection-over-union (tIoU) of 0.5075 for temporal localisation. Our cross-domain experiments reveal performance degradation under different recording conditions, while our movie case studies demonstrate the framework's potential to retrieve potentially violent scenes for further review. Our results highlight the practical value of multimodal intelligent systems in supporting human reviewers with the identification, classification, and temporal retrieval of violent content in films and streaming media.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of single-modality methods and short-clip analysis for violence understanding in untrimmed videos.
Fuses temporally aligned visual and audio features with attention-based adaptive fusion, then models time using a Transformer.

Cross-domain performance degrades under different recording conditions; movie case studies indicate practical retrieval potential.

papers.abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.
bullets: Targets physical and logical failures in multi-step video reasoning and planning.
Models solutions as causal state transitions with an explicit stopping decision.
Uses decision-focused training and Corrective Fine-tuning to repair failed decisions without policy-gradient optimization.
Reports an 83.8% average strict success rate across games, planning tasks, and robot-planning benchmarks, with generalization to larger puzzles and unseen layouts.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. (a) Instead of jointly generating a fixed-length clip, the model generates state transitions causally and ends with a visual EOS frame. (c) From the state hd before a failed decision, CFT resamples a successful continuation and trains the noise ϵ−d that produced the failed decision to generate the successful decision X+ d , shifting the decision distribution toward solvable moves.

papers.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval asks a system to find, in a large collection of untrimmed videos with subtitles, the video and the time interval that a natural-language query describes. We find that most top-ranked errors of a strong corpus-level scorer come from choosing the wrong video, not from imprecise boundaries, and that re-weighting the evidence the scorer already uses does not fix them. We present DiTraR, which addresses video selection from two complementary directions. A witness-interval scorer decomposes the query into probes and scores every candidate interval of every corpus video exactly; a multi-scorer energy ensemble averages the energies of independently trained scorers before one exhaustive search; and a transcript verifier, a frozen language model that reads the time-stamped dialogue of the highest-ranked videos, re-orders the moments without changing their boundaries. With all settings frozen on development data and a single evaluation, DiTraR reaches 24.36 and 13.55 R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 0.7 on the TVR validation split. The ensemble improves queries about visual content, the verifier improves queries about dialogue, and their gains largely add up.
authors: Mohammad Alijanpour Shalmani, Alale Rezvani Boroujeni, Ali Amini
bullets: Most top-ranked errors arise from selecting the wrong video rather than inaccurate temporal boundaries.
A witness-interval scorer evaluates query probes against every candidate interval across the corpus.
A multi-scorer energy ensemble combines independently trained scorers before exhaustive search.
A frozen language-model transcript verifier re-ranks top moments using time-stamped dialogue without changing boundaries.
On TVR validation, DiTraR achieves 24.36 R@1 at IoU 0.5 and 13.55 R@1 at IoU 0.7; visual and dialogue-query gains are complementary.

papers.abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.
authors: Fabio Guglietta, Tianyi Li, Francesco Viola, Luca Biferale
bullets: Cardiovascular imaging provides noisy, incomplete, and resolution-limited observations, making flow reconstruction inherently ambiguous.
Using a controlled digital twin of a healthy human left heart, the study evaluates unconditional generation and conditional reconstruction.
Repeated conditional samples produce plausible completions rather than a single deterministic estimate; their mean preserves key reference-flow features.
Compared with Gaussian process regression, diffusion-model ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations and better encompass ground-truth features.
The work is a quantitative proof of concept, with scope demonstrated on simulated healthy-heart data and potential application to in-vivo imaging augmentation.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based probabilistic reconstruction of temporally structured flow; transferable to video and world-model generation.
papers.title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
papers.tldr: Generative diffusion models can probabilistically reconstruct incomplete cardiovascular flow measurements while capturing diverse, physically plausible flow patterns.

papers.abstract: A comic-book character, a photorealistic cityscape, an oil-painted coffee cup -- such stylistically diverse references provide visual guidance across shots and frames, yet generating a coherent multi-shot video that unifies their visual styles while preserving subject identities and scene content remains challenging. Existing methods maintain cross-shot continuity through additional attention control or memory processing. However, they struggle to resolve disparate per-shot styles or handle reference-target duration mismatches within a single framework. We introduce Refrain, a unified model that learns cross-shot consistency through a self-supervised reconstruction task. Reference clips from the same original video are deliberately perturbed with distinct visual edits, and the model recovers the unedited source footage under a shared style prompt. The resulting pipeline yields DurMix-300K, which pairs independently edited references of varying durations with their original videos. Operating on the A$^2$O principle (Any Reference, Any Duration, One Timeline), Refrain maps image and video references onto a shared temporal canvas without auxiliary conditioning modules. For evaluation, experiments show that standard CLIP or DINO metrics frequently overlook stylistic clashes or misinterpret intended narrative cuts as inconsistency. We propose Shot-Debiased Consistency (SDC), which uses an extensive real-video bank to establish a baseline for style variation associated with content changes within shots. By discounting this baseline divergence, SDC evaluates cross-shot style shifts against real-world distributions, where smaller residual differences indicate higher stylistic continuity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Refrain achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-shot consistency, while excelling at shot timing, reference adherence, and text alignment.
authors: Hongru Yan, Yue Wu, Jian-Wei Zhang, Liangbin Xie, Mingzhe Zheng, Shenghua Gao
bullets: Addresses stylistic clashes and reference–target duration mismatches in multi-shot video generation.
Uses self-supervised reconstruction: perturbed reference clips are restored to their original footage under a shared style prompt.
Introduces DurMix-300K, pairing independently edited references of varying durations with original videos.
Implements the A²O principle—Any Reference, Any Duration, One Timeline—without auxiliary conditioning modules.

Proposes Shot-Debiased Consistency (SDC) to evaluate cross-shot style continuity against real-video variation; experiments report state-of-the-art consistency and strong timing, adherence, and text alignment.
