papers.abstract: Long-video understanding increasingly relies on agentic systems that actively acquire evidence rather than process fixed video representations. Their execution harnesses must coordinate language-level planning with video-level observation and evidence acquisition, yet are typically fixed across model stacks. We therefore introduce MoHA, a framework for model-conditioned harness adaptation that adapts a common initial execution harness to the specific planner and observer models it hosts. MoHA treats the harness itself as a model-conditioned optimization object: under the same task distribution and initialization, different planner-observer stacks can benefit from different executable harnesses. Starting from a common initial harness, MoHA analyzes failed calibration traces to diagnose model-harness mismatches and adapts both planner-side reasoning support, such as overview, memory, and verification, and observer-side capability assignments, including OCR and ASR specialists. After structural adaptation, MoHA separately calibrates observer execution configurations for the hosted model stack. Across three frozen planner stacks, MoHA improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2-27.1 percentage points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1-20.1 points over the fixed initial harness. Cross-model transfer further shows that the adapted harnesses generalize only partially to other models, highlighting the harness as a model-conditioned optimization layer for long-video understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/roverx12345/MoHA.
authors: Jianghan Chao, Wenhui Tan, Hang Su, Qiuyu Tian, Tanxiao Li, Bingzi Zhang, Zequn Liu, Ruihua Song, Yingce Xia
bullets: Targets the mismatch between fixed execution harnesses and diverse planner–observer model stacks.
Diagnoses failed calibration traces to adapt planning support, memory, verification, and observer roles such as OCR and ASR.
Separately calibrates observer execution configurations after structural harness adaptation.
Improves Video-MME Full accuracy by 6.2–27.1 points and Video-Holmes accuracy by 3.1–20.1 points across three frozen planner stacks.
Cross-model transfer is only partial, indicating harnesses remain strongly model-conditioned.

papers.abstract: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.
authors: Luca Glawion, Julius Polz, Harald Kunstmann, Benjamin Fersch, Patrick Ludwig, Antonio S\'anchez-Ben\'itez, Christian Chwala
bullets: Targets the gap between snapshot-based skill evaluation and temporal coherence needed for sub-daily climate-impact applications.

Trains a diffusion U-Net with a noised previous high-resolution state, enabling continuous interpolation between autoregressive and per-timestep-independent sampling through one inference-time noise parameter.
On hourly European precipitation and 2-meter temperature downscaling, autoregressive rollouts remain stable for up to six months, with only slight early ensemble-spread contraction.
Autoregressive precipitation better preserves daily maxima, while independent generation underestimates them by up to 2×; temperature differences are negligible.
Noise-free conditioning diverges, indicating that the noise-conditioned scheme is important for stable long rollouts.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed temporal-noise-conditioned diffusion framework. (a) Training: The conditional diffusion model learns to emulate high-resolution RCM fields from coarse GCM input. The previous-hour RCM state is additionally provided as temporal condition input, corrupted with randomly sampled noise. (b) Inference: The conditioning noise level is controlled by the parameter τ . At its maximum value (τ = 999), the temporal condition consists of pure noise, resulting in per-timestep independent (PTI) samples (dashed lines). This regime also serves to initialize the autoregressive rollout. At a lower noise level (e.g. τ = 50), the previous timestep’s prediction is perturbed with noise and used as the temporal conditioning input. This provides informative temporal context, resulting in temporally consistent autoregressive (AR) sampling (solid lines).

papers.tldr: A noise-conditioned diffusion downscaling model provides a tunable trade-off between temporally coherent autoregressive rollouts and independent per-timestep generation without progressive degradation.

papers.abstract: Gameplay videos are a rich source of experience for learning virtual-world dynamics, yet their frames contain heads-up displays (HUDs) that follow interface rules rather than scene dynamics. Removing HUDs would make this footage directly usable for learning world dynamics. However, training a removal model requires paired clips with and without HUDs, whereas real recordings contain only HUD-overlaid footage. Existing work synthesizes pairs by compositing HUD graphics onto HUD-free footage, requiring a separately curated clean corpus and producing HUDs that only approximate real ones. Models trained on such pairs leave 40 to 50% of real HUD elements untouched. We instead recover pseudo-clean targets directly from real recordings by inpainting HUD regions with a pretrained video diffusion model. Preventing HUD traces from leaking into recovered targets is challenging because latent video autoencoders mix information across mask boundaries. Our training-free recovery pipeline, GameScrub-Data, pre-fills HUD regions with flow-guided background estimates before encoding, excludes HUDs from scene conditioning, and confines restoration to masked regions through pixel-space compositing. The resulting pairs train GameScrub, a video diffusion removal model that handles diverse HUDs without inference-time masks or clean reference images. On the in-the-wild Game2World benchmark, GameScrub achieves an artifact-adjusted removal score of 71.95, compared with 57.86 for the strongest reference-free GameCleaner configuration, and removes 90.06% of annotated HUD elements versus 59.07%. These results demonstrate that real recordings with recovered targets can support effective HUD removal, advancing HUD-free gameplay data for world models and controllable video generation.
authors: Mohammad Areeb Qazi, Yiyan Hu, Yanan Wang, Xuezhi Liang, Xin Li, Fan Yang, Xin Gao, Guangyi Liu
bullets: Real gameplay is valuable for world-model learning, but HUD overlays obscure scene dynamics and lack clean paired training data.
GameScrub-Data recovers HUD-free targets using flow-guided pre-filling, HUD-excluded conditioning, and masked pixel-space compositing.
The resulting video diffusion model removes HUDs without inference-time masks or clean reference images.
On the Game2World benchmark, it scores 71.95 artifact-adjusted removal versus 57.86 for GameCleaner and removes 90.06% of annotated HUD elements versus 59.07%.
The approach is scoped to improving HUD-free gameplay data for world modeling and controllable video generation.

papers.abstract: Echocardiography assesses the structure and function of the heart. Cardiologists read each study across several standard views and report the findings visible in those views by cardiac structure. AI foundation models can learn to analyze these studies from clinical reports, reducing annotation burden and supporting clinical interpretation. However, existing models are trained by pairing each video with the full clinical report, including structures and findings its view does not show. This mismatch lets a model associate a finding with incidental or spurious signals rather than its visual evidence, which limits accuracy, anatomical grounding and clinical trust. Here we introduce EchoAlign, a vision-language foundation model developed on 2.87 million echocardiographic videos and images from 159 clinical centers. EchoAlign aligns each cardiac structure, video and study with its report text, and a visibility matrix restricts supervision to the views that actually depict each structure. We compare it with five public foundation models on 0.47 million test videos across ten unseen external datasets from more than 25 clinical centers. EchoAlign achieves the highest mean AUROC of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.881 to 0.897) for classification and the highest mean quadratic weighted kappa of 0.530 (95% CI, 0.511 to 0.544) for severity grading. Across 62 clinical findings, EchoAlign provides one model that detects findings, grades their severity, estimates measurements and segments cardiac structures.
authors: Ahmed Aly, Darya Taratynova, Lotfi Abdelkrim Mecharbat, Roman A. Sandler, Joseph Z. Sokol, Joshua Penn, Klaus H. Maier-Hein, Numan Saeed, Mohammad Yaqub

Uses multilevel alignment of cardiac structures, videos and studies with report text, guided by a visibility matrix.
Achieves mean AUROC 0.890 for classification and mean quadratic weighted kappa 0.530 for severity grading across 10 unseen external datasets.
Supports detection, severity grading, measurement estimation and cardiac-structure segmentation across 62 clinical findings.

papers.abstract: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.
authors: Chuhan Jiao, John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Guy Rosman, Andreas Bulling
bullets: Addresses visual perspective taking beyond state estimation, reconstruction, and discrete question answering.
Uses backbone-agnostic geometric modules with scene coordinate maps, 3D ray-space token alignment, and visual-memory-based view completion.
Handles extreme viewpoint changes, dynamic occlusions, and sparse overlap between collaborators’ views.
Across three video diffusion backbones on CoMind, improves visual quality, scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion over prior cross-view generation methods.
Enables applications in human–robot collaboration and synchronized multi-perspective video generation for robot learning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Ego2Ego. Given the ego person’s egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and both camera trajectories, Ego2Ego generates the collaborator’s egocentric video with a pretrained video diffusion transformer equipped with three geometry-grounded modules. All conditions are encoded by the frozen VAE and form a single token sequence with the noisy collaborator latent. (1) Since the same surface appears entirely different from the two viewpoints and hands occlude the scene, dense geometric rendering rasterises the point cloud into every view, colouring each pixel by its 3D coordinate in a shared frame, so that the same scene point carries the same colour across views and provides a shared spatial reference. (2) To relate tokens across substantially different viewpoints, relative geometric attention aligns the geometric components of keys and values to each query token’s ray-aligned frame. (3) To recover regions the ego person does not currently observe, the ego person’s visual memory supplies past ego-person frames together with their renderings.

papers.abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking
authors: Davide Gardenal, Mingxuan Liu, Flavio Vella, Quentin Guimard, Elisa Ricci
bullets: Introduces TTU, which requires continuous tracking through object transformations and maintenance of semantic state graphs.
Proposes TIPO, a training-free generate–evaluate–judge framework for detecting and labeling split and merge events.
Uses mask components, overlap-based proposal scoring, and MLLM verification for transformation understanding.
Introduces VISTA, a benchmark with 50 sequences, 124 assembly events, 132 disassembly events, and over 26,000 frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA and runs 6×–15× faster than prior methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of TIPO. At each frame It, the tracker provides the set of per-object masks. The pipeline operates in four stages (1–4): (1) extraction of the disjoint components and mask sampling, (2) generation of all possible assembly and disassembly states, (3) evaluation of the state proposals based on mask overlap metrics, (4) validation of the highest-scoring proposal by the MLLM Judge and semantic labeling. Lastly, the state graph and the tracker are updated with the validated state.

Figure 9. Overview of the VISTA Annotation Tool. Our custom interface couples automated object tracking with expert human verification to construct high-fidelity state graphs. (Top) The landing page features an interactive video player, central tracker controls, and lateral panels for object and graph management. (1) Add Object: The annotator registers a new distinct entity ID in the system. (2) Segment and Track: By clicking on the object within the video frame, the annotator prompts the segmentation model to extract the spatial mask and initiates temporal tracking. (3) Log Transformation: At the exact frame of a physical state change, the expert opens a dialog box to explicitly link the pre- and post-transformation object tracks and assign a semantic action label (e.g., “Unscrew”). (4) Transformation Logged: The validated event is immediately committed to the state graph and displayed in the right-hand panel for continuous review.

Figure 3. Qualitative results on VISTA. Visualizing the TIPO pipeline on cascaded transformations. The state graphs map part-whole interactions and semantic actions, while the masks show robust spatial continuity across multi-step assembly and disassembly sequences.

The top row details the multi-step construction of a drawer assembly from flat boards, while the bottom row shows a digital camera that receives its memory card and battery before being inserted into its pouch. These examples demonstrate the capability of the framework to model multi-step assemblies and part-whole interactions.

Figure 17. Failure cases of TIPO on the VISTA benchmark. We present two disassembly sequences from the Assembly101 [27] subset with their corresponding state-graph predictions. papers.abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.
authors: Changin Choi, Jungwon Park, Jungmin Ko, Jimyeong Kim, Wonjong Rhee
bullets: Targets the challenge of finding and connecting evidence across distant intervals in videos lasting hours or days.
Builds three memories: searchable segment captions, entity-event records, and entity-aware episode context.
Induces a compact library of memory skills from successful agent trajectories for iterative retrieval, reasoning, and verification.
Achieves the best results on three week-long egocentric benchmarks, with up to 9.4% improvement over the strongest baseline on Ego-R1 Bench.
Ablations show that all memory components and memory skills contribute, including better temporal evidence localization.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of VMSA. (b) Memory skills are induced from successful source trajectories. Coverage assessment determines whether each procedure is already covered, requires skill refinement, or requires a new skill. The skill libraries are updated accordingly and periodically consolidated to reduce redundancy while preserving procedural knowledge. (c) At inference time, the video agent receives the target query, retrieved memory skills, and entity-aware episode memory as input context. The agent then gathers and verifies evidence through tool calls to generate its answer.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. In practice, however, standard RL often improves the target reward without reliably preserving holistic generation quality, leading to unstable reward-quality trade-offs that we view as a form of reward hacking. Since Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is known to improve visual clarity, prompt alignment, and perceptual quality in generation, we investigate whether its underlying structure can serve as a useful prior during RL. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.
authors: Yunfei Zheng, Xiaolong Wang, Dandan Zheng, Xianjun Deng, Shenghao Liu, Wei Xiang, Yuqian Li, Laurence Tianruo Yang
bullets: Standard RL can increase target reward while degrading holistic generation quality, causing reward hacking.
The paper views CFG and RL updates as correction vectors and uses their alignment to diagnose structural preservation.
Geometric analysis suggests pretrained CFG directions encode quality-relevant information that RL may discard.
CCR applies the frozen reference model’s conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL.
Across multiple rewards and backbones, CCR maintains competitive reward while more consistently preserving quality than standard RL and generic regularization.

papers.abstract: A streamed video generator releases each chunk the moment that it is produced, so a safety decision that waits for the finished clip arrives after the harm has been seen. We measure a guardrail by exposure, the harmful frames a viewer is shown, and ask where a fixed moderation budget should be spent. The accurate detector reads decoded frames with a video language model and is too expensive for every chunk, so our guard reads hidden states the generator has computed already and spends a cheap score on deciding when to call it. On 599 streams from a distilled causal generator the undefended model shows 46.25 harmful frames of 81. The video model on every chunk leaves 0.91 frames at 80.1 scored per benign stream, and the same model triggered by our guard leaves 2.35 at 5.3. Spending that budget at random leaves 37.20 frames, so the gain is in the ordering, and a frame detector in the same role gives up almost six, so the judging stage must read the chunk as a clip. The ordering is worth more as the stream lengthens, and the guard carries to a second system. An independent guardrail model agrees with our oracle at $\kappa=0.74$, and a blinded audit by 50 participants puts its precision at 96.1% and recall at 82.8%. Warning. This paper contains examples of generated content that some readers may find disturbing or offensive in nature.
authors: Yuxin Cao, Ziqi Ding, Jiayu Zhang, Xianglin Yang, Wei Song, Jin Song Dong
bullets: Streaming generators can expose harmful frames before a completed-clip safety check finishes.

Clip-level judging was substantially more effective than using a frame detector, and the ordering benefit increased with stream length and transferred to a second system.
An independent guard agreed moderately with the oracle (κ=0.74); a 50-person blinded audit measured 96.1% precision and 82.8% recall.

papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion distillation reduces sampling cost but often weakens adjustable classifier-free guidance (CFG) and runtime negative prompting. We introduce PP-CFG, an architecture that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate and combines their attention responses with opposite signs within a shared visual backbone. Its Scale-Time Polarity Mixer refines each condition using the guidance scale and denoising timestep, allowing prompt influence to vary throughout generation. The student retains a continuous scale input and selectable negative prompts with one visual backbone pass per step. We evaluate PP-CFG on Wan2.1 for video generation with distribution matching distillation (DMD), and on Qwen-Image with both latent consistency model (LCM) distillation and DMD. PP-CFG achieves 81.46 VBench in four steps and lower video teacher-student distances across guidance scales than step-distilled DMD. On NegElement-1K, our benchmark of 1,000 matched image and video prompt cases, it achieves higher target-removal rates than the corresponding teachers. These experiments support the method's generality across attention architectures, generation modalities, and distillation objectives while retaining competitive generation quality.

Evaluated across Wan2.1 and Qwen-Image using DMD and LCM distillation, supporting broad applicability.

papers.abstract: Inference-time methods that lift a small open video generator toward a proprietary one are compared through preference scores, which never say how much of the gap to a target video they close. We introduce the oracle control ladder, which hands a fixed student progressively richer information from a target clip and reads the closure of each fidelity metric at each rung as an empirical headroom reference for the methods that must synthesize that information. On 954 clips of the principal student, a dense caption reproduces little of the appearance and almost none of the motion of a target, a first frame closes half of the appearance gap and a tenth of the motion gap, a depth video closes three quarters of the motion gap and leaves color untouched, and the two together close 64 to 94% of every fidelity gap across four teachers, while a second student agrees on the rungs that it accepts. An item response model forecasts which rung closes which clip with held-out AUC of 0.76 to 0.95 on the fidelity criteria and serves as the prior of a budgeted selection policy. When controls are free, a fixed dense-control rung is hard to improve upon, and once controls are priced the policy lies above the fixed-rung frontier at matched cost and survives critics that ruin critic-driven search.
authors: Ziqi Ding, Yuxin Cao, Kai Ye, Yaobo Yang, Wei Song
bullets: Preference scores do not quantify how much of a teacher–student fidelity gap inference-time methods close.

Dense captions add little appearance or motion fidelity; first frames mainly help appearance, while depth strongly helps motion.
Combining first-frame and depth controls closes 64–94% of fidelity gaps across four teachers, with similar rung behavior for a second student.
An item-response model predicts useful control rungs (held-out AUC 0.76–0.95), supporting a budgeted policy that beats fixed-rung choices at matched cost.

papers.abstract: General-purpose point tracking requires large-scale training data with diverse dynamics, yet existing datasets struggle to combine rich dynamic content, accurate scene geometry, and sufficient scale. We introduce TrajRealm, the first public synthetic point-tracking dataset to reach the ten-million-frame scale, constructed from games and embodied simulations. TrajRealm uses the rich environments and motion systems of modern games to capture diverse targets, activities, and interactions across diverse worlds, while embodied simulations add robot manipulation and indoor navigation data. The dataset provides RGB observations, depth, camera parameters, and persistent 2D and 3D point trajectories. These annotations provide precise, geometrically consistent supervision across foreground objects and static environmental surfaces. We also build TrajRealm-Bench with eight subcategories under Interaction and Locomotion to evaluate tracking across diverse scenes. Benchmark evaluations reveal the strengths and limitations of existing trackers in handling complex motion and maintaining long-term point correspondences. Training on TrajRealm improves the performance of existing tracking methods on synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
authors: Ni Yang, Weiguang Zhao, Jiafei Cao, Yankai Jiang, Haoyu Guo, Tao Yang, Chunhua Shen, Junting Dong
bullets: Combines game environments with embodied simulations to cover varied targets, interactions, robot manipulation, and indoor navigation.

Benchmark results expose strengths and limitations of existing trackers, especially for complex motion and long-term correspondences.
Training on TrajRealm improves existing trackers on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

papers.abstract: LLM-generated descriptions enrich zero-shot skeleton-based action recognition but repeat cues shared by confusable actions. Their contextual semantics also lack explicit links to skeleton features. To address these challenges, we propose CRAFT, which couples Concept Refinement and Feature-grounded Tokens. Hard-negative-conditioned generation and contrastive scoring identify concepts that distinguish each action from its closest rivals. Unique-QDPP selects complementary descriptions within each semantic slot and prevents their reuse across slots. This bank supervises learnable concept tokens that read motion and context cues from each skeleton. On fixed NTU-60 and NTU-120 splits, CRAFT improves five baselines spanning four recognition paradigms. ZSL accuracy and GZSL harmonic mean increase on every baseline-split pair, by 5.4 and 5.9 percentage points on average. Random-split experiments extend these gains to three datasets, including PKU-MMD. Code will be released after acceptance.
authors: Siyu Zhu, Feng Ding, Zixiao Jin, Kaizhi Li, Xin Dong, Haisheng Fu, Yuchen Zou, Guohe Zhang, Jie Liang
bullets: Targets redundant LLM-generated descriptions and weak links between semantics and skeleton motion.
Uses hard-negative-conditioned generation and contrastive scoring to find concepts that distinguish confusable actions.
Selects complementary descriptions with Unique-QDPP and assigns them to separate semantic slots.
Learns concept tokens that extract motion and contextual cues from skeletons.
Improves ZSL and GZSL performance across five baselines and multiple splits, with average gains of 5.4 and 5.9 percentage points on fixed NTU splits.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables real-time streaming generation, with each generated chunk serving as historical context for subsequent generation. To avoid the memory explosion of backpropagation through time, previous self-rollout methods typically truncate cross-chunk gradients or detach historical latents. As a result, earlier denoising computations receive no downstream feedback through the generated history on how to synthesize frames that facilitate subsequent generation, leading to visual drift and structural collapse as rollouts extend. To address this limitation, we propose Hindsight Forcing, which allows historical chunks to learn directly from future outcomes by decoupling forward generation from backward credit assignment via a latent straight-through bridge. In the forward pass, each chunk completes a full multi-step rollout to update the KV cache. In the backward pass, the bridge routes gradients from future losses back to a single selected denoising step per historical chunk, training both the context writer and historical denoiser on shared parameters without retaining the full trajectory graph. Remarkably, Hindsight Forcing requires no additional model parameters, architecture modifications, or separate trajectory replay. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that Hindsight Forcing outperforms existing baselines in overall visual quality and dynamic motion, while ablation studies validate the benefit of supervising historical denoising. Code is available at https://github.com/haonanAN309/Hindsight-Forcing.
authors: Haonan An, Yihang Tao, Yu Guo, Renlong Chen, Jiasheng Zhang, Yuguang Fang
bullets: Addresses visual drift and structural collapse caused by detached or truncated gradients across generated video chunks.
Uses a latent straight-through bridge to separate full forward rollout from efficient backward credit assignment.
Routes future gradients to one selected denoising step in each historical chunk, jointly training context writing and historical denoising.
Requires no extra parameters, architectural changes, or separate trajectory replay.

papers.abstract: Video fusion integrates complementary information in multiple source video streams into a single sequence for complete scene perception. Existing methods perform frame-wise fusion and lack unified spatio-temporal modeling across sequences, damaging temporal coherence across sequences. When dealing with degradations, they also ignore temporal dynamics and overload a single network with diverse degradations, leading to limited and imbalanced degradation suppression. To address these issues, we propose V2VFusion, the first unified video-to-video fusion framework that directly generates temporally coherent, high-quality fused videos from degraded multi-source inputs. By reformulating video fusion as a video-to-video conditional generation problem in latent diffusion space, our approach holistically models spatio-temporal dependencies across entire sequences and intrinsically ensures sequence-level consistency. On this basis, a text-guided degradation-conditioned ControlNet bridges high-level textual degradation descriptions with low-level visual priors, enabling interpretable and controllable guidance for structure-preserving fusion beyond purely data-driven conditioning. To handle heterogeneous and compound degradations, a state-modulated degradation-aware hierarchical mixture-of-experts module decouples expert selection into diffusion-state-aware filtering and degradation-aware routing. It prevents unreliable routing and fosters expert specialization to mitigate representation conflicts among diverse degradations. Experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, and multi-focus video fusion tasks and complex degradations validate that V2VFusion surpasses existing methods in fusion quality and temporal stability. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenDoubleJ/V2VFusion.
authors: Jiajun Chen, Han Xu, Yunfei Huang, Zhuoya Zhang, Guangcan Liu, Jiayi Ma
bullets: Targets frame-wise fusion methods that fail to model sequence-level spatio-temporal dependencies and diverse degradations effectively.
Reformulates video fusion as conditional video-to-video generation in latent diffusion space for improved temporal consistency.
Uses text-guided degradation-conditioned ControlNet to provide interpretable, controllable structure-preserving guidance.
Introduces a diffusion-state-aware, degradation-aware mixture-of-experts module for heterogeneous and compound degradations.
Experiments across infrared-visible, multi-exposure, and multi-focus fusion report improved fusion quality and temporal stability over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Many questions about videos ask for a number, such as how tall a person is, how far a cart travels, or how fast a ball leaves a ramp. We study this task, quantitative physical reasoning from video, where the inputs are a video, a question, and a prior of known facts such as object sizes, speeds, and distances from the camera to named objects. End-to-end video-language models lack an explicit metric scale and physical consistency, and their errors cannot be inspected. We present SceneRuler, which instead recovers a measurable physical scene and answers with that scene as evidence. Its central principle, Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction, builds, for each question, only the smallest scene that suffices to measure the asked quantity, and tests sufficiency on measurements rather than assuming it. The scene is written as a program whose structure a vision-language model writes and whose magnitudes are left to measurement. Physics-guided Fitting measures them through physical motion laws, so that gravity itself can anchor the metric scale, and marks every parameter, and the read-out of the asked quantity, as determined or undetermined. Each question receives a read-out and an answer. The read-out is the asked quantity evaluated on the scene, and it is empty when the scene does not fix that quantity. The answer is always given by a model that takes the scene as evidence. We evaluate on QuantiPhy and also apply the method to 27 in-the-wild videos that we collected, which have no ground-truth answers. On its validation split, the final answer reaches a mean relative accuracy of 0.709 against 0.624 for the strongest baseline, and the reconstruction determines the asked quantity on 47 of 158 questions, where the final answer reaches 0.781. Because every intermediate quantity is explicit, each answer can be traced to the objects, scale, and motion behind it.
authors: Yumeng He, Gezheng Kang, Fanlian Zeng, Yin Yang, Chenfanfu Jiang
bullets: Targets questions requiring physical quantities such as height, distance, and speed from video plus known prior facts.
Uses Minimal Sufficient Reconstruction to build the smallest question-specific scene that can determine the requested measurement.
Represents scene structure as a program, estimates magnitudes with physics-guided fitting, and can use gravity to establish metric scale.
Marks parameters and outputs as determined or undetermined; answers are generated with the reconstructed scene as evidence.
On QuantiPhy validation, achieves 0.709 mean relative accuracy versus 0.624 for the strongest baseline; fully determined cases reach 0.781 on 47 of 158 questions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.
authors: Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Yan Cui, Jinli Ou, Yuhua Zheng, Jianqiang Huang
bullets: Introduces Cognitive Inertia and Perceptual Inertia as two opposing failure modes of multimodal integration.
Presents TheaterBench, a benchmark featuring counter-intuitive videos that violate physical laws or common sense.
Finds severe Modal Polarization across current state-of-the-art video understanding models.
Reports that existing de-hallucination methods often shift the balance between the two inertias rather than resolve the conflict.
Positions perceptual-cognitive equilibrium as an important direction for future model evaluation and improvement.

papers.abstract: Existing game super-resolution methods typically operate at moderate upscaling factors, struggling to recover fine visual details from extremely low-resolution inputs (e.g., 120p). At such resolutions, super-resolution shifts from reconstructing existing information toward synthesizing missing visual details. While video diffusion models offer powerful generative priors for this challenging task, their dependence on future frames limits their applicability to interactive games. We present CIDER, a causal diffusion framework for extreme game super-resolution that synthesizes high-frequency details from current and past low-resolution frames, guided by G-buffers (depth and motion vectors) to preserve scene structure and temporal consistency. We collect data from two AAA games (Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong). To reduce inference load, we develop a lightweight latent projection encoder tailored to ultra-low-resolution inputs, fine-tune a decoder (TAE) on our high-resolution outputs, and distill the diffusion model to reach interactive frame rates. Our experiments demonstrate high-fidelity 8$\times$ upscaling from 120p to 960p at around 13 FPS, outperforming state-of-the-art game upscalers in visual quality and showing potential for 16$\times$ magnification.
authors: Christina Zhang, Jenna Kang, Colin Groth, Akshay Jindal, Stavros Diolatzis, Qi Sun
bullets: Targets extreme upscaling, where ultra-low-resolution inputs lack recoverable visual detail.
Uses current and past frames plus depth and motion-vector G-buffers to preserve scene structure and temporal consistency.
Combines a lightweight latent projection encoder, a high-resolution-trained decoder, and diffusion distillation to reduce inference cost.
Evaluated on Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong, achieving about 13 FPS for 8× upscaling and showing potential for 16× magnification.
Scope: designed for interactive games and relies on temporal context and G-buffer guidance.

papers.abstract: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/
authors: Jingchen Sun, Jiaxing Zhang, Qingqiao Hu, Dingqiang Ye, Yuqi Jia, Yijun Liang, Di Fu, Yunjie Tian, Dongdi Zhao, Changyou Chen
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of annotated or externally supervised video foresight training.
Uses on-policy self-distillation over past–future video pairs as a natural self-supervised signal.
Introduces a foresight score and contrastive privilege advantage to emphasize informative future content over irrelevant context.
Optimizes a tractable lower-bound surrogate combining true-versus-random future comparison with teacher–student distillation.
Improves base models by up to 14.2 points on open-ended prediction and 15.9 points on closed-ended planning, without harming general video understanding.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Future-OPSD and comparison with other training paradigms. (a) SFT learns annotated future descriptions y⋆ from past observations x using cross-entropy. (b) Naive OPSD uses a frozen future-aware teacher π0 to score the student’s own response ŷ, converting the teacher–student log-probability gap into token advantages for PPO. (c) Future-OPSD (ours) has a frozen teacher score the same response under the true future z (blue) and a reference future z̃ from another video (orange). The contrastive privilege advantage ℓzt −ℓz̃t compares the two futures, and the teacher–student distillation advantage ℓzt −ℓSt compares the true-future teacher with the past-only student. Their interpolation at down-weights context tokens supported by both futures (next / chop / the) while keeping content tokens specific to the true future (cilantro), helping the student focus on the most valuable future information. The advantages are clipped and centered into At for PPO, and inference uses only the student.

Figure 4. Case study: why Future-OPSD improves video foresight reasoning. On an EgoPlan-IT example with Qwen3-VL-8B, we compare the initial token advantages and trained predictions of Naive OPSD and Future-OPSD. A frozen teacher scores the same initial rollout under the paired future z and a reference future z̃ from another video, giving token log-probabilities ℓzt and ℓz̃t ; ℓSt is the past-only student’s log-probability. The context and content components are Ct = ℓz̃t − ℓSt and It = ℓzt − ℓz̃t . Before clipping and centering, Naive OPSD uses at = It + Ct, while Future-OPSD uses at = It + (1 − λ)Ct with λ = 0.75. Plotted values are initial advantages, with Ct and It below each token. Future-OPSD suppresses context information and amplifies decision-relevant content information, yielding the correct next-action prediction.

Figure 1. Not all of the future is equally important. To answer what will I do next? from what is seen now, only a small part of the future clip carries content information (rinse the knife); most of it is context information (tap, dish rack, sink, sponge) that neither answers the question nor reflects the expected action and trajectory of the ongoing event.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.
authors: Zirui Zhao, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong
bullets: Long-video token pruning and merging can lose accuracy because sparse frames may span unrelated scenes, causing 3D patch tokenizers to blend them before token selection.
The method analyzes frame similarity and tokenizer behavior across 16 open models to guide budget allocation.
A closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and tokenizer class to choose token grids and the reduction dimension before encoding.
Across five accelerators and three video LLMs, ESSENCE is more accurate in 58 of 60 matched-TTFT comparisons.
Using 80% of tokens, it matches full Qwen-model accuracy with 1.6× faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it improves accuracy by up to 3.4 points.

papers.abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.
authors: Mohammed El Amine Mokhtari, Matei Mancas, Virginie Vandenbulcke
bullets: Compared fixed perception agents and a common reasoning model using agent messages, a tool-explored evidence graph, flat text, or a single audio-visual model.
On 799 XD-Violence clips, flat text nearly matched the single model (F1 0.967 vs. 0.968), while graph and message interfaces were less accurate.
Sound events improved F1, consistent with annotators relying on sound or speech for most violent clips.
Stored-observation citations were generally faithful, but graphs did not improve faithfulness over flat text; the agent pipeline used about 3× the GPU time.
Results were broadly robust to prompt rewording and a larger reasoning model, though model scale changed the relative ranking of message passing and graph use.

papers.abstract: Surgical video analysis requires video object segmentation (VOS), yet existing methods are commonly based on pretrained model fine-tuning using a large number of expert labels. In-context segmentation (ICS) offers the promise of bypassing this high cost by segmenting a target video using a few annotated references, which are the sole source of surgical knowledge for a frozen model. However, existing ICS methods tend to draw such references at random, which concentrate on a few views that dominate a surgical video and can miss other objects of interest (e.g., transient instruments and small structures). To address these challenges, we propose INCISE, a training-free ICS framework for surgical videos. INCISE selects unlabeled frames from multiple surgical videos that jointly cover the local appearances of a target video, and then segments the target video using these references. With only 1.7% of training frames selected and annotated as references and no target video frame labeled, INCISE obtains 67.2% mean mIoU and outperforms the best SOTA fine-tuned method by 9.2 points. We hope INCISE can help establish ICS as a practical alternative to fine-tuning in surgical video analysis and other domains with a costly labeling burden.
authors: Yifan Xu, Bofang Zheng, Guangyu Meng, Nishchal Sapkota, Xianshi Ma, Xu Cao, Tianjiao Yu, Danny Z Chen
bullets: Addresses the high expert-labeling cost of fine-tuning-based video object segmentation.
Selects unlabeled frames across multiple surgical videos to cover the target video's local appearances.
Uses the selected frames as the sole references for a frozen model, with no target-frame annotations.
Using annotations for only 1.7% of training frames, achieves 67.2% mean mIoU.
Outperforms the best fine-tuned baseline by 9.2 percentage points, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) like CLIP have shown great success in image tasks, however, applying CLIP to open-vocabulary video recognition poses challenges. Due to the limited text information, directly fine-tuning CLIP on video recognition datasets may lead to overfitting and hinder its generalizability. A prevalent method is to enrich text information by generating prompts using Large Language Models (LLMs). However, limited efforts have been made to explore how to generate higher-quality prompts that can contribute to classify unseen categories, and how to further enhance vision-text alignment based on these prompts. In this paper, we propose P2CLIP (Prompt-guided CLIP), which aims to bridge this gap by exploring the impact of prompts across three aspects: category, video, and frame. At the category level, we argue that LLM-generated prompts under simple instructions may suffer from semantic overgeneralization, which can blur the category boundaries and hinder the performance of the model. To address this issue, we design Generic-Discriminative Prompt using LLMs to obtain discriminative category embeddings with rich semantic information. At the video and frame levels, we first use VLM and LLM to generate frame and video descriptions for enhancing vision-text alignment. Then we propose a Knowledge-Guided Temporal Aggregation mechanism, which leverages the expert knowledge derived from LLMs to guide the temporal modeling of videos and encourage a better construction of the joint visual-textual feature space. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, including zero-shot and few-shot settings, demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
bullets: Addresses CLIP’s overfitting and limited text-information challenges when adapting to open-vocabulary video recognition.
Generates Generic-Discriminative Prompts to reduce semantic overgeneralization and sharpen category boundaries.
Uses VLMs and LLMs to produce video- and frame-level descriptions for richer visual–textual alignment.
Introduces Knowledge-Guided Temporal Aggregation, using LLM-derived expert knowledge to guide video temporal modeling.
Experiments on multiple benchmarks in zero-shot and few-shot settings demonstrate the method’s effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models have made remarkable progress in generating high-fidelity visuals, yet their outputs still often exhibit physically implausible phenomena, including discontinuous dynamics and implausible event interactions. Existing representation alignment methods mainly transfer generic video features or short-range motion cues, treating physical plausibility as a single-level representation problem. To address this issue, we propose MiMaAlign, a hierarchical micro-macro alignment framework that transfers complementary dynamics-oriented and event-oriented knowledge into different abstraction depths of a pretrained video diffusion model. Specifically, micro-level continuous dynamics alignment imposes constraints by aligning diffusion features with a continuous-time motion representation learned by a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE), while macro-level event-commonsense alignment provides representations of object interactions and event semantics through an instruction-prompted vision-language model (VLM). With training-only auxiliary objectives, we align the complementary supervision from the two teachers with shallower and deeper generator features, respectively, enabling the generator to internalize the corresponding physical priors. Empirical evaluations show that, on CogVideoX-2B, MiMaAlign achieves a relative improvement of up to 21.0% in the Physical Commonsense (PC) score on the VideoPhy benchmark over the baseline, and also delivers substantial gains on the highly challenging VideoPhy2 benchmark, while maintaining general video quality on VBench and being supported by blind user comparisons.
bullets: Addresses discontinuous dynamics and implausible object-event interactions in T2V video generation.
Uses a Neural ODE to provide continuous-time motion supervision for shallow generator features.
Uses an instruction-prompted vision-language model to encode object interactions and event commonsense for deeper features.
Training-only auxiliary objectives transfer these complementary physical priors into the generator.
On CogVideoX-2B, improves VideoPhy Physical Commonsense scores by up to 21.0% relative to baseline, with gains on VideoPhy2 and preserved general video quality on VBench.

papers.abstract: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.
authors: Hidir Yesiltepe, Julius Berner, Arash Vahdat, Pinar Yanardag
bullets: Addresses reverse-KL distillation’s mode-seeking bias and resulting loss of sample diversity.
Uses exponentially reweighted student samples to match teacher posterior means at shifted noisy inputs.
Under Gaussian corruption, matching these means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior.
The stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without retraining.
On SDXL and FLUX.2 4B, PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods while remaining competitive on alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 4. PMD Training Framework. A noisy state zt is obtained through the student’s on-policy sampling process. The frozen teacher is evaluated at the shifted input zt + ρtλ, yielding the tilted posterior mean Tλ = Dt(zt + ρtλ, t). Conditioned on the same zt, the stochastic student generates multiple clean-image predictions using independent random inputs. These predictions are combined into an exponentially weighted mean, which is compared with the teacher target Tλ. PMD minimizes the resulting posterior-matching discrepancy through the loss LPMD, encouraging the student to recover the teacher’s conditional posterior distribution.

Figure 3. Exponential Tilting of the Teacher Posterior. Starting from the original teacher posterior q(x | zt), exponential reweighting by exp(λ⊤x) changes the relative prominence of its modes. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.
authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral, Kaan Oktay, Alec Helbling, Atakan Kara, Duen Horng Chau, Pinar Yanardag

They recover 90.0–96.3% of reward gains across six image models and 89.8% and 111.9% across two video models.

papers.abstract: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.

Experiments show leading instruction following on VTR, strong scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility, and higher realism than compared Code2Video baselines.

papers.abstract: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.
authors: Nathaniel Cohen, Nicolas Dufour, Am\'elie Royer, Alasdair Newson, Patrick P\'erez

AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time at 20.7 fps on one GPU; AURA 5B streams 720p at 9.7 fps.
Released resources include both model weights, 30K synthetic videos, and precomputed teacher trajectories.

papers.abstract: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce \textbf{WeMM-Video}, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.
authors: Changli Tang, Jie Yang, Tianyi Wang, Lei Li, Daoze Zhang, Zijie Xin, Zhan Liu, Li Li, Jinchang Xu, Fengyun Rao, Chao Zhang, Jing Lyu
bullets: Supports unified text, image, audio, and video processing in both fast instruct and explicit reasoning modes.
Offers 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants trained with progressive pre-training and multi-stage post-training.
The flagship 35B-A3B achieves a reported open-source state of the art on omni-modal video evaluations.
The 9B model reportedly surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct on these evaluations.
The model family, evaluation suite, and reproduction pipeline are publicly released for research.

papers.title: WeMM-Video: Pushing the Frontiers of Open-Source Omni-Modal Video Understanding

papers.abstract: Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution to a target data distribution. A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution, such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources. Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow matching with linear interpolation. Suppose the source distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an everywhere positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance $\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}$, and an $L$-Lipschitz score. Using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}(Ld\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}/\varepsilon)$ iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student's $t$ distributions with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommodating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.
authors: Yuchen Zhou, Lili Zheng, Yuxin Chen, Gen Li
bullets: Addresses limited sampling theory for heavy-tailed and multimodal flow-matching sources.
Analyzes Euler discretization with linear interpolation using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid.
Under positive differentiable source densities, finite total variance, Lipschitz scores, and a mild target second-moment condition, achieves error ε in ~O(Ld·TotVar_base/ε) iterations.
Covers multivariate Student’s t sources with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance.
Allows target distributions without smooth densities or bounded support.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a theoretical foundation for efficient sampling in flow matching with non-Gaussian sources, establishing non-asymptotic convergence guarantees that improve sampling efficiency.
papers.title: Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources: A Theory of Efficient Sampling
papers.tldr: Provides finite-step total-variation convergence guarantees for Euler flow-matching samplers initialized from broad non-Gaussian source distributions.

papers.abstract: Low-dose and thin-slice computed tomography (CT) images suffer from elevated noise that obscures anatomical detail, while clean references for supervised denoising are often unavailable. Although Noise2Noise permits self-supervised training from noisy pairs, direct regression tends to oversmooth fine structure. Averaging multiple independently generated samples mitigates this blur, though repeating multi-step diffusion sampling is costly. We introduce Noise2Noise with Improved Mean Flow (N2N-iMF) to accelerate this process via few-step sampling. N2N-iMF learns to generate one noisy image conditioned on its paired counterpart; at inference, independent outputs are sampled and averaged to suppress noise. We evaluated image quality and sampling efficiency on simulated thin-slice brain and low-dose abdominal CT across four sampling methods and averaging counts from 1 to 20, and validated the approach on real-world photon-counting CT (PCCT) brain scans. With ten samples per conditioning input and three network evaluations per sample, N2N-iMF achieved a mean absolute error of 2.60 HU on brain CT and 14.02 HU on abdominal CT, outperforming 50-evaluation denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) sampling (2.91 and 14.53 HU). On the same GPU, per-output generation time dropped from 7.29 to 0.43 s. Across eight PCCT cases, N2N-iMF reached a mean gray-white matter contrast-to-noise ratio of 1.341, versus 0.916 for Noise2Noise and 1.176 for DDIM. N2N-iMF accelerates self-supervised generative CT denoising without distillation while keeping the number of averaged outputs adjustable at inference.
authors: Xingyi Yao, Zhengtao Ma, Zhennong Chen
bullets: Addresses noisy low-dose and thin-slice CT when clean reference images are unavailable.
Trains on paired noisy images and uses Improved Mean Flow to generate denoised candidates with only a few network evaluations.
Averages independently sampled outputs to suppress noise and preserve fine anatomical structure.
Using 10 samples and 3 evaluations per sample, it improved MAE over 50-evaluation DDIM and reduced generation time from 7.29 to 0.43 seconds per output.
On eight real PCCT brain cases, it achieved higher gray-white matter contrast-to-noise ratio than Noise2Noise and DDIM.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces N2N-iMF, a method to accelerate self-supervised generative CT denoising via few-step sampling. This technique for improving diffusion model efficiency is directly transferable to video generation and world model research.
papers.title: Fast Self-Supervised Generative CT Denoising via Few-Step Sampling
papers.tldr: N2N-iMF enables fast self-supervised generative CT denoising by averaging independently generated outputs from few-step sampling, improving image quality while greatly reducing inference time.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers reuse key--value (KV) caches across denoising steps, which quickly becomes a bottleneck for long video generation. We find that quantizing temporally distant cache vectors leads to a large range and high quantization error, but that nearby video tokens in the KV-cache share a persistent pattern per channel. These patterns also vary across videos, motivating rotations that are adapted to each video's unique cache. We propose Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ), a method that rotates frames in the cache that are adjacent in time before quantization. For each block of temporally adjacent cache vectors, TRQ fits an orthogonal transform that maps the block's per-channel means to a vector that is close to a constant across channels. To keep the quantization format lightweight, we parameterize this rotation as a tree of $2 \times 2$ planar rotations, each stored with only two bits, followed by a fixed Hadamard transform shared across all blocks. The rotations are fit without gradients or changes to model weights, and we prove that a simple greedy fit is globally optimal for our 'mean-flattening' objective. The transforms are fit online for each new video, and we release fused Triton kernels to make this process efficient at inference. At 2-bit precision and matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over the state-of-the-art method QVG from 90.38 to 92.02 on LongCat-Video-13B and from 86.33 to 87.61 on HY-WorldPlay-8B, as well as improving other metrics.
authors: Ryan Lucas, Petros Prastakos, Rahul Mazumder
bullets: Temporal KV-cache reuse creates memory bottlenecks, while distant-token quantization suffers from large ranges and errors.
TRQ rotates temporally adjacent cache vectors to flatten per-channel means before quantization.
It uses gradient-free, online-fitted trees of 2-bit planar rotations followed by a shared Hadamard transform.
A greedy fitting procedure is proven globally optimal for the mean-flattening objective, with efficient fused Triton inference kernels.
At matched compression, TRQ improves VBench subject consistency over QVG on LongCat-Video-13B and HY-WorldPlay-8B, while also improving other metrics.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Temporal Rotation Quantization (TRQ) to improve KV-cache efficiency in Video Diffusion Transformers, directly addressing a bottleneck in long video generation and improving subject consistency.
papers.title: Online Temporal Rotations for 2 Bit KV-Cache Quantization in Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: TRQ enables accurate 2-bit KV-cache quantization for long video diffusion by learning lightweight, video-specific temporal rotations online.

papers.abstract: Tracking objects through transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. Recent work has extended traditional object tracking to detect state changes. However, existing methods require an initial object prompt and detect only its decompositions, missing assembly events, which begin with multiple objects rather than one. We therefore introduce a prompt-free formulation of this task, where the goal is to recover all object tracks and detect both decomposition and assembly events given only a video. Our key insight is that assembly is decomposition in reverse. Building on this insight, we present Atlas, a zero-shot system that constructs and jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions to recover object tracks and their transformations. We further introduce OmniST, a benchmark with dense annotations of objects and both transformation types. On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on existing benchmarks that only evaluate decomposition.
authors: Cheryl Lam, Yihong Sun, Bharath Hariharan
bullets: Addresses prompt-dependent tracking methods that miss assembly events involving multiple objects.
Introduces a prompt-free task: recover object tracks and both types of transformations from video alone.
Atlas is a zero-shot system that jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions.
Introduces OmniST, a densely annotated benchmark for objects, assemblies, and decompositions.
On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on decomposition-only benchmarks.
