papers.abstract: Real-time streaming video generation has gained rapid momentum in live content creation and interactive media. Deploying such systems in practice requires flexible scaling factors to accommodate diverse source resolutions, target displays, and computational budgets. However, extending fixed-scale generative video super-resolution (VSR) to varying target scales poses two challenges: downsampling from a larger fixed scale incurs redundant cost, while re-optimizing the diffusion transformer (DiT) is costly and alters the shared generative prior. To address both, we propose FlexVSR, a decoupled framework for continuous-scale streaming generative VSR with supervision at only a few scales. Our key insight is that naively resampling fixed-scale latents onto a new target grid induces scale-dependent input mismatch, which can be effectively addressed through parameter-efficient, scale-aware adaptation of the latent interface without updating the DiT. To this end, FlexVSR introduces ReLSA (Refined Latent Scale Adaptation), a lightweight latent adapter that constructs and refines target-grid latents before they enter the DiT, enabling a shared frozen VSR prior to generalize across continuous scales with only 0.274M trainable parameters and an adaptation cost of 7.3 H100 GPU-hours, while introducing no additional temporal dependencies and preserving the native causal streaming protocol. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive or superior reconstruction and temporal quality, lower latency than most native-scale streaming baselines and offline methods, and effective generalization to unseen continuous scales, filling the continuous-scale gap in real-time streaming generative VSR.
authors: Ji Wang, Haonan An, Jiasheng Zhang, Renlong Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and inefficiency of extending fixed-scale streaming VSR to diverse target resolutions.
Introduces ReLSA, a lightweight scale-aware latent adapter that refines target-grid latents before the diffusion transformer.
Uses supervision at only a few scales while generalizing to unseen continuous scales.
Preserves causal streaming and adds no temporal dependencies, with 0.274M trainable parameters and 7.3 H100 GPU-hours of adaptation.
Reports competitive or better reconstruction and temporal quality with lower latency than most compared streaming and offline methods.

papers.abstract: Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation transforms third-person recordings into first-person viewpoints, unlocking immersive AR/VR experiences and scalable demonstration synthesis for embodied robotics. Extending it to a streaming setting is expected to further enable live applications. However, existing methods suffer from degraded manipulation regions, overfitting and confinement to fixed-length clips with prohibitive latency. To address these limitations, we present StreamEgo, a real-time framework for unbounded, generalizable Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve intricate manipulation dynamics while supporting the streaming pipeline, a streaming dual-branch prior provides pixel-aligned guidance for translating appearance and skeletal kinematics. We also introduce a region-aware loss curriculum to improve generalization and stabilize multi-objective diffusion training. Furthermore, we distill the model into a chunk-wise autoregressive model, augmented with a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enabling high-quality, generalizable real-time streaming Exo2Ego generation at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.
authors: Tianyi Xu, Boyang Lyu, Yunkai Tang, Kairan Ding, Jiahang Li, Weiyu Guo, Yandong Guo, Shuchen Weng, Boxin Shi
bullets: Targets live AR/VR and embodied-robotics applications by converting third-person video into first-person views.
Uses a streaming dual-branch prior to provide pixel-aligned appearance and skeletal-kinematic guidance.
Introduces a region-aware loss curriculum to stabilize diffusion training and improve generalization.
Distills the system into a chunk-wise autoregressive model with region-aware corruption and first-chunk training.
Generates streaming video at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

papers.title: StreamEgo: Streaming Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation

papers.abstract: Personalized video generation faces a significant scalability challenge: as the number of custom subjects increases, existing methods suffer from severe identity leakage and semantic entanglement, resulting in videos with blended attributes and incoherent narratives. We identify that this stems from a lack of explicit binding between textual entity phrases and their corresponding visual patterns prior to fusion in diffusion models. To address this, we propose MultiBinder, a novel framework built on a ``bind-then-narrate'' paradigm. Our approach introduces a two-stage conditioning process before video diffusion. First, Cross-modal Entity Binding devises an entity-aware Q-Former to extract identity-centric features from each subject's reference image and tightly align them with its unique entity phrase, yielding disentangled ``identity tokens.'' Second, a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) acts as a ``narrative director'' in the Narrative-Aware Subject Arrangement stage, capturing the action of each subject from the text prompt and synthesizes contextualized subject features that encapsulate ``who is doing what'' and preserve role-specific distinctions. These features are then injected into a video diffusion model via dedicated conditioning pathways, ensuring precise attribute allocation. Extensive experiments on both general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks show that MultiBinder significantly outperforms existing methods in multi-subject identity fidelity.
authors: Wei Li, Yiheng Zhang, Zhaofan Qiu, Ting Yao, Xiaoyan Sun, Tao Mei
bullets: Addresses identity leakage, blended attributes, and incoherent narratives as the number of custom subjects grows.
Uses an entity-aware Q-Former to align each reference image with its corresponding entity phrase, producing disentangled identity tokens.
Employs an MLLM to determine each subject’s role and action, creating context-aware features that preserve subject distinctions.
Injects these features through dedicated conditioning pathways into a video diffusion model.
Experiments on general and newly curated multi-subject benchmarks report significantly better identity fidelity than existing methods.

papers.title: MultiBinder: Preventing Multi-Subject Identity Leakage in Personalized Video Generation

papers.abstract: Video-language models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on video-text retrieval and are increasingly used for egocentric video understanding. Yet, despite gains in zero-shot retrieval, they have shown limitations in compositional understanding, and it remains unclear whether they understand compositional relationships between verbs and nouns. In this work, we introduce Ego-ExBind, a compositional diagnostic protocol for analyzing pretraining exposure and verb-noun binding in egocentric video-text retrieval. Ego-ExBind consists of an Exposure Ledger built from the EgoClip pretraining corpus used by EgoVLPv2, which defines Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, and Unseen Atom splits for EPIC-KITCHENS-100 multi-instance retrieval (MIR). We further probe noun and verb binding channels through controlled noun-swap and verb-swap negatives. We find that zero-shot retrieval is positively associated with pair exposure within seen compositions, even after controlling for the marginal frequencies of verbs and nouns. However, higher pair exposure is associated with larger noun-swap margins and slightly smaller verb-swap margins. This asymmetry motivates us to test whether exposure reweighting can improve retrieval with little change in the measured swap margins. To isolate the effect of exposure input, we keep the trained checkpoint fixed and replace only the exposure input at inference. We demonstrate that this exposure reweighting can improve video-text retrieval without stronger verb-noun compositional understanding, and that the gain depends on the correct sample-level exposure correspondence. By separating exposure-driven retrieval gains from verb-noun binding, Ego-ExBind provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating whether future improvements in egocentric MIR reflect compositional understanding rather than pretraining familiarity.
bullets: Introduces a diagnostic protocol for separating pretraining familiarity from compositional binding in video-text retrieval.
Builds exposure-based Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, and Unseen Atom splits from the EgoClip corpus, with controlled noun- and verb-swap negatives.
Pair exposure correlates with zero-shot retrieval performance even after accounting for separate verb and noun frequencies.
Inference-time exposure reweighting improves retrieval while leaving measured binding largely unchanged, and requires correct sample-level exposure correspondence.
The framework helps assess whether future retrieval gains reflect genuine compositional understanding or pretraining exposure.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Swap margins relate differently to pair exposure. Within Seen Compositions, noun-swap (a) and verb-swap (b) margins are plotted against log10(1+ f (v,n)) over 8,592 frozen-model probes. papers.abstract: The proliferation of AI-generated videos has raised growing concerns about misinformation, fraud, and potential societal risks, creating an urgent need for detection. Reconstruction-error-based methods have shown strong empirical performance for AI-generated image detection by exploiting discrepancies between an input and its reconstructed version. Their extension to video detection, however, faces two challenges: (i) a fixed reconstructor is not optimized for the detection objective and may yield weak discriminative signals; and (ii) an additional raw-video feature stream is often introduced to model temporal dependencies, increasing architectural overhead. To address these challenges, we develop a detector that learns and exploits reconstruction errors as a unified source of spatiotemporal evidence. First, we jointly optimize a reconstructor and the downstream classifier to produce reconstruction errors that are more informative for detecting AI-generated videos. Second, we show that consecutive reconstruction errors alone carry temporal evidence, and thus a 3D convolution over them captures spatiotemporal evidence without a raw-video stream. Extensive experiments on over 30 existing AI-video generators demonstrate competitive performance against baselines.
authors: Jiahua Jiang, Jinglai Li, Jianru Zhang, Jin Zhu
bullets: Addresses weak detection signals from fixed reconstructors and the overhead of parallel raw-video streams.
Jointly optimizes the reconstructor and classifier for more discriminative reconstruction errors.
Uses consecutive reconstruction errors with 3D convolution to model spatiotemporal evidence.
Evaluated across more than 30 AI-video generators, achieving competitive performance against baselines.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video generation has made remarkable progress with diffusion models and transformer-based video architectures, yet generating coherent long videos from evolving textual descriptions remains challenging. Training long-video models from scratch requires substantial computation and large-scale multi-event data, while training-free multi-prompt generation must activate new prompt semantics without breaking temporal continuity. We identify a frequency-agnostic boundary coupling problem in existing transition strategies: weak coupling causes abrupt changes, flicker, and background jumps, whereas overly strong or coarse coupling may over-preserve source semantics and produce ghosting or duplicated subjects around prompt boundaries. To address this problem, we propose FreqSync, a training-free framework that formulates prompt transitions as frequency-selective boundary coupling. FreqSync combines Frequency-Synchronized Source-Conditioned Attention (FS-SCA) with Residual-Clipped Spectral Stitching (RCSS), enabling adjacent segments to share stable low- and mid-frequency structure and motion cues while keeping high-frequency prompt-specific details target-dominant under explicit residual constraints. Extensive experiments show that FreqSync achieves state-of-the-art transition smoothness and prompt alignment while maintaining strong perceptual video quality, demonstrating its effectiveness for coherent multi-prompt long video generation.
authors: Yipan Xu, Shuyong Gao, Jiyuan Fu, Keliang Yin, Jiayu Chen, Qianyu Guo, Yang Liu, Wenqiang Zhang
bullets: Addresses abrupt transitions, flicker, background jumps, ghosting, and duplicated subjects in multi-prompt long-video generation.
Combines Frequency-Synchronized Source-Conditioned Attention with Residual-Clipped Spectral Stitching.
Shares low- and mid-frequency structure and motion across adjacent segments while preserving target-prompt high-frequency details.
Experiments report state-of-the-art transition smoothness and prompt alignment with strong perceptual video quality.
Scope: training-free generation; effectiveness depends on frequency-selective boundary coupling and explicit residual constraints.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of FREQSYNC. Given a prompt sequence, FREQSYNC first encodes frozen text conditions and initializes overlapped latent segments with noise reuse. During iterative denoising, FS-SCA performs frequency-synchronized source-conditioned attention inside selected attention layers, while RCSS applies residual-clipped spectral stitching to denoised overlap predictions before the sampler update. After denoising, overlapped regions are removed and the clean latent segments are concatenated for VAE decoding, producing the final long video.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. On a three-prompt driving sequence, baselines suffer from viewpoint drift, weak prompt transition, ghosting, or duplicated traces. FREQSYNC preserves vehicle identity and motion while producing smoother semantic transitions.

Figure 6: Visual ablation of FREQSYNC. Isolated generation produces a hard cut. RCSS alone smooths the overlap region but lacks attention-level semantic handover. FS-SCA alone preserves the global layout but changes the chapel structure. Full FREQSYNC combines both modules for smooth transitions and stable identity.

Figure 2: Diagnostic observation. Strong frequency-agnostic coupling may over-preserve sourceside evidence and cause duplicated subjects. FREQSYNC transfers mainly low- and mid-frequency continuity cues while keeping target details controlled.
Figure 1: Teaser of FREQSYNC. Given a prompt sequence, FREQSYNC generates coherent long videos with smooth transitions, stable motion, and prompt-specific details.

Figure 9: Additional three-prompt generated examples. We show three representative three-prompt sequences, where each example spans two rows to cover a longer temporal range and two consecutive prompt boundaries. FREQSYNC maintains coherent temporal evolution across multiple semantic changes, such as scene, illumination, and action transitions. The results suggest that the proposed boundary coupling is not limited to a single transition, but can also support longer prompt sequences with successive target-prompt activations.

Figure 11: Additional qualitative comparison on a skateboarder sequence. The base prompt describes a young skateboarder gliding forward through an open public square, while the segment prompts transition from an empty dawn plaza to a festival plaza and then to a rain-washed night plaza. Kling2.6 [1] produces visually stable frames but shows limited scene progression. MEVG [33] and VideoInfinity [42] suffer from identity, viewpoint, or motion inconsistency. DiTCtrl [7] improves crosssegment continuity but introduces ghosting and blurred boundary artifacts. In contrast, FREQSYNC preserves the skateboarder’s motion trajectory while progressively changing the plaza environment and illumination.

Figure 12: Additional qualitative comparison on a hot-air-balloon sequence. The base prompt describes a hot air balloon, and the segment prompts change the lighting condition from early sunrise glow to bright daylight and then to violet dusk light. Kling-2.6 [1] preserves the balloon appearance but shows limited temporal and illumination transition. MEVG [33] and Video-Infinity [42] produce noticeable subject or scene inconsistencies, including multiple balloons, unstable scale, or abrupt viewpoint changes. DiTCtrl [7] maintains partial continuity but shows over-preserved source-side evidence and boundary-local artifacts. FREQSYNC better preserves the balloon identity and desert layout while producing a smoother lighting transition across the prompt sequence.

Figure 5: Temporal self-similarity around prompt boundaries. FREQSYNC preserves local diagonal continuity while reducing excessive cross-boundary similarity, supporting frequency-selective boundary coupling.

Figure 8: Additional two-prompt generated examples. We show eight representative two-prompt sequences. Each row corresponds to one generated video and visualizes key frames across a single prompt boundary. Across diverse transition types, FREQSYNC preserves the main subject, scene layout, and motion trajectory while allowing the target-prompt condition to emerge progressively. These examples further illustrate that the frequency-synchronized boundary coupling used by FS-SCA and RCSS can reduce abrupt visual changes without suppressing prompt-specific details.

Figure 10: Single-prompt long-video generation with FREQSYNC. We apply FREQSYNC to singleprompt long-video generation by assigning the same prompt to all segments. The four examples show a sunlit courtyard fountain, warm paper lanterns, a drifting maple leaf, and a Mars rover driving across a red crater plain. Even without semantic prompt changes, long-video generation still requires stable cross-segment continuation. FREQSYNC produces smooth motion and coherent visual content over extended durations, suggesting that its boundary-coupling mechanism can also benefit single-prompt video extension.

Figure 7: Boundary temporal-frequency analysis. FREQSYNC shows stronger low-frequency continuation and lower high-frequency variation around prompt boundaries. This supports our frequencysynchronized boundary coupling design, where low-frequency components preserve structural continuity and high-frequency instability is suppressed near transitions.

Table 5: Per-seed quantitative results of all compared methods. We report the results of MEVG [33], Video-Infinity [42], DiTCtrl [7], and FREQSYNC under three random seeds: 42, 123, and 999. The shaded average rows correspond to the results reported in the main paper. CSCV and Motion Smoothness are reported as percentages.

Table 4: Main hyperparameters in the supplementary configuration file. The table lists the core parameters included in config.yaml. FS-SCA controls frequency-selective attention-level source conditioning, while RCSS controls residual-constrained prediction-level boundary stitching.

Table 9: Paired OFAT sensitivity analysis. Absolute scores are shown for each configuration; the default is the reference. “DC+k” is the logged temporal-frequency-bin partition. No tested alternative dominates the default across all metrics.

Table 1: Quantitative comparison. Results are averaged over three seeds on the 130-case multi-prompt benchmark. FREQSYNC delivers the strongest overall performance, achieving the best scores on CSCV, Text-Image Similarity, T2V Alignment, and Physical Consistency, while remaining highly competitive on Motion Smoothness and Visual Quality with only marginal gaps to the best results. Best scores are in bold; second-best scores are underlined.

Table 3: Blind human evaluation on 40 anonymized cases with 30 participants. Mean five-point scores are reported, where higher is better in every column. For source leakage and artifacts, higher scores mean fewer artifacts. Best scores are in bold.

Table 2: Ablation study on a 40-case subset. Ablations are conducted on a representative 40-case subset covering all transition modes under a single random seed. CSCV is the primary boundarytransition metric. Segment-level Text-Image Similarity is reported as a prompt-fidelity reference and is not boundary-aware. Best results are in bold and second-best results are underlined.

Table 6: Paired 100-case analysis against DiTCtrl. Differences are FreqSync minus DiTCtrl; CSCV differences are in percentage points (pp). All listed confidence intervals exclude zero. Minor differences from subtracting displayed scores arise from rounding.
Table 8: Controlled 40-case frequency-routing ablations. Mean ± standard deviation; all scores are higher-is-better. The routing tuple gives source weights (L,M,H).
Table 7: Cross-backbone evaluation. All metrics are higher-is-better; CSCV and Motion Smoothness are percentages. Best results are bold within each backbone.

Table 10: Cutoff–layer interaction sweep. Every cell lists CSCV (%)/T2V Alignment. These interaction results come from a separate paired study and should not be combined numerically with the OFAT table.

Table 11: Inference cost as prompt count increases. Runtime is mean ± standard deviation over three timed runs (seconds); memory is peak allocated GiB. Counted FLOPs are in TFLOPs per sequence. Percentage increases are relative to DiTCtrl.
Table 12: Existing assets used in this work. We cite the original sources in the main paper and follow their corresponding licenses or usage terms.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free multi-prompt long video generation via frequency-selective coupling; fits video diffusion.
papers.title: Frequency-Synchronized Boundary Coupling for Training-Free Multi-Prompt Long Video Generation
papers.tldr: FreqSync is a training-free framework for generating coherent long videos from multiple evolving prompts by selectively coupling segment boundaries across spatial frequencies.

papers.abstract: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.
authors: Zhihao Hu, Jianqi Ma, Jun Zhang, Jiayang Bai, Haifeng Shi, Yanxiang Zhuang, Zhongqian Sun, Weidong Zhang, Wei Yang
bullets: Targets the challenge of jointly achieving high visual fidelity, frame rate, responsiveness, and long-term stability in interactive game video generation.
Redesigns the VAE for efficient 1080p decoding and real-time synthesis.
Uses diffusion forcing with an extended temporal training horizon to capture long-term dependencies and persistent memory.
Applies post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while preserving visual and temporal quality.
Experiments report improved fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the inference pipeline. During inference, the 3D UNet-based Diffusion Model takes noise as input, injects control signals via cross-attention, and propagates historical frame information through temporal attention. After multiple denoising steps, the reconstructed latents are decoded by the VAE decoder to produce the generated video frames.

Figure 2: Overview of the ADCS. Designed to capture rich features of AAA games—including diverse landscapes, dynamic interactions (e.g., climbing, swimming), and photorealistic lighting—the system achieves a daily throughput of >10M frames and densely covers KM2s of virtual terrain within several days.

Figure 7: Qualitative comparison with state-of-the-art approaches on Genshin Impact. We show our method and the competing approaches on four different cases over a one-minute rollout; rows are methods and columns are timestamps.

papers.title: Streaming-AAA: Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency

papers.abstract: Long-form video understanding, as a fundamental yet crucial vision task, is being revolutionized by multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based video agents. However, the retrieval-driven nature inherent to these agents creates a significant bottleneck, forcing them to reactively fetch clips based on local saliency without a global temporal plan. To address this, we present ForeSeek, a foresight-driven video agent that transforms long-video reasoning from reactive retrieval into predictive exploration. Rather than blindly probing the timeline, ForeSeek forms visually grounded expectations over unseen temporal regions, verifies them through targeted observations, and continuously refines its search based on emerging evidence, where failed expectations serve as informative signals for principled backtracking. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training framework that equips MLLMs with foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision making. Extensive experiments on five long-video benchmarks demonstrate that ForeSeek consistently improves the efficiency--accuracy trade-off of long-video reasoning, achieving competitive or superior accuracy while observing $2.5$--$4.4\times$ fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent. Code is available at https://github.com/harry0021/ForeSeek
authors: Yuchen Sun, Siyuan Cheng, Shi-Zhe Chen, Yixin Qin, Jinwen Luo, Zheng Wei
bullets: Addresses the lack of global temporal planning in retrieval-driven long-video agents.
Builds visually grounded expectations about unseen regions, verifies them with targeted observations, and backtracks when expectations fail.
Uses a two-stage training framework for foresight-guided reasoning and efficient decision-making.
Across five long-video benchmarks, achieves competitive or better accuracy while observing 2.5–4.4× fewer frames than the strongest search-based agent.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ForeSeek. ForeSeek enables foresight-guided reasoning by anticipating unseen regions and refining beliefs through evidence. Phase 1: sparse glimpses initialize a temporal belief and prediction. Phase 2: verification updates beliefs, with failed predictions guiding search redirection.

Figure 3: Unified analysis of ForeSeek. (a, top) Per-round frame-cap sweep on VideoMME, LongVideoBench, and LVBench; (a, bottom) Phase-1 initial-budget and compression-scale trade-offs, with EVA as a fixed-cost reference; (b) ablation of the prediction–verification mechanism (ForeSeek, w/o PV Supervision, and w/o PV Mechanism) under SFT and RL; (c) sub-linear budget scaling across VideoMME duration buckets.

papers.tldr: ForeSeek enables MLLM video agents to reason through long videos by predicting and verifying relevant future regions instead of reactively retrieving clips.

papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion models are widely deployed for their efficiency. However, reinforcing them with black-box rewards, as is routine for multi-step models, faces two structural challenges. First, a few-step generator is a sampler rather than a score model, so its velocity is not the forward velocity of the generated distribution. Second, it must be anchored to the undistilled teacher, which shares no transitions with it. Existing few-step RL methods handle the latter with a marginal KL to the teacher, but each pays for the former in its reward credit. We propose Shadow Posterior Matching (SPM), which renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and obtains the credit from their shadow posterior. From the KL-regularized reward objective, we derive a regression loss that turns reward values into a reward direction while anchoring the generator's outputs to the teacher and aligning the shadow inputs with the deployed inputs. Applied to 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step RL methods.
bullets: Few-step diffusion generators are samplers, making standard reward-credit assignment unsuitable because their velocity differs from the generated distribution’s forward velocity.
They also require anchoring to an undistilled teacher despite sharing no transitions with it.
SPM renoises generated samples into shadow inputs and uses their shadow posterior to obtain reward credit.
A regression loss derived from a KL-regularized reward objective converts reward values into a reward direction while aligning deployed and shadow inputs and anchoring outputs to the teacher.
On 4-step generators, SPM achieves higher rewards with less reward hacking than prior few-step reinforcement-learning methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Shadow Posterior Matching. (a) The deployed few-step sampler generates final samples without gradients, and their black-box rewards yield group-relative advantages. (b) Renoising with fresh noise pairs each shadow input ys with a posterior sample x and the velocity u. (c) Colored arrows show three velocity differences: u − F (ys, s) for shadow credit, and vT − F̂s and F − F̂s at (ŷ, τ) for teacher anchor and endpoint matching. A regression loss pulls the generator’s velocity vθ(ys, s) along their weighted sum Gs.
Figure 3. Qualitative comparison. Samples are generated from GenEval (left), OCR (center), and PickScore (right) test prompts.

Figure 1. Reward curves with a single black-box reward. The reward is GenEval (top) or OCR (bottom). Left: training reward on test prompts. Right: ImageReward on DrawBench prompts. SPM achieves higher task rewards with better image quality.

Figure 4. Ablation results on visual text rendering. Left: OCR reward on test prompts. Right: ImageReward on DrawBench prompts. EM and AW denote endpoint matching and adaptive weighting, respectively. α is the tilting temperature, with a default value of 0.1.

Table 2. Quantitative results. We report training rewards on test prompts, and image-quality metrics and preference scores on DrawBench prompts. Higher is better for all metrics. The best 4-NFE results within each task are shown in bold and second-best results are underlined.

Table 1. Few-step RL paradigms, distinguished by their reward credit. Reward value: the credit is computed from measured reward values, without the reward’s gradient or a learned proxy. Final call: the deterministic final call receives credit from a black-box reward (◦ means only through a learned proxy, and – means not applicable, since the paradigm needs the reward’s gradient). Sharp sample: no reference in the update is built from the generator’s own velocity, so the samples receive no shift toward the posterior mean and stay sharp. Reward direction: the reward provides an update direction independent of the anchor’s force instead of only reweighting the anchor. Teacher KL: the generator is anchored to the teacher by a KL between their marginal distributions.

papers.selection_reason: Reward fine-tuning method for few-step diffusion generators; technically transferable to video diffusion models.
papers.title: Reinforcing Few-Step Diffusion Models via Shadow Posterior Matching
papers.tldr: Shadow Posterior Matching enables more effective and less reward-hacking reinforcement of few-step diffusion generators by deriving reward guidance from renoised shadow samples.

papers.abstract: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: https://github.com/yermandy/TwinD
authors: Andrii Yermakov, Jan Cech, Mario Fritz, Jiri Matas
bullets: Existing detectors perform well on blending fakes but struggle on entire face synthesis (EFS), where blending traces are absent.
TwinD uses reconstruction twins to target neural decoder traces and blob twins to target blending artifacts, without requiring a generator or face-shaped mask.
Across 19 datasets, TwinD achieves 96.3% mean AUROC: 98.1% on blending datasets and 95.6% on EFS datasets.
Training on twins alone still achieves 94.3% mean AUROC across three seeds.
Code, trained models, and training data are publicly released.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of TwinD. (a) A twin is a fake made from a real frame. The traces of the autoencoder are amplified 10× for visualization. (b) Each fake is paired with the real frame it was made from. Both get the same augmentation, so they differ only by the manipulation. TwinD is a frozen PEcoreL with LoRA, trained on batches of such pairs. (c) Mean video-level AUROC (%) on the EFS and Blending datasets of Tab. 1. Gray bars show the best prior detector of each kind.

Table 3. Results per generator. Video-level AUROC (%) on DF26, OF and MV for each of their generators. The row of TwinD is the AUROC. Every other row is the difference to TwinD in percentage points, green if higher and red if lower. The prior detectors are the four best AIGC detectors and the four best facial deepfake detectors of Tab. 1. The other seven are in Tab. S11 in the supplementary. The rows under TwinD make the reconstruction twins with another autoencoder instead of CogVideoX. HV is HunyuanVideo, T2V is text-to-video and I2V is image-to-video. papers.selection_reason: Addresses the generalization gap in deepfake detection by training on 'twins' (reconstruction and blob twins) to handle entire face synthesis, a task within video understanding and manipulation detection.
papers.title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis
papers.tldr: TwinD improves deepfake detection on unseen entire-face synthesis by training on two generator-free synthetic “twin” manipulations that capture decoder traces and blending artifacts.

papers.abstract: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.
authors: Yutong Guan, Meixing Shi, Haoran Sun, Bing Sun, Yuxiang Cai, Yankai Jiang
bullets: Builds a hierarchical, time-indexed memory that aligns diverse evidence along a unified video timeline.
Uses temporal cues from retrieved evidence to constrain and guide subsequent memory access.
Introduces retrieval skills that adapt search targets, memory operations, temporal ranges, and stopping decisions based on the current evidence state.
Evolves skills through reward-guided policy improvement, accepting useful policy patches without updating model parameters.
Across four benchmarks, achieves 60.1% average accuracy and an 8.6-point average gain over prior best methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall pipeline of EvoMem: hierarchical time-indexed memory construction, skill-guided retrieval over textual, interval, and visual evidence, and reward-guided active skill bank updates without modifying model parameters.

papers.abstract: Flow matching enables high-quality image and video generation, but its iterative sampling process requires repeated evaluations of large neural networks. Existing few-step methods can distort the output and reduce its agreement with a many-step reference. We propose TrajCal, a training-free calibration framework for few-step sampling. Based on scatter search, a well-established metaheuristic for difficult optimization problems, TrajCal starts with diverse seed schedules, deforms and combines these candidates, and selects one fixed schedule by final output fidelity for reuse on new inputs. For both image and video generation, TrajCal achieves higher reference fidelity than all compared baselines at low evaluation budgets while maintaining competitive visual quality. The search is effective even with randomly generated seeds, while trajectory-based seeds further improve fidelity. For cross-style generalization, photography-calibrated schedules also improve fidelity on unseen image styles.
authors: Junchi Zhang, Zihan Gu, Jiangcan Jia, Lulu Zhao, Wenbo Su, Hua Zhang
bullets: Addresses quality degradation and reference mismatch caused by few-step flow sampling.
Uses scatter search to generate, deform, combine, and select candidate time schedules based on final-output fidelity.
Calibrated schedules can be reused across new inputs without retraining.
Improves reference fidelity for image and video generation at low evaluation budgets while retaining competitive visual quality.
Schedules transfer across styles, and trajectory-based seeds improve fidelity beyond random seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Improves few-step sampling in flow matching for video generation, enhancing efficiency and fidelity without sacrificing quality.
papers.title: TrajCal: Trajectory-Calibrated Time Schedules for Few-Step Flow Sampling
papers.tldr: TrajCal is a training-free method that searches for fixed few-step sampling schedules that better match many-step flow-generation outputs.

papers.abstract: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/
authors: Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Bing He, Ke Xu, Zhongyuan Wu, Yuxuan Xie, Wenzheng Wu, Zhongyuan Liu, Youcheng Cai, Ligang Liu
bullets: Targets generative renderers that lose continuity and fail to follow evolving gameplay conditions.
Uses Dynamic-Context Learning for chunk-level interaction supervision and Recurrent History Compression to maintain continuity within a bounded token budget.
Introduces Cross-Representation Flow Alignment to support generalization across diverse scene proxies and target appearances.
Provides WorldPrism, a dataset of agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos with renderings and chunk-level annotations.
Improves reconstruction and visual quality on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench; qualitative results show sustained interactive rendering under changing prompts and references.

figures.caption: Figure 3. ContextRenderer overview. (a) Refreshed text, subject references, and proxy chunks condition next-chunk generation alongside visual history. Recurrent History Compression keeps an anchor and multiscale rolling history; generated latents update future steps. (b) Proxy and target tokens share spatiotemporal RoPE coordinates at a fixed local temporal start after history; dashed text takes prefix RoPE slots (MiniMax-H3) or RoPE-free cross-attention (Wan). (c) Cross-Representation Flow Alignment jointly trains direct rendering, shared reconstruction, and reconstruction-to-target variation; inference uses the direct path. Scene images and token counts are schematic.

(b) Conditional synthesis and VLM filtering produce corresponding proxies and target variants. papers.abstract: Temporal action localization (TAL) detectors must identify actions and estimate their temporal boundaries, but localization remains a major source of detection errors. While understanding what determines boundary placement requires faithful attribution of temporal evidence, existing attribution methods have not sufficiently addressed the temporal structure of TAL or the need to tailor attribution to boundary localization. We introduce a structure-aware attribution framework that averages contributions across random evidence-restoration orders following the Shapley-Shubik principle. We make it tractable by using the detector's receptive field to limit which time steps are ordered individually, and by approximating each order with a soft gradient path. For boundary predictions, we further introduce cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references that selectively remove adjacent evidence. We also adapt faithfulness evaluation to assess the joint effects of contiguous temporal evidence and the direction of boundary displacement. Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer demonstrate improved attribution faithfulness over existing methods. Attribution analysis and controlled interventions further reveal that class-score changes do not reliably track boundary displacement, providing input-level evidence that classification relies on content less informative about boundary placement. Code and evaluation artifacts will be publicly released.
authors: Ruoshan Lan, Zongru Shao, Chieh Tsai, Mihai Surdeanu
bullets: Addresses the lack of faithful, boundary-specific explanations for temporal action localization errors.
Averages contributions over Shapley–Shubik-inspired evidence-restoration orders, restricted by the detector’s receptive field and approximated with soft gradient paths.
Uses cell-structured restoration orders and boundary-anchored references to model adjacent evidence and boundary displacement.
Introduces faithfulness evaluation for contiguous temporal evidence and directional boundary shifts.
Experiments on THUMOS14 and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with TriDet and ActionFormer show improved attribution faithfulness; analyses indicate class scores do not reliably reflect boundary placement.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Random-order path attribution, shared by all targets and used directly as the class map (Sec. 3.2). (a) A candidate q is one position of the detector’s feature pyramid; the example is a TriDet detection on THUMOS14 (CliffDiving, 118.1–120.7 s; start and end frames outlined). Its path attributions aπ are averaged over R random orders of the units into apath; the baseline is the dataset mean m. Two approximations reduce the cost: (b) only the steps in the receptive-field window Wq are ordered independently, and (c) each order is integrated along a soft path whose cost does not depend on the number of units N . (d) Each candidate uses the faster of exact forward differences and the soft path, which for the wide windows of coarse pyramid levels is the soft path.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses temporal action localization with a structure-aware attribution framework, contributing to the understanding of temporal dynamics in video.
papers.title: What Places an Action Boundary? Structure-Aware Attribution for Temporal Action Localization
papers.tldr: A structure-aware attribution framework explains which temporal evidence drives action-boundary placement in temporal action localization.

papers.abstract: Human proficiency estimation is challenging because skill is a high-level and often subjective property that is not captured by action identity alone. Existing approaches leverage multimodal observations such as ego-exo video, gaze, pose, and inertial signals, but the gap between sensor-level evidence and abstract proficiency labels remains difficult to bridge. We present SkillLens, a proficiency estimation framework that uses atomic action descriptions as temporal guidance, rather than direct semantic supervision, to localize proficiency-relevant windows for dense visual-dynamics extraction. Each window is summarized into an action-dynamics feature and scored by a high-low prototype margin against higher- and lower-proficiency executions from the same activity-action category. Fusing these ego/exo PDM cues with a global ego-exo-gaze baseline through CORAL ordinal calibration, our method achieves 0.542 accuracy on Ego-Exo4D. Our project page is available at https://skill-lens.net/
authors: Deokhyun Ahn, Hyukjin Kim, Jae-Ho Han, Bumsub Ham, Heeseung Choi, Ig-Jae Kim, Haksub Kim
bullets: Targets the gap between multimodal sensor observations and abstract proficiency labels.
Uses temporal action guidance to localize proficiency-relevant windows for dense visual-dynamics extraction.
Scores window features via margins between higher- and lower-proficiency executions within the same activity-action category.
Fuses ego/exo visual-dynamics cues with global ego-exo-gaze features using CORAL ordinal calibration.
Reports 0.542 accuracy on Ego-Exo4D; the abstract does not specify limitations beyond the task’s inherent subjectivity.

We concatenate both signals and use a CORAL ordinal head to predict the final proficiency level.

papers.title: SkillLens: Action-Guided Dense Visual Dynamics for Proficiency Estimation
papers.tldr: SkillLens estimates human proficiency by using atomic action descriptions to identify skill-relevant video windows and compare their dynamics against high- and low-proficiency prototypes.

papers.abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.
bullets: Single-reference squared-error evaluation may favor blurred or prematurely stopped videos that reduce prediction variance.
The authors formally decompose this bias and show that Physics-IQ can improve as generated futures collapse, even when their distribution worsens.
Kernel Physics-IQ removes the incentive in expectation using two independent samples per condition.
Across five image-to-video models, two-step sampling lowered Kernel Physics-IQ; for CogVideoX, the official score rose by 0.055 while the proposed score fell by 0.131.
Controlled physical-system tests show the new metric prefers the true outcome distribution over collapsed predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Tied official scores hide different futures. (a) Predictors in a pendulum world that swings left or right with equal probability: each card shows what the predictor draws (line weight: probability; dashed: never drawn), and the pixel mean blends both swings into one video (diamond: mean position). (b) Exact scores, averaged with a ball dropped onto a peg: the raw official composite ties the first four, whereas Kernel Physics-IQ ranks the true distribution first, as it does among all 34 predictors. (c) Mask distance: staying still wins below the thresholds of Prop. 2.

Two-step samples disperse less: the dispersion premium they collect (dashed) outweighs their kernel loss, so single-sample scoring prefers them. A second sample measures the self-dispersion, which Kernel Physics-IQ subtracts. Frames: paper-smoke 2 s after the switch frame (Wan2.2, two seeds). Brackets (root-mean-square) and bars: Wan2.2 ST IoU distances on whole clips, mean over 66 scenes.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes evaluation of video generators as world models and denoising-step effects; relevant to world models and video diffusion.
papers.title: What One Sample Cannot See: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Score Higher on Physics Benchmarks
papers.tldr: Physics-IQ can reward video world models for producing less varied, less realistic futures; Kernel Physics-IQ corrects this using two independent samples per condition.

papers.abstract: Current multi-shot video generators render only limited durations per pass, requiring long movies to be stitched from local segments across which narrative progression and visual identity drift. To synthesize long-horizon movies with Coherence across Time, we present CaT-Movie, a multi-shot generation system consisting of a global story planner and a local window renderer. The planner expands user requests via a large language model to preserve, infer, and complete story details, while deterministic code maintains the resulting storyboard across shots to compile self-contained shot prompts and index reference frames from generated history. To execute this guidance, the renderer applies reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention to route identities from the indexed frames while isolating per-shot textual conditions. Given the scarcity of high-quality open-source multi-shot data, we construct a dataset of over 350K film shots annotated with semantic state transitions, entity grounding, and multi-granularity requests. We further build CaT-MBench, a benchmark on held-out films with the same annotations. It gives every baseline its native format and counts cross-shot consistency only when a cut opens a new camera setup, preventing repeated framing from passing as consistency. On CaT-MBench, CaT-Movie attains the highest average score and the most consistent characters among all methods. The project page is available at https://jinplu.github.io/CaT-Movie/.
authors: Jinpeng Lu, Haoyuan Shi, Yuanshen Guan, Jiyuan Xia, Bin Wu, Yinda Chen, Zhiwei Xiong
bullets: Addresses narrative progression and visual-identity drift when stitching short video segments into long movies.
Uses an LLM-based planner and deterministic storyboard tracking to create self-contained shot prompts and retrieve relevant prior frames.
Applies reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention to preserve identities while isolating shot-specific conditions.
Introduces a dataset of over 350K annotated film shots and the CaT-MBench held-out-film benchmark.
Achieves the highest average score and most consistent characters among evaluated methods on CaT-MBench.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the dataset and benchmark. One film pool and one schema feed the training data, (a) curation and annotation and (b) entity grounding, and CaT-MBench, (c) stories and questions and (d) cut-gated judging. The center chart gives the composition of both.

Figure 2. Overview of CaT-Movie. A planner writes one storyboard, from which a prompt compiler maintains cross-shot state and derives per-shot text ck, the frames each shot recalls, and an identity line cref for each recalled frame. The renderer denoises each window jointly with reference-routed sparse self-attention and shot-wise cross-attention, placing recalled frames before the reading shot’s first latent frame.

(Right) State questions of the storyboard rows of Tab. 2 whose change the per-shot text states and the video shows, states but the video omits, or leaves unstated.

CaTMovie renders the reference storyboard, the first group retrains from the base model, and the last replaces it with the shot-list request compiled directly or our planner’s storyboard. papers.abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.
authors: Amit Feldman, Ilan Shimshoni, Rotem Dror
bullets: Addresses the need to identify and assess procedural mistakes before recovery is no longer possible.
Uses observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions to recognize completed steps, localize them temporally, and classify execution errors.
Compares separate modular components with a joint model that predicts step identity, timing, and correctness together.
The joint model improves binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 from 80.7% to 84.1%, with the largest gain for slips.
The dataset split is revised to include erroneous videos across all splits; omitted steps are identified only after the video ends.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the two approaches. At each call, the system receives the current window V [τ, t] (sampled at 1 fps), the task description d, the instruction list I , and its prediction history. (a) The modular approach chains a Step Identifier, which selects an instruction s ∈ I or EXTRA; a Temporal Localizer, which predicts the attempt’s boundaries [a, b]; and an Execution Verifier, which classifies the cropped attempt V [τ+a, τ+b] as CORRECT, MODIFICATION, SLIP, or CORRECTION, using its previous execution labels as context. Extra actions are labeled ADDITION without verification. (b) The joint approach predicts all fields in a single structured response, conditioned on up to 12 previous predictions. In both, a NOT COMPLETED output (dashed) keeps the window start τ and extends the window by ∆ = 5 s; an accepted record updates the history and starts the next window at the predicted end.

papers.abstract: Advances in video generation and avatar synthesis enable new ways to answer user questions through visual explanations. This task requires a system to formulate a correct answer, translate relevant information into visual material, and deliver the explanation through an avatar's speech and actions. Existing benchmarks rarely assess whether avatars point to the visual content being discussed. We introduce VisualTalk-Bench for question-driven avatar-led video explanations in finance and Chinese and English education. It includes 800 curated reference videos and 100 independent evaluation requests, assessing Content Factuality, Speech-Visual Consistency, Visual Quality, Motion Smoothness, and Avatar-Content Pointing. Yet end-to-end video generators often struggle to align gestures with specific visual targets. To explore this challenge, we develop Avatar-O Agent, a modular reference implementation with explicit interaction planning. Experiments across six agents show that factual precision and visual quality do not guarantee accurate pointing. A 26-participant study comparing four agents finds that Avatar-O Agent receives the highest average ratings for visual guidance, perceived pointing accuracy, and explanation effectiveness. We will release the data and code.
authors: Xin Zhang, Tujie Xu, Zhiyi Chen, Xiaodong Zhang, Sicheng Yang, Minglei Li
bullets: Introduces a benchmark spanning finance and Chinese/English education, with 800 reference videos and 100 evaluation requests.
Measures factuality, speech–visual consistency, visual quality, motion smoothness, and avatar-to-content pointing.
Presents Avatar-O Agent, a modular system that explicitly plans avatar–content interactions.
Across six agents, strong factuality and visual quality did not ensure accurate pointing.
A 26-participant study rated Avatar-O Agent highest for visual guidance, pointing accuracy, and explanation effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Sign language translation and recognition have been shown to benefit from various pretraining approaches. We propose a novel two-stage pretraining approach for the motion encoder, which first learns to reconstruct masked motion, followed by joint masked prediction of pseudo-gloss units and motion. Pseudo-glosses serve as an intermediate structured representation of natural language text and are obtained from the captions by a large language model. We curate a corpus of about 1,100 hours of American Sign Language from five public datasets, estimate 2D pose for all clips and define an evaluation protocol. We then reproduce state-of-the-art translation methods and evaluate them using the same train and test splits. We propose a translation model built on our pretraining strategy, and this model outperforms the previous state-of-the-art methods Uni-Sign and SHuBERT, as well as the YouTube-ASL baseline, on the How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki and OpenASL datasets. Furthermore, the gain from the joint pretraining using motion and pseudo-gloss grows as translation data shrinks. A classifier built on the same encoder also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ASL Citizen isolated sign recognition and outperforms our reproduction of Uni-Sign on WLASL2000.
bullets: Uses a two-stage motion-encoder pretraining strategy: masked-motion reconstruction, then joint masked prediction of motion and LLM-derived pseudo-gloss units.
Curates approximately 1,100 hours of ASL video from five public datasets, estimates 2D poses, and defines a common evaluation protocol.
The resulting translation model outperforms prior methods and the YouTube-ASL baseline on How2Sign, ASL STEM Wiki, and OpenASL.
Joint motion–pseudo-gloss pretraining is especially beneficial when less translation data is available.
The shared encoder achieves state-of-the-art isolated-sign recognition on ASL Citizen and surpasses a Uni-Sign reproduction on WLASL2000.

papers.abstract: Tracking a hidden object through a video is effortless for humans, yet it remains a bottleneck for vision language models (VLMs). In the shell game, where a ball is hidden under one of several identical cups that are then swapped, VLMs that answer directly stay near chance, thinking models fail on long games, and fine-tuning learns only the lengths it has seen. We argue that the limit is serial computation: each swap must be composed with the last result, and a VLM of fixed depth has only a fixed number of state transitions for it. To address this, we propose RecurrentVLM, which makes every attention layer of a pretrained VLM recur over time by computing the keys and values of finished frame groups from the layer's own output. With a single answer token, RecurrentVLM reaches 100% on VET-Bench and 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps. We also observe several interesting phenomena: length generalization emerges suddenly at an aha moment; without recurrence, each swap costs an attention layer; the ball's state forms in the first four attention layers; and recurrence keeps the latest state at the cost of details of earlier moments. These results suggest that recurrent VLMs are a potential solution for tracking the states of unobserved objects in video. Code will be released.
authors: Dingqiang Ye, Jiacong Xu, Wen Zhang, Yiqun Mei, Vishal M. Patel
bullets: VLMs struggle with shell-game tracking because each swap requires composing a new state with the previous one.
RecurrentVLM applies every attention layer recurrently, recomputing keys and values from completed frame groups while using a single answer token.
It achieves 100% on VET-Bench, 99.6% on MET-Bench, and 99% on 50-swap games after training on at most 30 swaps.
Length generalization appears abruptly, while recurrence preserves the latest state but loses details from earlier moments.
The findings suggest recurrence can support tracking unobserved object states in video.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Recurrent KV cache. (a) A standard attention layer of the LLM caches keys and values of its input tokens. (b) We cache keys and values of the layer’s own output, once per frame group, so every attention layer becomes a recurrence over time. (c) Each query reads keys and values of earlier tokens’ inputs in (a), but of earlier frame groups’ outputs in (b).

Figure 7 Tracking the ahamoment. (a) Over training: share of swaps on which the frame-wise answer equals the model’s own last answer updated by the current swap (black), and per-swap accuracy on swaps 31–50 (red). (b) Accuracy on 50-swap games with one head of attention layer 4 switched off; any single head of attention layer 3 or 5 keeps at least 60%. (c) Per-swap accuracy with head 2 of attention layer 4 off.

Figure 1 Current VLMs struggle with the shell game. Claude-Opus-5.5 thinks for thousands of tokens and still errs; fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B drifts on games longer than in training. RecurrentVLM stays correct at every swap with one token.

Figure 5 Probing the ball across attention layers. (a, b) Linear probes reading the ball position from every layer output (three GDN layers between attention layers) after each swap of 100-swap games, fit on the first 30 (inset: swaps 1–10). RecurrentVLM reads the ball after attention layer 4 at all swaps, while the baseline needs one more attention layer per about two swaps, which limits it to 10 swaps. papers.title: Recurrent Vision Language Models Solve the Shell Game
papers.tldr: RecurrentVLM enables vision-language models to track hidden objects through long sequences of swaps by repeatedly reusing their attention layers over time.

papers.abstract: JEPA-based video encoders learn strong representations for video and image understanding through prediction in latent space. However, their standard pretraining predicts features within individual images or video clips, without explicitly exploiting paired camera views of the same object or moment. Consequently, the learned representations may not reliably support matching across different camera viewpoints. To solve this problem, we introduce multi-view predictive post-training to strengthen cross-view instance and temporal correspondence while retaining independent single-view inference. A shared encoder processes masked context views independently, and a training-time predictor jointly predicts latent tokens for masked context regions and a fully held-out view. We alternate cross-view prediction with single-view masked prediction on general image and video data to help retain the encoder's pretrained capabilities. After only 9,000 post-training updates on a single GPU, MV-JEPA improves cross-view instance retrieval and coarse cross-camera moment retrieval on various datasets, with further gains in zero-shot action-phase retrieval and frozen-feature classification on AE2. Frozen-probe evaluations further indicate that post-training largely preserves motion recognition, image recognition, and dense semantic segmentation performance on the evaluated benchmarks. Together, these results demonstrate that multi-view predictive post-training can strengthen instance and coarse temporal correspondence in JEPA video encoders without modifying the encoder architecture or single-view inference interface.
authors: Yangchen Zhao, Ali Payani, Caiwen Ding
bullets: Addresses weak cross-view instance and temporal correspondence in standard JEPA pretraining.
Uses a shared encoder with a joint predictor for masked context views and a fully held-out view.
Alternates multi-view and single-view masked prediction to retain pretrained image and video abilities.
With 9,000 post-training updates on one GPU, improves cross-view instance retrieval, coarse cross-camera moment retrieval, and some zero-shot and frozen-feature tasks.
Evaluations suggest motion recognition, image recognition, and dense segmentation are largely preserved; scope is limited to evaluated benchmarks and coarse temporal matching.

papers.abstract: Human-object motion synthesis requires coordinated human participation as objects move toward specified goals. However, reaching object targets does not ensure that contact is established and maintained, while adjustments that improve contact may interfere with task completion. We introduce CoRelate, a diffusion framework that coordinates full-body human-object motion through explicit interaction relations and task feedback for rigid and articulated objects. We represent intended participation through hand-part relations that specify the participating hand, its part-relative reference position, and participation interval. These relations serve both as generation conditions and as references for measuring interaction realization. At each denoising step, a temporal refiner trained jointly with the generator combines relation deviations, task residuals, and motion features from the current prediction to jointly update human and object motion across the sequence. After generation, temporal motion correction addresses remaining contact failures by optimizing local motion segments while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion. Experiments demonstrate improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success over the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies support the benefits of relation conditioning and the complementary roles of task and relation feedback.
authors: Zhiwen Qiu, Daisy Lin, Diyu Zhou, Jialin Wu, Rosita Ji, Saleh Kalantari
bullets: Targets the challenge of achieving both object-goal completion and sustained human–object contact.
Conditions generation on participating hand, part-relative reference position, and interaction interval.
Uses a temporal refiner to jointly update human and object motion from relation deviations, task residuals, and current motion features.
Applies local temporal correction after generation to fix contact failures while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion.
Experiments report improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success; ablations support relation conditioning and combined feedback.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CoRelate. (A) From the task conditions and a task-only proposal X, we construct relations R: a hand, a wrist reference xrel in the part frame that moves with the part, and establish, hold, and release phases. (B) R conditions the generator Dθ and is the reference for relation feedback z (blue paths). At each denoising step, Fψ combines z, task residuals etask, and features f to update human and object motion, with R and goals g fixed. (C) Temporal correction then edits local hand motion with the object trajectory fixed followed by finger refinement.
Figure 4. Qualitative ablation visualization. We progressively add task and relation feedback to the no-feedback baseline and highlight incorrect interactions.

Table 1. Comparison on FullBodyManipulation dataset. CoRelate achieves lower object-target errors and higher contact F1 and complete interaction success than the evaluated baselines. † denotes task-adapted methods.
Table 3. Ablation study. Each design choice contributes and task and relation feedback show complementary gains when combined.

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based human-object motion synthesis, relevant to video generation.
papers.title: CoRelate: Coordinated Human-Object Motion Synthesis through Interaction Relations
papers.tldr: CoRelate synthesizes coordinated human–object motions by combining explicit hand–object interaction relations with task-aware diffusion refinement and post-generation contact correction.

papers.abstract: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised video encoders are commonly trained to either reconstruct pixels or predict latent features, yet it remains unclear how these objectives shape representations for downstream dynamics. We present a capacity-matched study isolating this choice: two identical video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck are trained under autoencoding and V-JEPA objectives on a continuous control environment. We introduce a simple asymmetric discretization scheme to apply the same bottleneck to the predictive model. The resulting representations exhibit a clear trade-off: the autoencoder preserves substantially more physical state information and achieves slightly better one-step latent prediction, while the predictive encoder accumulates less error under autoregressive rollout. Structural probes suggest that this advantage is associated with greater robustness to low-level visual perturbations and stronger dependence on temporal context. These results indicate that predictive and reconstructive objectives induce distinct representations of dynamics, trading state fidelity for properties that may benefit long-horizon prediction.

Introduces asymmetric discretization to apply the same discrete bottleneck to the predictive V-JEPA model.

Predictive representations accumulate less error during autoregressive rollout, with benefits linked to robustness to visual perturbations and stronger temporal-context dependence.
The objectives create a trade-off between state fidelity and properties useful for long-horizon dynamics prediction.

papers.abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. We benchmark 17 multimodal models and find that they struggle substantially on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding. Performance degrades consistently as reasoning complexity increases, with models frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders, revealing a systematic failure in role-action association rather than coarse aggression recognition alone. We further observe that increasing model scale or generic reasoning models experience limited improvement. Finally, we explore a simple role-graph prompting strategy that encourages structured reasoning over participant interactions, leading to improvements in compositional reasoning. Our findings highlight that reliable aggressive-scene understanding remains a major challenge for current MLLMs and motivate future research on role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection. papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (omni-modal LLMs) can respond to spoken requests directly through voice and video calls. Such requests rely on the scene shared by the user and the assistant, so the same utterance may call for different help or for no response. Most audio-visual benchmarks provide questions as separate text input, and interactive benchmarks mostly score a response as a whole. It thus remains unclear whether a model recognizes when the user is asking for help, and whether its reply meets the user's need once the request is recognized. We propose O-IN-Bench to evaluate how well omni-modal LLMs understand spoken intentions. A model watches a complete video with native speech and outputs one text response, or [SILENCE] when no response is needed. O-IN-Bench contains 1,000 Chinese and English samples in five categories and 16 subcategories. Contrastive pairs combine the same request with different scene conditions to test whether the response changes with the context. A sample-specific rubric judges language, intent, and content separately, and O-IN-Engine verifies each rubric against the video. Across 30 omni-modal model configurations, the best overall score is 59.6, achieved by Gemini3.7-Flash. Gemini3.7-Flash passes 74.4% of the intent judgments but only 42.6% of the content judgments. When the speech is a conversation between peers rather than a request to the assistant, even strong models often keep responding. When a reply must satisfy several people, the best score is only 25.9. These results indicate that recognizing a request and meeting its requirements are separate abilities, and O-IN-Bench measures each of them.
