papers.abstract: Training autonomous driving models requires large and diverse datasets, collected primarily by vehicles. Scaling them entails investment in fleet operation, data processing and annotation. Road infrastructure records traffic and multi-vehicle interactions, yet the viewpoint gap between roadside and onboard sensors limits its direct use for training. Here we introduce AnyR2V, a framework that transforms multimodal roadside observations into seven-camera surround-view videos for different vehicle perspectives. It aggregates sequential observations into a shared scene representation of geometry and road-user motion, then renders appearance, depth and layout conditions along target-vehicle trajectories. Supervised by spatiotemporally aligned roadside-vehicle pairs, AnyR2V generates surround-view videos guided by scene structure and road-user motion. Existing roadside 3D bounding boxes are transformed into target-vehicle coordinates and paired with generated images, allowing one traffic recording and its annotations to yield training data from multiple vehicle perspectives. We construct R2V360, a dataset of 89 real traffic sequences at an urban intersection, with aligned multimodal roadside data and onboard surround-view videos. AnyR2V outperforms six scene reconstruction methods in image fidelity and in depth and semantic agreement between generated and real onboard images. We further evaluate generated videos along other vehicles' trajectories by adding them to real training data. Adding generated frames equal to 50% of the original real training frame count improves mean average precision (mAP) by 3.3-3.4 AP-points across three 3D object detectors on the real onboard test set, relative to real-data-only baselines. These results demonstrate that roadside traffic records can provide training data from multiple vehicle perspectives, offering a new data source for autonomous driving.

figures.caption: Figure 8: AnyR2V framework for roadside-to-vehicle surround-view video generation. a, Construction of the shared roadside scene. Sequential roadside point clouds and images are aggregated using 3D tracking annotations to construct a static background and instance geometry for dynamic objects. Together with object trajectories, these form a shared scene that can be queried at specified times. Instance geometry remains fixed, while position and orientation vary along each trajectory. b, Rendering of target-view conditions. Camera poses and capture times are determined along the trajectory of the recording vehicle or another target vehicle. The shared scene is rendered into appearance, depth and layout conditions, which respectively provide observed colours, relative depth distributions, and object categories and spatial extents. c, Video generation with tri-modal conditioning. The three conditions are encoded by a frozen video encoder and concatenated. A trainable condition embedding and four control blocks inject conditioning residuals into the frozen video backbone, guiding the progressive generation of video latents from Gaussian noise. The seven videos for a given vehicle are generated jointly and decoded separately for each camera by a frozen decoder. Videos for different vehicles are generated independently using the shared scene and model parameters. Flames and snowflakes indicate trainable and frozen modules, respectively. papers.abstract: Purpose: Surgical training benefits from explicit comparison between cases: in patient condition, in technique and in skill proficiency. Surgical vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising and flexible interface for this purpose. Yet current VLMs typically see one video at a time, and they often fall short when asked to compare videos. Methods: We propose EndoComparer, a VLM for comparative surgical video question answering with two components. (a) A Pseudo-Siamese Visual LoRA (PSVL) gives each video slot its own low-rank adapter over a shared frozen vision encoder, separating the two videos in the visual pathway at the cost of a single encoder pass. (b) A Perceive-then-Compare chain of thought (PtC-CoT) trains the model to first state what each video shows, then derive the answer from these statements. We further curate EndoDiffVQA, a benchmark of nearly 11K multiple-choice questions on video-pair over cholecystectomy and gastric bypass procedures, covering anatomy, tool, action and skill. Results: EndoComparer outperforms strong generalist and surgical VLMs on detecting and specifying difference between videos. Ablations show that two proposed components contribute complimentarily, and the model remains more robust under a video-swap control that exposes confusion between the two videos. Conclusion: Providing a dedicated visual reasoning path through PSVL and PtC-CoT makes cross-case comparison of surgical videos more robust for VLMs. EndoDiffVQA and EndoComparer provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for this task. Project page: https://camma-public.github.io/endocomparer

papers.abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce systematically unfair demographic outcomes when prompts leave protected attributes unspecified. For example, prompts describing nurses without specifying gender may disproportionately generate videos depicting female nurses. Mitigating unfairness in T2V generation is particularly challenging: training-based methods that modify model internals require architecture-specific access and risk disrupting temporal consistency, while sampling-based methods often incur costly pre-deployment video generation. We present the first conditional online approachability formulation of attribute-level fairness for T2V generation. Building on this formulation, we introduce Mem2Fair, a plug-and-play framework that maintains concept-conditioned Fair Memory. Using generated videos at inference time as feedback, Mem2Fair selects prompt-level attribute interventions based on the deviation from each concept's prescribed fairness target, without training or separate pre-deployment sampling. Experiments demonstrate that Mem2Fair consistently improves fairness over the unmodified generator and existing baselines across multiple demographic attributes, prompt settings, and target distributions, while maintaining comparable prompt-video alignment and video quality. We further demonstrate its effectiveness on commercial black-box T2V models.

papers.abstract: Video-based fall detection could support timely assistance when a person cannot call for help. Unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels challenge deployment. We examine whether joint training improves cross-dataset detection and subsequent local training. We analyze 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset. Positive clips contain a fall or collapse transition, while negative clips do not. We hold out each dataset in turn, training on the other eight. We evaluate three vision-language models (VLMs), Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL, and three visual baselines, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. We evaluate the stored source model without target data for training or selection. For each label budget, we update a separate copy using labeled clips from the held-out target dataset. We call this target-site personalization. We compare the Source-initialized model with Target-only, which skips source training but uses identical target clips and updates. Across nine targets, source training raises mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from frozen-model values of 0.821 to 0.912 for Qwen, 0.883 to 0.947 for LLaVA, and 0.939 to 0.962 for InternVL. With five target examples per class and 26 updates per run, 95% confidence intervals for the AUROC benefit over Target-only lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. With full-target training, they lie above zero only for Qwen and LLaVA. Separate VLM analyses reveal threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections. The benefit varies by model and label budget.
bullets: Evaluates cross-dataset fall detection across nine datasets, holding out each target in turn.
Compares three vision-language models and three visual baselines under zero-target transfer and local target-site personalization.
Source training improves frozen-model mean AUROC for Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL from 0.821→0.912, 0.883→0.947, and 0.939→0.962, respectively.
With five labeled examples per class, source initialization benefits Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN over Target-only training.
Benefits are model- and label-budget-dependent; VLMs also show threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections.

The lower panel shows their difference with its pointwise 95% bootstrap interval and a zero-effect reference line. Intervals are displayed only on the difference scale. papers.abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.
authors: Austin H. Cheng, Marcel M\"uller, Andreas Burger, Yeonghun Kang, Tsz Wai Ko, Marta Skreta, Luka Mucko, Ella Miray Rajaonson, Cher Tian Ser, J\'er\^ome F. Gonthier, Alex Zook, Varinia Bernales, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik
bullets: Addresses the gap between language models’ controllability and specialist models’ ability to handle 3D molecular coordinates.
Uses causal-transformer next-token diffusion to autoregressively denoise continuous coordinate tokens without enlarging context.
Trained end-to-end across twelve 3D chemistry tasks, spanning microsolvation, conformer search, and metal-surface adsorption.
A single model performs all tasks and surpasses specialized baselines for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation.
Demonstrates the feasibility of generalist multimodal models for language-and-chemistry generation.

Figure 2 Next-token diffusion with Nahual. (left) Next-token diffusion provides both the clean current sequence and the noisy next sequence as input. Each token is noised at an independent timestep. papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly in image and video understanding, yet their ability to reason over paired aerial electro-optical and infrared (EO-IR) videos remains poorly understood. Such video poses a harder test than standard RGB video QA: targets are often small, evidence may appear only briefly, viewpoints change with the platform, and useful cues may appear in only one stream. We introduce RAVEN-Bench (Reasoning over Aerial Videos with EO-IR aligNment), a paired EO-IR video QA benchmark for low-altitude aerial multimodal understanding. RAVEN-Bench contains 100 temporally aligned EO-IR video pairs and 1,200 human-authored four-way multiple-choice questions, each independently audited for answer keys, modality requirements, evidence intervals, and group validity. It supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation, and uses hierarchical capability levels and structured question groups to diagnose paired-input gain beyond the stronger unimodal condition, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence. We evaluate frontier, open-weight, and remote-sensing MLLMs, showing that aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported EO-IR reasoning. RAVEN-Bench provides controlled modality conditions and group-level diagnostics for auditing whether progress on RGB video benchmarks transfers to aerial cross-spectral understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yuhu990424/RAVEN-Bench and https://huggingface.co/datasets/TerraSenseAnalytics/RAVEN-Bench.
authors: Yu Hu, Jianyang Gu, Yue Cao, Hao Liu, Kangnan Wang, Jozsef Hamari, Zheng Liu, Mohsen Zardadi

Supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation under hierarchical capabilities and structured question groups.
Diagnoses paired-input gains, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence.
Evaluations show aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported cross-spectral reasoning; code and data are publicly available.

papers.abstract: In cinematic storytelling, sound and visual transitions do not always coincide in lockstep: dialogue frequently bridges across cuts to reveal reactions or introduces new scenes via J- and L-cuts, while deliberate silences pace the scene. Existing audio-visual generative frameworks, however, lack explicit mechanisms to coordinate independent visual and acoustic timing over extended horizons. As narrative duration and shot complexity scale, these systems struggle to maintain long-range dialogue pacing, often hallucinating speech during intended silences or erroneously driving mouth movements on silent listeners. To enable fine-grained cinematic control, we present DECOUPAGE, a screenplay-driven framework for long-form, multi-shot, and multi-character joint audio-video generation. Rather than coupling modality boundaries by default, DECOUPAGE uncouples generation into independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks governed by persistent character identities. DECOUPAGE builds on a joint audio-video diffusion model with dual-schedule temporal cross-attention, incorporating a directorial Lip-sync mechanism that selectively decouples speech conditioning from visual facial dynamics during off-screen dialogue. On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, DECOUPAGE achieves precise control over shot transitions, audio timing, and visibility-aware lip synchronization, directing 15- to 60-second screenplay-driven audio-video generation with multimodal coherence.

bullets: Addresses the mismatch between visual and acoustic timing in cinematic multi-shot storytelling, including J/L-cuts and deliberate silences.
Uses independently bounded visual and acoustic tracks while preserving persistent character identities across shots.

On multi-shot conversational benchmarks, controls shot transitions, audio timing, and off-screen dialogue for coherent 15–60-second generations.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in audio-driven avatar video generation have enabled increasingly realistic synthesis, yet achieving precise lip-audio synchronization, natural, human-like motion, and visual consistency over long sequences remains challenging. We present LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6, which builds on LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 to improve expressive naturalness and reduce error accumulation during extended generation, e.g., exaggerated lip movements and overly red, temporally unstable lip coloration, enhance the naturalness of facial expressions and coordinated head and body movements. These improvements are driven by a refined post-training pipeline that integrates reinforcement learning, improved classifier-free guidance strategies for DMD-based few-step distillation, long-video rollouts, and on-policy distillation. Together, these refinements improve expressive realism and enable the generation of videos exceeding 10 minutes while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Arena evaluations show that LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 outperforms its predecessor and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the improved post-training pipeline.
authors: Meituan LongCat Team, Xunliang Cai, Yiqi Chen, Feng Gao, Xiaoyu Kong, Le Li, Hongyu Liu, Xiaoming Wei, Tianyu Yang, Yong Zhang, Sijie Zhao

Arena evaluations report improvements over LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models.

papers.abstract: Surgical workflow assistance is inherently anticipatory: systems must reason about how procedures evolve, not just recognize the current frame. However, many prior approaches perform prediction in pixel space by synthesizing future frames, which primarily focuses on appearance fidelity rather than the semantic representations required for downstream reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose a feature-space semantic forecasting framework that models temporal dynamics directly within the representations of a frozen Vision Foundation Model (VFM). Specifically, we build a hierarchical target representation from multi-layer VFM features, replace future-frame feature tokens with learnable \texttt{[MASK]} tokens, and train a masked transformer to forecast the corresponding future latent features from observed context, thereby formulating procedural evolution as masked future feature prediction. Experiments on public laparoscopic benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in phase anticipation, multi-label tool presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation over RGB-based forecasting baselines, while enabling a plug-and-play representation interface for lightweight downstream heads.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of pixel-space prediction, which emphasizes visual fidelity over task-relevant semantic reasoning.
Builds hierarchical multi-layer features from a frozen Vision Foundation Model and masks future feature tokens.
Uses a masked transformer to forecast future latent features from observed procedural context.
On public laparoscopic benchmarks, improves phase anticipation, tool-presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation over RGB-based baselines.
Provides a plug-and-play representation interface for lightweight downstream prediction heads.

papers.abstract: Long-video reasoning requires a system to localize sparse evidence over extended temporal sequences, preserve temporal structure, and generate answers despite substantial multimodal distractors. Existing video retrieval-augmented generation methods typically build indexes from uniformly sampled video segments. In long-video settings, this design readily introduces irrelevant context and is unreliable for questions with explicit temporal constraints. We propose VTG-RAG, a framework for long-video question answering that combines query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling with temporal graph retrieval. First, a two-stage sampling strategy selects core segments with high mean query relevance or high intra-segment relevance variance. The framework then integrates subtitles, speech transcripts, visual descriptions, entities, and relations from these segments into a temporally ordered multimodal graph. Finally, it performs temporally filtered, two-pass retrieval and reasoning across frame, text, and graph evidence spaces. A lot of experiments have proven the effectiveness of the VTG-RAG. Specifically, we evaluate the framework on Video-MME and LongVideoBench. On LongVideoBench, the reported Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 72B results improve from 48.16% to 50.56% and from 52.13% to 53.32%, respectively, with 24 answer-input frames. These correspond to gains of 2.40 and 1.19 percentage points. The ablation experiments of VTG-RAG further support that the contributions of each component are very important.

bullets: Addresses irrelevant context and weak handling of temporal constraints in uniformly sampled video retrieval.
Uses query-adaptive coarse-to-fine sampling based on segment relevance and intra-segment relevance variation.
Builds a temporally ordered graph combining subtitles, transcripts, visual descriptions, entities, and relations.
Performs temporally filtered, two-pass reasoning over frame, text, and graph evidence.
On LongVideoBench, improves reported Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 72B results by 2.40 and 1.19 percentage points, respectively, using 24 answer-input frames.

papers.abstract: Recognizing individual events does not guarantee correct execution of compositional instructions in streaming video. For example, given the request "Notify me when the pot boils after someone turns on the stove and leaves the kitchen", existing models may recognize the individual events yet notify too early or miss the intended moment, failing to track how their temporal conditions are satisfied over time. To evaluate this gap, we introduce CoTriggerBench, which composes annotated video events into temporally constrained instructions and verifies notification timing and silence through executable event plans and source-event replay. To address this challenge, we propose a real-time VLM agent, TEMPI. TEMPI decomposes instructions into atomic event queries and temporal constraints, and uses Scenario Memory to continuously maintain task progress as event evidence arrives, allowing earlier observations to support subsequent decisions beyond the detector's visual window. Even when no notification is required, relevant events continue to update the scenario state. On CoTriggerBench, TEMPI achieves 44.4% instruction-level success, outperforming the strongest closed-source and fine-tuned open-source VLM baselines by 15.6 (Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash-Realtime) and 18.1 (MOSS-VL-Realtime) percentage points, respectively. To support efficient on-device streaming inference, we further optimize the streaming inference pipeline by overlapping partial visual encoding and LLM prefix prefill with frame arrival. On an 8 GB RTX 5060, our optimized detector implementation achieves a 4.90$\times$ speedup.
authors: Yehua Huang, Penglei Sun, Xiang Li, Jinhao Zhou, Jiawen Wen, Qingqing Xiao, Zihan Yang, Wenqi Wang, Haolan Chen, Yu Xu, Xiaowen Chu

Scenario Memory preserves earlier evidence beyond the detector’s visual window and updates state even when no notification should be issued.
TEMPI achieves 44.4% instruction-level success, exceeding the reported baselines by 15.6 and 18.1 percentage points.
An optimized streaming pipeline overlaps visual encoding and LLM prefix prefill, yielding a reported 4.90× detector speedup on an 8 GB RTX 5060.

papers.abstract: As text-to-image diffusion models see widespread deployment, removing unsafe or undesirable concepts without retraining has become a pressing need. Spectral methods are attractive because they are training-free and reversible, yet current variants apply the same output-value (OV) circuit intervention at every denoising step, assuming concept information is temporally uniform. This wastes intervention where concept energy is low while degrading image quality, an inefficiency that compounds across concept types. Through timestep-resolved spectral analysis, concept-specific energy is found to follow a consistent temporal hierarchy: content concepts decay fastest, object concepts are intermediate, and style concepts persist longest. This paper proposes Timestep-Adaptive Spectral Nullification (TASN), which adapts suppression strength and spectral components to the concept energy profile. Cross-attention at each timestep is decomposed into concept-aligned and concept-orthogonal components, and it is proved that when the orthogonal component is approximately stable, the collateral-minimizing schedule sets suppression proportional to concept energy. TASN implements this with a timestep-adaptive spectral subset tracking only active concept directions, strictly generalizing uniform Spectral Nullification (SN). On five red-teaming benchmarks, TASN lowers attack success rate below uniform SN while recovering the majority of its quality loss; ablations confirm gains arise from temporal targeting rather than reduced suppression, generalizing across concept categories and architectures.
authors: Chanaka Thushitha Bandara, Lakmali Nadeesha Kumari, Sen-Ching Samson Cheung
bullets: Uniform spectral interventions waste suppression when concept information is weak, harming image quality.
Timestep-resolved analysis finds content concepts fade fastest, objects are intermediate, and styles persist longest.
TASN tracks active concept directions and adjusts suppression strength and spectral components throughout denoising.
Across five red-teaming benchmarks, it reduces attack success below uniform Spectral Nullification while recovering most of its quality loss.
Ablations attribute the gains to temporal targeting, with generalization across concept categories and architectures.

papers.abstract: Computer vision methods for video understanding, such as object detection and tracking, inherit the way videos are captured and displayed: as successive frames processed sequentially. However, a video is an inhomogeneous 2D+time volume of pixels, named voxels, and frames are only one family of cuts through it. In this frame-based representation, static backgrounds introduce computational redundancy, and motion can only be understood across several frames. In this position paper, we study another family of cuts: spacetime images (STIs), obtained by sampling any set of pixels other than frames, for instance a line of pixels followed over time. Such images are familiar in narrow forms, from line-scan inspection and kymographs to spatiotemporal slices for motion analysis, but have received little attention as a general input representation for computer vision and are often limited to (x,t) or (y,t) cuts. We define new cuts leading to STIs in their general form, explain how to read their content, and show that a family of cuts tiles the video so that existing dense annotations transfer at no cost. We also detail how motion appears in an STI, spatially and in the frequency domain, and discuss applications such as walking pedestrians, deposited objects, and dynamic scenes. Two pilot experiments illustrate the representation. The first trains a segmentation network entirely in the spacetime domain, on transferred annotations, and performs background subtraction on CDnet 2014 close to supervised frame-based methods, without explicit temporal modeling. The second recovers the pan speed of a camera as a moving cut, identified by a simple criterion on the frequency spectrum of the resulting image, turning a temporal estimation problem into the choice of a cut. Our position is not that STIs should replace frames, but that slicing the video volume is a design variable worth studying in its own right.
authors: Jade Lambert, S\'ebastien Pi\'erard, Anthony Cioppa, Marc Van Droogenbroeck
bullets: Problem: Frame-by-frame processing is redundant for static backgrounds and requires multiple frames to understand motion.
Method: Sample arbitrary sets of pixels over time to create STIs, including cuts beyond conventional (x,t) or (y,t) slices.
Contribution: Define general STI cuts, explain their spatial and frequency-domain content, and show that a family of cuts can tile videos while transferring dense annotations at no cost.
Results: Pilot studies perform background subtraction with a spacetime-trained segmentation network and estimate camera pan speed from STI frequency spectra.
Scope: STIs are proposed as a complementary design choice, not a replacement for conventional frames.

papers.abstract: Video generation models have become increasingly capable of synthesizing realistic human motion, yet they often lose track of the very structure that makes the motion plausible. As generated human motion becomes more complex, videos can suffer from progressive body deformation and appearance drift across frames. Existing motion-controlled methods use explicit representations to stabilize generation, but typically rely on pre-defined motion sequences as references. This raises a fundamental question: if the base generator already produces a usable coarse motion, why replace it with an external one? ReMoVe answers this question by treating the coarse output as a motion hypothesis rather than a final result. ReMoVe recovers and refines the underlying motion, then renders the refined motion as 3D mesh and transfers facial appearance onto it, thereby improving motion accuracy and identity consistency. We further derive depth from the same 3D scene and camera trajectory to impose scene-level spatial consistency beyond the mesh. By jointly conditioning video generation models on mesh and depth, ReMoVe synthesizes high-quality motion videos with controllable camera trajectories and enhanced spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReMoVe improves human structural stability, appearance consistency, temporal coherence, and motion-following fidelity, while retaining the base generator's motion prior and offering accurate camera control.
authors: Jie Li, Muxin Pu, Hongyi Cai, Mingkang Dong, Jianyuan Guo, Tao Huang
bullets: Addresses progressive body deformation, appearance drift, and weak scene-level consistency in complex human video generation.

Renders refined motion as a 3D mesh, transfers facial appearance, and derives depth from the same scene and camera trajectory.
Jointly conditions video generation on mesh and depth to improve structural stability, temporal coherence, appearance consistency, and motion-following fidelity.
Retains the generator’s motion prior while enabling accurate camera control, according to extensive experiments.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is wasteful and lossy when a multimodal model must re-encode the same video for every query: context limits force sparse sampling or truncation, and no reusable representation remains for later questions. We present VidEngram, an agentic video QA system that builds a persistent hierarchical memory once at ingest and answers later questions from that memory. VidEngram captions video and audio jointly with Qwen2.5-Omni, consolidates segment memories into episode and entity layers, and uses a text-only agentic planner with specialized retrieval tools to produce grounded answers. The web interface makes this process inspectable: users can watch memory formation, inspect retrieval traces, verify cited evidence in the video player, and explore entity relationships. On the full OmniVideoBench, VidEngram with a GPT-5-mini planner outperforms a strong single-pass Qwen2.5-Omni baseline (37.0% vs. 32.3%), with gains concentrated on longer videos where single-pass coverage becomes sparse. Because perception is paid once, subsequent queries use low-cost text-only planning.
authors: Zinuo Cheng, Yueqian Lin, Zhongxi Wang, Hai "Helen" Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: Addresses repeated video re-encoding, context limits, and information loss in long-video question answering.

Subsequent queries avoid repeated perception, reducing them to low-cost text-only planning.

papers.abstract: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. We find that distilled students maintain total activation variance comparable to their teachers, but concentrate it into substantially fewer directions. This directional collapse is localized to an identifiable intermediate block at the initial denoising step. Consequently, diversity collapse stems from a misallocation of activation variance rather than an inherent loss of generative capacity. Guided by this finding, we propose ReDiverse to reinstate the missing variance directions. At training time, ReDiverse-FT fine-tunes a lightweight adapter that regresses student activations onto the teacher's, reviving the teacher's feature variance characteristic. At inference time, ReDiverse-TF introduces a training-free mechanism that steers activations along precomputed teacher principal directions. Across image and video distillation benchmarks, ReDiverse consistently restores sample diversity while preserving generation quality, further supported by the user study.
bullets: Distillation reduces sampling latency but causes severe variation collapse across random seeds.
Student models retain overall activation variance, but concentrate it in fewer directions than their teachers.

Across image and video benchmarks, both methods restore diversity while preserving generation quality, with additional support from a user study.

papers.abstract: Narrative video understanding requires more than recognizing visible events: models must extract evidence from dialogue, bind it to speakers, and use it to infer narrative meaning. Existing video benchmarks evaluate aspects of this problem, including video question answering, audio-visual reasoning, and temporal grounding, but rarely test whether these abilities form a coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chain within the same clips. We introduce \textbf{CineMME}, a human-verified benchmark designed to diagnose dialogue-grounded plot understanding, supported by approximately $1,600$ expert person-hours of annotation. CineMME contains $975$ curated short narrative video clips and two linked tracks: \textit{CineMME-Grounding}, with $13,554$ timestamped speech segments and $33,083$ speaker face boxes for temporal dialogue localization, transcription, and active-speaker grounding; and \textit{CineMME-Reasoning}, with $1,600$ multiple-choice and $316$ open-ended questions spanning perception, audio, narrative, social, and scene-presentation understanding. Our main evaluation compares $20$ MLLMs on reasoning and $9$ omni-modal models on grounding. The results reveal a pronounced who-what-when decoupling: Gemini-3 Pro localizes dialogue in time ($68.34\%$ tIoU) and transcribes it with a WER of $28.99\%$, yet achieves only $7.74\%$ vIoU for active-speaker grounding while achieving $67.66\%$ MCQ accuracy on questions with extractable answers. Modality ablations further show that vision is not uniformly beneficial: it improves performance on perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning. CineMME provides a compact diagnostic testbed for evaluating how multimodal video models connect dialogue, speakers, visual evidence, and narrative meaning.
bullets: Targets a missing evaluation link: coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chains within the same narrative clips.
Includes 975 human-verified clips with grounding and reasoning tracks covering speech localization, transcription, active-speaker grounding, and narrative questions.
Evaluates 20 multimodal LLMs for reasoning and 9 omni-modal models for grounding.
Finds strong time localization and transcription but weak active-speaker grounding, revealing a who–what–when gap.
Vision helps perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning.

papers.abstract: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.
authors: Jianjun Zhou, Hua Geng, Haoyu Guo
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of directly diffusing high-dimensional raw video pixels.
Studies video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization for quality–efficiency trade-offs.
Achieves quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in class-conditioned and unconditional generation.
Supports joint pixel-aligned modality generation, demonstrated with camera-conditioned RGB–disparity videos.
RGB–disparity generation improves camera following and provides explicit scene geometry without an inference-time reconstruction model.

papers.abstract: Weakly Supervised Video Semantic Segmentation (WS-VSS) aims to learn temporally consistent semantic object masks in videos using only video-level labels. While fully supervised models successfully learn temporal relationships by means of cross-attention, training these temporal weights under weak supervision is unstable and even pushes the model below its single-frame baseline. Therefore, existing WS-VSS methods exploit temporal consistency by relying on external priors, such as optical flow. Unfortunately these cues are non-semantic, computationally expensive and noisy, degrading the supervisory signal. Instead of supervising attention weights directly or using external priors, we propose MemCAM, a WS-VSS transformer framework that learns temporal cross-attention directly through feature-space self-supervision. MemCAM introduces a CAM Propagation Algorithm that synthesizes a supervisory signal by propagating past CAMs according to patch-level feature similarities in the latent space. Specifically, we constrain their induced CAMs through a consistency objective between predicted and propagated maps, stabilizing temporal attention learning. Experiments on the YouTube-Objects v2.2 and WS$^2$ datasets demonstrate that MemCAM consistently outperforms the temporal localization and segmentation performance of WS-VSS alternatives, showing that cross-attention can be effectively trained in label-scarce video settings through internal self-supervision.
authors: Andrea Marelli, Alessandro Ardenghi, Giacomo Boracchi, Luca Magri
bullets: Targets temporally consistent object masks from only video-level labels.
Propagates past CAMs using patch-level feature similarities in latent space to create self-supervision.
Trains temporal attention with a consistency objective between predicted and propagated CAMs.
Experiments on YouTube-Objects v2.2 and WS² show improved temporal localization and segmentation over existing WS-VSS methods.
The approach is evaluated in label-scarce settings and avoids reliance on computationally expensive, noisy optical flow.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MemCAM architecture. Inputs (left) are encoded by the multi-class transformer backbone into class tokens V t cls (a1) and patch tokens V t p (b1). V t cls are pooled and fed to the classification head (a2) producing Lcls. V t p are refined via the MAM, (c) using context retrieved from the Memory Bank’s patch queue Qp. The memory-refined patch embeddings V t p ′ (b2) are reshaped (b3) and passed through the Patch-Level Supervision branch (PLS) to produce per-patch activations V t M and the patch-level loss Lp. Class-aware CAMs V t M ′ are obtained after attention-based refinement and stored in the CAM queue QM of the Memory Bank (d). CAMPA consumes the CAMs stored in QM to produce a propagated pseudo-CAM M̂ t, which is used to compute the consistency loss LM.

Figure 3. CAMPA overview: The current frame’s patch embeddings V t p and the memory queues from past frames patch queue Qp and CAM queue QM as input (section Setting). (a) A Similarity Matrix S is computed by comparing the current frame’s patch embeddings against all embeddings stored in the Qp queue. (b) We convert S into a Probability Matrix P, by keeping only the top K entries per row (and so per current patch) and then applying a per-row softmax. In this way, we can see P as a matching likelihood between current and past patches. (c) The final propagated CAM M̂ t is computed as a weighted aggregation of past CAMs (from QM ), using the probabilities from matrix P to weight the activation values. M̂ t will be used as pseudo-label to supervise the CAM of the current frame t. A step-by-step pseudo-code is given in Alg. 1 in Section B the Supp. Mat.

Figure 4. Detailed architecture of the MAM. Starting from the backbone patch embeddings V t p , the module refines representations through three stages, each equipped with a residual connection. Self-attention (left): current-frame tokens act as queries, keys, and values. The arrows entering the yellow block indicate that the attention matrix Aself t is learned from the input; its output Attn(qself ,kself ,vself) is added back to the backbone features, producing the self-attended representation V t,self

papers.abstract: Direct image-to-video diffusion models entangle pixel synthesis with implicit latent motion, precluding persistent 3D mechanical equilibrium, mid-rollout intervention, and counterfactual force control. Conversely, single-pass programmatic 3D reconstruction from an uncalibrated photograph leaves monocular depth and support clearance underconstrained, causing reconstructed scenes to interpenetrate or collapse under gravity. We present TelePhysica, a closed-loop framework that reconstructs an executable, multi-regime physical world from a single photograph to drive stateful 3D interaction and trajectory-grounded video synthesis. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models within a two-stage verification loop that pairs pixel-aligned silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium preflight. The verified world compiles into a unified solver coupling rigid bodies, articulated chains, co-dimensional cloth shells, and 3D tetrahedral elastodynamics, whose simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models through pixel-aligned structural streams. On a 100-scene single-image benchmark, closed-loop execution raises equilibrium-verified world recovery from $0\%$ in single-pass synthesis to $81\%$. Controlled constitutive ablations show over an order-of-magnitude larger localized corner displacement and out-of-plane pleating in finite-element cloth than in matched rigid-plate proxies. Conditioning video diffusion on simulated trajectories increases dynamic motion-mask overlap by $2{\times}\text{--}5{\times}$ and preserves motion direction under counterfactual force reversals where direct image-to-video models fail.
authors: Ruiqi Shu, Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses image-to-video models’ lack of persistent 3D mechanics and single-pass reconstruction failures such as interpenetration or collapse.
Uses a vision-language coding agent with silhouette critique and zero-force gravitational preflight to build verified visual meshes and physical models.
Compiles scenes into a solver supporting rigid bodies, articulated chains, cloth shells, and tetrahedral elastodynamics.
On a 100-scene benchmark, equilibrium-verified recovery improves from 0% with single-pass synthesis to 81% with closed-loop execution.

Simulated trajectory conditioning improves dynamic motion-mask overlap by 2–5× and preserves motion direction under reversed forces; finite-element cloth exhibits stronger deformation than rigid proxies.

papers.abstract: Hallucination benchmarks for text-to-image generation are predominantly designed around diffusion models, limiting their diagnostic value for visual autoregressive (VAR) models and the development of mitigation methods. We identify two limitations in existing prompt construction paradigms: many prompts are no longer challenging for modern generators, while category-based construction relies on recurring object-attribute-relation templates and rarely tests interactions among multiple visual requirements within a single image. We introduce InfiHall-Bench, a controlled benchmark of 411 prompts constructed by systematically composing five foundational and visually verifiable skills: attribute binding, spatial relation, action relation, part consistency, and scene consistency. Each prompt covers 4.05 annotated skills on average, enabling the evaluation of hallucinations under diverse combinations of visual requirements. Using this benchmark, we find that hallucinations in VAR models exhibit a scale-wise persistence pattern: semantic errors can emerge at different autoregressive scales and are rarely corrected by subsequent fine-scale steps. Motivated by this observation, we propose Confidence-Masked Hallucination Mitigation (CMHM), which estimates the prediction confidence of target visual tokens at each autoregressive scale during teacher-forced fine-tuning. CMHM downweights reliably predicted tokens, allowing optimization to focus on uncertain predictions across scales. Experiments show that InfiHall-Bench distinguishes models that existing compositional benchmarks rate as comparable, while CMHM consistently outperforms uniform LoRA fine-tuning for VAR-based text-to-image generation.
authors: Yuxia Qiao, Xinhao Zhong, Junhao Li, Yi Sun, Jiaxin Hong, Shuoyang Sun, Bin Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of diagnostic hallucination benchmarks tailored to visual autoregressive (VAR) models.
Introduces 411 prompts combining five verifiable skills: attribute binding, spatial and action relations, part consistency, and scene consistency.
Finds that VAR hallucinations can persist across autoregressive scales and are rarely corrected by later fine-scale steps.
Proposes Confidence-Masked Hallucination Mitigation (CMHM), which downweights confidently predicted tokens during teacher-forced fine-tuning.
Reports that the benchmark separates models judged similarly by prior compositional benchmarks, while CMHM outperforms uniform LoRA fine-tuning for VAR generation.

papers.abstract: Attention is essential for modeling spatio-temporal dependencies in video diffusion transformers, but its quadratic cost makes it a major inference bottleneck. Its high sparsity offers an opportunity to accelerate generation by focusing computation on important interactions. However, accuracy and execution favor different granularities: each query attends to its own key tokens, whereas GPU kernels work on tiles. We present Token2Tile, a training-free sparse attention operator that combines per-query scoring and a per-query residual with tile execution. An online low-rank space, computed directly from queries and keys to preserve attention logits, makes clustering, scoring, and residual approximation efficient. Token2Tile unites query-specific selections to allocate exact work across query clusters, then packs the selected keys into GPU tiles. On MiniMax-H3 and Wan2.1-14B, Token2Tile delivers 1.48-1.54x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3 with VBench scores within 0.5 points of dense. At comparable speeds on H3, it improves PSNR over SOL and SubBlock by 5.5-6.8 dB; on Wan, it exceeds SOL by 4.6-4.8 dB while running faster.
authors: Xuecheng Wu, Aichen Feng, Jinyan Chen, Qingjie Zhao, Julien Lai
bullets: Targets the quadratic inference cost of spatio-temporal attention in video diffusion transformers.
Uses per-query scoring and residual approximation in an online low-rank space derived from queries and keys.
Clusters query-specific selections and packs selected keys into GPU tiles for efficient execution.
Achieves 1.48–1.54× end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3, with VBench within 0.5 points of dense.
Outperforms SOL and SubBlock in PSNR at comparable or higher speeds on the evaluated models.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse attention for video diffusion transformers, improves efficiency.
papers.title: Token2Tile: Token-Wise Sparse Attention with Tile Execution through a Low-Rank Space for Video DiTs
papers.tldr: Token2Tile accelerates video diffusion attention by combining token-level sparsity with GPU-friendly tile execution while preserving near-dense quality.

papers.abstract: Cardiac cine MRI provides time-resolved visualization of cardiac motion and is essential for evaluating ventricular function and anatomy. In routine clinical acquisition, however, cine sequences are frequently temporally sparse or degraded by arrhythmia, motion, and scan-time constraints, which can hinder reliable quantification and downstream analysis. We present CardioTrace, a motion-aware cine synthesis framework that generates a full cardiac cine sequence from limited input while explicitly modeling and tracing cardiac motion. CardioTrace couples two complementary pathways: a pixel-translation branch that directly predicts cine frames in a residual formulation, and a flow-field branch that estimates time-resolved deformation fields from a reference phase to provide interpretable motion correspondences across frames. To further preserve anatomical plausibility, a segmentation branch supervises clinically meaningful cardiac structures at key phases, and a cross-branch consistency objective encourages the synthesized appearance dynamics to follow the explicit motion guidance, mitigating temporal drift and unrealistic shape transitions over long sequences. The framework also supports prompt-style conditioning to incorporate auxiliary patient or acquisition information, improving robustness across heterogeneous multi-center data. Experiments on public cardiac cine MRI datasets demonstrate that CardioTrace improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence over representative GAN- and diffusion-based baselines, while better preserving ventricular morphology throughout the cardiac cycle. \textit{Our codes are available after review}.
bullets: Addresses temporally sparse or degraded cine MRI caused by arrhythmia, motion, and scan-time constraints.
Combines a residual pixel-translation branch with a flow-field branch that estimates interpretable cardiac deformations over time.
Uses segmentation supervision and cross-branch consistency to preserve anatomy and reduce temporal drift or unrealistic shape changes.
Supports prompt-style conditioning with auxiliary patient or acquisition information for heterogeneous multi-center data.
Experiments on public cardiac cine MRI datasets show improved perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and ventricular morphology preservation over representative GAN- and diffusion-based baselines.

The Segmentation Branch does segmentation at end-diastolic (ED) and end-systolic (ES) frames.

Fig. 2. Qualitative comparison on the M&M dataset. From left to right: ground-truth reference, Pix2Pix, CycleGAN, Med-DDPM, TraceTrans, and the proposed CardioTrace. For each method, the top row shows the synthesized end-systolic (ES) frame conditioned on the end-diastolic (ED) input, with dashed boxes indicating regions of interest that are enlarged below. The bottom row visualizes the corresponding absolute error maps with respect to the ground-truth ES frame. Compared with baseline methods, CardioTrace better preserves ventricular morphology and boundary sharpness, while reducing errors in regions undergoing large cardiac deformation.

CardioTrace produces end-systolic images that are closer to the ground truth, with fewer artifacts and reduced errors in regions undergoing large deformation, demonstrating improved anatomical consistency across the cardiac cycle.

papers.abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.
authors: Keuntae Kim, Dongjun Kim, Yong Suk Choi
bullets: V-JEPA retains shared representations of dynamics such as direction, speed, order, and state, but standard caption-based training largely leaves them unused.
Counterfactual pixel transformations create answer-balanced video variants whose answers depend specifically on the visual change.
Models are trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples using 32 visual tokens per frame.
V-JEPA-LM models from 1B to 8B lead their size classes across eleven video benchmarks; the 4B model scores 72.1.
Controlled studies find counterfactual supervision improves average performance by 4.5 points and speed-question performance by 38 points on natural benchmarks.

papers.title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations
papers.tldr: V-JEPA-LM combines dynamics-aware video encoders with counterfactual supervision so language models can answer questions about motion and temporal change, achieving strong performance across video benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of assistants that respond only after user prompts.
Introduces Model-Initiated Conversation, Stream-Aware Tool Calling, and Interactive Visual Grounding.
Adds Long-Horizon Interaction Memory for continuity across extended video streams.
Uses a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and three-stage training scheme to integrate these behaviors.
Reports leading performance among open-source streaming models on public benchmarks and releases model weights and inference code.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the AURA 2.0 streaming interaction framework. The model incrementally processes video chunks together with user inputs and interaction history, producing either <|silent|> for silent observation or <|respond|> followed by a text response or tool call. Tool results are incorporated into the context to support subsequent responses. Dashed outlines indicate historical messages beyond the active visual window.

Figure 3. Data construction pipeline for AURA 2.0. The pipeline transforms collected videos into a verified streaming training mixture through three stages: (1) Video collection and preparation standardizes videos into clips and generates clip-level descriptions. (2) Task-specific data synthesis uses the clips and descriptions to construct General QA, MIC, SATC, and IVG trajectories. (3) Streaming assembly and quality assessment aligns the trajectories to video chunks and filters invalid or low-quality samples.

Figure 4. Training data composition and response-control statistics across the three training stages. (a) Sample distribution by stage (inner ring) and task (outer ring). (b) Stage-wise sample and token allocations and silent/response decision proportions. (c) Task-wise sample counts and shares aggregated across stages. Together, these distributions characterize the task coverage and supervision balance of the training mixture.

Figure 8. IVG examples with less salient and peripheral targets. AURA 2.0 (top, red boxes) localizes both the handbag and the partially visible bus. Qwen3.5-9B (bottom, blue boxes) incorrectly declares the handbag absent and produces no response for the bus. Both models accurately localize the remote control despite the salient cat.

Figure 7. Real-world weather query at t = 1 s. AURA 2.0 identifies Rome from the Colosseum and calls get_current_datetime and get_city_weather to retrieve the forecast. Without tools, the model reports that weather information is unavailable in the video; with tools, it provides the forecast for the visually identified city.

Figure 5. MIC example in the Visual-Dialogue Context setting. Before playback, the user mentions wanting to get home early despite heavy traffic, and the assistant advises caution around big trucks. Without any further user query, AURA 2.0 initiates two messages: at t = 66 s it warns about a large Amazon truck ahead, and at t = 78 s it advises keeping a steady speed and a safe distance as traffic tightens. Both messages build on the user’s expressed concern and the assistant’s earlier advice. Each frame is shown one second before the corresponding message onset.

Figure 6. SATC examples from the internal benchmark. Top: WebSearch identifies the “Zaochake” reservation as a breakfast experience at the water market. Bottom: WebSearch uses character names from the subtitles to identify Brotherhood of Blades II. Both examples correct answers generated without tools.

Figure 9. Cumulative effect of the inference optimizations on median TTFP with a single session. Each row adds one optimization to the preceding configuration, and the full configuration reduces median TTFP by 54.6%. The right column reports the change relative to the previous row.

papers.abstract: Physical plausibility is essential for realistic video generation. Existing methods impose physical guidance before synthesis via simulations or refined prompts, but this can limit dynamic diversity, miss errors that emerge only after generation, and require repeated regeneration when inconsistencies remain. We therefore study a generate-diagnose-repair paradigm that preserves the original generation capability and selectively repairs physical inconsistencies afterward, raising two key questions: what to repair and how to repair? To address them, we introduce PhysRepair, an agentic video generation framework that combines causal reasoning over the observed physical failure with prior repair experience to enable localized and adaptive correction. Specifically, Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints identify the first invalid physical state and its causally affected states, producing a repair specification that guides physically plausible local regeneration while preserving unaffected content. Experience-augmented In-context Learning combines the ongoing repair context with relevant experience from previous repairs, allowing the agent to adapt its repair decisions across diverse physical failures and accumulate completed trajectories for future cases. Experiments on Physics-IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism demonstrate that PhysRepair consistently improves the physical plausibility of generated videos over existing methods. Our project page is available at https://xxkkxxx.github.io/PhysRepair-Website/.
bullets: Addresses failures that emerge after video generation without requiring full regeneration.
Uses Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints to identify the first invalid state and affected downstream states.
Applies localized, adaptive regeneration while preserving unaffected content.
Combines repair context with prior repair experiences through in-context learning.
Improves physical plausibility across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism on Physics-IQ Verified.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PhysRepair. Starting from an initially generated video, a Physics Repair Agent diagnoses the realized physical failure and performs localized counterfactual repair. Spatiotemporal causal constraints determine what may change and what must remain fixed, while experience-augmented in-context learning retrieves relevant repair experience to adapt how to repair. The resulting counterfactual physical state guides video regeneration, followed by physicsand-preservation verification and experience distillation for subsequent repair.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison on multi-object spatiotemporal interactions. Top: fan–garment interaction; bottom: wrench–box interaction. Baselines exhibit incorrect contact timing, inconsistent motion, or object artifacts, whereas PhysRepair preserves object identity and coherent contact–response dynamics.
Figure 5: Analysis of PhysRepair. Memory efficiency and user-perceived physical consistency of PhysRepair.

Figure 1: Comparison of physics-grounded video generation paradigms. (a) Plan and Prompt Refine iteratively updates generation plans or physics-aware prompts, while (b) Simulator Program Refine iteratively updates physical programs or simulator configurations; both impose physical guidance before synthesis and may require repeated regeneration. (c) PhysRepair instead follows a generate–diagnose–repair paradigm: it diagnoses physical failures from the generated video (what to repair?) and performs localized, causally constrained repair, while leveraging prior repair experience to adapt the intervention and preserve generated already-valid content (how to repair?).

Table 1: Quantitative results on Physics-IQ Verified. SP, ST, and WS denote Spatial IoU, Spatiotemporal IoU, and Weighted Spatial IoU, respectively. The best, second-best, and third-best results for each metric are marked in bold, single underline, and double underline, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Agentic video generation framework that diagnoses and repairs physical inconsistencies, fitting video understanding and generation.
papers.title: Agentic Physics-Grounded Video Generation via Memory-Augmented In-Context Reasoning
papers.tldr: PhysRepair generates, diagnoses, and locally repairs physically inconsistent video content using causal constraints and memory-augmented reasoning.

papers.abstract: We study how to repurpose video diffusion models (VDMs), pretrained on millions of videos, for dense 3D point tracking, where training data is scarce. Doing so is non-trivial, as it requires representing 3D tracks as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution on which the VDM was trained. We thus systematically assess the effectiveness of two such video representations. The first, Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame and allows recovery of 3D trajectories directly from the generated video. The second, Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), labels each pixel with a canonical coordinate invariant through time. This is closer to a natural video and easier for the VDM to learn, but requires additional post-processing with an off-the-shelf 2D tracker to recover 3D tracks. RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a VDM can generate dense correspondence as a video. We instantiate both representations with LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor as a geometric scaffold. Trained with a single dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks. A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses additional training data brings further improvement, demonstrating the potential of this direction for dense 3D tracking. We hope our analysis will inspire future work that leverages VDM priors for dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction. Project page: https://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/track4d
bullets: RTV encodes per-pixel 3D offsets and directly recovers trajectories, yielding more accurate tracks.
NCMV uses time-invariant canonical coordinates, making the representation more natural for video diffusion but requiring a 2D tracker for recovery.
Both representations use LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, guided by point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor.
Trained on one dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot performance across four real and synthetic benchmarks.
A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses extra training data provides further improvement.

figures.caption: Figure 2: TRACK4D overview. (a) Generative readout. A frozen reconstructor supplies point maps P; the video VAE encodes them with video V into condition C. The LoRA-adapted video DiT denoises the RTV and NCMV latents, jointly by default, and the VAE decodes the videos. Hatched targets are noised in training and start from Gaussian noise at inference. Adding inverse-normalized RTV offsets to the query-frame point map gives 3D tracks; NCMV requires 2D tracking and lifting. (b) Regression readout. Point maps enter through a patch encoder, a private motion expert attends jointly with the video DiT, and a DPT head reads residuals without the output VAE (Section 3.4 and Figure 8). Flames denote trained modules, snowflakes frozen modules.

Figure 6: TrackCraft3R vs. the three TRACK4D readouts on DAVIS [70]. Each panel shows the point cloud of frame j and the last 12 frames of the predicted 3D tracks, from one fixed view (the frame-0 input camera rotated by 4◦). All methods receive the same VGGT-Ω point maps and draw the same 767 queries, the most-moving points of a dense grid, colored by image row. RTV and NCMV come from the joint Wan2.1-I2V-14B model (50 steps, no input-latent noise); NCMV tracks are read with CoTracker3, lifted with the same point maps, and frozen where NCMV support is lost (on camel, after the first frames). No ground truth or Sim(3) is used. More clips in Figures 9 and 10.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison of dynamic tracking on DAVIS [70]. Dense 3D tracking is visualized as colored point clouds, with color encoding query-frame identity of each tracked point. Left: input frames. Right: reconstructions from St4RTrack [19], TraceAnything [31], Any4D [23], and TRACK4D (ours). TRACK4D produces more temporally coherent trajectories with fewer outliers, particularly on articulated and deformable motion (e.g. moving mug, walking cows). All baselines are run from their official released checkpoints and inference scripts at the resolution recommended by the authors; sequences shown were selected to expose dynamic-object failure modes for the comparators. More DAVIS results appear in Figure 14.

Figure 4: Two video representations of dense 3D tracking on DAVIS [70]. Rows show RGB, RTV offsets, NCMV canonical coordinates, and recovered XYZ tracks. Adding inverse-normalized RTV offsets to the query-frame point map recovers the tracks. All predictions are TRACK4D outputs.

Figure 7: Submitted overview (reproduced from the submitted version). A monocular video V and point maps P from an off-the-shelf reconstructor are encoded by the video VAE into the condition C; the VDM jointly generates the RTV ∆ and the NCMV M, and the decoded residuals are added to the query-frame point map. Figure 2 shows the current overview.

Figure 13: Effect of backbone size. Specifically, we show our model’s performance on four samples from PStudio [90], with sequence names on the left. For each sequence, we compare the results from TRACK4D-5B (in orange) and TRACK4D-14B (in green). Both RTV and NCMV are visualized. The Wan-14B-based TRACK4D shows better foreground-background factorization and sharper motion, suggesting benefits from stronger video diffusion models.
Figure 10: More DAVIS clips (continued). Same setup as Figures 6 and 9.

Figure 12: Ablation: absolute XYZ prediction vs. residual prediction. We visualize 3D tracking results at t = 0 and t = 24 on ADT [89] and PStudio [90] sequences. Left: predicting absolute 3D coordinates directly (w/o Residual Pred). Right: our residual formulation (Equation (4)). Absolute prediction produces noisy geometry with scattered outliers, whereas the residual formulation yields cleaner reconstructions with more coherent motion.

Figure 3: Prediction formulations (adapted from VDPM [22]). Each entry Pi(tj) (short for Pi(tj , π0), with the reference frame π0 fixed) gives the positions at time tj of the surface points observed in frame Ii. P (diagonal): geometry at each frame’s capture time. Q (column): timeinvariant prediction [22], referring every frame Ii back to the reference time t0. R (row): dense 3D tracking, propagating the query-frame point map P0 across all timestamps. TRACK4D encodes R explicitly as 3D offsets (RTV) and Q as normalized canonical colors (NCMV), from which R is recovered by 2D tracking.

Figure 9: More DAVIS clips, TrackCraft3R vs. the three TRACK4D readouts. Same setup as Figure 6. Because the view is fixed at frame 0, subjects that the camera follows leave the view in later frames (car-shadow, kite-surf, parkour). Over all 91 DAVIS clips, the median second difference of the projected tracks over consecutive frames, counting points inside the frame, is 6.5 px for TrackCraft3R and 1.8 px for TRACK4D-Reg (672-px-wide frames), and it is smaller for TRACK4D-Reg on 90 clips. This measures temporal smoothness, not accuracy.

Figure 14: More qualitative results. We show seven zero-shot inference results from DAVIS [70]. The first row shows RGB input, with eight frames sampled uniformly from a 49-frame clip, and the second and third rows show RTV and NCMV predictions. The query frame is the first frame shown in the first row. RTV encodes 3D offsets on the query-frame grid; NCMV encodes persistent coordinates on each video frame’s grid.

Figure 11: Failure case. TRACK4D predicts near-zero deformation in this video, where the camera moves with the object. Limited coverage of such camera-following-object trajectories in the training data is a plausible, but not conclusively established, cause (Appendix G.9).

Table 2: Ablations of design choices. Baseline is TRACK4D (Wan 2.2 5B, STream3R). Top three rows modify one component each; bottom rows scale the VDM backbone (1.3B / 14B) and swap conditioning (DAv3 / STream3R). Green/red show gains/losses over baseline; intensity indicates magnitude. All models are trained and evaluated at 256×256 following [24]. Reported on ADT [89], PStudio [90], and DR [45]; PO [44] is excluded due to mismatched aspect ratios.

Table 16: Existing assets and their licenses, as stated by the official repositories and dataset pages (checked October 2026). Data and model weights may carry terms beyond the code license; we use every asset for non-commercial research only.
Table 3: Submitted version versus this version. The submitted column summarizes the described design; the training run that produced the submitted numbers is distinguished below.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual models improve egocentric action recognition by exploiting complementary cues, yet typically assume that both streams remain available at inference. Existing missing-modality methods operate on trimmed, single-event clips in which a stream is entirely present or absent, whereas real sensors fail and recover within long, untrimmed observations. We redefine egocentric modality missingness as temporally localized sensor outages within untrimmed, multi-event observations, with whole-clip absence as the limiting case. We introduce \textbf{MacJEPA}, a missing-modality-robust \textbf{Ma}sked-\textbf{c}ontext query \textbf{JEPA} that recognizes visual actions and acoustic events from supplied interval queries over audio-visual context. Window-local modality dropout simulates these sensor outages during training. MacJEPA further repurposes masking in JEPA from a self-supervised pretext into a supervised robustness objective, aligning masked and clean latent representations of both multimodal content tokens and the task-conditioned queries. All objectives are optimized jointly with recognition in a single stage, requiring no test-time adaptation. Across Epic-Kitchens-100 and Epic-Sounds, a single checkpoint remains competitive under complete input and consistently surpasses published missing-modality baselines when either the dominant or auxiliary stream is removed. MacJEPA thus unifies strong full-input recognition with temporal missing-modality robustness in a single model operating on untrimmed multi-event videos.
bullets: Reframes missing modality as within-video, time-localized outages, including full-clip absence as a special case.
Uses a masked-context query JEPA to predict visual actions and acoustic events from interval queries over audio-visual context.
Trains with window-local modality dropout and aligns masked and clean representations for content tokens and task-conditioned queries.
Jointly optimizes robustness and recognition in one stage, without test-time adaptation.
On Epic-Kitchens-100 and Epic-Sounds, one checkpoint remains competitive with full input and outperforms published missing-modality baselines when either stream is removed.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models have witnessed the paradigm shift from single-agent to multi-agent involvements, which can reveal more complicated dynamics and cross-agent interaction in the real world. However, existing approaches commonly adopt implicit inter-agent communications via cross attention, which lack explicit geometry constraints and unified 3D state, thereby leading to poor multi-view consistency and struggling with recovering out-of-sight agents. In addition, most of them assume a static background, failing to represent uncontrolled background dynamics. To address these problems, we propose Artemis: a geometry-grounded multi-agent world model with explicit memory sharing. An explicit 3D world map is reconstructed from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified 3D state across agents, offering high cross-view consistency. Specifically, an action-guided geometric injection module is developed to simultaneously render decomposed foreground-background control maps, which are then injected into a diffusion transformer through a designed GeoAdapter block. Compared to previous methods assuming static-only background, our GeoAdapter can also distinguish uncontrolled non-agent dynamics, which are conditioned on their own multi-frame history positions to provide consistent motion cues. Keyframes selected from progressive video rollouts are used to progressively update the reconstructed 3D world maps. To effectively capture complex dynamic patterns, we curate a novel dataset sampled from the CARLA simulator called MA-CARLA. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in terms of visual fidelity and cross-view consistency in the generated videos. In addition, our Artemis can support simultaneous multi-modal rollouts with both 2D video and 3D point map maintenance, scale to scenarios beyond two agents and multi-camera setting.
bullets: Addresses poor cross-view consistency, out-of-sight agent recovery, and static-background assumptions in prior multi-agent world models.
Reconstructs an explicit 3D world map from multi-agent observations to enforce a unified geometric state.
Uses an action-guided GeoAdapter to inject decomposed foreground–background control maps into a diffusion transformer.
Models uncontrolled background dynamics using their own multi-frame position histories, while keyframes progressively update the 3D map.
Introduces the MA-CARLA dataset; experiments report improved visual fidelity and cross-view consistency, with support for multi-modal 2D video/3D point-map rollouts and more than two agents.
