papers.abstract: Video reasoning hinges on a small number of visually decisive tokens embedded in otherwise largely language-driven chains of thought. Yet prevailing post-training methods such as GRPO overlook this structure, assigning coarse trajectory-level rewards while requiring multiple rollouts and often costly external judges. We introduce Visually-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (VIOS), a post-training framework that identifies where a model under-utilizes visual evidence and concentrates learning at those positions. Our key insight is that a model can audit its own visual reliance: the divergence between its next-token distributions with and without the video reveals how strongly each prediction depends on the visual input. Measuring this reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged teacher exposes a per-token reliance gap, identifying positions where the teacher exploits visual evidence that the student overlooks. VIOS translates this signal into dense, targeted supervision through three complementary components: an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher that co-evolves with the student, a contrastive objective that encourages predictions to depend on the video, and a reliance-gap gate that focuses learning on visually under-utilized tokens. Crucially, VIOS requires only a single on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers. Across 12 benchmarks spanning general, temporal, spatial, knowledge-intensive, and long-video understanding, VIOS consistently improves three model backbones and outperforms contemporary video-reasoning systems, while training in over 9x fewer steps, 60x fewer FLOPs, and 111x fewer generated tokens. Project page: https://vision.cs.utexas.edu/projects/VIOS/
bullets: Targets a limitation of GRPO-style post-training: coarse trajectory rewards, multiple rollouts, and costly external evaluation overlook token-level visual reliance.
Measures how predictions change with versus without video to estimate visual reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged EMA teacher.
Uses a contrastive visual-dependence objective and a reliance-gap gate to focus supervision on visually under-utilized tokens.
Requires one on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers.
Across 12 benchmarks and three backbones, it consistently improves performance while using over 9× fewer steps, 60× fewer FLOPs, and 111× fewer generated tokens than contemporary approaches.

papers.abstract: Attention heads in video Transformers vary greatly in functional importance. Understanding their contributions requires examining not only which heads are important, but also how they participate in collective computation within the network. We study this collective computation from two perspectives: the downstream use of head outputs and the composition of interactions across layers. Ablation analyses of four video Transformers show that high-importance heads identified on a single task also support other video understanding tasks and help preserve the representational structure that distinguishes different videos. Representational responses to head ablation correlate weakly with head importance after the attention module, but more strongly after the MLP in the same block. Adapting this downstream processing through MLP-only fine-tuning further improves the use of lower-importance head outputs. Meanwhile, through composition across layers, sets of heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances support stronger perturbation responses at distant tokens than sets with longer distances. Their joint ablation causes even greater performance loss than ablating equally sized sets of high-importance heads, revealing collective contributions not fully captured by individual importance rankings. These findings highlight collective computation as a key perspective for understanding attention head function: functional contributions depend on both how head outputs are used downstream and how local interactions compose across layers.
bullets: High-importance heads transfer across video understanding tasks and help preserve distinctions between videos.

papers.abstract: Optical flow requires reliable matching from sufficient visual context and precise motion at every pixel. Existing methods such as WAFT match and estimate flow on the same coarse grids, then recover dense flow through learned upsampling, without explicitly linking visual support for matching to dense flow reconstruction. Our key insight is that dense pixel-level flow does not require equally dense matching. We decouple correspondence scale from flow resolution by adapting the size and shape of spatial supports to image structure for reliable matching, while reusing these supports for precise dense flow reconstruction. We realize this in Flow from Adaptive Token Estimation (FATE), whose token supports expand within coherent regions and contract near motion boundaries. Shared pixel-to-token associations pool features for matching and reconstruct pixel flow from token motions. Flow supervision jointly trains pixel grouping, token matching, and flow estimation without grouping labels, allowing FATE to anticipate which pixels are likely to move together from appearance alone. Trained on FlyingChairs/FlyingThings3D, FATE achieves the highest zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI, a critical setting given scarce real-world flow labels. For visible pixels, FATE improves accuracy within coherent regions, and more near motion boundaries. Its largest gains occur where direct matches are unavailable: Occluded or out-of-frame pixels account for roughly 10% of valid pixels but 50% of WAFT's total error. Experiments show that adaptive correspondence through pixel-to-token grouping enables reliable matching and precise pixel-level flow, improving generalization to unseen real scenes.
bullets: Decouples correspondence density from flow resolution, avoiding uniformly dense matching.
Adapts token supports to image structure: larger in coherent regions and smaller near motion boundaries.
Shares pixel-to-token associations for feature pooling, token matching, and dense flow reconstruction.
Joint flow supervision learns pixel grouping without grouping labels and helps infer shared motion from appearance.
Trained only on synthetic data, FATE achieves the best zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI, with notable gains near boundaries and for occluded or out-of-frame pixels.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles use pedestrian crossing intention prediction (PCIP) to participate safely in traffic. Existing models are largely trained under favourable daytime conditions with sufficient daylight. Little is known about the robustness of these models under night-time and low-light conditions, due to the lack of datasets containing night-time footage. This paper investigates how a dataset, named NightSteps, can be constructed and evaluated as a baseline benchmark. The dataset is based on nighttime dashcam footage collected from six different cities around the world, capturing a wide variety of road conditions. The dataset consists of dashcam-recorded point-of-view footage, raw data of pedestrians' locations with corresponding 'track ids' and ground-truth labels containing accurate information about pedestrian crossing behaviour, resulting in a diverse dataset. Gemini, ChatGPT, and human assessment are used to demonstrate the usability of the dataset by predicting crossings in clips from the dataset and comparing the results with the initial ground-truth labels. These results show that human input achieves an accuracy of 88.17% and an F1-score of 80.21%. Predictions from Gemini and ChatGPT perform lower, with accuracies of 60% and 79.13% respectively, and F1-scores of 42.50% and 63.64%. The evaluation demonstrates that the NightSteps dataset can be used for future model evaluation to test the performance of PCIP, with the aim of improving road safety at night.
bullets: Addresses the lack of nighttime data for robust pedestrian crossing intention prediction.
Uses dashcam footage from six cities with varied road conditions, pedestrian locations, track IDs, and crossing labels.
Evaluates dataset usability with human assessment, Gemini, and ChatGPT predictions against ground truth.
Humans achieved 88.17% accuracy and an 80.21% F1-score; Gemini and ChatGPT performed lower.
Supports future evaluation and improvement of nighttime PCIP systems for road safety.

papers.abstract: As long-video understanding gains increasing attention, augmented reality (AR) devices are emerging as a compelling deployment platform. However, egocentric videos exhibit significant temporal redundancy, imposing substantial memory and computational burdens on resource-constrained AR hardware. To address this challenge, we introduce UTOPI, a plug-and-play pre-compression module designed specifically for egocentric long videos on AR platforms. First, we leverage user motion signals to estimate inter-frame overlap and propose a viewpoint-shift-invariant pruning algorithm. Second, we exploit eye-tracking sensors to identify user fixations, enabling the separation of attended foreground content from background and its preferential retention via a fine-tuned neural network-based adjustment mechanism. Across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, UTOPI achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance. Code and project page are available at https://sai-lab-nyu.github.io/utopi/.
bullets: Addresses the memory and computation costs of temporally redundant egocentric videos on resource-constrained AR hardware.
Uses user motion to estimate inter-frame overlap and perform viewpoint-shift-invariant token pruning.
Uses eye tracking to distinguish attended foreground content from background and preferentially retain it.
Works as a plug-and-play pre-compression module across multiple benchmarks and model backbones.
Achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Agentic autoregressive video generation combines semantic planning, sequential generation, and visual verification for controllable synthesis. Growing visual histories enlarge the key-value (KV) cache, increasing memory use and attention costs across candidate rollouts. Existing compression methods primarily optimize individual generators without the planner's semantic constraints, risking low priority for states supporting requested attributes or actions. We introduce SemanticKV, a training-free method for semantically aligned KV cache compression. To our knowledge, SemanticKV is the first KV cache compression method for agentic autoregressive video generation that explicitly uses planner-extracted semantic constraints to guide retention. Text cross-attention identifies constraint-related video positions, whose self-attention queries are collected into separate groups. Attention weights are averaged within each group and maximized across groups, giving each cached entry a high score when strongly used by any represented constraint. A single top-k selection retains high-scoring entries under the memory budget, leaving their keys, values, and positions unchanged. For fixed query groups and equal entry costs, this selection minimizes an additive upper bound on worst-group discarded attention. The method operates independently within each candidate without retraining or additional video generations. We evaluate four AR video backbones on three benchmarks for 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation. On Causal Forcing at a compression ratio of 0.7, SemanticKV obtains a VBench Total Score of 84.10, compared with 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV. It achieves a 1.22x speedup over Full KV and reduces KV-cache memory from 6.04 GB to 1.81 GB, a 3.35x reduction.
bullets: Addresses growing KV-cache memory and attention costs from long visual histories and candidate rollouts.
Uses planner-extracted constraints and text cross-attention to group relevant queries, then selects a single top-k set of high-value cache entries.
Training-free, operates independently per candidate, and preserves retained keys, values, and positions without extra video generation.
Across four backbones and three benchmarks, it supports 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation; on Causal Forcing, it reports a 1.22× speedup and 3.35× lower KV-cache memory.
At 0.7 compression on Causal Forcing, it reports a VBench score of 84.10 versus 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV.

papers.abstract: Aligning video generation models with human preference depends critically on the quality of the reward model that scores generated videos. Current video reward models, however, source their reward signal from a model's representational rather than generative capacity: they either repurpose vision-language models as pixel-space scorers, or train auxiliary scoring heads on top of frozen generator features. The generator's actual ability to predict velocities, denoise latents, and produce videos plays no role in scoring its own generations. We argue that this overlooks a structural property of offline preference learning. Any preference optimization objective that approximates an offline preference dataset mathematically targets a strictly defined KL-constrained optimal policy. By isolating the reward term from this analytical solution and mapping the exact generation log-likelihood to its flow-matching surrogate, the empirical reward emerges deterministically as the relative difference in continuous-time velocity-prediction errors. We formalize this equivalence into GenRM-Flow, a framework where a preference-tuned video generator inherently operates as a process-aware reward model directly in the noisy latent space. We further show theoretically that distinct fine-tuning objectives, whether contrastive like DPO and IPO or non-contrastive like RWR, are alternative optimization pathways toward the same optimal policy, each inducing a reward readout from the generator's velocity-prediction errors. Furthermore, the extracted process reward seamlessly substitutes external VLM scorers in FlowAWR. Operating purely on native latent outputs without auxiliary reward networks, this generative reward drives measurable improvements in downstream video generation.
bullets: Current video reward models score representations or add scoring heads, ignoring the generator’s denoising and video-generation capabilities.
GenRM-Flow derives an empirical reward from the relative difference in continuous-time velocity-prediction errors in noisy latent space.
The framework links preference objectives such as DPO, IPO, and RWR to the same KL-constrained optimal policy and reward readout.
The process reward can replace external vision-language-model scorers in FlowAWR.
Using native latent outputs, the approach yields measurable downstream improvements in video generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The pipeline of GenRM-Flow. Following preference optimization, the implicit reward RD(x, c) is algebraically extracted from the velocity-prediction errors. The scalar score is computed natively by contrasting the active policy (flame, θ⋆) against a frozen reference (snowflake, θref ), requiring no architectural modifications or auxiliary heads.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for video action recognition typically conflate spatial appearance and temporal dynamics into a single saliency or importance map. We propose a perturbation-based framework that disentangles these contributions into a spatial appearance mask ($M_a$) and a temporal motion mask ($M_m$). The two masks are jointly optimized against a frozen action recognition model through factored perturbation architecture, with nearest frame replacement to identify important temporal dynamics. A separation penalty discourages the appearance mask from spending budget on frames that the motion mask has already discarded. A ReLU-based area constraint penalizes explanations larger than an assigned budget. To evaluate these explanations, we introduce a separation protocol that sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames independently, backed by proofs characterizing the proposed method. Across EPIC-Kitchens-55, EGTEA Gaze+, and Something-Something V2, our method attains the lowest deletion AUC against leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.
bullets: Addresses the conflation of spatial appearance and temporal dynamics in existing video explanations.
Jointly learns an appearance mask and a motion mask against a frozen recognition model.
Uses nearest-frame replacement, separation penalties, and area constraints to isolate temporal and spatial importance.
Introduces a protocol that independently sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames to evaluate explanations.
Across three video datasets, achieves the lowest deletion AUC among compared baselines with masks about five times sparser.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient image-to-video transfer adapts frozen image foundation models to video via lightweight trainable adapters. Existing methods insert the same adapter at every transformer layer, implicitly assuming all layers require equal temporal modeling. A layer-wise sensitivity analysis across four video-native model families and two pretraining paradigms reveals that this assumption is wrong: temporal sensitivity increases with depth, and the pretraining paradigm determines its growth profile. Vision-only models exhibit a gradual rise, while vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery. This finding motivates STRAP, a training-free adapter placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model. Spatial adapters are assigned before this boundary and temporal adapters after it, without modifying the adapter architecture itself. On four fine-grained action recognition benchmarks, STRAP improves accuracy by up to 11.8% over uniform placement, reduces trainable parameters by 29 to 48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%. On standard benchmarks, it matches accuracy with fewer parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/th-nesh/STRAP.
bullets: Temporal sensitivity generally increases with transformer depth, but its pattern depends on the model’s pretraining paradigm.
Vision-only models show a gradual sensitivity increase; vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery.
STRAP is a training-free placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model.
Across four fine-grained action-recognition benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 11.8%, reduces trainable parameters by 29–48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%.
On standard benchmarks, STRAP matches accuracy with fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: Surgical procedures are inherently partially observable, requiring surgeons to continuously infer evolving anatomical dynamics and future surgical states beyond the current observation. However, existing self-supervised learning methods primarily learn from observed surgical videos through masked reconstruction or predicting representations within the camera's current field of view, lacking the capability to explicitly model the out-of-sight surgical dynamics. Inspired by latent predictive world models, we introduce SurgWorld, a video-native, self-supervised framework for surgical representation learning, which treats a specified spatial or temporal shift as a pseudo-action and learns to predict the target latent representation from a partial observation. Specifically, we propose Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling (OSDM) as the pretraining objective for predicting representations conditioned on relative spatio-temporal shifts. We further regularize the learned latent dynamics from OSDM with a Geometric Visual Similarity (GVS) objective by aligning patch-level relational structures between predicted and target representations, preserving spatial geometry and local visual coherence for dense perception. These two objectives are integrated through an agglomerative training framework that consolidates complementary supervisory signals from multiple teachers to learn a unified latent representation of surgical dynamics and visual geometry. Extensive transfer learning experiments on 17 surgical benchmarks show that SurgWorld consistently outperforms existing vision foundation models across surgical workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense visual perception. We further conduct tailored qualitative and quantitative analyses, demonstrating that SurgWorld effectively captures surgical dynamics beyond the directly observed context through latent prediction.
bullets: Addresses the partial observability of surgery, which limits methods focused only on visible content.
Uses spatial or temporal shifts as pseudo-actions and introduces Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling to predict target latent representations.
Adds Geometric Visual Similarity regularization to preserve patch-level spatial relationships and local visual coherence.
Combines complementary supervisory signals through an agglomerative training framework for unified dynamics and geometry representations.
Transfers effectively across 17 surgical benchmarks spanning workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense perception.

papers.abstract: Compressing continuous human motion into a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens is now the first stage of many motion understanding and generation pipelines. Vector quantization partitions a latent space into Voronoi cells around a finite codebook, but the geometry of that latent space is inherited from the input pose encoding, and it is unclear which encoding admits an efficient discretization. We study four encodings that place skeletal motion in different geometric spaces: Gaussian joint heatmaps on the pixel lattice, which we show to be a morphological dilation of the joint point set by a quadratic structuring function; root-relative joint positions in Euclidean space; local joint rotations on $\SO$ through a continuous 6D embedding; and a redundant full kinematic encoding. For each, we train VQ-VAE tokenizers whose codebooks lie on the unit hypersphere, varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension. Beyond reconstruction, we measure codebook utilization and the effective vocabulary size, i.e., the number of equiprobable spherical Voronoi cells with the same entropy as the observed token distribution. Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty. The smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings, and the effect of temporal stride depends on the encoding. Encodings of the same pose family can thus yield effective vocabularies differing by an order of magnitude, a difference that reconstruction loss alone does not reveal, which points to input geometry as a first-order design choice in motion tokenization.
bullets: Compares four pose geometries: joint heatmaps, root-relative positions, local rotations, and full kinematic features.
Trains VQ-VAE tokenizers while varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension.
Evaluates reconstruction alongside codebook utilization and entropy-based effective vocabulary size.
Rotation and position encodings continue benefiting from larger codebooks; full kinematic features saturate at a few hundred effective cells, while heatmaps remain below 60.
Small code dimensions generally maximize utilization, and temporal-stride effects depend on the encoding.

papers.title: Does Pose Encoding Matter? Analyzing Geometric Representations for Discrete Motion Vocabulary Learning
papers.tldr: Pose encoding strongly determines how efficiently continuous motion can be converted into discrete tokens, with rotation and position representations supporting much larger effective vocabularies than heatmaps or redundant kinematic encodings.

papers.abstract: Video understanding evaluations are intended to measure a model's proficiency in video perception and task solving. However, current VideoQA benchmarks struggle to isolate these capabilities due to their reliance on multiple-choice (MC) answer guidance, language priors, and fragile scoring pipelines. Disentangling these confounding factors reveals how much of a model's score is supplied by the evaluation context rather than earned through faithful perception. Across six VideoQA benchmarks of varying length, we find that accuracy is significantly above chance without any visual input. This is caused by shortcutting and option-prior reliance. We express these effects in the language of faithfulness: option-exploitation and answer-conditioned reasoning traces are unfaithful even when they are correct. Together, our results show that a VideoQA score is jointly determined by language priors, option timing, and how outputs and labels are converted into correctness. We produce a novel Option-Delayed Replay (ODR) mechanism that discloses options at controlled stages of an open-ended (OE) trajectory, to obtain objective MC scores from faithful option-free inference. Our work demonstrates that agentic methods with ODR and faithful inference can match option-exploiting performance. Finally, we formalize our diagnostic collection and ODR as a reproducible evaluation protocol, and we release a human-relabelled edition of LVBench (correcting $20.5\%$ of keys) to remove annotation noise as a confounding variable.
bullets: Across six VideoQA benchmarks, models perform above chance even without visual input, indicating reliance on language priors and answer-option exploitation.
The study identifies option timing, answer-conditioned reasoning, and scoring/label conversion as major confounds in VideoQA evaluation.
Option-Delayed Replay (ODR) reveals answer choices at controlled points during an otherwise open-ended, option-free inference process.
Agentic methods using ODR and faithful inference can match performance achieved through option exploitation.
The authors release a reproducible diagnostic protocol and a human-relabelled LVBench edition correcting 20.5% of answer keys.

Each column withholds or perturbs a single input while holding all other settings fixed relative to MC (full). Chance and Heuristic use no model at all (Appendix F). This equals the full split everywhere except LVBench open-ended (1,477 of 1,549 items) and the two QBench-Video Author-AVP replay conditions (622 of 868 items), where differences are taken over the shared subset. The two OE columns take the difference against the judge binarised at ≥ 80 (§G.7), not against the mean rating, so both sides of every entry are per-item correctness on one scale; the bracketed figures in Table 1 are these binarised scores. papers.abstract: Surgical video understanding is an important foundation for intelligent assistance in robot-assisted surgery. Similar surgical views can reflect different actions or procedural stages. Interpreting these views requires access to earlier observations, yet frame-centric prompting leaves this history unavailable. We introduce MemSurg, a framework that remembers surgical observations before reasoning over them. Its structured memory graph stores timestamped entity categories, locations, motion cues, and interaction summaries. Chronological links preserve recent context, while entity-associated links connect recurring observations across the procedure. Task-adaptive retrieval then supplies evidence-grounded prompts for scene and workflow reasoning, supporting both frozen inference and memory-conditioned supervised fine-tuning. Evaluation on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two complementary surgical benchmarks shows a 10.43-percentage-point gain over SurgRAW with GPT-4o. Memory conditioning adds 6.52 points under matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and an inference-time plug-in adds 7.04 points to EndoChat. These results support structured memory as a reusable source of procedural evidence for surgical video understanding. Our code will be publicly released.
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of similar surgical views that correspond to different actions or procedural stages.
Builds a memory graph containing timestamped entities, locations, motion cues, interaction summaries, and chronological or entity-linked context.
Uses task-adaptive retrieval to generate evidence-grounded prompts for frozen inference or memory-conditioned fine-tuning.
Improves performance by 10.43 points over SurgRAW with GPT-4o, by 6.52 points with matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and by 7.04 points as an EndoChat plug-in.
Evaluated on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two additional surgical benchmarks; code is planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Video fusion aims to integrate complementary cues from heterogeneous sources, producing visually informative videos with coherent spatio-temporal structures. Jointly learning cross-modal complementarity and temporal dependencies typically relies on large-scale, high-quality video datasets, whose storage and repeated use during optimization incur substantial costs, making data-efficient learning highly desirable. To address this challenge, we rethink video fusion from the perspective of dataset condensation and propose STAR-VF, the first framework that condenses spatio-temporal representations for data-efficient video fusion. STAR-VF condenses the original training set into a compact set of learnable spatio-temporal representations, which are decoded into synthetic video clips and optimized using feature-level supervision provided by a frozen proxy model. The resulting condensed data preserves fusion-relevant spatial and temporal cues without requiring ground-truth fused videos as supervision. To adapt fusion learning to condensed representations, we equip the final fusion model with flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation, enabling direct temporal interaction and adaptive selection of fusion-relevant information in representation space. Extensive experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion benchmarks demonstrate that STAR-VF, trained with only approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training set, achieves fusion quality comparable to methods trained on the full data. Further analyses validate the contributions of learned condensation and flow-free temporal modeling, and demonstrate the robustness of the condensed supervision across different proxy encoders and downstream fusion models. Project page: https://zju-xyc.github.io/STAR-VF-Project-Page/.
bullets: Targets the storage and optimization costs of large video-fusion training datasets.
Learns compact spatio-temporal representations, decodes them into synthetic clips, and optimizes them with feature-level supervision from a frozen proxy model.
Uses flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation for fusion directly in representation space.
Supports infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion without requiring ground-truth fused videos.
Using approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training data, it achieves fusion quality comparable to full-data training; robustness is shown across proxy encoders and downstream fusion models.

In Stage II, the learned condensed set is decoded into synthetic temporal samples to train the final fusion model 𝐹𝜃 with flow-free temporal alignment and query-driven intra-frame aggregation. During inference, only the trained fusion model is used, without the condensed set or proxy model.

papers.abstract: Endoscopic diagnosis unfolds over native video, where a single positive finding during traversal of the gastrointestinal tract sets off a multi-minute chain of reasoning over location, morphology, severity and intervention. Existing endoscopy multimodal benchmarks test only static images or single-disease videos, which miss the temporal and clinical reasoning that real-world reporting demands. We introduce EndoSCOP-V, a video-grounded multi-turn evaluation framework for structured endoscopy reporting and clinical reasoning. It contains 1,307 real-world endoscopy and colonoscopy videos (63.2 h; 97% 1080p) averaging about 174 s. Its 20,274 question-answer turns are instantiated deterministically from clinician-filled structured endoscopy-reporting EHRs, so no per-case annotation is synthetic or LLM-rephrased. They come from 1,033 clinician-reviewed templates, about 18 per disease, that span a clinically aligned 9-task x 30-sub-task reporting taxonomy over 54 World Endoscopy Organization (WEO) MST 3.0 diseases. 22% of procedures carry co-existing pathologies, up to six per case. A Markovian context-pruned oracle-forcing protocol evaluates the dialogue turn by turn, injecting the gold answer before each subsequent turn so that per-turn reasoning is isolated from cascading dialogue errors. A panel of 15 board-certified endoscopists sets a 78% strict-accuracy baseline on 1,500 questions. Across 14 open-weight LMMs, the best 27B-class model reaches 59.8% strict accuracy, falling to 53.4% once format-trivial disease-rejection items are excluded. On a between-subjects spot-check, the best of 3 frontier proprietary models trails the clinician panel by 23 pp on strict NDR accuracy. Sub-task analysis reveals consistent gaps in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading and intervention reasoning on long-horizon video. Data: Hugging Face (EndoSCOP-V). Code: GitHub (abhi25t/EndoSCOP-V).
bullets: Addresses the limits of static-image and single-disease benchmarks for temporal, multi-finding endoscopy reasoning.
Includes 1,307 real-world videos, 20,274 deterministic question-answer turns, 54 diseases, and a 9-task, 30-subtask reporting taxonomy.
Uses clinician-derived EHR templates and context-pruned oracle forcing to isolate turn-level reasoning from cascading dialogue errors.
The best 27B open-weight model achieves 59.8% strict accuracy versus 78% for 15 board-certified endoscopists; performance drops to 53.4% after excluding format-trivial items.
Models show persistent weaknesses in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading, and intervention reasoning over long videos.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) enable AI systems to interpret egocentric video. Yet continuous visual capture raises privacy concerns because sensitive content is pervasive and varies across users and contexts. We present EgoVeil, a personalized privacy reasoning system that determines which visual content to obscure based on individual preferences while retaining context useful for downstream assistance. It converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory for personalized privacy reasoning. This design supports personalization and continual adaptation as preference evidence accumulates. We evaluate on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol. EgoVeil achieves 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines. Our results show that personalized, adaptive privacy reasoning better aligns privacy preservation with individual preferences while retaining the visual context needed for effective smart-glasses assistance.
bullets: Addresses privacy risks from continuous egocentric video capture, where sensitive content varies by user and context.
Converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations for reasoning.
Combines a privacy reasoner with explicit user-specific memory to support personalization and continual adaptation.
Evaluated on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users using a cross-user chronological protocol.
Reports 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming the described baseline systems.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but attention over long spatiotemporal sequences makes inference computationally expensive. Sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only a subset of query-key interactions exactly, and recent training-free methods further approximate the remaining interactions. These methods, however, degrade quickly at high sparsity, which limits the achievable speedup. We present ESTRA (Extreme Sparsity Through Refined Attention), a training-free acceleration method that preserves generation quality even at extreme sparsity. ESTRA concentrates exact attention computation on a small set of important key-value tokens and approximates the remaining contributions with cluster representatives. To identify these tokens efficiently, it groups similar queries and uses their representatives to score individual keys. A variance-based correction further refines the attention weights of the cluster representatives, improving the accuracy of the approximation. Experiments on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B show that ESTRA establishes a new quality-efficiency frontier for training-free sparse attention, achieving $3.26\times$ and $4.71\times$ end-to-end speedups at 5% attention density while surpassing Sol-Attn and SVG-EAR in fidelity to dense generation and on most VBench dimensions. Even at 1% density, ESTRA remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5%, while reaching up to $5.39\times$ speedup.
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of attention over long spatiotemporal video sequences.
Selects a small set of important key-value tokens using clustered query representatives.
Approximates remaining attention with cluster representatives and applies variance-based weight correction.
At 5% attention density, achieves 3.26× and 4.71× end-to-end speedups on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B.
At 1% density, remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5% density, with up to 5.39× speedup.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free method for extreme attention sparsity in video diffusion transformers, relevant to video diffusion and efficient attention.
papers.title: ESTRA: Enabling Extreme Attention Sparsity for Training-Free Video Diffusion Acceleration
papers.tldr: ESTRA accelerates video diffusion transformers with training-free sparse attention, retaining high fidelity at extreme sparsity and delivering up to 5.39× speedup.

papers.abstract: Feature caching accelerates Diffusion Transformers by reusing intermediate computations across denoising timesteps, yet existing methods share a fundamental blind spot: they treat the standard reference denoising trajectory as the optimisation target, approximating its per-step states and thus inheriting its output as an implicit quality ceiling. We argue that this target is arbitrary -- what truly matters is the ideal result, not the intermediate path taken to reach it. We propose IdealCache, a training-free framework that abandons step-wise imitation of the reference trajectory. Instead, it anchors caching on a per-input ensemble of ideal trajectories constructed from candidate target results, aggregates their geometry into a single graph, and discovers optimal non-uniform schedules via a constrained shortest path on this graph. By decoupling from the reference process, IdealCache breaks the performance bottleneck of trajectory-approximation; our schedules can attain near-lossless fidelity in generation and even surpass on task-specific metrics (e.g., maintaining higher semantic consistency in image editing). Without retraining, IdealCache achieves 6.35x speedup on Qwen-Image, 5.84x on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32x on HunyuanVideo, with competitive or superior quality across tasks.
bullets: Existing cache schedulers optimize approximation of the reference denoising trajectory, imposing an implicit quality ceiling.
IdealCache constructs per-input ensembles of ideal trajectories from candidate target results and aggregates their geometry into a graph.
A constrained shortest-path search identifies input-specific, non-uniform caching schedules.
The training-free method reports speedups of 6.35× on Qwen-Image, 5.84× on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32× on HunyuanVideo.
It maintains competitive or superior generation quality, including higher semantic consistency for image editing.

papers.selection_reason: Cache scheduling for Diffusion Transformers; large speedups on image/video diffusion with near-lossless quality.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms is paramount for advancing model training and inference in a principled way. Here, we demonstrate that deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal geometric structure invariant to data modalities and diffusion model implementations. This structure can be largely explained by an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.
bullets: Motivates understanding the mechanisms underlying diffusion-based generative modeling.
Analyzes deterministic sampling trajectories across data modalities and diffusion implementations.
Identifies a universal geometric structure shared across these trajectories.
Explains much of the structure using an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.

papers.selection_reason: Universal geometric structure in deterministic diffusion sampling; transferable to video diffusion and generative modeling.
papers.title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion
papers.tldr: Deterministic diffusion sampling trajectories exhibit a modality- and implementation-invariant geometric structure that can be explained by an exactly solvable optimal-linear-denoiser model.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires models to answer user queries over continuously evolving video streams. Unlike offline video QA, SVU must handle queries whose evidence may lie in the past, appear in the current scene, or emerge only after future observations. Existing streaming video systems often rely on compact visual memories or fixed evidence-access schemes, which can lose fine-grained details and fail to adapt the answering process to the temporal intent of each query. In this paper, we propose TimeTraveler, a streaming VQA framework that performs temporal strategy planning with a Time Dictionary. Inspired by the need to search across different temporal regions of a stream, TimeTraveler stores each observed moment as a timestamp-indexed structured caption and uses this dictionary as an explicit source of queryable evidence. Given a query, TimeTraveler determines whether to recall past evidence, read the present context, or wait for future observations, and then applies a strategy-specific evidence acquisition process. Comparative experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show that TimeTraveler improves streaming question answering by preserving fine-grained temporal evidence and selecting the appropriate temporal strategy for each query. The project page is available at https://geppa.github.io/TimeTraveler.
bullets: Addresses streaming video queries whose evidence may occur before, during, or after the current scene.
Stores observed moments as timestamp-indexed structured captions for fine-grained, queryable temporal evidence.
Selects a query-specific strategy: retrieve past evidence, read present context, or defer answering for future observations.
Experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show improved question answering through temporal evidence preservation and strategy selection.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TimeTraveler. Incoming video frames are encoded into structured captions and stored in a timestamp-indexed Time Dictionary. Given a query, a Temporal Strategy Planner acquires evidence following temporal intent: past queries retrieve relevant captions through similaritybased lookback, current queries access local captions, and future queries continue observation until evidence appears. Then, the retrieved evidence is used to produce the final answer.

Figure 1: Conceptual comparison between prior memory-based SVU and TimeTraveler. Prior methods preserve streaming history as agentic memory [19], pruned tokens [22], or KV-memory recall [24], but rely on a single evidence-access path and do not ensure that retained evidence remains query-recoverable. In contrast, TimeTraveler plans whether each query should be grounded in the past, current scene, or future, and accesses a structured Time Dictionary accordingly.

Figure 3: Textual input sensitivity on OVO-Bench. We replace a fraction ρ of the Time Dictionary captions with irrelevant captions sampled from unrelated videos and measure the resulting Overall accuracy. Dashed lines indicate the baseline (no memory) and our full method (clean captions).

Figure 4: Qualitative example of lookback retrieval on OVO-Bench. Given a query at time tq, the similarity score over past captions (orange curve) peaks at the frame most relevant to the question. The retrieved Time Dictionary caption preserves fine-grained details such as on-screen text (“FRONT RAISE”), spatial layout, and highlighted muscle groups, which are essential for answering correctly.

papers.abstract: Deepfake videos generated by advanced generative models pose serious threats to digital security, misinformation control, and media forensics. Although numerous detection methods have been proposed, their reported performances are often based on heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, inconsistent data splits, and model-specific training protocols, hindering fair architectural comparison. This work presents a controlled and reproducible comparative study of convolutional neural networks (ResNet-18 and EfficientNet-B0) and a transformer-based architecture (ViT-B/16) within a unified, face-centric deepfake detection framework. All models are trained using identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization settings, and data splits on Celeb-DF v2 and FaceForensics++, and results are validated across three independent random seeds with bootstrapped confidence intervals. Experimental results show that while CNN-based models perform competitively at the frame level, their performance degrades after video-level aggregation. In contrast, ViT-B/16 demonstrates more stable video-level performance, achieving 92.8\% [95\% CI: 91.7--94.0] video-level accuracy and an AUC of 0.950 [95\% CI: 0.934--0.964] on Celeb-DF v2 (3-seed bootstrapped). Cross-dataset evaluation across the same three random seeds reveals a large, asymmetric generalization gap (AUC 0.79 FF++$\rightarrow$Celeb-DF vs. 0.64 Celeb-DF$\rightarrow$FF++), indicating that in-domain video-level stability does not transfer to unseen manipulation domains. These findings indicate that global self-attention improves robustness and video-level stability for deepfake detection within a given data domain, while highlighting the need for further work on cross-domain generalization.
bullets: CNNs perform competitively at the frame level but degrade after video-level aggregation.
ViT-B/16 achieves 92.8% video-level accuracy and 0.950 AUC on Celeb-DF v2, with bootstrapped confidence intervals across three seeds.
The study uses a unified face-centric pipeline with identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization, splits, and evaluation across ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, and ViT-B/16.
Cross-dataset performance shows an asymmetric generalization gap: AUC 0.79 from FaceForensics++ to Celeb-DF versus 0.64 in the reverse direction.
Results support improved in-domain stability from global self-attention, while emphasizing limited cross-domain robustness.

papers.abstract: Computer vision (CV) for policing has centred on recognising objects such as seized weapons, while body-worn video (BWV) is still reviewed by people, with existing AI tools using only its audio. Multimodal video AI could make BWV review faster and cheaper. At the object level, we present the KnifeHunter dataset, developed with UK law enforcement, with over 25,000 images of 543 knife classes and a protocol reflecting investigative conditions, and KHNet, a retrieval architecture fusing local and global features, which with about 125,000 distractor images attains 85.7% and 63.4% mean Average Precision (mAP) on the medium and hard protocols. At the event level, we present an evaluation protocol for video understanding pipelines, which describe a video as events and a transcript, that scores transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation and unsupported events. Whether each event is supported by the recording is labelled by a judge validated against blinded human labels. We apply it to complete pipelines, three 2026 omni-modal models and our hybrid NarrativeBridge-PAL-GPT-5 pipeline, on UKBWV-27, a pilot stress-test set of 27 publicly released UK BWV recordings (118 minutes). On this set the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures, yet it leaves 13.6% of predicted events unsupported and misattributes 27.7% of utterances, and every pipeline degrades on recordings from edited releases, long recordings and noisy audio. We propose readiness levels separating assistive tasks from those requiring verification of every output.
bullets: Introduces KnifeHunter, a law-enforcement-developed dataset with over 25,000 images across 543 knife classes and investigative evaluation protocols.
Presents KHNet, which fuses local and global visual features for knife retrieval, achieving 85.7% mAP on the medium protocol and 63.4% on the hard protocol.
Proposes an event-level evaluation framework covering transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation, and evidential support.
On 27 UK body-worn-video recordings, the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures but produces 13.6% unsupported events and misattributes 27.7% of utterances.
Performance declines for edited releases, long recordings, and noisy audio; the paper recommends readiness levels distinguishing assistive uses from outputs requiring verification.

papers.abstract: Benchmark scores license claims about the capabilities being evaluated. We audit the inference licensed by an evaluation protocol, rather than the predictive model alone. Using procedural action anticipation as a controlled case study, we study a broader evaluation-validity failure mode: a protocol can remain temporally causal and free of classical target leakage while still supplying a privileged intermediate representation. The failure is not merely optimistic accuracy, but a mismatch between the capability claimed and the construct actually measured. On Breakfast, matched recognizer-history and GT-history regimes score 30.3% and 62.3% (Delta_PH(R_BA) = +32.0, 95% Student-t interval [+24.1, +39.8]). A fixed-checkpoint 2 x 2 intervention isolates a +14.6-point test-time oracle contrast; a matched no-video provenance probe yields a +26.8-point gap; and a boundary-independent query/history control retains a +19.4-point gap. We refer to this discrepancy as a privileged-information gap, defined relative to a specified non-oracle recovery pipeline, and propose a reusable four-condition audit. Across five evaluation settings the gap is heterogeneous; a standard 50 Salads long-term-anticipation re-implementation provides cautious support beyond the audit-specific next-action construction.
bullets: Audits the validity of evaluation protocols, not just predictive models.
In Breakfast, ground-truth history scores 62.3% versus 30.3% for recognizer history, a 32.0-point privileged-information gap.
Controlled interventions show the gap persists without video and under boundary-independent history controls.
Proposes a reusable four-condition audit and finds heterogeneous gaps across five evaluation settings.
Evidence beyond the audit-specific setup is cautiously supported by a 50 Salads re-implementation.

papers.tldr: Evaluation protocols for action anticipation can appear causal yet overstate capability by giving models privileged intermediate information.

papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to construct a dynamic 3D scene (Draft Video) that provides structure and motion signals to downstream video generators. To support this paradigm, we design a dedicated data pipeline and curate two high-quality datasets, Video-Coder-SFT-6k and Video-Coder-RL-2k, which contain diverse prompts and ground-truth reference videos. We further develop the Video- Coder Harness, a unified interactive environment integrating code execution, 3D scene rendering, and execution feedback for agent training and inference. We then train Video-Coder with SFT fol- lowed by harness-native agentic reinforcement learning with dual reward feedback, which combines execution-based and video-based rewards. Additionally, we design an annealing training strategy that gradually reduces the execution reward over time, allowing the model to rely more on the video reward in the later training stages. Experiments show that Video-Coder achieves significant gains, improving Minimax-H3 by approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0. We hope this work can serve as an open foundation for coding agents in video generation, and we fully open-source our data, models, and code
authors: Chaoyang Wang, Sicheng Gao, Junan Hu, Kunyang Li, Dongyang Chen, Yiyang Zhou, Huaxiu Yao, Yong Jae Lee, Radu Timofte, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: Addresses difficulties in precise spatial structure, coherent motion, and controllable scene composition in video generation.
Uses code-driven 3D scene construction to produce draft videos with structural and motion signals for downstream generators.
Introduces a training pipeline with supervised fine-tuning, agentic reinforcement learning, and dual execution/video rewards.
Employs an annealing strategy that shifts reliance from execution feedback to video quality during training.
Reports gains of approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0, with data, models, and code released.

papers.abstract: 3D spatial reasoning from video remains challenging for VLMs because videos provide sequential, view-local observations rather than persistent metric scene records. Many questions must be answered in a query-specified perspective rather than the observed camera viewpoint, and prompting with a fixed set of RGB views may miss sparse or occluded visual cues. To address these gaps, we introduce BEV3SR, a training-free and backbone-agnostic framework for RGB-D videos with camera parameters. BEV3SR turns video observations into queryable metric bird's-eye-view (BEV) scene memory and formalizes each query into an evidence-aware spatial task. The Spatial Task Formalizer specifies the query's reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and evidence requirement. The evidence requirement determines the appropriate reasoning pathway. A query treated as requiring geometric evidence is handled by the Geometric Reasoner, which deterministically computes the answer using the metric BEV records in the query-specified reference frame. Otherwise, a query treated as requiring visual evidence is passed to the Visual Evidence Aligner, which uses BEV-indexed object records and their associated supporting views to retrieve object-consistent and scene-context RGB frames for VLM grounding. Within a standard 16-frame budget, BEV3SR consistently improves different VLM backbones across multiple 3D scene QA benchmarks, delivering large gains on spatially intensive questions and significant improvements on open-ended scene QA. These results demonstrate that BEV3SR offers an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for explicit 3D spatial reasoning from video.
bullets: Addresses view-local, sequential video observations, query-specific viewpoints, and sparse or occluded evidence.
Formalizes each query’s reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and required evidence.
Computes geometry-based answers deterministically from metric BEV records in the requested reference frame.
Retrieves object-consistent and contextual RGB frames for VLM grounding when visual evidence is needed.
Improves multiple VLM backbones across 3D scene QA benchmarks, especially spatially intensive and open-ended questions, within a 16-frame budget.

papers.abstract: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. Existing training-free video editing methods, however, assume full offline access to the entire sequence, while streaming approaches either rely on additional training or are limited to specific editing techniques. We show that this limitation can be removed by analyzing the self-attention dynamics of DMD-distilled autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. We uncover a key asymmetry: queries and keys remain stable and aligned with their source counterparts across denoising timesteps, while values diverge and encode the evolving content. Inherited from the non-distilled bidirectional teacher, this asymmetry is strongest at high noise, where few-step streaming models operate. The resulting mechanism is simple: a single forward pass suffices to capture source identity in the value features, which can be reused throughout generation. Starting from pure Gaussian noise and injecting only these source values reconstructs the input with fidelity matching or surpassing inversion-based methods, effectively eliminating inversion. Based on this insight, we introduce AR-Edit, a training-free, inversion-free method that caches source values once and selectively injects them during denoising. Across multiple AR backbones, AR-Edit enables real-time streaming editing with superior source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.
authors: Hovhannes Margaryan, Quentin Bammey, Christian Sandor, Vicky Kalogeiton
bullets: Addresses the need for online video editing without future-frame access, training, or technique-specific constraints.
Analyzes self-attention in DMD-distilled autoregressive video diffusion models and identifies stable query/key alignment but evolving value features.
Caches source values in a single forward pass and selectively injects them during denoising from Gaussian noise.
Across multiple autoregressive backbones, achieves real-time editing with improved source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.

papers.abstract: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at https://starry1001.github.io/AnimWeb-Bench-website/ .
authors: Zhongyi Zhang, Jingyu Xiao, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 124 real-world webpages across 7 domains and 33 animation types, paired with reference videos and original static assets.
Provides a two-dimensional evaluation protocol measuring static appearance fidelity and animation fidelity across aligned frames.
Finds that webpage animation reconstruction is harder than reproducing static visual appearance.
Shows that explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve coding-agent reconstruction quality.
Reports that rapid, continuous motion is more difficult to reproduce than discrete state transitions.

papers.abstract: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.
authors: Xiangqun Zhang, Likai Wang, Zekun Qian, Rui Zhou, Ruize Han, Wei Feng
bullets: Formulates cross-view dense video object captioning (CVDVOC), combining synchronized multi-camera evidence instead of processing views independently.
Constructs CRTrack-Cap with 425 global trajectories, 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, and canonical captions for 335 identities.
Introduces CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate cross-view tracking and caption quality.
The reference framework uses VECA for cross-camera association and CEG to integrate reliable, non-conflicting caption evidence.
It reports CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 in-domain and 33.48 cross-domain on scene-disjoint tests.

papers.abstract: We address geometric video alignment for the same scene captured by multiple freely moving cameras. Existing methods, which are based on image stitching or video stabilization, are typically limited to two cameras or must assume the restrictive setting of a fixed linear ordering of the cameras. We propose MViS, a lightweight test-time optimization framework for joint multi-view alignment with temporal consistency. MViS uses a spatial-transformer-inspired net to jointly process frames from all views within a short temporal window and predict per-view, per-time homographies. Optimization proceeds in two stages: geometry-guided alignment followed by appearance-based refinement, with both stages enforcing multi-view and temporal consistency across the sequence. The method requires no scene-specific hyperparameter tuning, handles arbitrary and time-varying view-intersection graphs, and remains robust under rapid camera motion. On a standard two-view video benchmark, MViS matches or surpasses the state of the art. To facilitate evaluation in more complex scenarios, we introduce an annotated dataset with more than two freely moving cameras and establish the first benchmark for this setting. Project page: https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/MViS-project/ .
authors: Shira Ifergane, Roy Amoyal, Shahar Benishay, Oren Freifeld

papers.abstract: The task of weakly supervised video anomaly detection is challenging. Existing approaches mainly model video frame features and determine whether anomalies are present based on their magnitudes. In this work, we propose a novel method that incorporates external knowledge into training to improve model performance, robustness, and generalization. We leverage textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) to establish prior information for the specific task, and employ dictionary learning to normalize and compress this information. Moreover, during experiments, we observed inconsistencies in the textual descriptions extracted from similar video frames by image caption models. To address this, we devise a method that leverages an LLM and auxiliary information to ensure consistency in the textual descriptions of similar frames within a video. Finally, we introduce a feature processing approach that incorporates prior knowledge and cross-modal attention mechanisms. This approach learns the relationships and characteristics among different modalities to construct more accurate and reliable feature representations, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of detecting anomalies from video-level supervision, where existing methods rely mainly on frame-feature magnitudes.
Uses textual prompts and an LLM to provide task-specific prior knowledge, then normalizes and compresses it through dictionary learning.
Improves consistency among textual descriptions of similar frames using LLMs and auxiliary information.
Integrates prior knowledge with cross-modal attention to learn relationships across modalities and build more reliable representations.
Experiments report that the method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches, though no specific datasets or metrics are provided.

papers.abstract: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
authors: Dian Jiao, Yuqian Yuan, Jiaqi Zhu, Mingjian Gao, Siwen Tan, Yunqi Cao, Jinhui Li, Sijing Li, Zhenxuan Fan, Haoyang Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Siliang Tang
bullets: Addresses MLLMs’ difficulty composing precise temporal and spatial evidence into coherent multi-step reasoning.
Represents videos as Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs and derives grounded reasoning chains from validated evidence paths.
Introduces a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark with grounded chain-of-thought annotations.
Finds that MLLMs often localize relevant evidence but struggle to compose it correctly, a weakness hidden by answer-only evaluation.
Fine-tuning with V-STORM improves answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) modeling is arguably the only way to extend a fixed-length video diffusion model to longer or even streaming videos. However, existing AR diffusion methods use only the previously predicted chunk as context for the next, discarding the intermediate predictions that constitute the chunk's generation history. In contrast, conventional AR models such as LLMs condition on the entire history of preceding tokens. To this end, we propose Trajectory Forcing (TraF), an AR diffusion method that exploits the denoising trajectories of previous video chunks as context. TraF operates under two training regimes: (1) with ground-truth videos, where pseudo-trajectories are constructed from Gaussian interpolations and re-predicted by the model, and (2) with a teacher model, where real trajectories are obtained from the student's own denoising rollout. The first regime naturally provides a strong initialization for the second. On the 5-second VBench benchmark, TraF achieves a Total score of 85.15, outperforming Self Forcing (+0.84) and Causal Forcing (+1.11), with Quality and Semantic improving simultaneously. On 30-second generation---6$\times$ the training horizon---TraF achieves the highest overall quality among all compared methods.
authors: Bohan Wang, Shuo Chen, Yunzhi Li, Zhaozheng Chen, Junzhe Zhang, Hanwang Zhang
bullets: Existing autoregressive diffusion methods retain only the previous video chunk, discarding its generation history.
TraF uses previous chunks’ denoising trajectories as context for generating subsequent chunks.
It is trained first with Gaussian-interpolation pseudo-trajectories and then with real trajectories from a teacher/student denoising rollout.
On 5-second VBench, TraF scores 85.15, outperforming Self Forcing and Causal Forcing while improving both quality and semantics.
It achieves the highest overall quality among compared methods for 30-second videos, six times the training horizon.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
bullets: Recasts long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem under a fixed budget.
Plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to refine candidate evidence segments into compact memory.
Combines sparse low-resolution global frames with dense high-resolution local frames from refined memory.
Outperforms budget-matched uniform sampling and frame-selection/agentic methods on LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench.

figures.caption: Figure 2: AdaAlloc pipeline. AdaAlloc splits a fixed visual-token budget B between low-res global context (blue) and high-res local evidence (orange). (1) From a sparse overview O, an MLLM planner picks a policy π and generates queries Q. (2) A temporal grounder (UniversalVTG) localizes Q; the MLLM refines the candidates into M∗, discarding an off-topic clip and the first return to the stove. (3) The MLLM answers from a global stream Eg and a local stream El drawn from M∗.

Figure 3: Qualitative example on LVBench. The overview supplies global context, while the question’s request to read a handwritten number motivates a LOCAL-HEAVY policy for detailed inspection. AdaAlloc retrieves multiple temporal candidates and refines them into a compact memory that preserves the decisive interval. AdaAlloc correctly answers 25, while Uniform predicts 5.

Figure 1: Visual token allocation for long-video reasoning. Uniform sampling preserves global coverage but loses fine details, while retrieval-based selection focuses on a few clips but can lose context. AdaAlloc allocates a fixed token budget between low-resolution global coverage and highresolution local evidence for both context and fine-grained verification.

Table 4: Contextual comparison with representative long-video understanding systems. Prior numbers are taken from the respective papers when available. We include methods that report results on comparable long-video benchmarks and specify a frame budget or sampling setting for similarscale systems. Visual inputs are reported in their original units, since frame-to-token conversion depends on the backbone, resolution, and compression scheme. Because methods differ in backbone MLLM, training data, inference pipeline, visual preprocessing, and evaluation protocol, this table is intended as a cross-paper comparison rather than a strictly controlled head-to-head evaluation. Bold marks the best result excluding proprietary models.

Figure 4: Distribution of selected allocation policies across benchmarks. We report the fraction of planner-routed examples assigned to each AdaAlloc policy on LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench. Examples that bypass planning and use direct answering are excluded.

Table 9: Component ablation under the 16K visual-token budget. All variants use Qwen3-VL8B-Instruct with the same final-answering visual-token budget and answerer. Planning & refinement denotes overview-conditioned planning with temporal-memory refinement; variants that use it share the same overview planner, grounding model, and refinement procedure.

Table 3: Comparison with recent frame-selection methods under the same backbone. All methods use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. †Approximate budgets converted from the reported 128- and 256-frame settings at about 150 visual tokens per frame [24]; these exceed AdaAlloc’s 16K and 32K budgets, making the budget favorable to the baselines. We report LongVideoBench and the medium/long subsets of VideoMMEw/o sub to match DIG [24].

Table 11: Discrete policy selection versus direct ratio prediction. Both variants use the same planner, grounding model, token budget, and answering pipeline, and differ only in whether the planner selects one of the five predefined policies or directly predicts the global/local ratio.

Table 2: Controlled main results under matched visual-token budgets. Following the protocol in Section 5, all methods use the same backbone, decoding setup, and visual-token budget within each block. We report accuracy (%) on four long-form video QA benchmarks in the video-only setting. Numbers in parentheses denote absolute gains over uniform sampling under the same budget.

Table 10: Sensitivity to overview density. The final answering budget is fixed at 16K and only the planner’s visual input changes. The 2× denser overview samples twice as many frames at the same resolution and spends additional planning compute, so it is a diagnostic rather than a budget-matched alternative.

Table 6: MLVU-Dev results. Accuracy (%) on the seven multiple-choice tasks of MLVU-Dev, grouped as in MLVU [78]: Topic Reasoning (TR), Anomaly Recognition (AR), Needle QA (NQA), Ego Reasoning (ER), Plot QA (PQA), Action Order (AO), and Action Count (AC). M-Avg is the mean over the seven tasks. All methods use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Numbers in parentheses denote absolute gains over uniform sampling under the same budget.

Table 7: VideoMME duration-split breakdown. We report AdaAlloc performance on VideoMME without subtitles under 16K and 32K visual-token budgets. VideoMME groups videos into short, medium, and long duration buckets.

Table 8: VideoMME sub-task breakdown. Accuracy (%) of uniform sampling and AdaAlloc on VideoMME without subtitles under the same 32K visual-token budget, broken down by the official sub-task categories. #Q is the number of questions in each sub-task.

Uniform sampling answers from uniformly sampled frames. Retrieval-only answers from segments localized by UniversalVTG using the original question. Fixed policy uses a BALANCED global/local split. W/o temporal memory refinement removes the refinement stage (Section 4.2).
