papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-video understanding and multimodal LLM reasoning under token budgets, with a novel token allocation framework.
papers.title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering
papers.tldr: AdaAlloc is a training-free framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between global context and localized detail for long-video QA, improving accuracy over uniform sampling by up to 10.5 points.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have achieved remarkable photorealistic RGB synthesis, yet generating videos with a native alpha channel remains an open challenge. Existing approaches often rely on matting-style data and non-native RGBA designs, causing them to specialize in real-object scenes and to degrade severely on visual-effect content whose semi-transparency is spatially non-local and non-elliptical. We present UniRGBA, a unified framework whose key insight is that RGBA generation does not require a dedicated alpha encoder or complex latent-space restructuring---a minimal, targeted extension of the existing RGB pathway is sufficient. UniRGBA-VAE extends a causal video VAE to 4-channel RGBA via zero-initialized channel expansion, symmetric selective layer unfreezing (5% trainable), and a six-term progressive reconstruction loss anchored by a KL reference loss that prevents latent drift, followed by a two-stage schedule that introduces a lightweight GAN objective. We then apply standard DoRA to the pretrained DiT, reusing the unified 4-channel latent without any alpha-specific architectural changes. On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, UniRGBA substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction while preserving RGB fidelity. For generation, UniRGBA outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA text-to-video tasks and matches or surpasses the original pretrained Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics, demonstrating that native alpha support can be integrated without compromising the underlying RGB prior or the model's architectural versatility.
authors: Lei Xu, Zhuo Li, Yongyi Jin, Aoyu Wang
bullets: Addresses failures of matting-based, non-native RGBA methods on visual effects with spatially non-local, non-elliptical transparency.
Extends a causal video VAE from RGB to RGBA using zero-initialized channels, selective unfreezing, progressive reconstruction losses, and a staged GAN objective.
Adapts the pretrained DiT with standard DoRA while reusing the unified four-channel latent, without an alpha-specific architecture.
On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, it substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha for reconstruction and improves RGBA text-to-video generation.
Preserves RGB fidelity, matching or surpassing the original Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Three-way qualitative comparison on visual-effect T2V prompts. Wan-Alpha (top), TransPixeler (middle), and Ours (bottom, DoRA on Wan2.1-T2V-14B) are stacked, all rendered on a checkerboard background to visualize transparency. Our method produces transparency and color content that is visually competitive with Wan-Alpha while clearly outperforming TransPixeler on challenging non-elliptical visual-effect scenes.

Figure 2: Overview of Alpha-aware downstream adaptation. For T2V, frozen umT5 text features and timestep embeddings condition adapter-tuned DiT blocks, whose denoised latents are decoded by UniRGBA-VAE. For I2V, a reference RGBA frame is additionally encoded into visual conditions in the same latent space and injected into the shared DiT backbone.

Figure 1: Overview of UniRGBA-VAE. UniRGBA-VAE extends the Wan2.1 VAE to 4-channel RGBA through zero-initialized channel expansion at Conv_in/Conv_out with selective layer finetuning (orange = trainable, blue = frozen). Training losses include pixel-level (Lrgb, Lalpha, Lcomp, Lhard_a), perceptual (Lperce), and regularization (Lkl, Lkl_ref) terms.

Table 3: Generation results on RGBA and RGB evaluation sets. Best results are shown in bold. For RGBA T2V, we compare our DoRA variant against Wan-Alpha and TransPixeler. For RGB T2V, we compare our pipeline against the original Wan2.1 to assess the effect of VAE replacement on standard RGB generation.

Table 1: Main reconstruction results on RGBA benchmark and RGB-only WebVid. Best results are shown in bold. The WebVid comparison confirms that the minor PSNR drop versus the original Wan2.1 VAE is an acceptable trade-off for enabling RGBA capabilities.
Table 2: Progressive loss ablation. Each row adds one loss component. Lkl_ref provides the largest single improvement, and Lcomp is essential for alpha-aware compositing quality.

papers.abstract: Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulator learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.
authors: Zheng Wang, Zhengwei Gong, Yuanzhi Liang, Chi Zhang
bullets: Targets physically inconsistent object motion in otherwise realistic video generation.
Learns object-level state evolution with a neural PDE solver focused on rigid-body dynamics.
Converts predicted trajectories into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model.
Uses diffusion matching plus a low-capacity decodability constraint to preserve object identity and position.
Improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience on evaluated benchmarks while maintaining comparable visual quality; scope is limited to rigid-body settings.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of MotionCore. (a) Stage 1 pretrains the occupancy autoencoder and the surface operator. Stage 2 freezes them and trains the neural simulator on rollouts of K frames. At inference the simulator rolls out the scene, and the decoded occupancy is rendered into a control video for the frozen Wan2.1-VACE [12]. (b) State adapter and latent neural operator. (c) Free-motion proposal. (d) Surface operator. (e) Collision operator: learned contact probabilities and coefficients enter a closed-form impulse update. Snowflakes mark frozen modules, and dashed red boxes mark losses.

Figure 2. Qualitative comparison on three Physics-IQ-Verified scenes. Blocks show (a) collision, (b) falling, and (c) rolling. Each block compares the reference video, MotionCore, native VACE-1.3B, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, and LTX-Video 0.9.5. Columns show the shared input and frames nearest the indicated times after the switch frame. “VACE-1.3B w/o simulator” denotes native VACE without our adapter or control-branch LoRA. These are selected examples rather than a controlled simulator ablation.

Figure 3. The rollout bound of Theorem A.4, measured term by term on held-out MOVi-Spheres scenes. (a) Centre error against rollout horizon, with the bound evaluated from the measured perstep defects and the amplification Lloc. (b) The bound’s two factors across 50 epochs: the mean per-step defect η̄ (left, log scale) rises fivefold after epoch 6 while the amplification implied by the observed accumulation, L⋆ (right), falls through one. The perturbation rate Lloc stays flat and tracks neither. (c) Substituting the encoded truth into one factor of the latent state at every step. Correcting the occupancy latent leaves the rollout unchanged, while correcting the object state collapses it to the per-step defect.

Figure 5. Actual loss over the 50 training updates. Each update uses its prescribed training window; all three learned arms see the same sequence. These raw state losses mix changing window difficulty with optimization, and are not fixed-validation convergence curves. The analytic arm is not trained.

Figure 4. Early state-error accumulation. Saved radiusnormalized position errors, averaged over valid objects at each prediction time on the same 16 test scenes. The vertical axis starts at zero. This is one training seed and a 20-step (≃ 0.333 s) rollout under the shared latent-slot interface, not a convergence or longhorizon video comparison.

Figure 6. Training the learned adapter on both corpora. The zero-initialised condition opens as training proceeds (centre), and the decodability constraint tightens (right); the flow-matching loss itself does not separate the variants, which is why obedience is judged by measurement after generation rather than by validation loss.

Table 1. Physical plausibility on the subset of Physics-IQ-Verified[38] and RigidBench[11]. Physics-IQ-Verified block uses the rigidbody subset. Both are tested on four random seeds (0, 42, 1989704766, 177674710).

Table 2. Shared latent-slot early-optimization pilot. All learned variants use 50 updates and seed 0; rollouts span 20 steps at 60 Hz. Test errors use the same 16 scenes, normalized by equivalent radius Req (floor 1 mm). Parameters count the active processor.

Table 3. The simulator against explicit alternatives, on 200 held-out windows of 20 frames. Error is the centre distance in scene units, averaged over the rollout and at its end. Contact F1 scores predicted against true contact events under one geometric criterion applied to all four rows, so it reads the raw predicted geometry rather than any learned contact head.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.
authors: Yukai Huang, Haoyu Albert Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Jialun Ma, Jiayao Ding, Yiran Lin, Xingyu Chen, Ziqi Gao, Yuguo Yu
bullets: Addresses noisy, temporally filtered calcium signals and limited paired neural–video data for visual reconstruction.
Separately derives layout and semantic controls from neural activity to condition a pretrained video diffusion model.
Using 7,863 V1 neurons, achieved 81.4% all-pairs identification accuracy on held-out natural-movie clips.
Virtual-population analyses across 11 datasets indicate reconstruction relies on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure.
Perturbations and temporal analyses show complementary layout/semantic information and preserved semantic dynamics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of the data pipeline and Ca2REAL architecture. a, Dynamic Sensorium data acquisition for the primary measured experiment. Awake, head-fixed mice viewed natural movies presented at 30 Hz while locomoting on a cylindrical treadmill, and V1 calcium activity was recorded with two-photon imaging. b, Neural-response synthesis with digital-twin encoding models. A spatiotemporal neural encoder maps each movie to the corresponding population response through a shared visual feature extractor, temporal processing, and population-specific readout. c, Neural and visual preprocessing. Movie frames were centrally cropped and resized to the generator resolution, while calcium responses were normalized neuron-wise using training-set statistics before decoding. d, Ca2REAL architecture. A multiscale temporal front end provides features to two neural-control pathways. The layout pathway predicts a low-resolution movie for spatial control of Wan2.1-VACE, whereas the semantic pathway predicts global and temporally ordered visual tokens that are adapted to the generator conditioning space.

Fig. 3 Neural-to-video decoding from a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons. a, Construction of the virtual population. Encoding models fitted to 11 independently recorded neural datasets predicted responses to common movie stimuli, and the predictions were concatenated across neurons. The lower panels show the contribution of each dataset and the cortical-area composition of the virtual population. b, Representative held-out target clips (GT) and reconstructions generated by Ca2REAL and baseline methods from the 116,705-dimensional encoding-model-predicted responses. Selected frames from one representative clip in each target cluster are shown. c, Quantitative comparison over 946 held-out segments.

Fig. 2 Natural-movie reconstruction from measured V1 calcium activity in a single mouse. a, Representative held-out target clips (GT) and reconstructions generated by Ca2REAL and baseline methods from measured responses of 7,863 V1 neurons. Selected frames from one representative clip in each of the four target clusters are shown. b, Quantitative reconstruction performance on 178 held-out measured clips.

Fig. 4 Complementary roles of the layout and semantic conditioning pathways. a, Representative reconstructions from measured and virtual-population activity using the full Ca2REAL model or with the layout or semantic pathway blocked at inference time. b, Mean oriented paired change in reconstruction performance relative to the full model after blocking either pathway. Signs are oriented so that negative values indicate worse performance for both higher-is-better and loweris-better metrics. Results are shown separately for the measured V1 population (n = 178 clips) and the virtual population (n = 946 clips).

Fig. 5 Distributed and stimulus-specific neural dependence of Ca2REAL. a, Effect of removing each source population relative to matched-size random neuron deletions (blue point, source-population removal result; gray line, matched-random 5–95% range; gray tick, median). b, Reconstruction performance as a function of the fraction of retained neurons. c, Robustness to progressive corruption of neuron identity. d, Robustness to replacing neural responses with responses evoked by a different stimulus. e, Robustness to random neuron dropout. f, Structured neuron-identity and cross-sample perturbations compared with magnitude-matched Gaussian perturbations. g, Effect of cross-sample substitution as a function of target–donor similarity defined in frozen SigLIP2 space; the outcome is SigLIP2-based all-pairs identification, and significance was assessed by a cluster-aware permutation test of the global Spearman trend. h, Denoising-objective pairing sensitivity at fixed diffusion noise level (σ = 0.7) in the full model and the model trained without Lpair, quantified by ∆pair = Lshuffled − Lmatched; asterisks indicate paired Full versus No-Lpair comparisons. For b–h, vertical bars indicate bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

Fig. 6 Ca2REAL preserves temporal semantic dynamics. a, Semantic trajectory spread retention (points, medians; thin bars, interquartile ranges; thick bars, bootstrap 95% CIs; dashed line, ideal ratio = 1). b, Semantic path-length retention, with conventions as in a. c, Within-clip temporal identification accuracy (dashed line, chance level = 0.5). d, Paired temporal-identification advantage of Ca2REAL over each baseline (points, mean paired differences; bars, bootstrap 95% CIs; dashed line, zero). Blue/red denote measured/virtual populations. Significance tests were Holm-corrected; asterisks denote significance and ns denotes non-significance.
Table 2 Reconstruction metrics. Arrows indicate whether higher (↑) or lower (↓) values indicate better reconstruction.

Table 1 Measured-response substitution tests functional compatibility with the virtual-population decoder. All-pairs identification accuracy after replacing available synthetic responses with matched measured activity or control responses on the full test set (n = 946 clips). ∆ denotes the change relative to the fully synthetic condition.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.
authors: Mingjia Huo, Yao Fu, Bo Chang, Yaqing Wang, Dawei Zhu, Dylan Zhang, Xinyang Yi, Lichan Hong, Ed H. Chi, Hao Zhang, Jiaxi Tang
bullets: Benchmarks VLMs on 20 Atari 2600 games using high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams.
Separates in-game dynamics from inference speed to test spatiotemporal perception, reasoning, and action grounding.
Finds failures in tracking object motion and direction, brittle sequential decisions, and over-reliance on textual history over new visual feedback.
Analyzes which game scores reliably reflect competence and examines the effects of memory design and prompting.
Highlights a persistent gap between passive visual understanding and active decision-making in dynamic environments.

papers.title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Aditya Desai
bullets: Top-p block selection can be sample-inefficient when video attention has high entropy.
It treats block selection as importance sampling: exact computation for top-scoring keys and inverse-probability-weighted samples for the rest.
Each query cluster shares a sampled set, preserving block structure for efficient GPU execution.
With SVG2, InstaGen improves PSNR at matched attention density and wall-clock time on Wan2.1-T2V models.
It also outperforms SVG-EAR on Wan2.1-T2V-14B while running faster at nearly the same density.

papers.abstract: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to temporally localize abnormal events in videos. Most existing approaches rely on dataset-specific training and curated annotations, limiting generalization in open-set scenarios. Recent zero-shot methods based on Large Vision- Language Models (LVLMs) alleviate this dependency but often lack temporal continuity and structured reasoning. We propose Cog-VADU, a fully training-free framework that reformulates VAD as a sequential cognitive reasoning task. Cog-VADU introduces Chain-of- Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP), which unrolls an LVLM into a recurrent reasoning chain across video segments. By propagating structured rationales over time, the model maintains implicit temporal memory, enabling robust discrimination between com- plex anomalies and high-motion normal activities. To improve reliability, we further design a cross-modal re-ranking stage that aligns textual rationales with visual embeddings, enforcing semantic consistency and temporal coherence for refined and stable predictions. Extensive experiments on multiple public VAD benchmarks demonstrate that Cog-VADU achieves competitive zero-shot performance. Moreover, cross-model evaluations show that CoADTP consistently enhances reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic manner, pro- viding interpretable and generalizable anomaly understanding for real-world applications.
bullets: Addresses the limited generalization and weak temporal reasoning of dataset-specific and existing zero-shot VAD methods.
Uses Chain-of-Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP) to propagate structured rationales across video segments as implicit temporal memory.
Applies cross-modal re-ranking to align textual rationales with visual embeddings, improving semantic consistency and temporal coherence.
Reports competitive zero-shot performance across multiple public VAD benchmarks.
Cross-model evaluations indicate that CoADTP improves reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic way.

figures.caption: Figure 19: Qualitative comparison on a video reasoning benchmark. Our training-free framework CogVADU (blue) correctly identifies the anomaly by reasoning over temporal visual inconsistencies, detecting that the second puppy’s nose and tongue morph unnaturally across frames. In contrast, training-based VAD approaches (orange), including HAWK Tang et al. (2024), HolmesVAU Zhang et al. (2025b), and VAD-R1 Huang et al. (2025), either hallucinate unrelated changes (e.g., ear color or fur texture) or fail to localize the correct anomaly despite similar visual evidence. This example highlights the advantage of reasoning-driven anomaly detection in capturing subtle semantic inconsistencies that are not easily modeled by conventional training-based approaches.

Figure 1: Comparison of video anomaly detection paradigms. (a) Vision-only methods rely on supervised training and produce anomaly scores without semantic reasoning. (b) Multimodal LLM-based VAD generates anomaly confidence and provides post-hoc explanations. (c) Cog-VADU employs a frozen LVLM with structured prompting and temporal cues to perform joint, training-free anomaly detection and reasoning.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on VANE. Cog-VADU generates structured, evidence-grounded reasoning (Observation → Anomaly → Reasoning → Answer), correctly identifying the anomaly (B). In contrast, prior multimodal VAD methods, including RL-based VAD-R1 Bharadwaj et al. (2025), often produce weakly grounded explanations.

Figure 13: Case 1 — Visually anomalous, semantically normal. Comparison of four state-of-the-art VAD methods on an open-web arm wrestling video (ground truth: Normal). URDMU Zhou et al. (2023a) produces a strong false alarm (peak ≈ 0.999); HolmesVAD Zhang et al. (2024b) hallucinates an unrelated “man in a blue shirt” scene; HAWK Tang et al. (2024) fabricates a basketball court context; and HolmesVAU Zhang et al. (2025b) contradicts its own reasoning by labelling recognized wrestling activity as “anomaly events.” In contrast, Cog-VADU correctly identifies the professional-wrestling context and outputs a calibrated score of 0.15 (Normal).
Figure 2: Comparison of prior-aware prompts for zero-shot VAD.

Figure 10: Structural analysis of annotation distributions under the proposed unified protocol. (a) Anomaly perception word cloud illustrating semantically enriched anomaly categories introduced through re-annotation, including subtle, contextual, and effect-based states that were under-represented in the original benchmarks. (b) Temporal relation word cloud highlighting causal, escalation, and aftermath relations, emphasizing the necessity of modeling complete cause-effect chains rather than isolated trigger events. Together, these visualizations provide linguistic and structural evidence that the original annotations are biased toward trigger-centric labeling, while our unified protocol captures temporally consistent and semantically grounded anomaly states.

Figure 17: Qualitative results of our Cog-VADU method on two test videos, from UCF-Crime Sultani et al. (2019). For each video, plot the frame-wise anomaly scores and show keyframes with their most relevant temporal summaries (green for normal, red for abnormal). These examples illustrate alignment between predicted anomaly scores, visual content, and descriptions. Ground-truth anomalies are highlighted in red.

Figure 15: Failure case — categorical labelling error under graceful degradation. Cog-VADU is applied to an open-web video of a sensory room being flooded with water. The model produces a factually accurate description (“water starts flooding the room, causing objects to float and move around”), correctly identifies the reasoning (“not a normal activity and poses a safety concern”), and outputs a well-calibrated anomaly score of 0.92. However, the predicted anomaly type is Suspicious instead of the more precise Flood. The root cause is structural rather than reasoning-related: our predefined anomaly database does not contain a Flood category, and the model gracefully defaults to the generic Suspicious class. This failure is correctable in a training-free manner by simply extending the textual anomaly database, in contrast to opaque training-induced failures observed in baselines.

papers.abstract: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
bullets: Targets DiTs’ inefficient uniform processing of mostly sparse visual content.
Routes tokens independently through MLP and self-attention operations, adapting compute by token, image, and denoising timestep.
Processes as few as 12.5% of tokens, substantially reducing training and inference costs.
Higher sparsity and model depth improve generation performance over unrouted baselines.
Token allocation is interpretable, correlating with visual content, noise level, and video motion.

papers.abstract: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning six action-video tasks. With only narrow-domain data, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.
bullets: Addresses the lack of native metric-3D human-action representations in modern video models.
Supports action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation.
Uses a role-adaptive action renderer and cross-stream action-video coupling to align motion with visual dynamics.
Covers six action-video tasks and generalizes from narrow-domain data to unseen scenes and interactions.
Provides effective action control and visual quality while preserving pretrained visual knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of EgoGeneralist. Role-adaptive rendering (Sec. 3.2) tailors the visual representation of metric 3D action to its task role: an ego-view map with a fixed 3D anchor for conditioning, or a multiview Posegrid for generation and metric readout. A shared frozen video VAE encodes rendered action and video into two latent streams. Cross-stream coupling (Sec. 3.3) uses joint self-attention and attention LoRAs activated only for generation targets, retaining the backbone weights and per-stream input structure. The bottom panel illustrates condition–target assignments for the three prediction directions defined in Sec. 3.1.

Figure 5. World-action policy on HOT3D. Top: EgoGeneralist’s generated video and 3D action in ego and side views. Bottom: action predictions from all three methods in a shared top view. GT object meshes and scene points are used only for visualization. Additional examples are provided in supplementary Fig. S7.

Figure 3. Action-conditioned image-to-video generation. Comparisons on EgoDex (left) and Xperience-10M (right, out-of-distribution). Adapted only on EgoDex, EgoGeneralist generalizes to in-the-wild scenes. The generated videos follow the prescribed motion with physically coherent interactions, correctly removing the purple block (left) and tilting the bucket (right).

Figure 6. Text-only joint action–video generation. Each example shows jointly generated video and 3D action, with the action projected onto video frames. Insets show the generated 3D upper-body skeleton and camera pose. Best viewed in the supplementary video.

Figure 4. Action-conditioned text-to-video generation. EgoGeneralist generates videos that share the same prescribed 3D motion while varying scenes and object appearances according to different text prompts. Actions are drawn from EgoDex (top) and Xperience-10M (bottom).

All methods receive an initial observation and instruction. VITRA and EgoGeneralist also receive initial action states. †Being-H0 uses a single wrist-anchored rigid alignment to the GT initial hand.

Our method maintains competitive action adherence across text-specified visual contexts.

PCK, IoU, and Failure are in percentages; best and second-best are bold and underlined. EgoSimO/EgoSimQ use dataset-provided/Qwen-generated prompts.

papers.abstract: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) is a long-established problem that aims to detect defects in industrial products during manufacturing for quality control. Most existing studies focus on static visual patterns as the basis for detection. However, in real manufacturing environments, many anomalies are dynamics-based, such as irregular movements that cannot be perceived from static cues alone. We observe that even recent Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based approaches fall short in identifying such dynamic anomalies due to limited temporal modeling capability. To address this, we introduce MUSTARD: MUltimodal SpatioTemporal Anomaly Reasoning and Detection, a framework that equips MLLMs with fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics awareness for detecting and reasoning about dynamics-based defects. MUSTARD introduces optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to capture critical motion irregularities through local motion patterns and global dynamic evolution. Its normal pattern-based reasoning pipeline requires only a few normal reference samples as the detection basis, avoiding any model updates. This enables efficient adaptation across various products and provides high decision interpretability. MUSTARD is the first MLLM-based framework for dynamics-based IAD. Experiments demonstrate its superior performance in detecting spatiotemporal anomalies and providing plausible explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/racercode/Mustard
bullets: Targets dynamics-based industrial anomalies, such as irregular movements, that static visual methods may miss.
Uses optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to model local motion patterns and global temporal evolution.
Employs normal-pattern reasoning without model updates, supporting efficient adaptation across products.
Experiments show strong detection of spatiotemporal anomalies and plausible explanations.
Scope: designed for motion-related defects; the abstract does not quantify performance or specify datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2. An overview of the proposed MUSTARD framework. It consists of three main stages. (1) Spatiotemporal Dynamics Awareness: Leverages optical flow to select keyframes and derive three complementary descriptive modalities, including raw frames for visual context, trajectory frames for visualizing local motion, and a flow magnitude curve for representing global temporal dynamics. (2) Normal Pattern Extraction: Extracts multi-faceted normal patterns from a small set of reference videos. (3) Pattern Reasoning (Inference): Compares the test video’s description with the extracted normal patterns to detect deviations, producing a final anomaly judgment and explanation.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: https://fudan-generative-vision.github.io/WAM-Sim.
bullets: Targets structural drift, identity drift, and visual quality decay in autoregressive driving world models.
Uses pose-aligned structural tokens, read-only scene tokens, and write-once instance tokens to preserve roads, appearance, and traffic-participant identities.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models generate text by reversing a stochastic masking process. Unlike autoregressive LLMs, which generate text one token at a time, they can reveal many tokens in parallel, at the price of an error, since tokens revealed together are drawn independently. We show that this trade-off maps onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems. (i) For any data, the error of parallel generation is the entropy production of the generation process relative to the reversed masking process. (ii) For Markov data, generation is a random sequential adsorption process with labelled gaps, which we solve exactly for any number of steps. (iii) For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system: the unmasking schedule plays the role of the driving protocol, the number of steps that of its duration, and the error is set by a thermodynamic metric that we obtain in closed form from the mutual information between tokens. Optimal schedules are geodesics of this metric. The exact solution shows how correlations in the text shape both the error and the quality of the output. The longer the correlations, the more the error concentrates at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps then gain more, both in path error and in perplexity, and need fewer steps to reach their asymptotic behaviour.
bullets: Parallel decoding introduces error because tokens revealed together are sampled independently.
For arbitrary data, this error equals the entropy production relative to the reversed masking process.
For Markov data, generation maps to random sequential adsorption with labelled gaps and is solved exactly for any number of steps.
In the many-step regime, error is governed by a thermodynamic metric derived from token mutual information; optimal unmasking schedules follow its geodesics.
Longer-range correlations concentrate error early, favoring schedules with initially smaller steps that improve path error and perplexity with fewer steps.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal models can answer questions about video, but their predictions rarely show which participant, event, or interval supports an answer. Moreover, answer-level supervision alone does not teach a model to interpret structured video evidence. To systematically mitigate this issue, we present THG-Omni, a human-centric graph-supervision framework that links Segment Anything Model~3 participant tracks with temporally grounded Qwen3-VL annotations. Candidate semantic claims are checked against the source video and available audio before they are used to construct training questions, while track geometry provides explicit spatial and temporal supervision. The resulting questions teach an omni-modal reasoning model to interpret participant attributes, actions, affect, interactions, and their timing from a structured graph. At inference, THG-Omni uses a predicted graph constructed from the evaluation video. Experiments on IntentBench show consistent improvements over the unadapted backbone across social reasoning, emotion understanding, and deception perception. On NExT-QA, THG-Omni achieves 89.54\% accuracy with the matched graph, compared with 85.10\% without graph input. Further validation experiments show that compact graph input achieves 78.22\% accuracy, compared with 78.02\% using the full graph and 77.58\% without graph input. A complementary diagnostic demonstrates that the predicted graph preserves evidence useful for answering questions even without the source video and audio. Together, these findings show that THG-Omni improves human-centric video reasoning while grounding its evidence in identifiable participants and events. Our codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/review-n94hhfcwp5666/
bullets: Addresses the lack of evidence traceability and limitations of answer-only supervision in omni-modal video models.
Builds structured graphs from participant tracks and temporally grounded annotations, with claims checked against video and audio.
Trains models to reason about participant attributes, actions, emotions, interactions, and timing.
Improves over the unadapted backbone on IntentBench; on NExT-QA, matched graph input reaches 89.54% versus 85.10% without graph input.
Compact graphs retain comparable performance to full graphs, and predicted graphs preserve useful evidence even without the source video or audio.

papers.abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.
bullets: Addresses short, ambiguous questions whose visual referents cannot be uniquely identified.
Uses three cooperating agents to propose interpretations, ask clarifying questions, and answer using resolved intent and visual evidence.
Applies a bounded, cost-aware policy to trade off information gain against user effort and limit clarification complexity.
Learns from interactions through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization.
Evaluations report better answer accuracy and joint answer-grounding performance, plus zero-shot transfer across datasets.

papers.abstract: Action recognition, and more specifically egocentric action recognition, is a core task in computer vision, with applications such as monitoring the daily life activities of elderly people and task assistance. Recent methods rely on visual modalities such as RGB video or depth. However, in egocentric video, an action is largely defined by its objects, which these methods rarely model. We propose a method that combines a frozen SlowFast video expert with an attention-based object expert by late fusion. Each object is represented with its affordances, that is, what can be done with it, generated zero-shot by a vision-language model. Since datasets such as MECCANO annotate only the objects involved in each action, evaluating with these boxes tells the model which objects are active. We therefore train on annotated boxes and evaluate the method with detections from the official active-object detector, and with annotated boxes as an upper bound. Without affordances, our fusion reaches 68.4% Top-1 with annotated boxes but 49.0% with detections. About half of this drop comes from non-active detections. To remove them, the same vision-language model generates an interaction affordance that decides whether a hand is manipulating each detected object. On MECCANO, objects raise the Top-1 of the video expert from 44.9% to 49.0%, and the two affordances raise it to 49.9%, above SlowFast and object-aware RGB baselines. Code will be released upon acceptance.
bullets: Egocentric actions are strongly defined by the objects being manipulated, which standard RGB/depth methods often underuse.
The method late-fuses a frozen SlowFast video expert with an attention-based object expert.
A vision-language model generates object affordances and an interaction affordance to filter detections that are not actively manipulated.
On MECCANO, objects improve SlowFast from 44.9% to 49.0% Top-1, while both affordances reach 49.9%.
Performance is substantially higher with annotated object boxes than with detector outputs, highlighting sensitivity to non-active detections.

papers.abstract: Capturing scenes with extreme motion and high dynamic range is fundamentally constrained by trade-offs among temporal resolution, spatial detail, signal-to-noise ratio, and dynamic range under practical bandwidth, power, and quantum-efficiency limits. Conventional frame-based cameras therefore suffer from temporal undersampling, exposure-induced motion blur, and sensor saturation. The Complementary Vision Sensor (CVS) addresses these limitations by decomposing visual information across two complementary pathways, a spatially dense, temporally sparse, long-exposure RGB pathway and a temporally dense, spatially sparse, short-exposure patiotemporal difference pathway. Their complementary measurements provide appearance, structural, and motion cues across a wide dynamic range that enable reconstruction beyond conventional imaging. We present CoGenRec, a complementarity-driven generative reconstruction framework that unifies video deblurring, high-temporal-resolution frame interpolation, and HDR fusion. CoGenRec encodes complementary measurements into multi-scale spatiotemporal features using exposure-aware appearance modeling and bidirectional temporal propagation. These features constrain a video diffusion model and are injected into the VAE decoder to recover fine structures lost during latent-space compression, combining the scene fidelity of physical measurements with the appearance recovery capabilities of learned video priors. On SportsSloMo-CVS, CoGenRec improves PSNR over the strongest general-purpose baseline by 4.40 dB for deblurring, 3.89 dB for frame interpolation, and 5.04 dB for HDR fusion, respectively. It also achieves strong perceptual quality on 129 unseen scenes captured with real CVS. These results establish a unified approach to advance high-quality reconstruction under challenging motion and illumination conditions. Project page: https://cogenrec.github.io/.
bullets: Targets temporal undersampling, motion blur, and saturation caused by conventional frame-based cameras.
Encodes complementary spatially dense RGB and temporally dense difference measurements with exposure-aware modeling and bidirectional temporal propagation.
Conditions a video diffusion model and injects features into the VAE decoder to preserve fine details lost during latent compression.
Unifies video deblurring, frame interpolation, and HDR fusion in one reconstruction framework.
Reports PSNR gains over a general-purpose baseline on SportsSloMo-CVS and strong perceptual quality on 129 unseen real CVS scenes.

papers.abstract: Post-training aims to enhance desired attributes in visual generative models while preserving their general generation capabilities. Reward-guided post-training faces two challenges: real training data may mismatch the generator's output distribution, and attribute supervision may be confounded by unrelated content. Unbounded reward maximization can also cause overoptimization and degrade generation quality. We propose a framework combining Generator-Aligned Reward Modeling (GARM) and Target-Aware Bounded Optimization (TABO). GARM mitigates distribution mismatch through generator-support matching and reduces content confounding using content-matched real contrasts, yielding generator-relevant, attribute-focused reward supervision. TABO maps the learned reward to a smooth, upper-bounded function calibrated from real target-positive examples. This transformation is independent of the optimization algorithm and supports both direct reward-gradient and policy-based optimization. We further introduce Target-Aware GRPO (TA-GRPO), an adaptation of Flow-GRPO that combines fixed stage-wise advantage scaling, a generator-to-target curriculum, and timestep-balanced credit assignment for flow-based video optimization. Experiments show that GARM improves target-attribute expression while maintaining competitive generation quality. TABO better balances attribute enhancement and visual quality than unconstrained reward maximization, while TA-GRPO improves target enhancement over vanilla Flow-GRPO and reduces unintended attribute leakage on neutral prompts. These results highlight the importance of generator-aligned reward supervision and controlled, data-calibrated optimization for targeted visual generation.
bullets: Addresses generator–training-data distribution mismatch, content-confounded attribute supervision, and reward overoptimization.
GARM matches reward supervision to generator outputs and uses content-matched real contrasts for attribute-focused signals.
TABO smoothly upper-bounds rewards using real target-positive examples and works with both gradient-based and policy-based optimization.
TA-GRPO adds curriculum learning, fixed stage-wise advantage scaling, and timestep-balanced credit assignment for flow-based video optimization.
Experiments show improved target-attribute expression, competitive visual quality, better quality–enhancement balance, and less leakage on neutral prompts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our framework. Because this reward transformation is independent of the update rule, it can be used with differentiable optimization (VADER) and policy optimization (TA-GRPO).

papers.abstract: One-step generators built on MeanFlow synthesize a video in a single function evaluation, yet inherit a rigid treatment of classifier-free guidance (CFG): the guidance scale is frozen during training or, at best, exposed as a single scalar. This conflicts with mounting evidence that the optimal guidance is not a constant but a field that varies with the noise level, with spatial content, and, for video, with frame position. Every existing remedy presupposes a multi-step sampler along which guidance can be re-scheduled--an assumption one-step models violate by construction. We resolve this tension through a single observation: because the MeanFlow target is an integral over a noise interval, an arbitrary guidance field can be absorbed into the target itself and compiled into one evaluation. We formalize this as the interval-integrated CFG identity, prove that the compiled guidance carries no schedule-discretization error and can thus match or exceed any finite multi-step sampler, and instantiate it as AGAVE, which equips the average-velocity field with a learnable temporal schedule, a free motion-saliency spatial modulation, and a frame-position asymmetry. Adding fewer than ten scalars at zero inference cost, AGAVE surpasses all one-step baselines on VBench, UCF-101 and MSR-VTT while matching multi-step guided sampling. Project repository: https://github.com/YMlinfeng/AGAVE.
bullets: One-step MeanFlow generators traditionally use a fixed or scalar CFG scale, despite guidance varying across noise levels, spatial content, and video frames.
The proposed interval-integrated CFG identity absorbs an arbitrary guidance field into the MeanFlow target.
AGAVE adds a learnable temporal schedule, spatial motion-saliency modulation, and frame-position asymmetry.
It uses fewer than ten additional scalars with no inference-time cost.
The method surpasses one-step baselines on VBench, UCF-101, and MSR-VTT, while matching multi-step guided sampling.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of AGAVE. A single MeanFlow DiT uθ emits a conditional/unconditional velocity pair whose guidance gap ∆v is modulated along three axes – a learnable Beta schedule over noise level τ , a free motion-saliency map M over space, and a learnable frame-position profile ρ(f) – forming a continuous guidance field ω(zτ , τ, f). The interval-integrated CFG operator (Thm. 1) absorbs this field into the average-velocity target, compiling a full time-, space- and frame-varying schedule into one evaluation. The schedule parameters ϕ are learned by distilling a multi-step adaptively guided teacher; inference remains strictly 1-NFE.

Figure 9. Qualitative comparison. Rows are methods, columns are boundary and interior frames of one clip, with magnified insets. AGAVE removes the saturated highlights of scalar guidance on static regions and sharpens fast-moving foreground, while keeping more diverse boundary frames. More results are in Appendix E.

Figure 2. VBench 16-dimension radar (14B). AGAVE (filled) against the one-step baselines iMF, rCM and CFG-Zero⋆. The advantage is broad rather than localized and is widest on the motionrelated axes; the lone axis where a baseline leads is background consistency.
Figure 4. Compilation gap. A K-step adaptive sampler only reaches the VBench total that AGAVE attains at K=1 (dashed) as K grows, visualizing the Θ(1/K) error of Prop. 1.
Figure 8. Test-time controllability. Sweeping the scale ωmax, the AGAVE field (amber) dominates the iMF scalar (blue) over the entire FVD–CLIP-T curve, so the field is strictly more controllable.

Figure 5. Recovered noise-time schedule. The learned ω(τ) (bold, inside the Beta family in light red) is bell-shaped and vanishes at the high-noise end, recovering the iMF constant (dashed) and the CFG-Zero⋆ step (dotted) as special cases.
Figure 7. FVD–CLIP-T trade-off (UCF-101, 14B). At a single evaluation AGAVE lies beyond the front traced by the multi-step teacher and rCM, the empirical face of Prop. 1.
Figure 6. Learned frame-position profile. ρ(f) (line) peaks on interior frames and is lightest at the clip boundaries; the per-frame temporal-consistency gain (bars) follows the same shape.

Figure 3. Interval-integrated CFG. The learnable Beta schedule ω(τ) (red) vanishes at the high-noise end (zero-init) and peaks mid-interval. The average-velocity target integrates the whole schedule over [r, t] (shaded), while the boundary term reads only the local value ω(t) (blue dot). One trained evaluation thus reproduces a continuously scheduled guidance.

Table 2. Zero-shot FVD, fidelity and cost (14B). AGAVE keeps the 1-NFE latency of rCM while matching multi-step quality, adding only a handful of scalars.
Table 3. One step vs. multi-step adaptive CFG (14B). AGAVE at 1-NFE matches or beats adaptive guidance run on the 50-step teacher, with the lowest over-saturation (lower is better).

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk and have made efficient video generation practical. However, further accelerating these models toward real-time generation remains challenging, as few-step distillation leaves little cross-step redundancy for existing training-free caching methods to exploit. We revisit this regime and identify two token-level redundancy patterns: cross-frame redundancy from static content shared across adjacent frames, and cross-step redundancy from tokens that converge early during denoising. Crucially, we find that early clean estimates along the model's own denoising trajectory provide an effective online signal for locating both patterns, requiring no retraining, auxiliary predictor, or reference video. Based on these findings, we propose PreSTP (Predictive Spatio-Temporal Token Pruning), a training-free framework that constructs a unified token-wise redundancy mask from cross-frame similarity and cross-step convergence. Tokens marked as redundant skip subsequent computation under a consistent last-computed-value restoration rule, and a content-adaptive mask reuse strategy further reduces dense probing cost. On 5-second generation, PreSTP achieves 1.52x-3.20x speedups and a better efficiency-fidelity trade-off than coarse-grained caching baselines such as TeaCache and FlowCache. On 30-second generation, it reaches up to 1.96x speedup while improving VBench-Long and suppressing long-horizon drift. Notably, it continues to reduce inference cost even in the extreme one-step regime, where cross-step redundancy vanishes entirely and coarse step-wise caching is no longer applicable.
bullets: Targets limited cross-step redundancy in few-step autoregressive video generation.
Uses early clean denoising estimates to detect cross-frame similarity and cross-step convergence online.
Applies a unified token mask, last-computed-value restoration, and adaptive mask reuse without retraining or auxiliary predictors.
Reports 1.52×–3.20× speedups for 5-second videos and up to 1.96× for 30-second videos, with improved long-horizon fidelity.
Remains effective in the one-step regime, where cross-step redundancy and step-wise caching are unavailable.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of PreSTP. Together, Ms and Mf form the next-step mask M , which selects active tokens for computation.

papers.abstract: We study action-conditioned monitoring of autonomous-vehicle behavior in semantically unusual driving scenes. The target is whether the executed ego action is appropriate for the scene: the same scene can admit both normal and anomalous behavior, so visual unusualness alone does not determine the monitoring label. A Vision-Language Model (VLM) first predicts the scene-required action from an outcome-hidden video window; the monitor then compares that expectation with the realized ego-motion trajectory under an explicit compatibility rule. To study this monitoring task, we contribute a six-field taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios spanning both failure polarities (42 derived from documented incidents), a generated video corpus with estimated trajectories, and an exploratory two-stage monitor on that corpus. On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, the two-stage protocol with a fixed T-2.5 s window obtains 83.0% accuracy and anomaly recall 0.773, versus 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage video-only baseline; specificity is 0.880 versus 0.928.
bullets: Targets whether the ego action is appropriate for the scene, not merely whether the scene looks unusual.
Uses a two-stage process: predict the required action from an outcome-hidden video window, then compare it with the realized trajectory using an explicit compatibility rule.
Introduces a six-field taxonomy of 112 paired scenarios, including 42 derived from documented incidents, plus a generated video corpus with estimated trajectories.
On 235 clips from 15 scenario families, achieves 83.0% accuracy and 0.773 anomaly recall, compared with 74.5% and 0.536 for a single-stage baseline.
Specificity is lower than the baseline: 0.880 versus 0.928; evaluation uses a fixed 2.5-second observation window.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is usually studied as frame selection: which few frames should a vision-language model see? We introduce VideoRouteAudit, a controlled audit that separates this choice from two alternatives, injecting non-visual evidence and routing to another answering model. It holds the backbone, frame budget, decoding, prompt and grader fixed while varying one decision at a time. On the full Video-MME long bucket (n=900, K=8), no tested selector significantly improves over uniform sampling. The largest selection-only estimate is +1.9 pt (95% CI [-1.2,+5.0]) and our cascade is +1.2 pt [-1.7,+4.1]; all are equivalent to uniform within +/-5 pt. The same contrasts are unstable at the n=200 subset scale commonly used: three of four are up to 3.8x larger, one reverses sign, and resampled 200-item subsets reverse the full-bucket effect's sign in 35.8% of draws. The audit also corrects our own first results. The anomaly-domain "+ASR" arms injected no text, so the pooled +4.7 pt gain was selection plus a development prefix. With transcripts, ASR lowers XD-Violence accuracy by 10.0 pt when appended after the question and not at all when placed before it, and lowers UCF-Crime by 13.0 pt either way; on Video-MME, placing it first adds about 4 pt (7 on Qwen2-VL) to uniform sampling and to the cascade alike (post hoc, unadjusted). Swapping the answering model gives the largest contrast (+15.1 pt on MUSIC-AVQA, +33.3 pt on its worst type), but the same audio-visual expert with its soundtrack silenced keeps 92% of the gain (69% with a mismatched soundtrack), so the contrast is mostly a model swap. Code, per-item predictions and scripts that recompute every statistic are available at https://github.com/mikeslin-ir/long-video-qa-audit.
bullets: On all 900 long-bucket Video-MME items, no tested frame selector significantly beats uniform sampling; estimated gains remain within ±5 points.
Results from 200-item subsets are unstable: effects can grow by up to 3.8×, reverse sign, and disagree with the full-bucket effect in 35.8% of resamples.
A claimed anomaly-domain “+ASR” gain was partly caused by a development prefix; transcript placement also changes performance substantially and inconsistently across datasets.
Routing to another answering model produces the largest contrast, but most of its gain persists when the soundtrack is silenced, indicating a model-swap effect rather than selection.
The audit releases code, per-item predictions, and scripts for reproducing all statistics.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has become an effective approach for improving video generation, but its success depends heavily on reliable reward models. Existing methods either map videos directly to opaque scalar scores or generate free-form rationales that are not explicitly optimized as the basis of the final judgment. We propose ArtiVidRM, a verifiable, artifact-as-rubrics video reward model that follows an observe-then-score paradigm. It first identifies visible generation artifacts and organizes them into a structured artifact list, then uses these artifacts as explicit rubrics for quality assessment. This intermediate representation grounds each score in concrete video-level evidence, making the reward more interpretable and informative for optimization. We further introduce a multi-reward reinforcement learning strategy to jointly optimize artifact prediction and quality assessment. The reward decomposes into complementary objectives that evaluate artifact prediction quality, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency, together with a pairwise preference objective that supervises quality ranking through score differences. By jointly optimizing the intermediate artifact representation and the downstream preference prediction, the model learns to produce informative artifact lists while improving the accuracy of video quality assessment. Experiments show that ArtiVidRM achieves state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks, provides effective signals for video diffusion optimization, and enables artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.
bullets: Addresses opaque scalar rewards and ungrounded free-form rationales in video-generation reinforcement learning.
Uses an observe-then-score pipeline: predict a structured list of visible artifacts, then assess quality based on those artifacts.
Jointly optimizes artifact prediction and pairwise quality ranking through multiple reward objectives, including semantic coverage and prediction efficiency.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on video preference benchmarks and useful signals for video diffusion optimization.
Supports artifact-guided refinement of closed-source video generators.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models for video generation have achieved remarkable success, yet precise motion control under explicit user guidance remains challenging. Recent noise-warping methods introduce temporal correlations by warping the noise according to the user-provided motion signal. However, standard spatial warping generally disrupts the noise's i.i.d. Gaussian structure, requiring distribution correction, such as Jacobian-based correction, but at a substantial computational overhead. We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), which encodes the motion signal into the noise through a sequence of Householder reflections that together form an orthogonal transformation applied to each location's channel vector. HME exactly preserves the spatial Gaussian structure within each frame while introducing cross-frame correlations that promote temporally consistent video. HME is agnostic to the network architecture and integrates directly into standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines. Experiments on different scenarios show that HME matches or outperforms the state of the art, while achieving a 2.7x speedup over noise warping. These results demonstrate that channel-space Householder transformations offer a principled and efficient alternative to noise warping for motion-controllable video generation.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of precise motion control in video diffusion models.
Uses a sequence of Householder reflections as an orthogonal channel-space transformation guided by user motion.
Preserves each frame’s spatial i.i.d. Gaussian noise structure while creating cross-frame temporal correlations.
Architecture-agnostic and directly compatible with standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines.
Reportedly matches or outperforms prior methods across scenarios and runs 2.7× faster than noise warping.

papers.abstract: Flow matching (FM) generators often face a quality-coverage tradeoff. Inference-time techniques such as classifier-free guidance raise quality, but at the cost of coverage. We revisit a basic property of FM -- an intermediate noisy image corresponds to multiple valid targets, which is collapsed into a single mean velocity by design. This can cover multiple modes of the distribution under ideal conditions, but is it optimal in practice? We instead investigate if directly modeling the modes of intermediate states better covers the modes of the full distribution. To do so, we augment the predictor with a randomly drawn low-dimensional code $z$, sampling $K$ candidate velocities for each training sample. We then apply the loss only to the best-matching candidate. This winner-take-all objective enables different codes to specialize and collectively cover different modes. Furthermore, this term naturally enables a new form of guidance, auxiliary conditioning scaling, which complements traditional guidance methods. Together, these two guidance mechanisms show that our method substantially improves the quality--coverage frontier. We validate on ImageNet-256, using two different testbeds, SiT and RAEv2. Given less than 3% of the original SiT pretraining compute for post-training, at the 67% Recall point, our method reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 19.22 to 5.91. On RAEv2, at the 70% Recall point, it reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 16.83 to 3.18.
bullets: Flow matching can collapse multiple valid targets for a noisy intermediate image into a single mean velocity, limiting coverage.
The method adds a random low-dimensional code to predict multiple candidate velocities and uses a winner-take-all loss so candidates specialize in different modes.
This enables auxiliary conditioning scaling, a new guidance mechanism that complements classifier-free guidance.
On ImageNet-256, the method substantially improves quality–coverage metrics on both SiT and RAEv2 testbeds, with less than 3% of SiT pretraining compute for post-training.

papers.abstract: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.
bullets: Introduces a dual-timeline benchmark for localized manipulations in open-scene, long-form audio-visual videos.
Includes 16,650 pristine–manipulated twin pairs spanning 998 hours and 27 editing configurations.
Zero-shot AV-LLM prompting performs near chance for detection and poorly for temporal localization.
NFSR uses separate audio and visual temporal decoders over frozen AV-LLM features, achieving the best localization in-domain and across three out-of-distribution settings.
The benchmark exposes errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation and is intended for public release with code and model weights.

papers.abstract: Masked discrete diffusion models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, but iterative sampling can be costly, and intractable sequence likelihoods complicate reward fine-tuning. We introduce IDRF, a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion generators. Starting from a standard reverse-KL-regularized objective, IDRF replaces the intractable sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization. With an optimal auxiliary denoiser, we prove that the population inverse-distillation loss upper-bounds the sequence-level KL divergence to the reference distribution. IDRF optimizes a trajectory-based surrogate of this loss without reference-model rollouts, so the student keeps its own few-step sampler. We view few-step generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and optimize reward with a clipped policy-gradient objective over the student's trajectories. Across DNA, image, and text generation, IDRF achieves high reward with up to $32\times$ fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.
bullets: Targets expensive iterative sampling and intractable sequence-level KL regularization in masked discrete diffusion.
Replaces the sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization and proves an upper bound under an optimal auxiliary denoiser.
Optimizes a trajectory-based, clipped policy-gradient objective over the student’s own few-step sampler.
Across DNA, image, and text generation, achieves high reward with up to 32× fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.
