papers.abstract: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance often struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion. We study center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking are unreliable under self-occlusion. We propose STATERA, which adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. To support this task, we introduce the HiddenMass Benchmark, comprising 50K MuJoCo trajectories and a 63-sequence real-world test set with physically calibrated CoM ground truth. In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, we observe a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Nevertheless, our phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that demonstrates consistent movement toward the true hidden offset. While this leads to a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error compared to a static geometric centroid, it improves physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%. These results suggest that frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation.
bullets: Targets CoM localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies where visual geometry and tracking are unreliable.
Adapts pretrained V-JEPA features with a temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories.
Introduces HiddenMass Benchmark: 50K simulated MuJoCo trajectories and 63 real-world sequences with calibrated CoM ground truth.
Reduces normalized simulation CoM error from 41.7% to 25.2% and improves real-world physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%.
Zero-shot transfer remains challenging: phase-aware supervision moves predictions toward hidden offsets but can cause overshoot, while phase-agnostic targets may collapse toward centroids.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Qualitative Kinematic Trajectories. A comparison of 2D predicted paths during multiaxis tumbling within a static observation window. (Left) Spatial models (e.g., DINOv2) suffer from visual-kinematic aliasing, tracking high-contrast surface distractors instead of momentum. (Right) STATERA-50K-Crescent successfully isolates the smooth Newtonian parabolic arc of the hidden mass, directionally aligning with the verified Ground Truth despite a Euclidean vector overshoot.

Figure 2: STATERA Architecture. A 16-frame video sequence is processed via a partially-frozen V-JEPA 2.1 backbone. Temporal tubelets are mixed using a 1D Convolution before passing through the Spatial Preservation Decoder. The network bifurcates to output a continuous spatial heatmap (Head A) and a regularizing 1D Z-Depth scalar (Head B).

Figure 6: The Vector Overshoot Artifact. (Left) An architecturally complete model (1K-Anchor) correctly learns to bound the hidden mass phase within realistic 3D physical constraints. (Right) Ablating the absolute 1D Z-Depth regularizer (1K-No-Z-Depth) causes the 2D spatial extractions to lose physical scale constraints, leading to a severe, unregularized Euclidean explosion far beyond the physical boundaries of the rigid body.

Figure 1: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematic Tracking. (Left) The HiddenMass-50K training environment featuring procedurally generated asymmetric masses. (Right) Zero-shot inference on real-world video sequences. While spatial baselines collapse to the visual centroid, STATERA successfully identifies the directional phase of the offset Center of Mass. The prediction pulls away from the visual center along the true kinematic vector (noting an empirical Euclidean overshoot inherent to the 2.5D spatial projection).

Figure 4: Curriculum Label Smoothing. Target probability distributions across training epochs. By mathematical design, at Epoch 0 (κ = 0), both targets initialize as identical broad Gaussian rings (σ = 12.5). Over the curriculum, the phase-agnostic baseline (Sigma) decays into an isotropic impulse (σ = 3.0), omitting phase data. Conversely, the phase-aware SOTA (Crescent) scales its Von Mises angular mask (κ → 50.0), forcing the network to continuously optimize for rotational torque direction.

Figure 5: Visual-Kinematic Aliasing (Bimodal Split). During high-torque rotations where groundtruth phase is highly ambiguous, models trained on static phase-aware targets output high-variance, bimodal probability heatmaps. The network essentially “hedges its bets” between two physically plausible mass locations, resulting in expectation collapse and severe temporal jitter.

Figure 7: HiddenMass Benchmark Profile. The Unified HiddenMass Score (HMS, orange) is calculated as a weighted composite: 25% Kinematic Accuracy, 25% Tracking Stability, and 50% Physics Disentanglement, explicitly penalizing statistical reward-hacking. Low Disentanglement (teal) reveals that DINOv2 and STATERA-50K-Sigma are deceived by visual and heuristic aliasing, defaulting closer to the geometric centroid. STATERA-50K-Crescent actively breaks this heuristic, achieving substantial positive physical disentanglement and securing the highest overall HMS (59.6).

Table 2: Zero-Shot Real-World Transfer (N=63). STATERA-50K-Sigma achieves the lowest spatial and jitter errors. However, unclamped Disentanglement analysis reveals DINOv2 and STATERA50K-Sigma struggle to fully disentangle the offset. STATERA-50K-Crescent remains the only architecture to achieve substantial positive disentanglement toward the hidden mass. Point trackers were evaluated via an idealized Dynamic Surface Centroid Proxy (initializing a uniform point grid around the object’s initial bounding center and gracefully falling back to the geometric center upon track death).
Table 1: In-Domain Simulation Performance (10,000 Sequences). Evaluated on the held-out MuJoCo validation set. Lower is better for all metrics.
Table 3: Temperature Pareto Sweep. The impact of the Soft-Argmax temperature (τ ) on physical capture versus Euclidean error. Evaluated on STATERA-50K-Crescent.

papers.selection_reason: Video representation learning for physical property estimation from motion, fitting video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: STATERA: Hidden Mass Estimation via Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematics using Frozen Temporal Tubelets
papers.tldr: STATERA uses mostly frozen video representations plus a lightweight temporal mixer to estimate hidden centers of mass from monocular motion, achieving strong simulation performance and meaningful zero-shot transfer to real objects.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.
authors: Yihong Luo, Tianyu Pang, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Addresses quality loss and unreliable student-score estimation in few-step distillation.
Introduces Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), using a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields.
Unifies score, Fisher-based, and moment matching while motivating new training objectives.
Uses trajectory distribution matching with online transition-aware velocity learning and dual-form supervision.
Achieves state-of-the-art four-step text-to-image and text-to-video results, including scaling to the 33B MiniMax-H3 model.

papers.abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.
authors: Yequan Bie, Dengyang Jiang, Zhixuan Chen, Xiaozhuan Liang, Haoxuan Che, Quande Liu, Xi Chen, Hao Chen
bullets: Introduces Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, requiring models to render events, infer their consequences, and reveal plausible outcomes later—even off-screen.
Uses a vision-language “world brain” to track evolving state and reason about transitions, paired with a segment-autoregressive video renderer.
Provides EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency.
Experiments report improved event-conditioned causal evolution while preserving visual quality and consistency.
Targets limitations of existing diffusion video models, which often produce visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent scenes.

papers.abstract: Scene Graph Anticipation (SGA) predicts object relationships in future video frames. Continuous-time SGA models evolve each subject-object pair with an independent Neural ODE, so relationships sharing an entity cannot influence one another during integration, and nothing prevents mutually exclusive predictions, such as "sitting on" and "standing on", for the same pair. We introduce CoupledSGA, which links such relationships through a Relationship Interaction Graph with graph attention inside the ODE vector field, and adds a Structural Consistency Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{SC}$) based on a matrix of mutually exclusive predicates. Developing CoupledSGA revealed a limitation of the evaluation protocol. With-Constraint evaluation keeps one predicate per group for each subject-object pair, so its R@K and mR@K cannot capture the within-group violations targeted by $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$: we prove they are unchanged whenever each group's winning predicate and its score are held fixed. We further show that the gradient of $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ depends on predicate scores rather than ground-truth labels: for two-predicate rules it amplifies the ordering the model already holds, and when all scores in a group are equal it suppresses predicates in more exclusion rules more strongly, explaining why the penalty can lower recall while improving consistency. On Action Genome, activating $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ after two warm-up epochs reduces R@20 from 42.21% to 35.18% while lowering the No-Constraint contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07% (matched-budget R@20: 40.48% CoupledSGA vs. 44.78% SceneSayerODE). CoupledSGA is a testbed, not a state-of-the-art claim: With-Constraint recall captures the cost of enforcing structural consistency but not the improvement. We recommend reporting No-Constraint results alongside a contradiction rate for methods that constrain predicate co-activation.
authors: Zeno Nongmaithem, Anushttha Srivastava, Anshit Sinha, Apoorv Sisodia, Suman Chowdhury, Prerana Mukherjee, Rajesh P. Barnwal
bullets: Independent Neural ODEs in continuous-time SGA cannot model interactions among relationships sharing an entity and may produce mutually exclusive predicates together.
CoupledSGA adds graph-attention coupling through a Relationship Interaction Graph and a Structural Consistency Loss based on mutually exclusive predicates.
The authors prove With-Constraint R@K and mR@K cannot reflect within-group violations when each group’s winning predicate and score remain fixed.
On Action Genome, the consistency loss reduces contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07%, but R@20 falls from 42.21% to 35.18%; matched-budget R@20 is 40.48% versus 44.78% for SceneSayerODE.
The paper recommends reporting No-Constraint results with contradiction rates; CoupledSGA is presented as a testbed rather than a state-of-the-art method.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.
authors: Shuai Dong, Kanghui Tian, Linghan Chen, Wenqi Shao, Hongrui Wu, Haowen Hou, Yongfu Zhu, Xuehui Wang, Ziyue Wang, Wenpu Liu, Weichu Xie, Yuqi Xu, Congcong Wang, Kaiwen Tuo, Caoyuan Ma, Taiqiang Wu, Ji Zhao, Wenzheng Chang, Dianyi Wang, Siyuan Wang, Zhongyu Wei, Yu Qiao, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Streaming video models must repeatedly choose whether to respond or keep observing, but trajectory-level credit can reinforce redundancy or suppress useful follow-ups.
TurnWise computes turn-level group-relative advantages from silence-completed prefix scores and each decision’s remaining return.
Turn-mean policy optimization gives response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of token output length.
The framework requires neither a learned critic nor additional rollouts.
Experiments report improved performance over prior RL methods for streaming video understanding.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Overview of TurnWise. Given streaming video input x, user queries, dialogue history, and an observation plan, the policy samples a group of trajectories {τi}Gi=1. TurnWise converts trajectory rewards Ri into group-relative remaining-return advantages Âi,t through silence-completed prefix scoring. Turn-mean aggregation then gives every response-or-wait decision equal weight in the trajectory loss Li.

TurnWise subtracts group-relative accrued reward before each decision, allowing later turns to receive credit according to their remaining return. The dialogue is illustrative. The advantage plot uses recorded TurnWise advantages and the corresponding GRPO counterfactual.

papers.abstract: Online reasoning video segmentation (Online RVS) requires a model to segment query-referred objects as a video streams in, using only the frames observed so far. Existing formulations largely assume a fixed target set throughout the video, overlooking a fundamental property of streaming reasoning: as new events occur, the objects that satisfy a query may change over time. To address this, we propose a new task, Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation (GRVS), where the target set depends on query-relevant events accumulated over the observed video history. As new evidence accumulates, the target set can evolve from empty to one or multiple objects, requiring a model to continuously maintain target validity while localizing the valid objects currently in view. To evaluate GRVS, we build Isekai, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 videos and 197 queries across 11 temporal query families, with 12,569 scoring points whose target sets are causally annotated over time. We further propose Sekai, an online framework with two complementary components: an Event Memory Reasoner (EMR) that maintains query-relevant events and evolving target states in structured memory, and a Memory-Grounded Decoder (MGD) that identifies valid targets from this memory and localizes them in the current frame. Experiments show that Sekai significantly outperforms existing online RVS methods, achieving 50.33 J&F and improving over the strongest baseline by 3.2 points. Code, example annotations, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zenastangbi/Sekai.
authors: Zhengtao Liu, Jinrong Xu, Shiu-Hong Kao, Huixin Sun, Yicong Li
bullets: Problem: Existing online video segmentation assumes a fixed target set, while streaming events can change which objects satisfy a query.
Method: The Event Memory Reasoner maintains query-relevant events and target states; the Memory-Grounded Decoder selects and segments valid objects in each current frame.
Benchmark: Isekai contains 60 videos, 197 queries, 11 temporal query families, and causally annotated target states across 12,569 scoring points.
Result: Sekai achieves 50.33 J&F, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.2 points.
Scope: The task focuses on online, causal reasoning where target sets may evolve from empty to one or multiple objects.

papers.abstract: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.
authors: Yunhao Huang, Kaushik Bhargav Sivangi, Tianyi Yu, Fani Deligianni
bullets: Targets the trade-off among pose localisation, temporal motion quality, and energy use in non-event-driven video.
Uses a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder for spatial evidence and MAM to estimate joint motion, align past heatmaps, and fuse them adaptively with current predictions.
Evaluated on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset using localisation, motion-error, and estimated arithmetic-energy metrics.
Compared with an architecture-matched ANN using MAM, it reduces estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% with a 1.12-point PCK_HB(0.5) decrease.
Adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46%, respectively, with minimal computational and parameter overhead.

papers.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.
authors: Mingzhe Zheng, Yue Wu, Jing Tan, Chang Zou, Dengyang Jiang, Zeyue Tian, Xuanhua He, Ryan Xu, Yunyang Ge, Sihui Ji, Yunlong Lin, Kaihang Pan, Hongru Yan, Sixiang Chen, Dianyi Wang, Julian Zhang, Weijie Kong, Changlin Li, Lanqing Guo, Zhao Zhong, Qifeng Chen, Harry Yang
bullets: Addresses subjective, context-dependent emotional video evaluation and reward hacking risks from fixed reward weights.
Plans emotion-specific grounding cues, scores videos with heterogeneous reward signals, and gates them by phase, facial confidence, conflict, and subtlety.
Uses RewardMemory to infer signal reliability from prior training traces and set bounded fusion-weight multipliers for subsequent runs without updating reward models.
Experiments across HunyuanVideo 1.5, SD 3.5, and FLUX support improvements and transferability across RL algorithms and agentic reward comparisons.
Scope: effectiveness is evaluated for visual generation and relies on evidence reliability learned within emotional regimes and prior training runs.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video models rely on historical key-value (KV) caches to preserve scene consistency over extended rollouts, making KV storage and repeated attention over history a growing memory and computational bottleneck. Aggressive compression can degrade generation quality, while reconstructing full-dimensional KV leaves attention computation largely unchanged. We introduce NanoKV, a frozen-backbone framework for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. NanoKV exploits redundancy across tokens and attention heads by storing shared content in cluster centers and encoding joint head-channel residuals into low-bit coefficients. Crucially, NanoKV uses different fitting objectives for Keys and Values according to their distinct roles in attention: Key decoders are optimized to preserve downstream block outputs, whereas Value encoders and decoders are fitted for faithful reconstruction through the deployed quantization path. Building on the same compressed representation, the optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention, reducing computation without modifying the video backbone. Across three autoregressive video backbones, NanoKV consistently improves the quality-storage trade-off. On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV achieves $26.09\times$ effective KV compression, nearly twice that of KVTC, while improving PSNR by 1.0 dB. NanoKV-Fast retains $20.53\times$ effective compression and achieves an approximately $1.15\times$ end-to-end speedup over KVTC.
authors: Jiacheng Lu, Haoyi Zhu, Sipei Yi, Enze Xie, Cheng Zhuo, Yu Li
bullets: Addresses KV-cache memory and historical-attention costs in long video generation.
Uses cluster centers and low-bit joint head-channel residual coefficients to exploit token and head redundancy.
Fits Key and Value compression differently: Keys preserve downstream block outputs, while Values prioritize reconstruction through quantization.
Across three video backbones, it improves the quality–storage trade-off; on HY-WorldPlay, it reaches 26.09× effective compression and improves PSNR by 1.0 dB over KVTC.
NanoKV-Fast enables mixed-dimensional attention, retaining 20.53× compression and delivering an approximately 1.15× end-to-end speedup over KVTC.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of NanoKV for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. (b) The encoder compresses residuals into INT4 coefficients; the decoder reconstructs them and adds back centers. (c) Key decoders use block-output alignment; Value encoders and decoders use quantizationaware fitting. (d) A fixed policy routes history to full- or low-dimensional attention. The latter reduces Queries and restores output dimensions before LSE merging.

papers.abstract: Portrait video relighting aims to modify the illumination of a portrait video while preserving photorealism and temporal stability. The task becomes particularly challenging under dynamic lighting, where illumination direction, intensity, and color vary over time. To tackle this problem, we introduce FlashRelight, a novel two-stage framework for dynamic portrait video relighting. FlashRelight first suppresses the source illumination through delighting, and then synthesizes the target dynamic lighting on an illumination-neutral portrait video. FlashRelight supports three complementary control modalities: envmap sequences for explicit frame-level lighting control, dynamic lighting text for semantic illumination editing, and lighting reference videos for visual lighting transfer. Training follows a low-cost hybrid strategy that combines static one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos, covering both controlled illumination variation and realistic portrait motion. Extensive experiments show that FlashRelight achieves temporally coherent and photorealistic dynamic relighting while enabling flexible cross-video lighting transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/vivoCameraResearch/FlashRelight
authors: Jiahui Sheng, Le Li, Limin Lin, Jiahao Li, Wansen Feng, Hong Gu, Shuhan Chen, Xiaorun Li, Rui Hu
bullets: Addresses dynamic lighting changes in portrait videos while preserving appearance and temporal consistency.

Trains with a hybrid of static OLAT data and generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos.
Experiments demonstrate coherent, photorealistic relighting and flexible cross-video lighting transfer.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained action understanding requires vision-language models to ground what an agent does, how it acts, and why it acts in spatio-temporal evidence. However, richer supervision can backfire: fine-tuned models may generate detailed action descriptions grounded in static scenes and salient objects rather than motion, a failure we call Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination (EGAH). To mitigate EGAH, we propose Staged Attention Rectification and Reinforcement (STARR), an action-centric video-text alignment framework that breaks scene-action shortcuts through Action-Environment Dissociation and reinforces action-focused grounding with an Attention Consistency Reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization. We further construct FineActionR&R, combining temporally localized captions with hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data. Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, FineActionVLM-R1 improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points over its base model and achieves 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench. Qualitative comparisons further indicate more faithful fine-grained action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.
authors: Zhiliang Zhu, Jiazheng Huang, Dawei Zhao
bullets: Fine-grained vision-language models can hallucinate actions from static scenes and salient objects, termed Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination (EGAH).
STARR uses Action-Environment Dissociation to break scene-action shortcuts and an Attention Consistency Reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization to reinforce action-focused grounding.
FineActionR&R combines temporally localized captions with hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data.
Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, FineActionVLM-R1 improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points and reaches 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench.
Qualitative results suggest more faithful fine-grained action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Staged Attention Rectification and Reinforcement method for fine-grained action understanding. (a) Attention Rectification: SFT is used to train on distractor videos that combine an action clip with irrelevant backgrounds, forcing the model to focus on true action regions. (b) Attention Consistency Reinforcement: GRPO optimizes a reward encouraging stable attention on key action-relevant visual tokens throughout generation.

Figure 1: Illustration of Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination. (a) VLM often generate accurate environment descriptions but incorrect action ones. During SFT, the model develops a strong tendency to anchor action predictions on easily perceived static backgrounds rather than true spatio-temporal evidence, leading to systematically incorrect action descriptions even when its environment descriptions remain accurate. (b) When environmental information is explicitly described in fine-grained action description tasks, it can easily trigger hallucinated actions unrelated to the actual video content.

papers.abstract: Adversarial training enables one- and few-step image and video generation, but conventional adversarial losses supervise critic values without directly specifying the gradients used to update the generator. We present NEXTGAN, which trains a scalar critic by regressing its input gradient onto displacements between independently paired reference and generated features at interpolated locations in frozen representation spaces. For a fixed generator, this regression is equivalent to an adversarial objective with a gradient-energy penalty, while the generator retains the standard potential-based GAN update. The same objective adapts pre-trained image and video generators with up to 14B parameters, without auxiliary losses, online teacher scores, or trajectories. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, NEXTGAN achieves one-step FIDs of 2.87 with pixel-space JiT-B and 1.54 with latent-space DiT-XL/1; its adversarial form further reaches 1.36. For text-to-video generation, a single trained Wan2.1-1.3B model supports one-, two-, and four-step sampling, achieving the highest VBench total scores among the compared 1.3B methods at one and two steps. At two steps, NEXTGAN scores 83.13, exceeding rCM and AnyFlow by 1.25 and 0.47 points, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/LINs-lab/NextGAN.git.

papers.abstract: Video-LLMs are typically trained on paired video-text data for temporal tasks, yet collecting precise temporal annotations and training on large-scale video datasets are both costly. We investigate whether a text-only LLM, with no vision-language pretraining, can be trained on textual video descriptions alone to perform temporal grounding and receive video only at inference time. This setting removes paired video data from training altogether and is a step toward training multimodal models without paired annotations. We generate a 134K-example corpus of textual sequences with up to 100 time steps, adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, and evaluate on Charades-STA and QV-Highlights without training on videos from either benchmark. LLM2CLIP, whose text encoder supports longer inputs, represents detailed descriptions better than CLIP (61.54 versus 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid) and transfers them better to video. Still, replacing text with frame embeddings at inference yields only 4.99 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 11.12 on QV-Highlights, revealing a large modality gap. To bridge it, we propose Nearest Entity Replacement (NER), a training-free mapping that represents each video frame by the normalized mean of its nearest text-entity embeddings, so that the model receives the kind of input it was trained on. NER reaches 14.45 mtIoU on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights, outperforming the strongest of four families of modality-gap baselines by 5.00 and 1.71 points. NER thus enables partial transfer from text to video, while more reliable grounding will likely require encoders with better-aligned text and visual representations.
authors: Divyanshu Mishra, Sabine Sternig, Rakshith Shetty, Erhan Gundogdu
bullets: Motivation: avoid costly paired video-text data and precise temporal annotations by training solely on textual video descriptions.
Method: adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA on 134K time-indexed text sequences using CLIP or LLM2CLIP text embeddings, then provide video only at inference.
LLM2CLIP transfers better than CLIP, achieving 61.54 vs. 53.86 mtIoU on Temporal-TextVid.
Nearest Entity Replacement maps each frame to nearby text-entity embeddings, improving mtIoU to 14.45 on Charades-STA and 20.72 on QV-Highlights.
Scope: transfer remains partial, indicating that better-aligned text and visual encoders are needed for reliable grounding.

papers.abstract: Online scam videos pose significant threats to individuals and society. Existing studies primarily focus on binary classification, offering limited insights into how scams work and the reasoning behind detection decisions. Moreover, they often overlook the challenge of distinguishing scam videos from superficially similar non-scam content, such as advertisements, and the robustness of detection models against misleading arguments. These limitations hinder reliable scam video detection. To address these limitations, we introduce MechScam, a benchmark comprising 6,614 videos covering diverse scam mechanisms and non-scam categories. MechScam provides explanations supported by video evidence, annotations of potential scam elements and their context, and misleading arguments constructed from genuine evidence. Recognizing that genuine evidence can still be used to justify misleading conclusions, we further propose ScamCourt, a debate framework in which trained prosecution and defense debaters present opposing arguments, while a trained judge makes decisions based on a transcript with verified citations. Extensive experiments show that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle to distinguish scam videos from similar non-scam content. ScamCourt outperforms larger MLLMs and same-backbone fine-tuned baselines, reducing false positives and showing stronger resistance to misleading arguments. Together, MechScam and ScamCourt contribute to more reliable and interpretable scam video detection. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/SuperYFan/MechScam.
authors: Yifan Wang, Junyu Lu, Shun Zhang, Chaozhuo Li, Fanliang Bu, Rong Yin, Lingbin Bu, Changrong Min, Peng Chen
bullets: MechScam contains 6,614 scam and similar non-scam videos spanning diverse scam mechanisms and categories.
It includes video-supported explanations, scam-element/context annotations, and misleading arguments based on genuine evidence.
ScamCourt uses prosecution and defense debaters plus a citation-verifying judge to evaluate competing claims.
Experiments find that state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle with scam-versus-advertisement discrimination, while ScamCourt reduces false positives and resists misleading arguments.
The work targets more reliable and interpretable web scam video detection; its scope is defined by the benchmark’s annotated mechanisms and categories.

papers.abstract: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, with progress driven largely by scaling model size and omni training data. We ask whether a model needs to hear the audio directly at all, and present SleuthVLM, an agent harness built on a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech will be transcribed into text, and the VLM will sleuth the video on its own without any predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, SleuthVLM achieves the best average accuracy: \textbf{75.0%}, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it also tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with \textbf{77.8%}; with an open-source 27B VLM, it beats all open-source omni models. We draw three findings: SleuthVLM beats a model that glances; hearing is not the bottleneck, agentic ability is; omni understanding needs better agentic ability, not just more omni data for modality alignment. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for doing omni video understanding. Omni understanding needs better agents, not just bigger models that hear.
authors: Peiran Wu, Fangfei Gou, Zhaoxi Mu, Changhao Zhang, Jian Liu, Weiqiang Wang, Yuntao Wang, Yuanchun Shi, Junxiao Shen
bullets: Challenges the assumption that omni video models must directly hear audio.
Uses a VLM agent that receives speech as text and autonomously investigates video without a predefined workflow.
Achieves 75.0% average accuracy across four omni benchmarks and 77.8% on Video-MME-v2, as reported in the abstract.
With an open-source 27B VLM, outperforms all open-source omni models evaluated.
Concludes that improving agentic reasoning may be more valuable than simply scaling omni data or model size.

papers.title: SleuthVLM: Do We Really Need Audio-in-Video for Omni Video Understanding?

papers.abstract: Motorized Two-Wheelers (MTWs) dominate personal transport across much of the Global South, yet remain largely overlooked in predictive perception research for autonomous driving and ADAS. We introduce MotoVerse, a benchmark for predictive perception from an MTW's ego-centric perspective. MotoVerse comprises 949 maneuver clips collected in dense, unstructured traffic and trajectory annotations for over 31,000 surrounding road agents, including over 16,000 MTWs, enabling two complementary tasks: Ego-Rider Maneuver Anticipation (ERMA) and Traffic Agent Trajectory Prediction (TATP). Each clip is further annotated with an MTW-specific challenge taxonomy comprising dynamic ego-motion, weak traffic structure and contextual occlusion, enabling challenge-aware evaluation. We benchmark established conventional prediction models, general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs), driving-specific VLMs and vision-language-action models. Our experiments reveal three key insights: (i) video backbones reach most of their full-observation accuracy from the first fifth of a maneuver, whereas zero-shot VLMs need most of the maneuver to be observed; (ii) zero-shot VLMs, whether general-purpose or driving-specific, largely remain close to simple baselines on both tasks; a preliminary LoRA study shows that adaptation lifts anticipation sharply but leaves trajectory prediction behind conventional models; and (iii) the rider's own motion drives forecasting difficulty: for every model, including a static baseline, errors are highest during left turns and rise under dynamic ego-motion. We believe MotoVerse will serve as a challenging benchmark for safer and more robust predictive AI for intelligent two-wheelers. The dataset and evaluation code are publicly available at https://github.com/VarunIIITH/MotoVerse.
authors: Varun A. Paturkar, Shankar Gangisetty, C. V. Jawahar
bullets: Contains 949 maneuver clips and trajectory annotations for more than 31,000 agents, including over 16,000 motorized two-wheelers.

Video backbones achieve most of their full-observation accuracy early, while zero-shot VLMs generally remain near simple baselines.
LoRA adaptation substantially improves maneuver anticipation but does not close the gap with conventional models for trajectory prediction.
Forecasting is hardest during left turns and under dynamic ego-motion across all evaluated models.

papers.title: MotoVerse: A Benchmark for Predictive Perception of Motorized Two-Wheelers in Dense Unstructured Traffic
papers.tldr: MotoVerse introduces a benchmark for predicting MTW rider maneuvers and surrounding-agent trajectories in dense, unstructured traffic from an ego-centric viewpoint.

papers.abstract: Video editors often work with large collections of fragmented footage and must select and organize relevant clips into a coherent story. However, many existing video editing and summarization methods assume a temporally ordered source video and aim to preserve its original narrative and temporal structure. In this paper, we introduce Clips2Story, a training-free, LLM-based pipeline that enables users to create keyword-specified short videos from a pool of video clips. Given a pool of clips and a user-specified keyword, we first extract text-based multimodal descriptors for each clip and retrieve the clips most relevant to the keyword. We then provide the textual descriptors of these candidate clips to an LLM, which selects and arranges them into an editable storyboard with connective narrations. Finally, we assemble the selected clips and retrieve accompanying visuals for the narrations to compose the output video. To evaluate the proposed pipeline, we construct a synthetic evaluation dataset from 100 long-form videos across five genres by segmenting each video into short clips using a scene-change detection model and shuffling the resulting clips to remove their temporal order. Through objective evaluation and qualitative examples, we demonstrate that Clips2Story can effectively retrieve keyword-relevant clips and compose coherent storyboards based on user-specified keywords. Human evaluation further shows that Clips2Story outperforms a strong baseline in terms of narrative coherence, keyword alignment, and overall realism.

papers.abstract: For decades, diagnostic pathology has relied on thin two-dimensional (2D) tissue sections, despite biological tissues exhibiting inherently three-dimensional (3D) morphological organization. Because a single section captures only one focal plane, important morphological cues along the z-axis are inevitably discarded, limiting tissue representation for both human interpretation and computational analysis. In this work, we propose a generative framework that learns z-axis morphological priors from pathology z-stack data, offering a cost-effective alternative to dedicated volumetric imaging, and transfers this knowledge to conventional single-plane histopathology. Specifically, an image-to-video (I2V) latent diffusion model (LDM) is trained to synthesize a pseudo z-stack from a single 2D image, capturing plausible morphological variations across adjacent focal planes rather than reconstructing physical tissue volumes. To enable deployment on large-scale clinical datasets without native z-stack acquisition, we further introduce a prior-preserving mixture fine-tuning strategy that adapts the model to new domains while retaining the learned z-axis morphological prior. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the synthesized pseudo z-stacks exhibit realistic cross-plane morphological continuity and consistently improve downstream prostate cancer classification compared with conventional 2D representations. Our results suggest that learning transferable z-axis priors from limited z-stack data provides a practical way to enrich routine pathology images with complementary morphological information. Code: https://github.com/QuIIL/PathoS2VD.
authors: Jiamu Wang, Keunho Byeon, Ji-Uk Kim, Jin Tae Kwak, Heounjeong Go
bullets: 2D tissue sections lose morphological cues along the z-axis, limiting pathology interpretation and analysis.

Experiments show realistic cross-plane continuity and improved downstream prostate cancer classification over conventional 2D representations.

papers.abstract: Diffusion drafters accelerate speculative decoding by denoising multiple draft tokens in parallel. Their training uses anchor sampling to construct compact draft queries and performs cross-attention with a block-sparse mask over a much longer context. We empirically show that acceptance length remains stable as context scales with a fixed query budget, while increasing the query budget yields diminishing quality gains, jointly establishing a practical regime with queries far shorter than the context. No existing context parallelism (CP) method jointly exploits this query--context asymmetry and meets the nonlinear, sample-dependent load-balancing requirement created by anchor sampling. We present Split-KV, an exact CP method that keeps key/value shards local and limits per-layer attention communication to query-sized tensors, making this communication independent of context length. Its global query view further enables a cost-aware longest-processing-time-first (LPT) strategy that balances context key/value chunks by their realized attention cost. At a CP size of 64, Split-KV retains 85--91\% weak-scaling efficiency and achieves up to $3.67\times$ speedup over the fastest available CP baseline. LPT achieves $<$1\% imbalance and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best load-balancing baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/zxgx/verl.
authors: Geng Zhang, Fangzhao Zhang, Cong Xie, Tiantian Fan, Yang You
bullets: Diffusion drafters use compact draft queries to attend over much longer, block-sparse contexts.

A global query view enables longest-processing-time-first scheduling to balance sample-dependent attention costs.
At context-parallel size 64, Split-KV achieves 85–91% weak-scaling efficiency and up to 3.67× speedup over the fastest baseline.
LPT reduces load imbalance to below 1% and plans three orders of magnitude faster than the best compared balancer.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates few-step video diffusion transformers by computing a few key blocks exactly and compensating for the rest. However, existing sparse attention still faces key challenges, including identification overhead from finding critical blocks at every denoising step, suboptimal budget allocation that sets sparsity budgets uniformly or by local metrics, and cross-step error accumulation as reused masks or clusters go stale. Observing that the errors left on skipped blocks cancel each other once every key is compensated, we propose DecoupAttn, a new paradigm of decoupled sparse attention: semantic clusters compensate every key, and exact attention corrects their error on a few blocks fixed once offline by position. To support this paradigm, we introduce Distortion Budget, a rate-distortion objective for budget allocation that places exact computation across timesteps, layers, and heads where it removes the most distortion that compensation leaves in the final latent. Built on this budget, we further propose Reassign Cache, in which each step reassigns the drifting keys to cached centroids and refreshes compensation while the budgeted blocks stay fixed. Moreover, DecoupAttn is training-free: a few calibration clips compile one plan offline, and inference runs standard block-sparse kernels with one fused compensation kernel. Our code will be released after submission.
authors: Yanjin Li, Bingbing Qiu, Qiang Huang, Rui Qian, Yanfeng Li, Jian Wang, Xiaoying Tang, Mingda Zhang

Uses Reassign Cache to update drifting key-to-centroid assignments and refresh compensation at each denoising step.
Compiles the plan from a few calibration clips and performs inference with block-sparse kernels plus one fused compensation kernel; no training is required.

papers.abstract: Identity-preserving video generation aims to synthesize high-quality and visually realistic videos from textual and visual conditions while faithfully maintaining the subject's identity across diverse motions. Prior methods have extensively introduced reference-guided control signals and identity-aware conditioning to improve facial alignment from reference images. However, improving static identity alignment alone creates a fundamental tension between identity fidelity and temporal controllability, which frequently causes identity drift or motion suppression under large pose variations and multi-segment sequential actions. To address this, we propose Chronos, a framework that unifies single-segment facial identity preservation and multi-segment sequential action generation under a common temporal formulation. Specifically, Chronos integrates Semantic Prompt Anchoring to adaptively refine the user prompt, Visual Frame Anchoring to transform conditions into visually grounded keyframe anchors for visual guidance, and Metric-Guided Candidate Routing to select the highest-quality videos from heterogeneous generators via multi-dimensional evaluation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our approach, which achieved first place in both Track 1 and Track 2 of the ACM MM 2026 Identity-Preserving Video Generation Challenge, demonstrating its effectiveness across both facial identity preservation and sequential action generation settings.
authors: Mengqi Huang, Wenchuan Wang, Zhendong Mao, Yijing Tu, Zhike Liu, Luoni Wang, Ning Tong, Xiaoxiao Sheng, Tianyu Huang, Xuecheng Qi, Yongdong Zhang
bullets: Addresses the conflict between strong identity fidelity and controllable motion, which can cause identity drift or motion suppression.
Unifies single-segment facial identity preservation with multi-segment sequential action generation in a common temporal framework.
Uses Semantic Prompt Anchoring to refine prompts and Visual Frame Anchoring to create visually grounded keyframe guidance.
Applies Metric-Guided Candidate Routing to select high-quality videos from heterogeneous generators.
Won first place in both tracks of the ACM MM 2026 Identity-Preserving Video Generation Challenge.

The enhanced prompt and anchors are passed to track-specific video generators, followed by metric-guided evaluation and automatic routing to obtain the final video.

papers.abstract: Digital human e-commerce video generation requires preserving product appearance, human identity, and overall video style during dynamic demonstrations. Although recent models support multiple reference images, their general conditioning schemes do not explicitly distinguish the asymmetric roles of "what is presented" and "who presents it." Consequently, generated videos may favor a single reference, resulting in product distortion, identity drift, or single-reference collapse. To address this issue, we propose DualCast, a role-addressed dual-image conditioning framework for video generation. By explicitly modeling the distinct roles of product and human conditions, DualCast reduces role ambiguity and feature competition between references. First, a dual-spatiotemporal slot injection mechanism VAE-encodes the product and human images separately and places their latent features at the front and rear boundaries of the DiT sequence, enabling sequence-level condition separation and directed injection. Second, a mask-guided region-weighted loss strengthens supervision over product, face, and product-face overlap regions, improving generation fidelity in critical areas. Third, image condition dropout enables a single model to support dual-image, product-only, and human-only generation. In addition, we construct a curated dataset of 10K e-commerce videos for model training. Experimental results demonstrate the strong performance of DualCast.

Uses separate VAE-encoded product and human features injected into opposite ends of a diffusion-transformer sequence.
Applies mask-guided region-weighted loss to emphasize product, face, and product–face overlap regions.
Uses image-condition dropout to support dual-image, product-only, and human-only generation.
Trained on a curated dataset of 10K e-commerce videos; the abstract reports strong experimental performance without specific metrics.

Compared with existing methods, our approach demonstrates advantages in three aspects: (1) Facial Feature Consistency — Our method preserves the source person’s facial identity during video generation, avoiding identity drift or distortion; (2) Product Consistency — Product details from the reference image, including appearance, texture, and logos, are accurately reproduced, maintaining high visual fidelity; (3) Style Decoupling Capability — The overall style of the generated video is not irreversibly influenced by the reference image, achieving flexible decoupling between content transfer and style control, making the generation results more suitable for e-commerce live streaming scenarios.

C (Human-only): When the product condition is omitted, the model generates high-quality presenter-led promotional videos based on the person.

papers.abstract: Holistic perception for autonomous agents requires reliably segmenting and associating scene elements across time and camera views, including objects outside a fixed semantic taxonomy. Existing open-set panoptic benchmarks focus on individual images or views, while panoramic tracking benchmarks assume closed-set taxonomies. Consequently, these benchmarks do not evaluate whether unknown objects can be consistently segmented and tracked across synchronized multi-camera sequences. We introduce WayPOP, a panoramic open-set panoptic tracking benchmark built on real Waymo PVPS sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets from Objaverse. Inserted objects are placed at fixed locations in the 3D scene and rendered using calibrated vehicle-mounted cameras as the ego vehicle and surrounding traffic move, providing temporally and cross-view consistent panoptic annotations and auxiliary LiDAR range observations. WayPOP contains approximately 670 curated assets instantiated as 980 unique unknown-object tracks, yielding 53,452 unknown-object mask annotations across 21,300 camera images. Our evaluation protocol defines a hierarchy of tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking, using known/unknown PQ and (w)STQ metrics. We benchmark representative open-set and open-vocabulary segmentation methods with temporal and cross-camera association. Our results reveal substantial limitations of current methods in truly open-set scenarios, highlighting robust unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views as major open challenges.
authors: Rohit Mohan, Maximilian Luz, Swarnava Chowdhury, Yao Lu, Florian Drews, Thomas N\"urnberg, Yakov Miron, Federico Tombari, Stefano Gasperini, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses the gap between image-level open-set benchmarks and closed-set panoramic tracking benchmarks.
Builds on real Waymo sequences augmented with diverse out-of-taxonomy 3D assets and temporally cross-view consistent annotations.
Provides unknown-object tracks, camera masks, and auxiliary LiDAR observations for evaluation.
Defines tasks from view-independent open-set panoptic segmentation to full panoramic open-set panoptic tracking.
Benchmark results show current methods struggle with unknown-object localization and identity association across time and views.

papers.abstract: Many temporal approaches for video recognition rely on explicit cross-channel aggregation projections, which have quadratic complexity in the number of channels, introducing significant computational overhead. In addition, the spatio-temporal representation used for video recognition is biased either toward local order interactions (for CNNs) or toward global order interactions (for transformers). Starting from the multi-order spatial representation of MogaNet, our method introduces two complementary contributions to tackle these problems. First, for the temporal modelling, we introduce parallel multi-order processing with depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating-based aggregation, which is linear in the number of channels, inducing a considerable computational reduction. Second, we propose a dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions, which allows a better spatio-temporal representation without increasing the computational cost. By combining these two contributions, our proposed VideoMogaNet achieves performance on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition approaches across multiple video benchmarks (UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, Diving48), while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.
authors: Kevin D. Nguetche, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli
bullets: Targets the quadratic channel cost of explicit cross-channel aggregation in temporal video models.
Uses parallel multi-order depthwise-only convolutions with implicit gating-based aggregation for linear channel complexity.
Introduces dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions to improve representation without added computational cost.
Matches or exceeds state-of-the-art action-recognition performance across UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, and Diving48.
Scope: focuses on reducing temporal modeling overhead while balancing local and global order interactions.

The architecture demonstrates precise focus on discriminative spatial regions where fine-grained object transformations occur (e.g., hand movements, object manipulations), while maintaining temporal consistency through multi-order temporal modulation (MOTM). Highlighted regions show the model’s ability to capture both spatial part-whole compositions via SMixer (SMOGA) and temporal dynamics via MOTM, validating the synergistic coordination between spatial and temporal modalities for fine-grained action understanding.

papers.abstract: Existing benchmarks for joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation evaluate perceptual quality and audiovisual alignment, but balanced sound-source sam?pling and separate reporting by shot structure remain limited. This makes it dif?ficult to determine whether a specific sound is missing, attributed to the wrong source, or lost across shot transitions. To address this, we introduce CAST?BENCH, a benchmark designed to trace every generated sound back to its in?tended source in multi-shot audio-video generation. The core idea is to formu?late T2AV correctness as an audiovisual contract in which each requested sound must be emitted by the right source, synchronized with the corresponding visual action, and carry the right semantic content. Concretely, the benchmark orga?nizes 900 prompts into 9 sound-source categories, with 100 prompts per cate?gory, spanning speech, animals, instruments, ambient sounds, and other emitter types. The prompts include 439 single-shot and 461 multi-shot narratives, each derived from a structured specification that links every audio event to its emit?ter, subject, and temporal slot. The benchmark provides an 18-metric evaluation suite covering three dimensions: Visual Performance, Content Consistency, and Audio & Semantic Alignment. We further benchmark 12 representative gen?erators and find that visual quality is nearly saturated across leading systems, yet audio semantic scores still differ markedly. Across the nine shared mod?els, multi-shot prompts receive lower aggregate scores under the subset-specific scoring rules and yield different model rankings. Multi-person speech, con?sistent speaker identity across shots, and cross-shot event retention remain the main unresolved challenges. All prompts and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/yucong-liu/CAST-Bench-public.
authors: Yucong Liu, Qi Tian, Shuyuan Tu, Kaihang Pan, Weijie Kong, Chao Pan
bullets: Introduces an audiovisual-contract framework for tracing each generated sound to its intended emitter, semantic content, and temporal slot.

papers.abstract: Diffusion image generators are successful due to accurate denoising networks and strong numerical samplers. Yet the two components are not fully matched. During sampling, the denoiser predicts for the next step based on flawed input that differ much from the real data. This train-test gap, or exposure bias, caps image generation quality (i.e., blurry, lacking in details or awkward in shape). To mitigate the problem, we propose PEEK, a novel training-free deterministic sampler plugin. At each eligible denoising step, PEEK first performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser once at the look-ahead state, and interpolates it with the one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. By taking the additional step, we obtain a generally more-image-like prediction from the higher-signal noisy state, mitigating the exposure bias. To optimize the interpolation positions, PEEK searches for an interpolation schedule search made efficient by the prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches. On 8 pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided, and text-guided settings across various output resolutions, PEEK consistently improves over NFE-matched baselines, with FID improvements up to 49.3\% at minimal extra computation cost (e.g., the one-time-per-model calibration takes at most 2.2 minutes across our experiments.). Project website is at https://dachengruoque.github.io/PEEK-Video/.
authors: Yunwei Bai, Ying Kiat Tan, Tsuhan Chen

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation is increasingly moving toward autoregressive rollout, where each newly generated segment becomes part of the evidence used for future prediction. Recent causal decoders, long-context training, and KV-cache mechanisms have extended feasible duration, but most inference pipelines still decide the visible past implicitly through recent windows, compressed caches, or external memory. This raises a direct question: \textbf{can the choice of which past frames or segments to show to the decoder be treated as an explicit test-time decision?} We answer this question with \textsc{ReCR}, a training-free method that formulates autoregressive video decoding as representation-guided context rewriting. At each step, \textsc{ReCR} builds a selected visible context from the generated history by using internal decoder representations to favor context units that match the global rollout state, avoid redundancy with the recent continuation, preserve temporal boundary coverage, and widen the range of spatial layouts in view. The selected units are then mapped onto a compact causal axis before decoding the next block. Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, \textsc{ReCR} consistently improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets. Empirical analyses such as representation-space diagnostics and transition-count prompt switching further show that improving what remains visible is an effective path toward more stable long-video decoding.
authors: Lixuan He, Jihyeon Je, Yang You, Leonidas Guibas
bullets: Frames or segments shown to the decoder are treated as an explicit test-time selection decision.
The training-free method uses internal representations to select globally relevant, nonredundant context.
It preserves temporal boundary coverage and increases the diversity of visible spatial layouts.
Selected context units are placed on a compact causal axis before generating the next video block.
Across long-horizon text-to-video benchmarks, ReCR improves multiple autoregressive backbones under matched visible-token budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the ReCR framework. Instead of exposing the full generated history or a fixed recent window, ReCR scores context units with unit-level representations and selects a compact visible context. The selection objective favors high representation utility, preserves boundary coverage over early and recent context, and discourages redundant selected units. At most one spatial-range exchange, not drawn here, then refines the selection (Sec. 3.2). The selected context is then temporally reindexed onto a compact causal axis before being passed to the causal video decoder.

Figure 1: Qualitative overview of ReCR across backbones. ReCR is applied as a training-free context rewriting module on top of different autoregressive video backbones. On 60-second rollouts, ReCR reduces common long-horizon failures such as scene drift, visual artifacts, and oversaturation. On 300-second ultra-long rollouts, ReCR further extends backbones with stable visual continuity.

Figure 3: ReCR further strengthens training-free decoding methods. Qualitative comparisons on two 60-second prompts. For both methods, ReCR improves temporal consistency and visual fidelity over time: it reduces drift and artifacts in Deep Forcing, and further improves the stability and text-alignment ability of Infinity-RoPE. These results show that ReCR is a complementary context-rewriting module that can be added on top of strong training-free methods.
Figure 5: Qualitative transition examples. ReCR improves cross-segment consistency of persistent visual anchors and requested local actions under the same directive-switch schedules.

Figure 4: Dynamic allocation of ReCR’s selected visible context. (a) Selection frequency over rollout time and context-unit index. (b) Composition of Ct and normalized DINO feature velocity over rollout. (c) Representation-utility space induced by gt and ℓt, with selected units highlighted.

Figure 6: Transition-count prompt-switch scaling. (a) Overall text alignment (TA) to the active directive versus transition count K. (b) Early post-switch alignment, summarized by AUC over 0–8 seconds, versus K. (c) Absolute DINO tail shown as a radial dot plot: each spoke corresponds to a transition count, and distance from the center represents the metric value; closer to the center is better. All panels share the same method colors and markers. Higher is better in (a,b), and lower is better in (c).
Figure 7: ReCR’s results on more backbone and more frame.
Figure 8: Mechanistic robustness analysis. We compare four context construction rules under controlled perturbations: contiguous recent context, Full Context, random intermediate context, and ReCR.

papers.tldr: ReCR improves long-horizon autoregressive video generation by explicitly rewriting which past content remains visible to the decoder.

papers.abstract: Existing multimodal video highlight detectors typically assume that visual, audio, and textual streams are continuously available. In practice, however, inputs may suffer from localized frame missingness or complete-stream outage. We formulate this robustness challenge along two dimensions: temporal missingness, where frames are missing independently in each modality, and stream-level missingness, where one modality is unavailable throughout a video. Moreover, we find that the mean squared error (MSE) loss is misaligned with both the evaluation metrics and the peak-driven nature of highlights. Therefore, we propose Temporal-Stream Modality Dropout (TSMD), which combines structured missingness simulation with a joint objective comprising pointwise MSE, per-video Pearson correlation, and peak-oriented RankNet loss terms. TSMD has three variants: temporal, stream-level, and mixed dropout. On the MoSu and Mr. HiSum datasets, TSMD-Temporal improves mAP@15 by 7.06 and 3.41 points over TripleSumm under 50% independent temporal removal, whereas TSMD-Stream performs the best under complete-stream removal. TSMD-Mix retains most of these complementary benefits and ranks the best or the second-best across the evaluated temporal and stream-level conditions.
bullets: Addresses two missing-input settings: independent temporal frame loss and complete stream outage.
Uses Temporal-Stream Modality Dropout with temporal, stream-level, and mixed variants.
Combines pointwise MSE, per-video Pearson correlation, and peak-oriented RankNet losses.
On MoSu and Mr. HiSum, TSMD-Temporal improves mAP@15 under 50% temporal removal, while TSMD-Stream performs best for complete-stream removal.
TSMD-Mix ranks among the best across both missingness conditions.

Solid and dashed curves denote clean and temporal-dropout training, respectively. Their separation shows the complementary contributions of the joint objective and temporal-dropout training.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Temporal-Stream Modality Dropout (TSMD) to improve robustness of video highlight detection against missing visual, audio, or text streams.
papers.title: TSMD: Temporal-Stream Modality Dropout for Robust Video Highlight Detection
papers.tldr: TSMD improves video highlight detection robustness to missing frames and unavailable modalities through structured dropout and a highlight-aware training objective.

papers.abstract: Tracking-by-propagation (TBP) methods perform end-to-end multi-object tracking by propagating track queries across frames, jointly handling detection and identity association without heuristic post-processing while naturally modeling temporal information. However, as detection and association are tightly coupled, detection queries in TBP are expected to discover currently untracked objects and provide complementary current-frame evidence for challenging tracks whose queries and identities are retained. Existing methods largely inherit detection-query formation from single-frame detection and construct such queries before the decoder with little awareness of trajectory states. Consequently, currently untracked objects may be missed, while challenging tracked objects with reduced visibility under occlusion may lack complementary evidence, causing association failures or duplicate responses. To address these issues, we propose TAQ-MOTR, a tracking-aware detection query formation framework that employs a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator (HQG) to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory. By conditioning detection queries on trajectory states, TAQ-MOTR adapts them to \rev{the discovery of currently untracked objects and tracked-object complementation We further introduce a training-only auxiliary detection branch whose one-to-one label assignment is decoupled from that of the main tracking branch, providing additional detection supervision to strengthen the shared HQG and decoder for the discovery of currently untracked objects. TAQ-MOTR improves performance on DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and BFT, achieving 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set. Code is available at https://github.com/Magicmiya/TAQ-MOTR
authors: Hanyang Liu, Hong Zhang, Ding Yuan, Yang Han, Yifan Yang
bullets: Addresses missed untracked objects and association failures for occluded or difficult tracks in tracking-by-propagation methods.
Uses a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory.
Adds a training-only auxiliary detection branch with independently assigned labels to strengthen query and decoder learning.
Reports 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set, with improvements also reported on SportsMOT and BFT.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of TAQ-MOTR. TAQ-MOTR forms tracking-aware detection queries before decoding. In the main tracking branch, HQG uses image-based detection proposals as queries and reads track memory and learnable memory as keys/values. The generated detection queries are concatenated with updated track queries and jointly decoded. During training, an auxiliary detection branch shares the detection proposals and HQG layers but removes track memory, producing a separate detection-query group supervised by all current-frame objects. Attention masks isolate this auxiliary group from the main query groups. The right panel shows an HQG layer.

Figure 3: Prior carriers used in HQG. Learnable memory provides learnable detection priors that are independent of specific trajectories. Track memory encodes existing trajectory states from propagated track queries, including content, position, and disappearance-time information. Detection proposals provide current-frame object evidence and coarse spatial priors.

Figure 4: Positive label assignments during training on DanceTrack. All ratios use the total GT count per epoch, including clip-initial frames. The auxiliary branch is disabled on each clip’s first frame, so Auxiliary Detection/GT remains below 100% while enabled. Dashed lines mark clip-length changes; shading marks branch shutdown from epoch 24. The auxiliary-only ratio is then zero and omitted. Epoch numbering starts at 0.

Figure 1: Detection query formation before decoding. (a) MOTR: learnable queries; (b) MOTRv2: detector-guided queries; (c) TAQ-MOTR: tracking-aware queries. The comparison highlights currentframe information, trajectory-state priors, and learnable embeddings.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison of detection-query formation strategies on DanceTrack. Green boxes denote ground truth. Yellow, red, and blue boxes denote tracking outputs from three queryformation variants: image-based detection queries without HQG, learned queries, and HQG-generated queries (TAQ-MOTR), respectively. The status tables report matched IDs and tracking states: “Lost” denotes no matched result, “IDSW” an identity switch, and “track” correct tracking. In the illustrated frames, TAQ-MOTR preserves the queried identities through occlusion, crossing, and overlap; this comparison provides qualitative evidence of association behavior.

Figure 7: Query-focus visualization of detection queries on DanceTrack. The heatmaps aggregate cross-attention between detection queries and multi-scale image features in the first decoder layer; each panel is independently normalized, so heatmap colors indicate relative spatial focus rather than absolute attention magnitudes. Green boxes mark established tracking outputs and red boxes missing or unstable outputs; these colors do not indicate track-query retention. Panels (a)–(b) show video initialization, and (c)–(e) show target discovery and challenging tracking in a crowded scene. TAQ-MOTR attends to missing or unstable output regions and crowded regions where existing tracks may require additional current-frame evidence, complementing the SA masking analysis in Table 11.
Figure 5: Module-level efficiency analysis of TAQ-MOTR. Rounded parameter counts and reported per-frame runtimes are shown for the backbone, hybrid encoder, decoder, HQG, and query updater.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.
authors: Christian Pipal, Eva-Maria Vogel, Morgan Wack
bullets: The study examines how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement validity in MLLM-based video analysis.
