papers.selection_reason: Studies input-representation validity in MLLM-based video analysis, relevant to multimodal video understanding.
papers.title: What Does the Model See? Representation Validity in Multimodal LLM-Based Video Analysis
papers.tldr: Input choice strongly shapes MLLM video-analysis validity, and the best classifier is not necessarily the best tool for reproducing human-coded estimates.

papers.abstract: Clustering faces by identity in long, continuous video streams is a challenging task that serves as a building block for human-centric video analysis. The majority of existing face clustering models are offline, i.e., they assume the entire data to be available altogether. In many practical scenarios, however, the entire data is either unavailable or poses computational challenges to be processed in its entirety. A handful of online methods that exist rely on geometric visual features and simple thresholding techniques, which fail when the faces exhibit significant appearance variations in long, unconstrained videos. To this end, we present VISTA, the first vision language framework for online face clustering in long videos. VISTA leverages semantic reasoning in a controlled, uncertainty aware fashion to maintain both high cluster purity and long range identity continuity. This makes it robust to the variations in illumination, pose, and costume changes that the faces and characters exhibit in long real world videos. Extensive experiments on the VPCD benchmark dataset (with 15 full episodes from The Big Bang Theory [2007-2019], Buffy the Vampire Slayer [1997-2003], and Sherlock [2010-2017]) demonstrate that VISTA achieves a robust precision and recall balance, consistently improving over the strongest matched online unsupervised baseline (COFC) under identical detector, embeddings, and evaluation protocol. Code and supplementary material: https://github.com/SkyJiashu/VISTA.
authors: Jiashu Liao, Joanne Garde-Hansen, Sanjay Sharma, Tanaya Guha
bullets: Addresses the need for online face clustering when complete video streams cannot be processed offline.
Combines visual features with controlled semantic reasoning to maintain cluster purity and long-range identity consistency.
Targets challenging variations in illumination, pose, and costumes across unconstrained videos.
Evaluated on 15 full episodes from three TV series in the VPCD benchmark.
Consistently improves the precision–recall balance over the matched online unsupervised COFC baseline under the same protocol.

papers.abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

papers.abstract: Long instructional videos are increasingly used in medical education, industrial training, and procedural knowledge transfer, yet their evidence is often incomplete or unreliable: subtitles may be missing, ASR noisy, OCR sparse, and decisive actions briefly shown without narration. Existing VideoQA systems typically return labels or free-form text, making answer support difficult to inspect. We study Long Video Moment Question Answering (LVMQA), where a system returns timestamped answer-supporting evidence. We propose EP-LVMQA, an evidence-preserving coarse-to-fine framework comprising an Uncertainty-Aware Multimodal Evidence Timeline, a Coarse Evidence Planner, and an Evidence-Conditioned Fine Localizer. An evidence card transfers planner scores, matched cues, source-confidence proxies, modality-specific evidence, neighboring context, and a temporal prior between the latter two modules. On MedVidQA, EP-LVMQA achieves 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, improving the strongest non-ours results by 6.3 and 5.1 points. It raises Suff.@2 and Ver.@2 to 25.4 and 22.6, gains of 9.5 and 8.8 points. Under matched low-quality perturbations, average relative degradation is reduced from the strongest non-ours value of 14.6% to 11.1%. On Ego4D-NLQ and QVHighlights, EP-LVMQA remains broadly comparable to established task-specific localization methods.

On MedVidQA, reports 26.1 R1@0.5 and 31.8 mIoU, with improved sufficiency and verifiability scores over the strongest non-ours results.

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion and flow matching models are ubiquitous in state-of-the-art generative video models. While highly effective, relying on pretrained autoencoders to compress the data into a lower-dimensional latent space also comes with drawbacks. First, training proceeds in two stages: autoencoder pretraining, with compression and reconstruction objectives, followed by latent generative model training, precluding fully end-to-end training. Second, autoencoders also lead to an inherent loss of signal, and the trade-off between reconstruction quality and generative performance in the latent space is still an active area of research. In this paper we explore the viability of generative video models directly in pixel space. We analyze recent approaches in pixel-space generative modeling of images that rely on basic transformer designs, and identify several shortcomings that limit their effectiveness for the high-dimensional pixel-space video generation. To overcome these limitations, we propose a UNet-like transformer architecture along with improvements to the training recipe and sampling strategy. We conduct controlled experiments, training latent and pixel-space models from scratch on Kinetics-600. For the standard frames-to-video task at 128 resolution, our U-JiT model improves generative FVD by 27% over prior state-of-the-art results, and by 14% against the JiT pixel-space baseline. Scaling to higher 256 resolution, we find the improvement over pixel-space and latent-based models grows as we increase the spatiotemporal compression rate up to $64 \times 64 \times 8$. Finally, we find that U-JiT improves per-frame FID by 27% over latent models and 61% over pixel-space models on class-to-video generation, with respectively 9% and 56% reduction in FVD.
authors: Th\'eophane Vallaeys, Jakob Verbeek, Matthieu Cord
bullets: Addresses the drawbacks of autoencoder-based latent video generation, including two-stage training and information loss.
Introduces a UNet-like transformer architecture with improved training and sampling for high-dimensional pixel-space video.
Trained pixel-space and latent models from scratch on Kinetics-600 for controlled comparison.
At 128 resolution, improves frames-to-video FVD by 27% over prior state of the art and 14% over the JiT pixel-space baseline.
At 256 resolution and for class-to-video generation, gains over latent and pixel-space models increase with spatiotemporal compression.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have achieved strong performance on many video understanding tasks, yet remain vulnerable to temporal hallucination in time-sensitive reasoning scenarios such as scene transition understanding and event ordering. Existing solutions either require costly retraining or introduce inefficient multi-pass inference and external supervision at test time. In this work, we show that temporal evidence is already encoded in Video-LLM hidden representations but is not fully exploited during standard inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose Single-Pass Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD), a training-free framework that recovers suppressed temporal evidence through analytical hidden-state manipulation in a single forward pass. SPOD consists of two components: Frame Distinctiveness Analysis (FDA), which identifies salient frames from middle-layer hidden-state geometry, and Temporal Delta Subspace (TDS), which constructs orthogonal temporal and prior subspaces from weighted inter-frame hidden-state differences. By decomposing final hidden states into temporal, prior, and residual components and rescaling them independently, SPOD enhances dynamic information, suppresses static appearance bias, and preserves complementary information. Experiments on VidHalluc, EventHallusion, and VideoMMMU show that SPOD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines across temporal reasoning tasks and model architectures while retaining near-vanilla inference efficiency. These results suggest that improving temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs may depend not only on additional supervision, but also on recovering temporal evidence already present in their internal representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/VioAgnes/SPOD.
authors: Yangguang Lin, Quan Fang, Xiaoyan Liu, Zefan Xu

papers.abstract: Video character replacement aims to replace actors while preserving facial expressions, motions, and scene dynamics. Existing methods typically rely on masked generation with pose guidance, limiting fine-grained expression and motion preservation in complex scenes. We propose ReXMo, an end-to-end framework that supports single-, multi-, and selective character replacement scenarios. ReXMo introduces paired triplet supervision, where synthesized driving videos and original videos share identical performances but different identities, enabling scalable training through synthetic data generation. An In-Context Diffusion Transformer learns identity transformation by jointly conditioning on driving videos, reference identities, and text prompts, while an Expression Enhancement Adapter improves facial expression preservation in multi-person scenes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReXMo outperforms existing methods in identity fidelity, motion consistency, expression preservation, and visual quality. Our dataset and code will be publicly released.
bullets: Addresses limitations of masked generation and pose guidance in preserving fine-grained expressions and motion in complex scenes.

Employs an In-Context Diffusion Transformer conditioned on driving videos, reference identities, and text prompts for identity transformation.
Adds an Expression Enhancement Adapter to improve facial expression preservation in multi-person scenes.
Experiments report improved identity fidelity, motion consistency, expression preservation, and visual quality over existing methods; code and data are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Most video anomaly understanding (VAU) systems still infer anomaly judgments from evidence collected in a feed-forward way under predefined rules, typically sampled frames, or events clustered from such frames. This protocol fails when the collected evidence is incomplete under imperfect predefined rules, because once reasoning begins the model can no longer search for the missing evidence. We address this limitation with SEEK-VAU, which reframes VAU as an agentic search-and-verify interaction protocol under a bounded search budget: instead of passively reasoning over pre-collected evidence, the policy actively gathers evidence across the three stages of an anomaly event chain (precursor, trigger, and aftermath) and verifies its sufficiency before finalization, turning event-chain completeness into an explicit design rather than an outcome of predefined rules. A bounded budget caps the cost of this search, but does not by itself teach the policy where to look or when to stop. To make this behavior learnable, we introduce evidence-faithful counterfactual verification (EFCV), which rewards selected evidence that remains supportive, compact, and necessary under counterfactual verification. We further introduce SEEK-Bench, featuring video-level episodes with temporal interval annotations, semantic QA and event-chain stage labels. Together, SEEK-VAU and SEEK-Bench establish a strong foundation for evidence-faithful and actively verifiable VAU.
authors: Minghe Wang, Weijun Zeng, Dapeng Luo, Xinyue Wang, Nong Sang
bullets: Addresses incomplete evidence caused by feed-forward systems that rely on predefined frame or event sampling.
Uses an agentic search-and-verify protocol covering precursor, trigger, and aftermath stages.

papers.abstract: Audio-based piano transcription is hampered by the sustain pedal and by noisy or missing soundtracks, problems that video-only transcription avoids, since a top-view video shows directly when each key is pressed and released. Most visual transcription networks, however, describe the whole keyboard with one global feature vector and must learn where each key is. In this paper, we propose KeyWise, a lightweight per-key architecture that exploits the known geometry of the keyboard instead of learning it. The rectified keyboard is divided into 88 equal tiles that serve as regions of interest (ROIs), and one small recurrent network, shared by all keys, follows each key over time. On PianoVAM, KeyWise reaches the onset accuracy of the state-of-the-art V2N (95.0% vs. 94.7% onset F1 at 50 ms and 97.8% vs. 97.0% at 100 ms) with 1.3 M instead of 28.2 M parameters, and it runs 4.7 times faster on the same GPU. At 100 ms, it is also significantly more accurate when the key releases (97.0% vs. 95.5% F1) or the velocities (89.4% vs. 84.5% F1) must be correct as well. On PianoYT, KeyWise pre-trained on PianoVAM reaches 69.4% onset F1 at 100 ms, comparable to the best published result, although it needs fine-tuning for new recording conditions.
authors: Anastasios Chatzigiannis, Natalia Panagou, Maria Koziri
bullets: Avoids audio issues such as sustain-pedal ambiguity and missing or noisy soundtracks by using top-view video.
Divides a rectified keyboard into 88 fixed regions of interest, replacing learned keyboard localization with known geometry.
Matches V2N onset accuracy on PianoVAM with 1.3M parameters instead of 28.2M and runs 4.7× faster on the same GPU.
Also improves release and velocity accuracy at a 100 ms tolerance.
Transfers to PianoYT with comparable published onset accuracy, but requires fine-tuning for new recording conditions.

papers.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) aims to infer and segment target objects specified by reasoning queries in videos. Existing methods typically first infer the target and generate a few segmentation tokens for it, which are then fed into a mask decoder for mask prediction. However, such segmentation tokens tend to be both semantically monotonous and spatially ambiguous, making them largely insufficient to represent the target to guide mask prediction. In this paper, we propose an explicit visual object grounding framework for VRS. Specifically, we first propose a spatial-aware prompt generation and refinement scheme, in which we query a multimodal large language model to generate explicit spatial prompts (i.e., bounding box and point set) for the target and then refine them through multi-step dialogue. Furthermore, we introduce a query diversification and alignment module to generate auxiliary queries that describe the same target from different perspectives. We then enforce cross-query consistency between their predicted spatial prompts to alleviate the training bias caused by query limitations. Finally, we select several reliable frames using a prompt-based keyframe selection strategy to support mask decoding and propagation. Extensive experiments on eight datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/viscom-tongji/EVOG.
authors: Jun Huang, Junyang Zhang, Zijie Yue, Bingkun Wang, Yong Luo, Miaojing Shi
bullets: Addresses the semantic and spatial ambiguity of conventional segmentation tokens in VRS.

Selects prompt-based reliable keyframes to support mask decoding and propagation.
Reports significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across eight datasets.

papers.abstract: Moving Object Segmentation (MOS) detects and separates dynamic objects from the static background in a video, which plays a fundamental role in dynamic-scene understanding. Most MOS methods rely on pure visual motion cues alone, such as optical flow or point tracks, which is inherently ambiguous due to the compounded camera and object motions as well as motion-induced appearance changes, e.g. shadows and reflections. Naive fusion of additional information such as depth and semantics, however, cannot leverage their complementarity to the fullest extent. We therefore propose DynOSeg, a novel MOS approach that takes on a two-stage fusion structure. DynOSeg first combines a geometry-aware residual map and depth encoding into a geometric representation of motion, delineating camera motions and object dynamics. We then further incorporate semantic features to refine object understanding. We have additionally curated a diverse training corpus including CARLA-MOS, a new synthetic urban-driving dataset for MOS training. Our experiments show that DynOSeg consistently outperforms published state-of-the-art MOS methods across a diverse range of datasets. Our code and pretrained models can be found at https://github.com/ACFR-RPG/DynOSeg
authors: Xu Han, Yiduo Wang, Yiran Wang, Viorela Ila
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in visual-motion-only MOS caused by camera motion, object motion, shadows, and reflections.
Uses two-stage fusion: geometry-aware residuals with depth first, followed by semantic features for object refinement.
Introduces CARLA-MOS, a diverse synthetic urban-driving training corpus.
Reports consistent gains over published state-of-the-art MOS methods across diverse datasets.
Code and pretrained models are publicly available.

papers.abstract: The advancement of multimodal learning is heavily constrained by the scarcity and high annotation cost of high-quality instruction data. While raw videos offer an abundant and dynamic source of visual knowledge, transforming them into precise instruction data remains highly challenging. To bridge this gap, we present VidUEU-Agent, an automated pipeline that synthesizes instruction data from raw videos for multimodal understanding, editing, and unified tasks. VidUEU-Agent follows a four-stage pipeline: it performs global perception to filter low-quality shots, mines keyframes and multimodal signals, constructs metadata and routes the metadata to synthesize instruction samples. More importantly, our agent framework can autonomously iterate the data distribution based on downstream training results, thereby optimizing data quality, balance, and training effectiveness. Scaling this pipeline, we construct VidUEU-100K, a large-scale dataset of 100K training samples spanning multiple domains and tasks, providing a robust foundation for developing comprehensive multimodal capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning baseline models on VidUEU-100K yields significant and consistent performance gains across diverse representative benchmarks, validating the effectiveness of our proposed agent framework and dataset.

papers.abstract: Counterfactual sketch animation explores how a static sketch evolves under a hypothetical intervention. We present CounterSketch, a physics-grounded framework that transforms natural-language ``What if...?'' queries into physically plausible sketch animations. The framework integrates VLM-guided scene grounding, causal event-chain reasoning, constraint-based trajectory generation, and verification. It models physical transitions to update the scene graph, computes continuous object trajectories, and validates them against physical, geometric, and semantic constraints. The verified trajectories are then projected into object-level motion bounding boxes to guide downstream sketch-video synthesis. Experiments on CounterSketchBench (80 questions) demonstrate that physics-grounded trajectories provide stronger motion guidance than direct VLM predictions.

papers.abstract: Continuous video scales in cost with camera count, resolution and recording duration, yet many monitoring tasks seek events rather than complete images and can operate on a compact single-pixel measurement stream. Recovering a chosen interval as video is then desirable, but at 0.24\% of the pixel count the scene correlation image looks like noise and per-clip optimization takes minutes. Correlating the residual of an estimate with the coding patterns nevertheless gives a residual image, the gradient of a centered measurement loss. Lifted through a pretrained video decoder, its agreement with the true error exceeds that of control decoders. Video-latent inversion (VLI) then outperforms frame-wise image-latent reconstruction at 1{,}000 bucket values. Measurement-Gradient-Conditioned Video Flow (MGV-Flow), trained once to read the lifted residual image with preceding frames, reconstructs five frames in 1.55\,s at 22.9\,dB median PSNR, against 398\,s and 18.1\,dB for VLI, with the largest gains in high-motion scenes. Directional fidelity ranks 30 coding configurations and selects one needing a third fewer bucket values. On a physical system, MGV-Flow outperforms per-frame reconstruction without retraining. A sliding window over the bucket-value stream yields 3.2 frames per second on one RTX~4090 and, in theory, 20 frames per second on a data-centre accelerator. Demonstrations are available at https://cavedweller509.github.io/MGV-Flow.
authors: Hongjun An, Shuaizhe An, Tong Tian, Zhe Sun
bullets: Single-pixel monitoring can detect events without recording full video, but reconstructing chosen intervals is difficult because measurements are only 0.24% of the pixel count and residual images resemble noise.

The method correlates measurement residuals with coding patterns, lifts the resulting gradient-like image through a pretrained video decoder, and conditions a video flow model on it and preceding frames.
MGV-Flow reconstructs five frames in 1.55 s at 22.9 dB median PSNR, compared with 398 s and 18.1 dB for video-latent inversion at 1,000 bucket values.
It performs especially well in high-motion scenes, ranks coding configurations to reduce required bucket values by one third, and works on a physical system without retraining.
A sliding-window implementation reaches 3.2 frames per second on one RTX 4090; the approach targets selected intervals rather than continuous full-video recovery.

papers.abstract: Novels tell rich stories, but their textual form cannot directly present the sights and sounds of the worlds they describe. Film adaptations offer an audiovisual experience but require substantial production effort and viewing time; film recaps are shorter but depend on existing footage. Neither route directly provides a concise audiovisual account of a novel. We therefore study novel-to-recap video generation: producing a self-contained, source-grounded audiovisual retelling directly from a novel within a fixed viewing-time budget. This task requires compressing the story while preserving causal connections, allocating sufficient time to retained events, and aligning narration with newly generated visuals. We propose ReVi, a dual-loop multi-agent framework guided by edit first, generate second. Its Inner Loop plans story content, narration time, and corresponding shots before video generation. Across novels, its Outer Loop performs recursive self-improvement by revising both the editing policy and the meta policy that governs its revision. Experiments on two evaluation sets show that ReVi improves recap quality and duration compliance over representative baselines, with human ratings and multi-round improvement results providing further support.
authors: Kyrie You Wu, Chaozhuo Li, Songyang Liu, Xueyang Feng, Ziluowen Luo, Chenxu Wang, Ji Qi, Jinfu Zhu, Litian Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of self-contained audiovisual summaries of novels without relying on existing film footage.
Uses a dual-loop multi-agent framework: an inner loop plans story events, narration timing, and shots before generation.
An outer loop recursively improves both the editing strategy and the policy governing that improvement.
Experiments on two evaluation sets show better recap quality and duration compliance than representative baselines.
Human evaluations and multi-round improvements further support the approach.

papers.abstract: Multi-instance partial-label learning (MIPL) addresses inexact supervision in both the instance and label spaces, which can be applied to video classification. However, bag-level labels do not explicitly supervise the correspondence between candidate classes and temporal evidence. We propose {\ours}, which couples label disambiguation with temporal evidence allocation through a joint class--time assignment. Occupancy-regularized spherical matching associates contextualized video features while learning nonuniform temporal mass and discouraging excessive concentration. During training, candidate-restricted inference recomputes the assignment within the candidate label set. A dual-marginal KL projection then constructs a structured teacher that incorporates momentum-refined class beliefs while preserving the proposal's temporal occupancy. A single plan-level KL objective aligns the full-space predictor with this teacher. Our analysis characterizes when candidate re-solving differs from masking and shows that, under the stated construction, the joint objective decomposes into class-marginal and class-conditional temporal supervision. We construct VCMIPL benchmarks from Breakfast, DoTA, and FineAction using model-generated candidate labels and evaluate the method across four feature representations. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that PIVOTMIPL outperforms existing MIPL algorithms in both effectiveness and efficiency.
bullets: Addresses weak supervision where videos have candidate labels but unclear class-to-time correspondence.
Uses occupancy-regularized spherical matching to assign contextualized video features to classes and learn nonuniform temporal importance.
Re-solves assignments within candidate labels and applies dual-marginal KL projection to create structured teaching targets.
Optimizes a plan-level KL objective that decomposes into class-level and class-conditional temporal supervision.
On VCMIPL benchmarks from Breakfast, DoTA, and FineAction across four feature types, it outperforms existing MIPL methods in effectiveness and efficiency.

papers.abstract: Physical parameter estimation from video aims to recover the parameters of a known family of governing dynamical equations from pixel observations. Existing identifiability theory for this setting has focused on linear time-invariant (LTI) second-order systems, leaving open what can be identified for nonlinear scalar dynamics. We develop an identifiability theory for nonlinear scalar second-order ODEs, organized by how their velocity dependence interacts with changes of the learned state coordinate. Under a shared non-collapsed state map and explicit same-state velocity-coverage conditions, we show that parameter identifiability depends on the ODE family: some parameters are uniquely identifiable, while in other families only invariant parameter combinations are identifiable or external physical calibration is required. For laws that are at most linear in velocity, compatibility forces affine coordinate alignment, yielding explicit parameter relations, invariants, and calibration conditions. This affine conclusion extends to broader finite velocity-feature families when coordinate curvature can be separated from the declared velocity dependence. For families admitting a squared-velocity term, nonlinear coordinate ambiguity can remain; a law-derived normalization instead enables affine comparison between canonical laws. Experiments on synthetic systems and real pendulum and free-fall videos support the predicted parameter relations, coverage effects, and calibration requirements.
bullets: Addresses the gap between existing LTI theory and nonlinear scalar dynamics observed through pixels.
Identifiability depends on velocity dependence, state-coordinate transformations, and sufficient same-state velocity coverage.
For laws at most linear in velocity, compatible coordinate maps are affine, giving explicit parameter relations, invariants, and calibration conditions.
Squared-velocity laws can retain nonlinear coordinate ambiguity; a law-derived normalization enables affine comparison.
Synthetic, pendulum, and free-fall experiments support the predicted identifiability and calibration behavior.

papers.abstract: Diffusion distillation is widely adopted to accelerate sampling, and the resulting few-step models are broadly believed to match or even surpass their multi-step teachers in generation. However, standard evaluations such as GenEval2 typically draw only one sample per prompt, so improved scores may fail to reveal losses in distribution coverage. We therefore revisit whether distilled models truly match their teachers beyond single-draw performance using \textbf{pass@$\mathbf{k}$}, which measures the probability that at least one of $k$ independent samples satisfies a quality criterion. At $k{=}1$, pass@$k$ reduces to standard single-draw evaluation. As $k$ grows, the curve reveals whether additional draws find genuinely different successes or merely revisit the same modes, directly exposing how broadly a model covers the space of valid outputs. We first show that classifier-free guidance (CFG), whose quality--coverage tradeoff is well established, is the clearest case: higher guidance improves pass@$1$, but its advantage shrinks and reverses at larger $k$. Applying pass@$k$ to few-step distilled models, we find the same tradeoff splits along training objectives: distribution-matching objectives concentrate the student's output distribution, boosting early-hit rates while eroding large-budget coverage, whereas consistency and trajectory-based objectives better preserve the teacher's coverage even at large $k$. We further show that this tradeoff extends to few-step causal video generation. Our findings reveal a previously overlooked cost of diffusion distillation: across both image and video generation, the choice of training objective fundamentally determines whether a few-step model inherits its teacher's distribution coverage or trades it away for single-draw quality.
bullets: Single-draw metrics may hide distribution-coverage losses because they use only one sample per prompt.
Pass@$k$ measures whether any of $k$ samples meets a quality criterion, exposing how coverage changes with more sampling attempts.
Higher classifier-free guidance improves pass@1 but can reduce performance at larger $k$, indicating narrower coverage.
Distribution-matching distillation favors early successes but concentrates outputs, while consistency and trajectory-based objectives better preserve teacher coverage.
The same quality–coverage tradeoff appears in few-step image and causal video generation.

papers.abstract: Learning from human data offers a scalable path toward embodied intelligence, yet it requires models to accurately understand fine-grained human actions from egocentric observations. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association. We introduce EgoActionBench, a benchmark that represents continuous human manipulation as temporally localized atomic actions associated with the left hand, right hand, or both hands. EgoActionBench contains 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined action annotations. To evaluate such dense predictions, we propose an evaluation protocol that retrieves temporally eligible candidates, selects a prediction by content agreement, and scores semantic fidelity and temporal overlap alongside action precision and recall, jointly capturing what happens, when it happens, and which hand performs it. We benchmark 20 baseline models and systems on EgoActionBench and further adapt two backbones, Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B, through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on automatically annotated training episodes. EgoAction improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two backbones, and both adapted models outperform all open-source baselines. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations of current models in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association, highlighting the gap between general video understanding and the action understanding required for embodied intelligence.
bullets: Introduces 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined annotations of temporally localized atomic actions linked to the left hand, right hand, or both.
Proposes an evaluation protocol measuring semantic fidelity, temporal overlap, action precision, and recall.
Benchmarks 20 models and systems, including adapted Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B backbones.
Supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two adapted backbones.
Finds persistent limitations in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association.

papers.abstract: High frame rate HDR video is important in applications such as autonomous driving and scientific imaging, where rapid motion and extreme illumination often occur simultaneously. Conventional frame cameras face a trade-off between temporal resolution and dynamic range, while event cameras provide complementary high-speed brightness-change measurements over a wide illumination range. These properties have motivated event-based HDR reconstruction, with existing methods broadly following event-only and hybrid event-frame paradigms. Event-only HDR reconstruction, however, suffers from brightness and color drift due to the lack of absolute intensity references. Hybrid event-frame methods alleviate this ambiguity using low-dynamic-range (LDR) frames as anchors, but most perform one-to-one HDR reconstruction at available LDR timestamps. In this work, we investigate single-reference HDR temporal expansion, reconstructing N HDR frames from one LDR reference and events instead of N aligned LDR observations. We develop HIVE-Diff, an event-conditioned video diffusion framework that decomposes the task into event-guided temporal generation and HDR content completion. Because paired real HDR-event data are scarce, we train on synthetic data and adapt the model to real event domains using LDR-event sequences as proxy supervision with teacher-student distillation. Experiments on synthetic and multiple real-world datasets demonstrate strong reconstruction quality and robust real-data adaptation.
bullets: Addresses the need for simultaneous high temporal resolution and wide dynamic range in fast, high-contrast scenes.
Generates N HDR frames from one LDR reference and events, avoiding the need for aligned LDR frames at every timestamp.
Uses event-guided temporal generation followed by HDR content completion in a video diffusion framework.
Trains on synthetic data and adapts to real event domains through teacher-student distillation with LDR-event proxy supervision.
Reports strong reconstruction quality and robust real-data adaptation across synthetic and multiple real-world datasets.

papers.abstract: Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce \emph{replacement-aware cross-audio supervision}: paired-audio samples use full-frame reconstruction, whereas unpaired replacement-audio samples mask out source-mouth reconstruction losses and supervise the mouth solely through audio--visual synchronization while preserving unmasked facial regions and background. Because offline dubbing provides the complete source video and target speech beforehand, we present \method, a full-context diffusion editor that uses matched trajectory regression to transfer CFG-guided teacher trajectories to a two-step student and distribution matching to recover visual quality after compression. We will release the curated training dataset, VidDub-Bench, fixed paired- and cross-audio evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833. At two NFE, the final student provides the strongest cross-audio synchronization and visual-speech recognition among the evaluated methods, with competitive visual fidelity and source preservation.
bullets: Existing self-reconstruction training conflicts with replaced target speech because the source mouth is an incorrect target.
Replacement-aware cross-audio supervision masks source-mouth losses for unpaired replacement audio while preserving other facial regions and the background.
A full-context diffusion editor uses matched trajectory regression and distribution matching to produce a two-step student.

Masking improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833 across three training seeds; the two-step student achieves the strongest reported cross-audio synchronization and visual-speech recognition, with competitive fidelity and source preservation.
The authors will release VidDub-Bench, evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code.

papers.abstract: Streaming digital humans produce detailed video while continuing speech as new text arrives. High-resolution denoising is costly, and text updates can cause repeated or interrupted speech. We present TaoMate-HD, an autoregressive model for high-resolution audio-video streaming. For each short segment, or chunk, two denoising steps establish coarse video structure at low resolution. A final step refines the video to high resolution, with audio generated throughout the same trajectory. Each stage passes its audiovisual predictions to the same stage of the next chunk as history. Across text updates, the model retains this history to infer what has already been spoken. Continuation training utilizes asymmetric text conditioning, with separate text windows for generation and distillation. Experiments show a 1.6x speedup over direct high-resolution generation with the same model and hardware. Optimized stage-parallel deployment provides a further 1.9x overall speedup over serial progressive generation. Our continuation training reduces character error rate by 11.18 percentage points relative to the baseline. The model also supports hour-long audiovisual generation. Our project page is https://taoliveaigc.github.io/TaoMate-HD.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of high-resolution denoising and speech interruptions caused by incremental text updates.
Uses low-resolution coarse denoising followed by high-resolution refinement, while generating audio along the same trajectory.
Passes stage-wise audiovisual predictions between chunks and retains history to continue previously spoken content.
Achieves 1.6× speedup over direct high-resolution generation, with stage-parallel deployment adding a further 1.9× speedup.

papers.abstract: Low-quality facial videos suffer from missing fine details, while AI-generated videos may additionally contain implausible teeth and lip movements that do not match the speech. Restoring the mouth region is particularly challenging: enhancing existing details can preserve structural errors, whereas regenerating them risks changing facial identity and articulation. We propose an audio-guided facial video restoration framework that reconstructs unreliable mouth details and aligns lip movements with the speech while preserving facial identity and temporal consistency. Built on a video diffusion transformer, our framework mixes input video latents with noise to retain useful source information while allowing corrupted details to be regenerated. Audio guides lip movements, reference images constrain facial appearance, and previously generated frames promote temporal consistency. We train the model in two stages, first learning visual restoration from degraded images and videos, then learning audio-guided lip correction from degraded dubbed videos. The resulting model supports both restoration with the original audio and visual dubbing with replacement audio. On talking-head restoration benchmarks, our method achieves the lowest LPIPS and DISTS and the best lip synchronization scores among the evaluated restoration baselines. Qualitative results on AI-generated videos further show improvements in facial detail and mouth-region appearance, including clearer tooth boundaries and lip contours.
bullets: Addresses low-quality or AI-generated talking-head videos with missing facial detail and speech-inconsistent teeth or lip movements.
Uses a video diffusion transformer that mixes video latents with noise, combining source information with controlled detail regeneration.
Audio guides lip motion; reference images preserve facial appearance; prior frames support temporal consistency.
Trains in two stages for visual restoration and audio-guided lip correction, supporting original-audio restoration and visual dubbing.
Achieves the best reported LPIPS, DISTS, and lip-synchronization scores among evaluated restoration baselines, with qualitative gains in tooth boundaries and lip contours.

papers.abstract: Multimodal retrieval must integrate complementary evidence from views that may be missing, noisy, or unequally informative. When a sample provides limited reliable evidence, learning from its views alone can hinder the acquisition of useful retrieval representations. Semantically related training samples may provide complementary observations, yet existing volume-based objectives jointly align modalities within each sample without explicitly enabling information exchange across samples. We therefore propose a training-time hypergraph fusion framework that connects observed modalities both within samples and across semantically related samples, allowing representation learning to draw on evidence beyond an individual sample while leaving the retrieval pipeline unchanged at inference. The framework includes HyVol as a special case and introduces two configurations: wHyVol learns view contribution weights and symmetric semantic affinities, whereas wRHG additionally models typed interactions and participant roles through relational propagation. Missing modalities are omitted rather than imputed, and the hypergraph is discarded after training, incurring no additional inference cost. Experiments on eleven zero-shot video-text and audio-text retrieval benchmarks demonstrate broad improvements with both GRAM and HyperGRAM. Across 17 video benchmark-modality settings evaluated in both retrieval directions, wRHG outperforms GRAM in all 34 comparisons and HyperGRAM in 33 of 34. Mean text-to-video R@1 increases from 63.4 to 68.2 with GRAM and from 64.8 to 68.4 with HyperGRAM, while the largest video-to-text gain reaches 13.3 percentage points on ActivityNet. Under missing-modality evaluation, both weighted configurations retain positive text-to-video gains over GRAM across seven benchmarks at every evaluated missingness rate, even when 90% of clips lack one modality.
bullets: Addresses noisy, missing, or unevenly informative modalities and the limits of per-sample alignment.
Connects modalities within samples and across semantically related samples through hypergraph regularization.
wHyVol learns view weights and semantic affinities; wRHG further models typed interactions and participant roles.
Improves retrieval broadly across 11 zero-shot video-text and audio-text benchmarks, with no added inference cost.
Maintains positive gains under missing-modality conditions, including when 90% of clips lack one modality.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. (a) Existing methods score each clip alone: a clip’s score depends only on the caption and the clip’s own views, and every other clip in the batch, even a related one, is pushed apart as a negative. (b) Our training-time hypergraph: observed views form vertices, document hyperedges group the views of each clip, and caption-guided semantic hyperedges connect related clips through same-modality and cross-modality links; missing views have no vertex and are not imputed, and each vertex receives a learned reliability weight. (c) At test time the hypergraph is removed: each clip is encoded and scored independently with the original backbone score, so the inference cost equals that of the backbone.

Figure 2: Overview of training-time hypergraph refinement. Each observed modality becomes a weighted vertex, and stop-gradient captions connect semantically related candidates through mutual top-k neighbors. Information is then exchanged either by weighted additive propagation (WHYVOL) or by typed relational messages (WRHG), and the refined embeddings are scored by the unchanged GRAM/HYPERGRAM objective. The hypergraph is used only during training and is removed at inference.

Figure 4: Zero-shot text-to-video retrieval under missing modalities with the GRAM backbone on seven video benchmarks. Each panel shows the R@1 gain of +HYVOL, +WHYVOL and +WRHG over GRAM (dashed line at zero) as a fraction r of the gallery clips that lose one randomly chosen modality; the per-clip masks are fixed and identical for all methods, and r=0 is the standard setting. papers.title: Fuse To Align: Multimodal Representation Learning for Retrieval via Hypergraph Regularization

papers.abstract: Fingerspelling - the sequential signing of letters that compose proper names, technical terms, and out-of-vocabulary words - is an integral component of any sign language. Despite Russian Sign Language (RSL) being used by more than 150,000 native signers, no public fingerspelling dataset for RSL exists, in contrast to American, British, German, and several other sign languages. We introduce Znaki the first open RSL fingerspelling dataset: 37,252 video recordings (35.4 hours) of 1,593 unique sequences - proper names sampled from 16 domain categories - recorded by 68 native RSL signers (37 Deaf, 29 hard-of-hearing, and 2 certified interpreters) through a crowdsourcing pipeline with a two-stage signer qualification procedure and expert validation. The dataset covers all 33 Cyrillic handshapes, and its letter-frequency distribution matches the Russian National Corpus. As reference points for future research, we establish two baselines adapted from American Sign Language fingerspelling recognition: a Squeezeformer-based encoder-decoder, reaching a character-level accuracy ($1-\mathrm{CER}$) of 0.932 and a sequence accuracy of 0.596, and Fingerspelling-PoseNet, reaching 0.886 and 0.545, respectively.
bullets: Addresses the lack of public RSL fingerspelling data despite widespread use of RSL.
Contains 37,252 recordings totaling 35.4 hours, covering 1,593 sequences across 16 proper-name domains.
Includes contributions from 68 native RSL signers and all 33 Cyrillic handshapes.
Uses crowdsourced collection with two-stage signer qualification and expert validation.
Provides two baselines: Squeezeformer achieves 0.932 character-level accuracy and 0.596 sequence accuracy; Fingerspelling-PoseNet achieves 0.886 and 0.545.

papers.abstract: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of dense scaling for complex, multi-request video editing.
Introduces MoE-Attention, which routes key–value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens.
Scales from a 5B initialization to 14B and 56B parameters, activating approximately 8B parameters per token in both variants.
Analysis finds routing responds more to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories, with sensitivity to object-level semantics.
Identifies decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling; evaluations compare against existing methods and complementary MoE baselines.

(b) Mean video-level Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence across controlled and cross-sample comparisons. Larger values indicate stronger global expert reallocation.

Figure 4 Object-semantic expert routing. Top: source frames (red contour marks the tracked person mask). Bottom: gate weights of a representative MLP expert (Layer 14, σ = 0.355), which track the moving subject and recede at its initial location (dashed).

papers.abstract: Pose-driven human video diffusion animates a person from a single reference image and a target pose sequence, yet it struggles to preserve identity, rendering the face and garments unfaithfully as the pose departs from it. Personalization is the standard remedy, but its supervision is missing: one image fixes identity at a single pose, while a multi-pose subject video cannot be assumed in practice. Instead, we synthesize the missing supervision. A domain-tuned, pose-conditioned generator produces pseudo-ground-truth frames at selected key poses. An inference-time reference-only sampler steers these candidates toward the subject and keeps the most identity-consistent. A per-subject low-rank adapter then trains on static clips of them, configured from the reference alone, with no subject video, ground truth, or labels. Although lower in fidelity, these synthetic frames supervise more effectively than real ones. Real frames as captured carry motion that erodes the temporal prior, while a static clip conveys appearance alone. On TikTok and UBC Fashion, the adapted model improves the base on every metric, inverts the identity-versus-motion trade-off, and matches or surpasses adaptation on five real frames despite using none. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/SadmanPinon/one-image-is-enough.
bullets: Addresses identity drift in faces and garments when the target pose differs substantially from a single reference image.
Generates pseudo-ground-truth frames at key poses, filters them with a reference-only sampler, and trains a per-subject low-rank adapter on static clips.
Requires only one reference image—no subject video, ground-truth frames, or labels.
On TikTok and UBC Fashion, improves the base model on every reported metric and matches or surpasses adaptation using five real frames.
Synthetic static clips can supervise more effectively than real motion videos because they preserve appearance without disrupting temporal priors.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method overview. From one reference image xref and a driving pose sequence P , a pose-conditioned generator G synthesizes pose-targeted pseudo-ground-truth frames Dpseudo of the subject. (a) Reward-guided generation: for each key pose, G draws several candidates as an interacting particle system and resamples them in-loop toward a DINO body-similarity reward to xref , then selects the final frame by ArcFace face identity. Every reward is read from the reference alone (our reference-only reward-guided sampler). (b) Test-time personalization: a per-subject LoRA ∆θ adapts the frozen base animator Fθ on static clips of the selected frames. The adapted model Fθ+∆θ renders the personalized video V̂ . No subject video, no ground truth, and no human feedback are used.

Figure 3. Temporal stability. Top: the driving frames. For Base (middle) and Ours (bottom), the leftmost column is that method’s output frame and the remaining columns are consecutive framedifference maps over the same frames. The non-personalized base produces widespread inter-frame residual across the face and torso (temporal flicker), whereas our adapted model confines residual to true motion boundaries and stays stable, reducing mean interframe residual by 60% over the frames shown. Brighter indicates larger frame-to-frame change.

Figure 7. Human preference study. Distribution of 1–5 ratings for ours, Animate-X, the unadapted base, and Moore-AnimateAnyone, on four axes. Thirty-four respondents, 180 ratings per bar group. Ours places 93% of appearance-alignment ratings at 4–5, against 38% for the base model; the ordering is the same on all four axes. Protocol in Appendix B.2.

Figure 8. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Motions and Backgrounds. Examples illustrating variations in background, motion complexity, and clothing style. Our approach consistently preserves holistic appearance and pose alignment while producing sharper, more realistic details than competing methods.

Figure 9. In-Domain Comparisons: Diverse Appearance and Illumination. Examples covering variations in skin tone, lighting conditions, and clothing texture. Our approach maintains consistent subject appearance and realistic fine-grained details across all scenarios, clearly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Figure 6. Pose-conditioned generator G. G is built on FLUX.1 Kontext [21] paired with a pose ControlNet [57]. The target pose is VAE-encoded and read by a frozen ControlNet (14 joint blocks, 38 unified blocks), whose pose-aware features condition the main DiT. The reference image and initial noise are encoded and denoised by the main DiT, into which we inject the trainable LoRA [13]; a text encoder supplies the prompt. The output latent is VAE-decoded to the subject rendered under the target pose. Backbone weights are frozen (snowflake); only the LoRA adapters are trained (flame).

Figure 5. Pseudo-frame count and supervision source. (a) FVD (orange) is lowest at K=5; FaceID (teal) dips at K=9 and peaks at K=21 at a similar FVD (values from Tab. 6). (b) Seven-metric comparison of supervision sources (outward = better, per-axis min–max over the rows of Tab. 5): Ours forms nearly the outer envelope, while self-distillation collapses on body similarity and temporal consistency.

Figure 4. Qualitative comparison on hard poses. For two subjects we show the reference and driving pose alongside the base, our adapted model, and ground truth. Insets crop the face. The base reconstructs identity and garment detail inconsistently as the pose departs from the reference, while our adaptation preserves both.

Figure 10. Cross-Domain Comparisons: Animated Characters. Examples from the Unseen100-Val evaluation set featuring 2D and 3D animated characters unseen during training. Our approach generalizes beyond photorealistic subjects, faithfully preserving stylized appearance details and character proportions while maintaining temporal coherence under complex motion.

Figure 11. Adaptation is bounded by pseudo-frame quality. Top (HQ): high-quality pseudo frames (Supervision) yield faithful adapted outputs (Output frames). Bottom (LQ): degraded pseudo frames for the same subject yield weaker outputs. This is why the reference-only sampler selects high-quality frames before adaptation.

Table 12. Sensitivity to the generator’s domain tuning. G’s LoRA receives from no tuning (off-the-shelf FLUX.1 Kontext with the pose ControlNet) to our default of 4,000 steps, with the rest of the pipeline fixed. Teacher is the fidelity of the selected pseudo-frame to the real frame at that pose, and downstream is the adapted model’s video quality (trim, 3 TikTok sequences).

Table 2. Quantitative comparison on cross-domain performance on the Unseen100-Val set after training on TikTok. Off the training distribution, our adaptation reaches the only FVD below 100 (92.5) and the lowest dtSSD, while every other method stays above 125.

Table 4. Component ablation. Each designed component is removed and compared against real-frame supervision (Real-5) and the unadapted base. FaceID and BodySIM are over the full video. Generator G is a per-frame reference with no temporal model, so it lacks FVD/dtSSD and is not ranked.

Peak GPU is the maximum resident device memory during the stage, and Alloc. the torch allocator peak where the pipeline reports it (protocol in Appendix F.1).

Table 7. Reward-design ablation (on a tuning subset). The two reference-only rewards assigned to in-loop steering versus final selection. Steering with DINO and selecting with ArcFace is best.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models proposed in the literature outperform recurrent baselines, with the best-performing Transformer achieving BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, respectively, as well as ChrF = 18.09 and ROUGE-L = 10.51. These results indicate that the task remains promising and warrants further investigations.
bullets: Addresses the underrepresentation of South African Sign Language in sign-language processing resources.
Collects SASL videos from public sources such as news broadcasts with minimal human intervention.
Uses ASR transcripts, video cropping, and motion-based sentence-boundary detection to create weakly aligned sign–text pairs.
Benchmarks recurrent neural networks and Transformer models for sign-to-text translation.
Transformers outperform recurrent baselines, though the reported translation scores show the task remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Real-time omnimodal assistants are expected to support people in everyday life, but audiovisual understanding alone does not establish whether they can provide timely and appropriate help. We introduce Omni-Life, a benchmark grounded in real-world user needs, deployment scenarios, and device-dependent observations. It combines controlled video synthesis for hazardous situations and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol. The benchmark contains 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance, with 555 required intervention events, and 110 requiring silence throughout to test whether models can withhold unnecessary responses when no assistance is needed. We evaluate twelve configurations featuring mainstream real-time omnimodal models, jointly assessing event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output. At most 4.48% of videos requiring assistance are handled completely correctly. To examine practical deployment strategies, we study task reminders and response-latency tolerance. Reminders can improve recall by 17.12 percentage points but add approximately 4.6 unwanted responses per minute of reference silence. Increasing latency tolerance by 10s improves recall by at most 5.95 percentage points. These results show that existing models remain insufficient to deliver reliable assistance in real-life applications, calling for tailored model optimization in instruction following, timely proactive intervention, and withholding responses when assistance is not needed.
bullets: Evaluates assistance quality across event coverage, response content, timing, and unwanted output.
Combines controlled videos of hazards and edge cases with annotated real-world videos under a shared temporal protocol.
Includes 400 videos: 290 requiring assistance and 110 requiring silence, covering 555 intervention events.
Across 12 model configurations, at most 4.48% of assistance-needed videos are handled completely correctly.
Reminders improve recall but substantially increase unwanted responses; greater latency tolerance offers limited recall gains.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models (AR-VDMs) enable real-time, long-horizon video generation but degrade rapidly once the inference horizon outruns the training horizon, due to compounding exposure bias. To stabilize long rollouts, recent methods heuristically adopt frame sink, keeping initial frames as a persistent model context, inspired by attention sinks in LLMs. We revisit this design and find that the mechanism by which initial frames stabilize long-range consistency in AR-VDMs is not an LLM-style attention sink; instead, long-range consistency is anchored through a sparse subset of attention heads, while the majority of heads predominantly capture local temporal dynamics. This observation reveals an over-conditioning pathology in existing frame-sink strategies: by universally exposing every head to the pinned initial-frame context, the model becomes prone to collapsing motion toward the low-dynamic modes of the teacher during model distillation. We propose Disen-Forcing, a distillation-time plug-in for AR-VDMs that disentangles and reinforces this head specialization through disentangled context routing and motion-disentangling regularization. On long-horizon video generation benchmarks, Disen-Forcing simultaneously improves long-range consistency and motion dynamics of base AR-VDMs, a trade-off that sink-based methods fail to balance.
bullets: AR-VDMs suffer compounding exposure bias when generating beyond their training horizon.
Long-range consistency relies on a sparse subset of attention heads, not a universal LLM-style attention sink.
Conventional frame-sink strategies over-condition all heads and can collapse motion toward low-dynamic modes.
Disen-Forcing uses disentangled context routing and motion-disentangling regularization during distillation.
Experiments show improved long-range consistency and motion dynamics without the trade-off of sink-based methods.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) elevates joint audio-video generation, but optimizing heterogeneous, modality-specific audio and video rewards often introduces cross-modal interference. On-policy distillation (OPD) alleviates this issue by transferring the capabilities of specialized audio and video RL teachers into a single student model. However, a significant imbalance in cross-modal token counts leaves audio with sparse supervision, causing unstable distillation. We observe that naively increasing the audio loss weight fails to solve this problem since audio learning relies heavily on visual context, indicating richer visual cues are crucial to offset sparse audio signals. To address this, we propose OmniOPD, a modality-wise on-policy distillation framework designed for balanced and stable audio-video generation. First, we construct privileged visual information using asymmetric noise scheduling, allowing the audio teacher to generate more informative targets from cleaner video context. Second, we introduce grouped multi-noise sampling to expand audio supervision coverage and stabilize training. Third, we introduce timestep-wise importance weighting based on teacher-student transition divergence, preserving reliable supervision while down-weighting unreliable learning signals, to stabilize fluctuations in audio learning. Evaluated on JavisBench and VBench demonstrate OmniOPD preserves audio quality while significantly enhancing video generation, achieving effective joint distillation.
bullets: Joint audio-video RL can suffer from cross-modal interference when audio and video rewards are optimized together.
Audio receives sparse supervision because audio has fewer tokens, and simply increasing its loss weight is ineffective.
The method uses asymmetric noise scheduling to provide the audio teacher with cleaner, more informative visual context.
Grouped multi-noise sampling broadens audio supervision, while timestep-wise importance weighting down-weights unreliable signals.
On JavisBench and VBench, OmniOPD preserves audio quality while significantly improving video generation.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient generation, yet maintaining consistency over long rollouts remains challenging, especially when subjects or scenes reappear after going out of sight. Despite progress in fidelity and rollout robustness, existing distillation methods do not fully exploit richer historical information to constrain the student's current prediction. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{History Forcing}, a unified on-policy distillation framework that strengthens historical supervision for few-step autoregressive video generators. The framework uses the residual between teacher predictions with and without informative historical context to decouple this supervision. Such a historical context can be obtained using earlier generated chunks with less accumulated drift or a fixed-view teacher rollout that keeps the scene visible while the student looks away. The residual is then weighted and added to the score or velocity prediction used for distillation, forming a corrected target. By aligning the student with this corrected target through distillation, History Forcing incorporates long-range historical constraints into autoregressive generation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance among 1.3B models, with a VBench quality score of 85.07 for 15s video generation and a VBench-Long aggregate score of 79.82 for 60s generation. For out-of-sight world modeling, evaluations further demonstrate more plausible scene evolution and more consistent states when the camera returns, with Evolution Quality improving from 2.35 to 2.70 on PlayWorld and Object Consistency from 58.43 to 62.18 on MemoBench.
bullets: Addresses scene and subject inconsistency when content reappears after going out of view.
Uses teacher-prediction residuals between context-rich and context-poor rollouts as corrected distillation targets.
Historical context comes from earlier, less-drifted chunks or fixed-view teacher rollouts that preserve scene visibility.
Reports strong results for 15–60-second generation and improved out-of-sight scene evolution and object consistency. The abstract does not state limitations.

papers.abstract: Understanding how objects and their spatial relationships evolve in 3D space over time remains challenging for vision-language models (VLMs), particularly under changing viewpoints. Recent approaches incorporate geometric information into reasoning, but explicit supervision for temporally ordered 4D state evolution and its use as intermediate evidence remains limited. We introduce \textbf{Trace4D}, which trains VLMs to predict 4D state sequences and reason over their inter-timestep changes alongside temporal visual observations. Its 4D-grounded chain-of-thought (CoT) explicitly represents 4D states, analyzes temporal visual context, and connects both as evidence for the answer. We construct Trace4D-Train from in-the-wild videos with 600K 4D perception examples and approximately 70K grounded QA examples, and train with joint supervised fine-tuning followed by geometry-aware GRPO. At inference, Trace4D predicts 4D states and reasoning directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model. Experiments on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D show improved QA accuracy over the base VLMs and benefits from reasoning over 4D state changes and temporal visual observations.
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty in tracking object states and spatial relationships over time under changing viewpoints.
Predicts temporally ordered 4D states, analyzes their changes, and combines them with temporal visual observations in grounded chain-of-thought reasoning.
Trains on in-the-wild videos with 4D perception and grounded QA supervision, followed by geometry-aware GRPO.
Performs inference directly from video without reference annotations or an external geometric model.
Shows improved QA accuracy on Trace4D-Bench and VLM4D over the base VLMs.

papers.abstract: Hyperspectral videos provide rich spectral signatures for robust tracking under challenging conditions such as camouflage and low illumination. However, limited hyperspectral annotations and the large RGB-hyperspectral domain gap hinder the direct use of modern temporally pretrained RGB trackers. We propose SProTrack, a multimodal framework that transfers temporal knowledge from pretrained RGB trackers to the hyperspectral domain through latent spectral prompting. The key idea is to decouple temporal modeling from spectral adaptation, allowing temporal dynamics to be inherited from RGB foundation models while hyperspectral information is learned from unlabeled data in a self-supervised manner. Unlike band-selection methods that discard most spectral information or prompt-based approaches that rely on local-search crops, SProTrack learns a global, scene-level spectral representation from the full hyperspectral frame using an autoencoder. This latent representation is used to guide spectral prompt extraction while a pretrained RGB tracker preserves strong temporal modeling on RGB-compatible inputs. By encoding spectral-spatial structure into compact latent prompts, SProTrack bridges the RGB-hyperspectral modality gap without extensive retraining or dense supervision. Experiments on HOT2020 and HOT2023 demonstrate that SProTrack achieves the best overall performance, with strong results across all spectral domains.
bullets: Addresses limited hyperspectral annotations and the RGB–hyperspectral domain gap in object tracking.
Uses an autoencoder to learn global spectral-spatial representations from full hyperspectral frames.
Decouples temporal modeling from spectral adaptation, retaining RGB tracker dynamics while adapting spectral information.
Avoids discarding bands and reliance on local-search crops by generating compact latent prompts.
Reports the best overall performance on HOT2020 and HOT2023, with strong results across spectral domains.

(c) Spectral-Spatial block: a spectral branch models inter-band dependencies via Mamba and a spatial branch captures local patterns via convolution; their fused outputs, stacked across blocks, form the encoder, with a symmetric decoder for reconstruction. papers.abstract: Surgical video understanding is essential for intraoperative assistance such as workflow monitoring, instrument preparation and procedural documentation. Delivering such assistance in real time requires a model to jointly perceive the ongoing scene, remember past surgical events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass. Existing approaches provide limited support for jointly retaining procedural evidence and deciding when to respond in streaming surgical video. In this work, we propose SurgStream, a workflow-anchored proactive streaming framework for real-time surgical video understanding. We first introduce Workflow-Anchored Memory (WAM) to record structured instrument-action-target observations and fold them into phase-level summaries, providing compact and queryable surgical memory. Deadline-aware Transition Learning (DTL) is then devised to supervise response states within clinical windows, enabling timely responses before procedural deadlines. We further introduce SurgStream-Bench, comprising 11.7K streaming interactions across various tasks covering real-time perception, backward memory queries, forward proactive QA, proactive alerts and caption memory. Experiments on SurgStream-Bench show gains over state-of-the-art methods, especially in memory and forward proactive QA. The source code will be available.
bullets: Targets streaming assistance that must perceive scenes, remember prior events, and respond before clinically relevant moments pass.
Workflow-Anchored Memory records instrument–action–target observations and compresses them into phase-level summaries.
Deadline-aware Transition Learning supervises response timing within clinical windows.
Introduces SurgStream-Bench with 11.7K streaming interactions spanning perception, memory queries, proactive QA, alerts, and caption memory.
Experiments report gains over existing methods, particularly for memory and forward proactive QA.

papers.abstract: Stress is a leading contributor to long-term physical and mental health decline. The automatic assessment of stress is a promising approach for continuous monitoring and mitigating human biases. However, the development of automated systems remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of physiological and behavioral signals. This paper presents MUPA${}^2$S, a multimodal framework for automatic stress assessment that combines facial video and ECG signals within a unified perception architecture. Both modalities are mapped into a shared token representation without modality-specific components, and processed through asymmetric attention comprising segment-local cross-attention and global self-attention across segment states. Experiments on a newly collected 58-subject stress dataset, evaluated under a stratified subject-level protocol, show that facial video achieves 69.44% test accuracy, while ECG-only performance remains close to chance under the proposed representation. Unified Video-ECG fusion achieves a test accuracy of 69.58% at approximately half the number of parameters of feature-level fusion, with negligible additional computational cost. Feature-level fusion does not exceed the video-only baseline, while unified input-level integration provides a parameter-efficient mechanism for jointly processing the two modalities.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of heterogeneous physiological and behavioral signals in automated stress assessment.
Maps facial video and ECG into a shared token representation without modality-specific components.
Uses segment-local cross-attention and global self-attention across segment states.
On a 58-subject dataset, video-only accuracy is 69.44%, while ECG-only performance is near chance.
Unified video–ECG fusion reaches 69.58% accuracy with roughly half the parameters of feature-level fusion and negligible extra computation.

papers.abstract: Event-based optical flow estimation using spatiotemporal planar approximation inherently assumes constant velocity and tends to average out temporal velocity variations. In this paper, we propose a flow estimation method that extends this planar approximation along the temporal axis. The resulting event-based optical flow constraint allows existing variational optical flow formulations to model temporal motion variation. Specifically, we partition the space-time volume into sub-intervals and apply a two-step planar approximation to track object edges consistently. Moreover, a spatial compensation mechanism and a temporal regularization term are incorporated to compensate for edge displacements and temporally stabilize the flow estimation, respectively. The experimental results show that modeling temporal motion variation improves flow estimation accuracy over conventional methods.
bullets: Addresses the constant-velocity assumption in conventional spatiotemporal planar approximation.
Partitions the space-time volume into sub-intervals and applies two-step planar fitting to track object edges.
Adds spatial compensation for edge displacement and temporal regularization for stable flow estimates.
Integrates with existing variational optical-flow formulations.
Experiments show improved accuracy when temporal motion variation is modeled.
