papers.abstract: Embodied agents need physical intelligence to understand their surroundings through physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning. These capabilities must work together to interpret events and make quantitative judgments. Existing benchmarks advance physical understanding and general-purpose tool use, yet the coordination of these capabilities in physical scenarios remains insufficiently characterized. Inspired by Popper's Three Worlds, we introduce TriPhysBench, a benchmark of 410 questions from 200 videos that brings physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning into a shared evaluation setting. Its measurement-grounded and knowledge-grounded subtasks impose complementary demands on obtaining observations and acquiring external specifications, then applying them to quantitative problems. Among six representative vision-language models, the best achieves an answer accuracy of only 50.38%, revealing limited performance on tasks that require these capabilities to work together. We further introduce TriPhys, a framework that learns a unified policy for physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and quantitative reasoning from complete tool-integrated trajectories. The policy uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into subsequent physical inference. On 110 questions from videos excluded from training, TriPhys improves answer and solution scores across three Qwen configurations, with a 17.7% relative gain in answer accuracy for TriPhys-27B over its Qwen3.6-27B backbone. This work provides a benchmark and a learning pathway toward embodied agents that move beyond recognizing events to understanding and reasoning about the physical processes behind them.
bullets: Introduces 410 questions from 200 videos covering physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning.
Measurement- and knowledge-grounded subtasks test whether agents can obtain observations or specifications and apply them quantitatively.
The best of six evaluated vision-language models reaches only 50.38% answer accuracy, indicating substantial difficulty with coordinated physical reasoning.
TriPhys learns a unified policy that uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into later inference.
On 110 held-out questions, TriPhys improves answer and solution scores across three Qwen configurations; TriPhys-27B achieves a reported 17.7% relative answer-accuracy gain over its backbone.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about surgical video -- which phase is underway, which instruments act, and when events occur -- underpins operative documentation, workflow analysis, and skill assessment. Yet surgical visual question answering is still largely built on single frames and closed labels that cannot express a duration, an ordering, or a count, and the video models that lift the frame limit typically compress every clip the same way regardless of the question, discarding the temporal evidence the answer needs. Worse, the answers are structurally heterogeneous, spanning five incompatible structures -- binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal -- that no single training signal scores uniformly well. We propose SurgQ-VLM, a two-stage model for surgical video question answering. Stage 1 trains a question-conditioned dual-stream (slow/fast) compressor for a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-VL-7B: cross-attention conditions both streams on the question, and each clip's visual tokens shrink 49x from the raw ViT patches (11x vs. post-merge backbone tokens). Stage 2 post-trains with GRPO under an answer-type-aware reward that scores each question on the metric matching its answer structure (micro-F1 for label sets, normalised error for counts, a content-timing blend for temporal windows). On a sealed 21,840-question test split over Cholec80 and CholecT50, SurgQ-VLM reaches 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10x BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot; GRPO adds 2.5 pp K-Acc (2.0 pp attributable to the answer-type-aware reward), concentrated in the structurally hard types, with answer format unchanged (ROUGE-L). Code is available at https://github.com/DhruvMakwana/SurgQ-VLM.
bullets: Targets limitations of frame-based and uniformly compressed video QA, especially for duration, ordering, and counting questions.
Uses a two-stage architecture: question-conditioned slow/fast visual compression followed by GRPO post-training.
Applies answer-type-specific rewards for binary, classification, multi-label, counting, and sentence-temporal answers.
On a sealed 21,840-question test split from Cholec80 and CholecT50, achieves 0.779 keyword accuracy and a 10× BLEU-4 gain over zero-shot.
GRPO improves keyword accuracy by 2.5 percentage points, with gains concentrated in structurally difficult answer types.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation has achieved impressive results on short clips, yet generating long videos remains challenging due to error accumulation over extended horizons, where each predicted frame depends on potentially imperfect previous frames. Existing approaches typically rely on static context management strategies, such as sliding-window caches that discard early frames or fixed sink frames that permanently preserve initial content. These designs either lose critical long-range context or anchor generation to outdated information, which can lead to degraded fidelity, motion stagnation, and reduced diversity. In this paper, we propose Learning to Memorize (L2M), a learned context memory management framework that dynamically retains, evicts, and evolves historical frames according to predicted importance. The framework consists of an importance prediction router that estimates the relevance of each historical frame, degradation-aware training that improves robustness to noisy or corrupted context, and a dynamic memory initialization and evolution mechanism that updates long-term memory using exponential moving average (EMA) importance scores. This allows high-quality frames to replace stale anchors and enables memory to adapt naturally to scene evolution. Trained with a teacher-student distillation objective and sparsity regularization, L2M makes efficient use of a fixed KV-cache budget while preserving the most informative contextual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that L2M improves long-horizon video generation quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines, providing a learned strategy for context memory management in long autoregressive video generation.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and degraded quality in long video generation caused by static context strategies.
Uses an importance-prediction router to retain, evict, and update historical frames based on relevance.
Combines degradation-aware training, EMA-based memory evolution, teacher–student distillation, and sparsity regularization.
Experiments report improved long-horizon video quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines.
Scope: focuses on learned context management within a fixed KV-cache budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of L2M. (a) Training phase: Given the current chunk feature f̄b and historical latent frame features {f̄i}i<(b−1)Bf+1, the importance-aware frame router predicts importance scores for each historical latent frame. Binary frame selection masks mi ∈ {0, 1} are obtained via GumbelSoftmax discretization. The pruned context is fed to the student network, which is supervised by the teacher operating on the full context. Degradation-aware training augments a subset of historical frames with degradations, encouraging the router to assign them lower retention probabilities. (b) Inference phase: The router predicts frame importance scores, and low-scoring latent frames are evicted to meet the cache budget. High-scoring frames are dynamically selected as long-term memory and periodically updated using maintained EMA scores, continuously promoting informative historical frames.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers have become the most powerful models for visual generation, but still suffer from massive computation costs. To solve this problem, feature caching has been proposed to cache the features of diffusion models in the previous computation steps and then reuse them in the following caching steps, which brings significant acceleration but also degradation in generation quality. To address this problem, this paper proposes Z-cache as a feature caching method that can maintain high-quality generation through self-reflection. Concretely, we observe that the error from feature caching tends to be sharply reduced after each full computation. Based on this observation, Z-Cache is designed to first predict the features in the future caching steps and then perform a full computation. After that, Z-Cache returns to the caching steps and re-predicts them based on the previous and the current computation steps, which brings correction in features. Experiments demonstrate that with Z-Cache, diffusion transformers achieve comparable generation quality to the original model but with faster inference speed, for instance, 6.22X acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation. Our code is released on GitHub.
bullets: Feature caching reduces diffusion-transformer computation but can degrade image quality.
Z-Cache predicts features for future caching steps, periodically performs full computation, and uses it to correct subsequent predictions.
Experiments report comparable generation quality with faster inference, including 6.22× acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation.
The method targets inference acceleration for diffusion-transformer-based visual generation.

Traditional feature caching forecasts an active window from a past full-computation anchor and directly moves to the next window. In contrast, Z-Cache treats the window as provisional: after obtaining the next scheduled full-computation anchor, it revisits the same window, constructs dual-anchor hidden estimates, re-samples the window trajectory, and commits the reflected window-end latent. Z-Cache therefore performs in-loop trajectory correction without adding extra full-computation steps.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have enabled generative video compression to reconstruct details lost during coding using pretrained spatiotemporal priors. However, a substantial gap remains between codec-induced degradation and the perturbation trajectories learned by flow-matching models. In this paper, we identify a compression-dependent directional mismatch that degradation-strength-based timestep calibration alone cannot resolve. Compressed latents remain strongly aligned across codec operating points, while their reconstruction residuals vary substantially in magnitude and direction. To bridge this gap, we propose RIFT, a Residual-Informed Flow Transfer framework for one-step generative video compression. At its core, RIFT introduces a Residual Geometry Inducer (RGI) that converts the pretrained flow prediction into a content-adaptive restoration update using decoder-visible codec cues. RGI integrates flow-timestep conditioning with a learned full-band residual-strength estimate and content-conditioned direction and gain modulation, aligning the orientation and magnitude of the update with the compression-dependent residual geometry. Extensive experiments on three public video compression benchmarks show that RIFT outperforms competing generative video compression methods. The code is publicly available on RIFT.
bullets: Compression artifacts differ in residual magnitude and direction, which timestep calibration alone cannot address.
RIFT uses decoder-visible codec cues to make restoration updates content-adaptive.
Its Residual Geometry Inducer combines flow-timestep conditioning with learned residual strength, direction, and gain modulation.
Experiments on three public video-compression benchmarks show RIFT outperforms competing generative compression methods.
The method targets one-step reconstruction using pretrained spatiotemporal priors.

papers.abstract: A poor start lowers the ceiling, but does not negate the value of finishing well. In autoregressive video temporal grounding, models systematically exhibit an endpoint performance asymmetry, predicting ends significantly worse than starts. A committed flawed start acts as an immutable physical constraint, irreversibly capping the attainable overlap as a sunk loss. While models should minimize the remaining conditional regret, standard post-training paradigms fail to teach this adaptation. Specifically, teacher-forced SFT suffers from strict prefix exposure bias, and holistic trajectory evaluation in standard GRPO inadvertently penalizes conditionally optimal ends if they follow a poor start. To address this, we introduce FinishStrong, a novel two-stage post-training framework explicitly designed to teach optimal continuations. First, Online-start SFT exposes the end prediction to the model's own generated contexts. Second, Conditional-tree GRPO restructures the sampling topology, centering end rewards exclusively within the same-start branch to mathematically isolate the conditional end quality from the inherited start penalty. FinishStrong-9B achieves a state-of-the-art 61.7\% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench, remarkably outperforming flagship closed-source models like Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.8-Max. Crucially, when forced to continue from imperfect starts, it reduces the subsequent end prediction error by 36.5\%, proving its exceptional ability to end well after flawed starts. Code will be open.
bullets: Autoregressive models predict temporal segment ends worse than starts, and flawed starts can cap the achievable overlap.
Standard teacher-forced SFT and holistic GRPO do not adequately reward conditionally good continuations after poor starts.
The two-stage framework uses Online-start SFT to expose models to their own generated starts.
Conditional-tree GRPO evaluates end quality within the same-start branch, separating continuation quality from inherited start errors.
FinishStrong-9B reports 61.7% overall IoU on TimeLens-Bench and reduces end prediction error by 36.5% after imperfect starts.

papers.abstract: Recently, speech-driven facial and oral animation technologies have been used in various fields such as education, speech therapy, and healthcare. But methods to objectively evaluate the quality of generated results are still limited. Accordingly, we propose the Fréchet Oral Distance (FOD), which uses embeddings from an Oral Motion Encoder (OME) and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution. In experiments, FOD reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based metric, Lip Vertex Error (LVE), and showed trends consistent with user preference. Our framework provides objective and reproducible benchmarking without relying on expensive equipment or subjective evaluation, and it can be extended to compare a variety of 2D/3D models.
bullets: Addresses the limited availability of objective evaluation methods for generated facial and oral animation.
Computes distance between Oral Motion Encoder embeddings and a TIMIT-Vis reference distribution.
Reproduced model rankings similar to the coordinate-based Lip Vertex Error metric.
Showed trends consistent with user preference in experiments.
Enables reproducible evaluation without expensive equipment or subjective assessment, with potential use across 2D and 3D models.

papers.abstract: A causal video generator writes every segment it produces into a key--value (KV) cache, and later segments know the past only through it. Self-rollout training stops the gradient at this cache, and Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) restores it, but applies it to the same weights that generate the current segment. We find that writing and generating are different roles: in a pretrained generator the written KV already differs from the KV used for denoising, and on shared weights the gradient from future reads is negatively aligned with the gradient of generation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV), which gives the write its own parameters, a low-rank residual used only when a segment enters the cache, and trains them with the gradient of the later segments that read what they wrote. Opening this gradient through the cache in common use exhausts GPU memory. We trace this to checkpoint replay re-writing the cache, not to the gradient path, which removes the need for the second reconstruction pass of SGF. dKV Forcing keeps the cache as persistent differentiable pages and computes the exact gradient in one temporal traversal, with an $11\%$ lower memory peak and $28\%$ less resident memory. With pages that store hidden states, it trains 15\,s clips on which the two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory. Trained on 5\,s clips, dKV Forcing reaches the highest VBench-Long quality score at 60\,s and 240\,s and outperforms SGF by $3.6$ and $6.1$ points of aesthetic quality, with a higher dynamic degree.
bullets: Shared generation and cache-writing weights receive conflicting gradients, motivating separate write parameters.
A low-rank residual writes segment representations into a persistent, differentiable KV cache.
The method computes exact gradients in one temporal traversal, avoiding SGF’s second reconstruction pass.
It reduces peak memory by 11% and resident memory by 28%; hidden-state pages enable training 15-second clips where two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory.
When trained on 5-second clips, it achieves the highest reported VBench-Long quality at 60 and 240 seconds and improves aesthetic quality over SGF by 3.6 and 6.1 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2. A separate writer learns what to store from the segments that read it, in one temporal traversal. For each segment the shared generator Gθ (gray) predicts x̃ts i , which enters the video loss, and the memory writer Kθ,ϕ (orange, with the writer LoRA ϕ) turns the detached prediction into the KV of that segment. The KV is committed once to a write-once slot of the page table, and later segments read it through handles. In backward (purple, dashed) the gradient of every later prediction returns through the handles to the page it read and to the writer that produced it, while replay only reads the pages.

Figure 3. Only pages and handles carry the memory gradient through replay. (a) Self Forcing detaches the cache: each replay is released, and the writes receive no gradient. (b) With the gradient passing through the in-place cache, every replay writes the cache again and its activations stay attached until backward runs out of memory. (c) dKV Forcing stores the values in a page table, written once outside replay, and a zero-valued handle h carries the gradient to the write, so replay only reads and is released.

Figure 11. Where the memory of one generator update goes. Measured component accounting for the four training schemes. Panel titles give the generator-update time. CF++ (detached writes) keeps only exit-forward boundaries and its backward is short. The naive mutable cache keeps both forwards’ boundaries and the sampled trajectory, and its backward exhausts memory while replay attaches new graph to the external cache (purple: engine-allocated gradients and temporaries). The two-pass reconstruction keeps no graph in the rollout but retains the whole second-pass forward (violet) and replays it layer by layer in backward (cyan), with the cache resident between steps (red). dKV Forcing allocates the page table once (green), keeps only group entry states during the rollout, and in backward adds one contiguous gradient per page (light green) and the local replay of five-block groups.

A data-free handle (purple circle) preserves the gradient connection to the writer without retaining the page data. Each forward reads a snapshot of the visible pages (orange dashed arrows), while backward returns an independent, contiguous gradient buffer (purple rectangles) to each page’s writer (purple dashed arrows).

papers.abstract: Video inpainting for object removal is scored over the whole hole, although the background behind the object is visible in other frames of the shot for some hole pixels and in no frame for others. A whole-hole score therefore mixes copying with generation and cannot show which of the two a remover does well. To separate the two, we propose recoverability-stratified evaluation, in which a point tracker run on the clean video labels each hole pixel by whether and how far away it is observed, so that fidelity and temporal stability can be reported per stratum against a copy reference. To reuse the observed content, we also propose evidence-guided sampling (EGS), which blends tracked colors into the clean-latent prediction of a video diffusion remover without training. On DAVIS, the perceptual advantage of three diffusion removers over flow propagation shrinks where the content is visible a few frames away (LPIPS difference-in-differences +0.046 to +0.056 against E2FGVI-HQ), and real paired captures show the same pattern for two of them. Their DAVIS hole warping error is two to four times that of ProPainter, and copying along clean-video tracks lowers their recoverable LPIPS by a quarter to two fifths. EGS closes 43% and 56% of the gap to this copy reference on held-out DAVIS when its colors come from clean-video tracks. With colors tracked on the masked input, a pre-registered confirmation finds no gain on MiniMax-Remover and a loss on ROSE. Diffusion removers thus leave observed content unused on DAVIS, and training-free reuse does not yet hold with tracked evidence.
bullets: Whole-hole metrics conflate pixels recoverable from other frames with pixels requiring generation.
A point-tracker-based evaluation stratifies fidelity and temporal stability by how recoverable each hole pixel is.
Evidence-guided sampling (EGS) injects tracked colors into diffusion predictions without additional training.
On DAVIS and paired real captures, diffusion advantages shrink for content visible nearby; their warping error is 2–4× ProPainter’s.
EGS closes 43% and 56% of the recoverable LPIPS gap with clean-video evidence, but masked-input evidence gives no gain for one remover and hurts another.

papers.abstract: Streaming video question answering (QA) requires real-time reasoning over continuous video streams under strict latency and active-context budgets. Current streaming vision-language models (VLMs) often give confident yet ungrounded answers when queries are ambiguous or have false premises, or when relevant visual evidence is no longer in the active context. Proactive clarification can help, but must satisfy the same latency and memory constraints. We present StreamClarify, a training-free framework for grounded streaming QA that combines a pre-answer uncertainty check with hierarchical memory. The check uses the entropy of a binary pre-answer judgment as a lightweight uncertainty score to decide whether to answer directly or request clarification. To support re-answering, a temporal-pyramid KV cache maintains a bounded active visual context, while a CPU-side semantic retrieval archive provides access to historical frames. We further construct StreamClarify-QA, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,837 QA pairs from StreamBench and OVO-Bench, spanning standard, referential ambiguity, and unanswerable scenarios. Across three VLM backbones, StreamClarify improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points over backbone-matched baselines. At comparable trigger rates, entropy-based selection achieves more than 18 points higher precision than random selection in identifying initially incorrect answers. Under oracle user guidance, clarification improves Macro accuracy by up to 3.5 points. We also report a controlled, oracle-assisted Qwen3-VL simulation on Ambiguous QA with generated questions and referent-only user replies, where the entropy-gated condition improves accuracy by 8.3 points.
bullets: Targets confident but ungrounded answers caused by ambiguous queries, false premises, or missing active-context evidence.
Uses a training-free entropy-based pre-answer uncertainty check to decide between answering and asking for clarification.
Maintains bounded visual memory with a temporal-pyramid KV cache plus CPU-side semantic retrieval of historical frames.
Introduces StreamClarify-QA, a 1,837-pair diagnostic benchmark covering standard, ambiguous, and unanswerable scenarios.
Across three VLM backbones, improves Macro accuracy by up to 8.2 points; oracle clarification adds up to 3.5 points, while entropy selection substantially outperforms random triggering.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of StreamClarify. The framework augments a frozen streaming VLM with a pre-answer uncertainty check in a twostage generation loop and hierarchical memory. (a) When pre-answer entropy does not exceed the trigger threshold, the system answers directly using the active temporal-pyramid KV (TP-KV) cache. (b) TP-KV keeps recent frames at full resolution and compresses older observed frames within a fixed active budget. (c) When entropy exceeds the threshold, the system requests clarification and converts the resulting user guidance into a retrieval query. (d) Semantic search retrieves relevant past clips from the archive and combines them with the active TP-KV context for answering after clarification.

papers.abstract: Streaming video LLMs can now commentate live gameplay, but they are trained and tested on the same games. We study cross-game streaming commentary, in which a model trained on one game commentates games it has never seen, and find that current commentators transfer their timing but not their knowledge of the game world. We propose StreamDuo, which pairs a trainable commentator with a frozen research agent that reads the wiki of the game being played. When the commentator sees something it cannot name, it sends the current frames, and the research agent returns a few wiki entries two seconds later while the stream continues. We train only the commentator, on a single game, in two stages. Information-gain labels teach it to ask only where an answer would help it say what the human caster said, and on-policy self-distillation from a copy of itself that sees the ideal answer teaches it to use noisy answers. Trained on Baldur's Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, StreamDuo raises entity recall from 0.082 to 0.116 over Proact-VL trained on the same data, cuts source-game leakage from 9.9% to 1.0%, and achieves the best timing and the highest judged liveliness and overall quality among streaming models.
bullets: Cross-game commentators preserve timing but struggle to recognize and understand unfamiliar game worlds.
The system queries relevant wiki entries when it encounters an unknown entity, while commentary continues with a short delay.
Training uses information-gain labels and on-policy self-distillation, requiring commentator training on only one game.
Trained on Baldur’s Gate 3 and tested on ten unseen games, it improves entity recall, reduces source-game leakage, and achieves strong timing, liveliness, and overall quality.
Results are scoped to streaming commentary on unseen games and rely on available game-wiki information.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators produce videos block by block from historical context. They are trained within a bounded horizon, whereas inference can extend far beyond it, causing temporal consistency to gradually decrease. Existing methods focus on eliminating this mismatch, but we instead ask whether the historical context used in training remains suitable for inference. Each block reads historical context in two stages, when denoising generates it and when committing writes it into the KV cache for later blocks. We find that older historical context such as the sink helps denoising but can hurt later blocks when read during committing, even in generators trained to read it there. We also show that as committing reads more preceding blocks, clip-to-clip Subject Consistency rises, plateaus, and then declines. We therefore propose Commit Forcing, a training-free rule that organizes committing into a chain. Each committing pass reads only the preceding block's stored KV, while denoising keeps the base historical context. Commit Forcing improves 60-second VBench Quality and Total on all 6 generators, by up to 1.27 and 1.10 points. Its consistency gains extend to 240-second videos, and it achieves an 82.9% win rate in overall human preference on 120-second LongLive videos.
bullets: Long-video autoregressive generators lose temporal consistency when inference extends beyond their training horizon.
Older context can help denoising but harm later blocks during KV-cache committing, revealing a mismatch in how history is used.
Subject consistency rises, plateaus, and declines as committing reads more preceding blocks.
The training-free Commit Forcing rule makes committing read only the preceding block’s stored KV while preserving the base context for denoising.
It improves VBench Quality and Total across all six generators, with consistency gains extending to 240-second videos and an 82.9% human-preference win rate on 120-second videos.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses long-horizon autoregressive video generation and KV-cache history handling in denoising-based block generation.
papers.title: What Helps Denoising Can Hurt Memory: Rethinking History in Long Video Generation

papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of mobile devices has democratized video recording, but a stark aesthetic divide persists between casual, low-cost captures and high-cost cinematic productions. Bridging this gap requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements, such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials, without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage. However, this task is heavily bottlenecked by two important challenges: 1) Lacking a high-quality paired training data specifically designed to handle complex low-to-high appearance shifts. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current video editing models to perceive and enhance the multiple low-cost compositions. To address these issues, we present CineCraft-120K, a large-scale dataset of aligned low- and high-cost video pairs annotated with pair-aware editing prompts. CineCraft-120K features a diverse, high-resolution and high-cost Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories. It also provides element-level mapping between low- and high-cost counterparts, offering pair-aware rich textual prompts that precisely detail the required aesthetic transformations while anchoring structural layout. Architecturally, we propose a simple yet effective dual-memory feature adapter, where a text-memory expands semantic capacity for low2high appearance changes, and a hint memory supplies layer-wise visual feature corrections of high-cost element before context injection. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the superiority of CineCraft-120K for low-to-high-cost video editing, alongside the effectiveness of our dual-memory adapter.
bullets: Addresses the gap between casual mobile videos and high-cost cinematic productions without changing core layout, identity, or temporal motion.
Introduces CineCraft-120K, a high-resolution dataset of aligned low-/high-cost video pairs with pair-aware editing prompts.
The dataset covers five broad domains and 23 fine-grained categories, with element-level mappings and structural editing guidance.
Proposes a dual-memory feature adapter: text memory expands appearance semantics, while hint memory provides layer-wise visual corrections.
Experiments and ablations report effective low-to-high-cost video editing and validate the adapter design.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SEU-VIPGroup/GO-SSL.
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison learned by prior within-instance self-supervised methods.
Pairs two visual instances, mixes their local elements, and trains the model to separate them by origin while restoring spatial, temporal, or geometric order.
Uses diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum to create richer automatically verifiable rewards from unlabeled data.
Applied to cross-image jigsaws, 3D depth, and video temporal ordering, with reported gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding across benchmarks.
Evaluations across model scales and families indicate broad generality, though the abstract does not specify quantitative results or limitations.

papers.abstract: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).
bullets: Targets inefficiency and quality degradation in chunk-wise autoregressive video generation, including camera drift during long rollouts.
Uses chunk-wise causal attention, staggered multi-step denoising, and replicated model pipelines to produce one chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill.
Introduces three-stage training with mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history.
Wave Runtime combines early K/V delivery, communication-computation overlap, optimized kernels, and pipelined VAE decoding.
On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, 5-step WF has quality comparable to Rolling Forcing with higher Dynamic Degree; 4-step WF reaches 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs.

papers.abstract: We report the end-to-end deployment and measurement of MiniMax H3, a 20.38-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer (DiT) - the count measured from the safetensors headers of the Q8 checkpoint as deployed locally (Section 3.2) - running entirely on consumer Apple Silicon hardware: an Apple Mac mini with M5 Pro chip and 64 GiB of unified memory. Using the official bf16-to-Q8 (8-bit, group size 64) quantization path executed locally on the machine, we produced a working text-to-video pipeline with no cloud dependency. We document the full deployment procedure, including two non-trivial blockers and their fixes, and report measured figures for build time, peak memory, and per-clip render latency across four resolution tiers (Draft 384x640 through Native 768x1344). A 15.08-second 576x1024 clip rendered in 4838.49 seconds with a measured MLX peak of 27.467 GiB. We further operated the system as an unattended production pipeline, completing 17 clips in 26.49 hours with zero render failures. A blind human review of the 17 production clips (generation prompts withheld) averaged 3.12, 3.18, and 2.94 out of 5 for structural integrity, temporal consistency, and visible artifacts. All figures in this report are our own measurements except where explicitly labeled as third-party data. This is a systems/empirical report; we make no claim of model innovation.
bullets: The system ran on Apple Silicon with 64 GiB unified memory using the official locally executed bf16-to-Q8 quantization path.
The report documents the deployment workflow, including two blockers and their fixes, plus measurements across four video-resolution tiers.

An unattended run produced 17 clips over 26.49 hours with zero render failures.

papers.abstract: We present \textbf{UniCaMo}, an unified framework for joint control of camera and object motion in image-and-text-to-video diffusion models. Given a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory, UniCaMo constructs motion-consistent input noise that directly encodes the desired motion. Our 3D-grounded noise construction combines reference-derived noise propagation with a spherical Gaussian noise representation for newly revealed regions, providing a simple and effective motion prior without requiring reconstruction of unseen scene geometry. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications or dedicated control modules and can be adapted using lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with low training data volume. Experiments on standard controllable video generation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality with minimal inference overhead.
bullets: Uses a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory as control inputs.
Constructs motion-consistent noise through reference-based propagation and spherical Gaussian noise for newly revealed regions.
Avoids reconstructing unseen scene geometry and requires no architectural changes or dedicated control modules.
Supports lightweight LoRA adaptation with low training data volume and minimal inference overhead.
Reports state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality on standard controllable video-generation benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The UniCamo pipeline begins with 3D-lifting the input reference image to a 3D point cloud, within which per-frame control signals are defined via an interactive GUI, producing 3D point tracks and camera trajectories. From these, a 3D-grounded scene representation from three noise components: foreground noise derived from 3D point tracks, background noise from depth cues, and 3D spherical noise for persistent out-of-view anchors, which is then merged by a depth-aware noise composition step. The 3D-grounded noise is consumed by a LoRA finetuned video diffusion model to generate a video exhibiting corresponding object and camera motion.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models and more recently Flow models have widespread application. In this work we consider degenerate Diffusion models in which the per-step generator is deterministic. We construct a modified variational framework and show a formal equivalence between Flow models and Degenerate Diffusion models. For our discrete-time variational objective we show that the optimal degenerate generator recovers the data distribution in the limit of an infinite number of generator steps. Our work therefore provides a unified perspective, showing that discrete-time implementations of flow matching and the discrete-time Degenerate Diffusion model can be considered within the same simple variational framework, removing the need for the continuous-time machinery normally used to justify flow matching models.
bullets: Studies degenerate diffusion models whose per-step generators are deterministic.
Constructs a modified variational objective for these discrete-time models.
Formally establishes equivalence between flow models and degenerate diffusion models.
Shows convergence to the data distribution with infinitely many generator steps.
Avoids relying on continuous-time machinery to justify flow matching.
papers.selection_reason: General flow-matching/diffusion theory with a unified variational objective; transferable to video diffusion and video world models.
papers.title: A Discrete-Time Variational Objective for Degenerate Diffusion and Equivalence to Flow Matching
papers.tldr: A discrete-time variational framework unifies degenerate diffusion and flow matching, showing that optimal deterministic generators recover the data distribution as the number of steps grows.

papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in long-form video understanding, current benchmarks mostly focus on short clips or hour-scale videos. This leaves a major gap in evaluating ultra-long video understanding, where videos often last tens of hours. To bridge this gap, we introduce DramaVQA, a large-scale benchmark built upon long-form TV dramas. Containing approximately 20K question-answering (QA) pairs, the scale of DramaVQA exceeds previous long-video datasets, such as Video-MME and LVBench, by an order of magnitude. Our benchmark has two main features that make it stand out from existing datasets. First, we establish a scalable, LLM-assisted annotation pipeline that uses multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to generate complex questions, followed by strict human checking to ensure high data quality. Second, DramaVQA introduces a multi-level time structure; queries are designed across different video lengths, with the hardest questions requiring overall understanding across the entire drama. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art MLLMs face major challenges when tested on these very long videos, highlighting the need for agentic AI algorithms capable of managing long-term memory. The project is available at https://github.com/xinyuehuo/DramaVQA
bullets: Targets a gap in video benchmarks: understanding dramas lasting tens of hours rather than short clips or hour-scale videos.
Provides approximately 20K question–answer pairs, exceeding prior long-video datasets by an order of magnitude.
Uses an LLM-assisted pipeline to generate complex questions, followed by strict human verification.
Organizes questions across multiple temporal levels, including whole-drama reasoning.
Evaluations show state-of-the-art MLLMs struggle with ultra-long videos, motivating agentic methods with long-term memory.

papers.abstract: Answering a complex question about a long video is a grounding problem: the answer turns on a few seconds of evidence, and vision-language models remain well below human accuracy at finding them. The standard way to spend extra test-time compute on this kind of video reasoning is best-of-N selection: sample several chain-of-thought answers from a fixed model, then let a second model re-watch the video and pick one. Such pipelines are reported by a single headline number, their margin over a majority vote. That number conflates two effects with opposite deployment consequences: the benefit the second model adds by selecting among candidates, and the benefit it would have supplied by solving the question itself. We separate them, measuring the Selection Increment (SI) -- selection accuracy minus the same verifier's accuracy with the candidates withheld -- alongside the margin over self-consistency, across five long-video benchmarks. The Selection Increment is largest for the weakest verifiers: a verifier that solves poorly on its own leaves the candidates the most room to help. Beating the majority vote follows the opposite profile: where the vote already sits near its ceiling no verifier we test improves on it; below that ceiling only the strongest do. On Video-Holmes, the two come apart on a single pool of candidates -- a weak verifier gains +19.3 points from the candidates yet lands 7.1 points below the vote, while the frontier verifier gains the least and beats the vote. The weakest verifier also shows a failure mode: on EgoSchema it picks by where an option sits in the list rather than by what the video shows. Read as a merit score, SI puts a verifier that fails to beat a majority vote at the top of its ranking; read as an audit, it says which of the two effects a headline number delivers. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/best-n-selection-video-reasoning.
bullets: Introduces Selection Increment (SI): verifier accuracy with candidates minus its accuracy when candidates are withheld.
Across five long-video benchmarks, weaker verifiers gain more from candidate answers, while stronger verifiers are more likely to beat majority vote.
On Video-Holmes, a weak verifier gained 19.3 points from candidates but remained 7.1 points below the vote; the frontier verifier gained less but surpassed it.
The weakest verifier showed positional-choice bias on EgoSchema, selecting based on option order rather than video evidence.
SI is useful as an audit of where gains come from, but is misleading as a standalone merit ranking.

figures.caption: Figure 1: What a best-of-N verifier pipeline measures. A base generator (Qwen3.5-27B) samples N=8 chain-of-thought rollouts per question, each ending in a candidate letter. Three rules score that same pool: majority voting; the verifier selecting among the candidates after re-watching K frames; and the same verifier with the candidates withheld. Their differences define our two axes, ∆maj and SI.

papers.selection_reason: Separates selection versus solving effects in best-of-N video reasoning, directly relevant to video-language understanding and VLM evaluation.
papers.title: Selecting or Solving? What Best-of-N Verification Delivers in Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: Best-of-N video reasoning gains must be split into candidate-selection benefit and the verifier’s own solving ability, because these can point to opposite conclusions.

papers.abstract: Dense action detection requires precisely localising multiple overlapping actions in long untrimmed videos. Transformer-based methods achieve strong accuracy but their $O(T^2)$ self-attention cost limits scalability. We present PAM-Mamba, a linear-time $O(T)$ architecture built on Mamba with a multi-branch temporal encoder. Gated Learnable Positional Encoding (GLPE) controls positional signal injection via a scalar gate initialised to zero, starting training without added positional signal. A Hub-and-Spoke Funnel extends the non-hierarchical multi-scale design of PAT with a direct residual from the original full-resolution input to each coarse branch, providing each coarse branch with a projection of the input features. Bi-TemBa (Bidirectional Temporal Mamba) first extracts local motion cues with a shallow Temporal Convolution Module, then applies a cascaded bidirectional Mamba scan; the backward pass refines the forward-scanned representation from the opposite direction, giving each temporal position access to context from both directions in linear time. Uncertainty-Based Mixup uses prediction entropy to guide the selection of mixup partners. Using the PAT evaluation implementation, we obtain 26.82 (Charades I3D), 34.59 (Charades CLIP), 46.56 (MultiTHUMOS I3D), and 46.92 mAP (MultiTHUMOS CLIP), with 26.1-27.9M parameters, 61-63% fewer than PAT.
bullets: Targets precise localization of multiple overlapping actions in long, untrimmed videos without Transformer self-attention’s quadratic cost.
Uses a multi-branch temporal encoder with GLPE, a Hub-and-Spoke Funnel, and bidirectional Bi-TemBa scanning for local and global temporal context.
Introduces entropy-guided Uncertainty-Based Mixup to select training partners.
Reports 26.82/34.59 mAP on Charades and 46.56/46.92 mAP on MultiTHUMOS with I3D/CLIP features.
Uses 26.1–27.9M parameters, reported as 61–63% fewer than PAT.

figures.caption: Figure 3. PAM-Mamba architecture overview. Pre-extracted I3D or CLIP features receive gated learnable positional encoding (including dropout 0.1) and input dropout 0.5 before entering the three-branch encoder. The full-resolution fine branch supplies a shared representation to two independently downsampled coarse branches. Each coarse branch also receives a strided projection of the encoder input. Projection blocks include LayerNorm. The Bi-TemBa inset follows the implementation: TCM is Conv1d, LayerNorm and GELU; the forward scan feeds the backward scan through temporal reversal. The backward output is reversed back, summed with the forward output and normalised, then added to the original block input. Both Mamba scans use pre-normalisation. SimpleFuser projects branch outputs to 1024 dimensions, linearly upsamples coarse outputs and combines them using learned softmax weights. Separate fine and coarse classifiers produce logits Zfine and Zcoarse, blended with the reported 0.25/0.75 weights; a sigmoid gives per-class probabilities.

papers.selection_reason: Linear-time Mamba architecture for dense action detection in long untrimmed videos, fitting video understanding.
papers.title: PAM-Mamba - Efficient Dense Action Detection using Mamba
papers.tldr: PAM-Mamba enables efficient dense action detection in long videos with linear-time Mamba processing while retaining strong multi-scale temporal context.

papers.abstract: Tracking points that leave the camera's field of view (FoV) requires reasoning about unobserved scene dynamics, a fundamentally different problem from tracking visible correspondences. We present TAP-Out, an offline method that makes this out-of-view (OOV) reasoning explicit by leveraging generative video outpainting as a world-model prior. Given a narrow-FoV input video, TAP-Out outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, locates target objects within the panoramic scene via video object segmentation, and synthesises object-centred perspective crops on which standard in-frame trackers operate. This decoupled design composes off-the-shelf foundation models without requiring task-specific architectural modifications. On the TAPVid360 benchmark, TAP-Out achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving OOV tracking accuracy by approximately 3x over the best prior method. We demonstrate its flexibility on out-of-frame object segmentation and detection and we provide detailed diagnostic analyses across motion regimes, static versus dynamic content, and hallucination quality, characterising when and why the approach succeeds or fails. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/finlay-hudson/TAP-Out
bullets: Addresses out-of-view tracking, which requires inferring unobserved scene dynamics rather than matching visible correspondences.
Outpaints a complete 360° equirectangular video, segments target objects panoramically, and generates perspective crops for conventional tracking.
Combines off-the-shelf foundation models without task-specific architectural changes.
Achieves approximately 3× higher out-of-view tracking accuracy than the prior best method on TAPVid360.
Also supports out-of-frame segmentation and detection, with analyses of motion, scene dynamics, and hallucination quality.

Figure 6: TAP-Out applied to out-of-frame object tracking on the LaSOT benchmark [14].

Figure 5: Eliminating re-identification failures on LaSOT [14]. A standard tracker (SAM2, left) tracks a white ball when visible (blue circles) but fails to re-identify it upon return (red circle) after extended absence. papers.selection_reason: Leverages generative video outpainting as a world-model prior for out-of-view point tracking, transferable to video world models and video understanding.
papers.title: TAP-Out: Tracking Any Point in 360° via Outpainting
papers.tldr: TAP-Out tracks objects after they leave view by outpainting a narrow-FoV video into a 360° world model and applying standard trackers to synthesized object-centred views.

papers.abstract: The hardest part of understanding a long video is not pinpointing any one moment but synthesizing many, e.g., answering a question that requires tracking what develops across hours of content and articulating how the pieces fit together. To date, most long-video QA datasets require only a short answer or a multiple-choice selection, oversimplifying the long-video understanding task to retrieval. We introduce LF-VideoQA, a dataset for long-form, open-ended question answering over long narrative videos built on theory-of-mind questions: a character's belief depends on everything they have seen or been told, so each question demands assembling and reasoning from evidence distributed across the video. The dataset contains more than 6,300 questions on 94 recent films; each requires reasoning over scenes spanning an average of 23 minutes and comes with a question-specific rubric for recall and precision scoring. The dataset is created entirely automatically by annotating screenplays with scene events and each character's first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs, then generating (question, answer, rubric) triples through LLM-based question generation and verification; human studies validate their quality. We evaluate four families of state-of-the-art open-source VLMs across three settings and find the task highly challenging: (i) even an oracle with access to the screenplay falls well short of complete answers; (ii) the best non-oracle model attains barely half of the recall level of the oracle; (iii) unlike on prior long-video benchmarks, captions and subtitles underperform the video itself, indicating that the questions need visual evidence; and (iv) recall is the predominant bottleneck, with answers omitting many required rubric claims.
bullets: Contains over 6,300 questions covering 94 recent films, with evidence spanning an average of 23 minutes.
Questions require tracking characters’ beliefs and meta-beliefs across multiple scenes rather than retrieving a single moment.
Built automatically from screenplay annotations using LLM-generated and verified question–answer–rubric triples; human studies validate quality.
Evaluations of four open-source VLM families show substantial difficulty: the best non-oracle reaches barely half the oracle’s recall.
Visual video evidence outperforms captions and subtitles, while incomplete recall is the primary failure mode.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dataset Construction on an Example. This figure shows (question, answer, rubric) from Deadpool & Wolverine (2024). Preprocessing: screenplay scenes are time-stamped against the subtitles and decomposed into scene events. Character belief annotation: scene by scene, we extract and verify each character’s first-order beliefs and meta-beliefs. Question generation and verification: for a center character (Wolverine) and an anchor (scene 113), we generate the triple and verify every rubric claim against the screenplay.

Figure 3: A second-order belief (Q6) example from Oppenheimer (2023), whose center character is Strauss’s Senate aide and whose anchor scene is S261. At 00:11:50 Strauss watches Einstein walk past him after a private word with Oppenheimer and concludes that Einstein disapproves of him; by 02:41:48 this has hardened into the false belief that Oppenheimer turned Einstein against him. The aide models that belief (meta-beliefs, bottom lane), suggests a better explanation that Strauss rejects, and the film reveals what was actually said only at the very end. Strauss never revises the belief. The question asks what the aide takes Strauss to believe, a belief about a false belief.

Figure 2: A knowledge-split (Q1) example from Sinners (2025), anchored at S82 with Annie as center character. At 01:18:22 Sammie glimpses Stack and Mary in the back room and tells the others that Stack is busy; Smoke, Delta Slim and Annie adopt the same false belief. Each then revises it at a different moment, depending on what they witness: Smoke when he sees Mary feeding (01:19:22), Delta Slim when she runs past him (01:20:03), Annie and Sammie when Stack dies (01:20:08). Meta-beliefs track who knows that Sammie missed each step. The question asks for this knowledge split at the anchor scene; its rubric separates core claims a correct answer must contain from supporting context claims.

Figure 4: An accepting-a-claim (Q7) example from Barbie (2023), with Sasha as center character and S51, Gloria’s car, as anchor scene. Told that a sad girl is causing her malfunction, Barbie misses the scene where Gloria shows her sad sketches (00:35:36) and wrongly concludes that the girl is Sasha; she revises only when Gloria explains in the car (00:52:19). Sasha hears the same true account and rejects it, while her own meta-belief records that Barbie accepts it. The question asks what Sasha makes of her mother’s explanation: noticing that Sasha rejects a true account, and that she is mistaken, is the task.

papers.selection_reason: Long-video QA dataset with theory-of-mind questions directly targets long-form video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: LF-VideoQA: Evaluating Long-Video Understanding with Long-Form Theory-of-Mind Questions
papers.tldr: LF-VideoQA introduces a challenging benchmark for evaluating whether models can synthesize distributed visual evidence in long videos to answer open-ended theory-of-mind questions.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have achieved impressive visual quality, yet they often fail to produce physically consistent dynamics due to the lack of explicit modeling of underlying physical processes. Existing approaches either rely on simulators with strong assumptions or use coarse semantic guidance, and further struggle to effectively inject physical priors into generation models. In this work, we propose Seeing the Unseen, a unified framework for physics-grounded video generation. Our approach decomposes the problem into two stages: learning physical dynamics and injecting them into video synthesis. First, we introduce a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS) that learns generalizable physical interactions from data and predicts plausible 3D motion trajectories. Second, we propose a Visible--Invisible Motion Field (VIMF) that captures both motion observable in the input frame and motion that emerges over time due to object dynamics. This representation enables more complete and structured motion guidance compared to conventional physical signals. By integrating these trajectories into a diffusion-based generator, our method produces videos that are both visually coherent and physically consistent. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and reduced physical artifacts compared to strong baselines.
bullets: Addresses physically implausible dynamics in video generation caused by weak or coarse physical modeling.
Uses a lightweight Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator to learn interactions and predict plausible 3D trajectories.
Introduces a Visible–Invisible Motion Field that represents observed motion and motion emerging over time.
Injects the learned motion guidance into a diffusion-based video generator.
Experiments report improved motion accuracy, interaction consistency, and fewer physical artifacts than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed framework. Given an input image, we first lift it into a 3D scene particle representation. A particle-based graph dynamics simulator then predicts physically plausible 3D motion trajectories, which are rendered into reference-visible and future- merg nt motions to guide physically consistent video generation.

Figure 3: Architecture of the physics-guided video generation model. The visible and future visible motion fields are encoded by a frozen 3D VAE and concatenated with the noisy video latent along the channel dimension. A zero-initialized injection strategy preserves the pretrained model behavior while progressively incorporating motion guidance.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison with existing methods. Our method produces physically plausible dynamics with accurate object interactions (e.g., correct collision responses and domino chain propagation), while baseline models frequently exhibit artifacts such as object interpenetration, implausible motion trajectories, or failure to trigger expected physical events.

Figure 8: Unified motion encoding and injection pipeline. The visible tracking video Vvis and future-visible tracking video Vfv are encoded using a frozen 3D VAE to obtain two latent sequences. These are concatenated with the noisy video latent to form a multi-channel input to the diffusion transformer. To preserve pretrained behavior, the patch embedding weights corresponding to tracking channels are zero-initialized, while the original weights are copied from the pretrained model. The first frame is injected via noise replacement to provide appearance conditioning.

Figure 7: Architecture of the Particle-based Graph Dynamics Simulator (PGDS). The simulator follows an Encode–Process–Decode pipeline. Given particle states, a graph is first constructed based on spatial proximity. Node and edge features are encoded to capture material properties and geometric relations. A message-passing processor then iteratively propagates interaction effects across the graph. Finally, a decoder predicts particle velocities, which are used to update positions and roll out future dynamics.
Figure 6: Comparison with different physical prior injection methods.

Figure 5: Pairwise human evaluation comparing our method against baseline models. For each comparison, human annotators judge which method produces better results across three criteria: (a) instruction-following, measuring how faithfully the generated video adheres to the given text prompt; (b) video quality, assessing visual fidelity, temporal coherence, and artifact severity; and (c) overall preference. Results are reported as win/tie/lose rates (%).

papers.selection_reason: Physics-grounded video generation with particle dynamics and diffusion, relevant to video world models and video diffusion.
papers.title: Seeing the Unseen: Unified Visible--Invisible Motion for Physically Consistent Video Generation
papers.tldr: Seeing the Unseen generates more physically consistent videos by learning 3D dynamics and guiding diffusion synthesis with both visible and emerging motion.

papers.abstract: Online Temporal Action Localization (OnTAL) aims to detect and localize action instances from untrimmed streaming videos in real time. Unlike offline approaches, OnTAL models have no access to future frames and cannot go back and refine earlier predictions, which makes the task considerably harder given the strict real-time constraints and narrow temporal window available. Most existing OnTAL methods lean on either brief anchor-based context or a single-scale memory of past frames, which limits how well they can capture actions unfolding across multiple time scales or requiring long-range reasoning in Procedural Videos. To address these gaps, we present DUGO (Dual-Scale Encoding and Gaussian Memory Online), a new OnTAL framework that jointly models local motion dynamics and long-range temporal dependencies. At its core, DUGO uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder, pairing depth-wise local representations with global self-attention so it can pick up both fine-grained temporal patterns and broader contextual cues. We also introduce a Gaussian Memory Bank, which represents action memory as stochastic, input-conditioned Gaussian prototypes, allowing for richer temporal memory through gated cross-attention applied at both the encoder and anchor-query stages. Extensive experiments on procedural egocentric datasets (EGTEA, EPIC-Kitchens-100) demonstrate that DUGO achieves state-of-the-art performance while also providing substantial improvements on non-egocentric benchmarks such as Muses. The project page is available at: https://aman554-eq.github.io/DUGO
bullets: Targets Online Temporal Action Localization without access to future frames or the ability to revise past predictions.
Uses a Dual-Scale Temporal Encoder to capture both fine-grained motion and long-range temporal context.
Introduces an input-conditioned Gaussian Memory Bank with gated cross-attention at encoder and anchor-query stages.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on EGTEA and EPIC-Kitchens-100, with improvements on the non-egocentric Muses benchmark.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: DUGO Architecture. DSE replaces the single-granularity encoder with dual branches consisting of depthwise temporal convolutions for local modeling and self-attention for global temporal reasoning, followed by fusion through a learned projection. GMB replaces deterministic history compression with a stochastic mixture of Gaussian prototypes injected at two stages: encoder memory refinement (Pass 1) and decoded anchor query enhancement (Pass 2) through per-head gated cross-attention.

Fig. 1: Motivation. Egocentric procedural videos require fine-grained motion discrimination, memory of prior steps, and procedure-aware framing. Prior OnTAL methods rely on single-scale encoding with absent or one-shot deterministic memory; DUGO introduces dual-scale encoding and a twice-injected stochastic Gaussian memory that preserves multi-modal procedural ambiguity.
Fig. 3: Gaussian prototypes Kg analysis of DUGO on EGTEA and EPIC-Kitchens-100 datasets across various tIoU thresholds.

papers.selection_reason: Online temporal action localization in egocentric procedural videos with a dual-scale encoder and Gaussian memory bank; directly fits video understanding and temporal action reasoning.
papers.title: DUGO: Dual-Scale Gaussian Memory for Online Temporal Action Localization in Egocentric Procedural Videos
papers.tldr: DUGO improves real-time action localization in streaming egocentric videos by combining dual-scale temporal modeling with stochastic Gaussian memory.

papers.abstract: Dense 3D tracking from monocular video requires establishing point correspondences over time, estimating their depth, and inferring their trajectories during occlusion. Existing methods typically learn these tasks jointly, a demanding objective given the scarcity of 4D supervision. We show that strong pretrained 2D trackers and 3D geometry models provide an effective foundation: lifted trajectories, with occluded segments simply interpolated, already rival dedicated 3D trackers using the same geometry. However, lifted trajectories inherit correspondence and depth errors, and under occlusion, their depth comes from the occluder rather than the tracked point. We introduce ReLift, an efficient feed-forward framework that recasts dense 3D tracking as geometric trajectory repair and completion. At its core, a trajectory corrector alternates attention along and across trajectories to preserve reliable observations, repair corrupted positions, and complete missing motion. Using only geometric inputs allows us to train directly on 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, decoupling training from images and from any specific tracker or geometry model. Concentrating 4D supervision on trajectory refinement yields a reusable model that consistently improves lifted trajectories across trackers and geometry providers without retraining, so it benefits directly from future advances in either component. On WorldTrack, ReLift achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy, improving on the strongest baselines by 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 on dynamic points, with faster configurations remaining competitive with leading 3D trackers while running faster than 4RC. Visit our supplementry page for more examples and code.
authors: Assaf Singer, Maroun Khriesh, Noam Rotstein, Yoni Kasten, Or Litany
bullets: Addresses correspondence, depth, and occlusion errors inherited from lifting 2D tracks into 3D.
Uses a feed-forward trajectory corrector with attention along and across trajectories.
Trains only on geometric 3D trajectories with simulated lifting errors, independent of images, trackers, or geometry models.
Improves trajectories across different trackers and geometry providers without retraining.
Achieves state-of-the-art WorldTrack accuracy, with gains of 2.1 APD on all points and 3.0 APD on dynamic points; faster variants remain competitive.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Inference pipeline of ReLift. Frozen pretrained models lift video observations (a–b) into corrupted and incomplete 3D trajectories (c). The corrector adds residuals to initialized XYZ coordinates to produce the final trajectories (d–e). The output head predicts frame-level XYZ residuals, which are added to the initialized trajectories. We train the corrector on simulated lifts from clean trajectory annotations (Sec. 3.4).

papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) trains a few-step student using the difference between a teacher's score and an online critic's estimate of the student distribution's score. We investigate what the critic needs, in capacity and in information, to provide a reliable training signal. On the capacity side, controlled experiments across seven SiT model sizes on ImageNet show that increasing teacher size while keeping a small critic fixed can degrade student quality and cause training collapse. Scaling the critic alongside the teacher, a strategy we call joint scaling, prevents collapse in our experiments and allows the student to benefit from larger teachers. On the information side, rather than forcing the critic to model a step-agnostic mixture of student outputs, we introduce a step-aware critic (STAC) that conditions on the student's generation step to estimate step-specific scores. Together, joint scaling and STAC consistently improve few-step distillation across class-conditional ImageNet generation, text-to-image generation with SDXL and FLUX.2, and text-to-video generation with Wan2.1.
authors: Zongze Wu (Adobe), Xianbang Wang (MIT), Zhengyang Geng (Adobe), Mingdeng Cao (Adobe), Zhoutong Zhang (Adobe), Richard Zhang (Adobe), Eli Shechtman (Adobe), Ruiming Cao (Adobe)
bullets: Larger teachers can hurt student quality and trigger training collapse when the critic remains small.
Joint scaling—growing the critic alongside the teacher—prevents collapse in controlled ImageNet experiments.
STAC conditions the critic on the student’s generation step instead of modeling a step-agnostic output mixture.
Joint scaling and STAC improve few-step distillation for class-conditional images, text-to-image, and text-to-video generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview. We study (a) step conditioning and (b) joint teacher–critic scaling. In (b), T and F denote teacher/critic capacity: T > F can be unstable, T < F inefficient, and T = F favorable here.

Figure 1: Few-step students distilled with a critic as large as the teacher. Top, samples of a 4-step FLUX.2 [klein] 4B student distilled with a 32B teacher and a 32B critic with STAC. Bottom, three frames each of six videos from a 4-step Wan2.1 1.3B student distilled with a 14B teacher and a 14B critic with STAC. (Settings: FLUX.2 1024× 1024, Wan2.1 480p.)
