STAC leads in VBench total at every evaluation in both regimes. (Settings: 1.3B teacher, student, and critic; ODE initialization from the CausVid repository (Yin et al., 2025); 4 steps, 480p, 2k iterations; bidirectional DMD uses no backward simulation, while the autoregressive runs use an online Self Forcing rollout.)

Figure 6: Generation quality varies sharply across steps. Clean predictions of a 4-step SDXL student along one generation path with a shared prompt and seed. Colored boxes and insets magnify the regions discussed below. The first step already fixes the overall color and layout but still carries significant artifacts; the second step refines the image substantially, yet artifacts remain in detailed regions such as the face and the wheel; the third step retains only small residual artifacts around the mouth, which the last step removes.

Figure 4: Per-update training compute versus FID. Best FID versus TFLOPs per student update for every non-collapsed teacher/critic pair of the S-student grids at (a) 1 and (b) 4 steps. Matched pairs are labeled by size and joined in size order; the nonlinear FID axis expands the low-FID region. At comparable per-update compute, matched pairs sit at or near the lowest FID, while most mismatched pairs lie above them. (Settings: ImageNet 256× 256, w/o CFG; learning rates as in Figure 10; FLOPs from Table 6.)

Figure 5: Scaling the teacher and critic on ImageNet. Every panel varies the teacher and critic sizes while the student is fixed. (a) FID over training for a 1-step B student under four teacher/critic pairs (B/B, XL/B, B/XL, XL/XL); the mismatched XL/B pair degrades only late, so (a) runs to 200k updates to expose it. (b, c) A 1-step S student over a grid of L, XL, and H teachers and S-to-H critics: (b) reports the best FID over training, and (c) the FID at a fixed 100k-update budget. Red boxes mark the diagonal, matched teacher/critic pairs. For both students, matched pairs give the lowest FID, while mismatched pairs often degrade and sometimes collapse (best FID of 100 or higher). (Settings: ImageNet 256× 256, w/o CFG; (a) default learning rates; (b, c) the best learning-rate pair per cell by the lowest FID over training.)

Figure 11: Guidance for DMD students and their teachers. FID against guidance scale for (a) 1-step B students distilled under CFG, (b) their teachers sampled with CFG, and (c) students distilled with a weak B model as the autoguidance reference. The students’ best CFG scale, about 1.3, lies below the teachers’ 1.5, and autoguidance does not improve on CFG. (Settings: ImageNet 256× 256, F = T for M, XL, and H; students report their best FID over training.)

Figure 19: SDXL samples of 4-step students across distillation methods. Each row shares a prompt and seed across PCM, SDXL-Lightning, DMD2, and its STAC continuation, with the prompt given below it. Compared with the other methods in this figure, DMD2 + STAC gives sharp images with coherent objects and faithful attributes. (Settings: 4 steps, 1024× 1024, shared seed per prompt.)

Figure 20: Wan2.1 samples of 4-step 1.3B students across teacher/critic pairs. Each row shows four frames of one video, and the three rows of a block share the prompt given below them. Big and small denote the 14B and 1.3B models. Frame change is the mean absolute luminance difference between consecutive shown frames, expressed as a percentage of the intensity range; higher values indicate greater temporal change, which may reflect either motion or artifacts. Red boxes mark artifacts. Relative to the big-teacher/small-critic pair, matching the critic to the big teacher recovers part of the temporal change and yields more plausible videos. (Settings: autoregressive Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B students with the Self Forcing rollout, 4 steps, 480p; teacher/critic pairs of Table 5.)

Figure 9: Joint scaling and STAC on a two-dimensional example. Samples of a 2-step, depth-3 student at each sampling step (rows), with energy distance (ED) to the target. The first column shows the single-roll target and an undistilled depth-3 teacher sampled with 20 Euler steps. The next three columns vary the teacher (T ) and critic (F ) depths, and the last adds STAC to the depth-6 pair. Deepening only the teacher makes both steps worse, deepening the critic as well reverses this, and STAC brings both steps closer to the single roll. (Settings: 4k DMD updates, five critic updates per student update; Table 13.)

Figure 13: More critic updates for a small critic. FID during training with the student-size critic at one and five updates per student update, and with an XL critic at one update, for (a) a B student with an L teacher, (b) a B student with an XL teacher, and (c) an S student with an XL teacher. Five updates speed up early training and avoid the collapse in (a), though the student-size critic stays at a higher FID than the single-update XL critic. (Settings: ImageNet 256× 256, 1-step students, w/o CFG.)

Figure 14: Critic warm-up. (a) FID of a 1-step S student under an H teacher with an S critic. The S critic is either trained concurrently from the start or warmed up for 10k/40k updates before student training begins. Both warm-ups fail to prevent collapse compared to the matched H critic. (b) Validation loss of an S critic fitted to a frozen student. (Settings: ImageNet 256× 256, w/o CFG.)

Figure 12: Teacher scaling under velocity KD and MeanFlow distillation. Best FID against teacher size for (a) an S student regressed onto each larger teacher’s velocity (the S teacher was not evaluated) and (b) S and B students distilled with MeanFlow at 1 and 4 steps. No teacher collapses these students, and the gain from a larger teacher shrinks as it grows. (Settings: ImageNet 256× 256; KD: learning rate 10−4, 200k updates; MFD: official MeanFlow recipe with default guidance coefficients, 200k updates for S and 60k for B students.)

Figure 3: The joint scaling phenomenon. Starting from an S-sized teacher, critic, and student and fixing the student size, each panel scales (a, left) the teacher, (b, middle) the critic, or (c, right) both along the ladder, with the horizontal axis the parameter count of the scaled network. Scaling only the teacher initially improves FID but eventually degrades it and causes collapse at H; scaling only the critic yields marginal gains; scaling both improves the student at every size. (Settings: 1-step S student, ImageNet 256× 256, w/o CFG; best FID with the per-cell learning-rate selection of Appendix B.2.)

Figure 10: The expanded teacher–critic scaling grid. Best FID per teacher/critic pair for S and B students at 1 and 4 steps. Red boxes mark the matched pairs, and hatched cells mark collapsed runs, whose best FID is 100 or higher under all nine learning-rate pairs. Every collapse occurs with a critic smaller than its teacher. (Settings: ImageNet 256× 256, w/o CFG, 200k updates; learning-rate selection as in Figure 5b.)

Figure 18: FLUX.2 samples of 4-step 4B students across teacher/critic pairs. Each row shares a prompt (listed below) and initial noise. The first two columns display the 50-step 4B and 9B teachers for reference. The subsequent columns show 4-step students distilled under the 4B/4B, 9B/4B, and 9B/9B teacher/critic pairs, alongside the 9B/9B pair combined with STAC. (Settings: students initialized from FLUX.2 [klein] base 4B, 4 steps; teachers sampled with 50 Euler steps at CFG 2.0; resolution 512× 512.)

Lower bound on the mutual information I(K;Xt) from a classifier predicting the step index of a 4-step B student, evaluated at (a) 30k and (b) 100k updates with online weights, and (c) at 100k updates with EMA weights. (Settings: ImageNet 256× 256, XL teacher and critic, w/o CFG; 10k fixed noise–class pairs, 8k/2k training/held-out split.)

papers.abstract: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.

Trains PanoVideoReasoner using Panoramic CoT SFT and evidence-privileged on-policy self-distillation.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation enables efficient inference through streaming prediction. However, existing methods are typically restricted to fixed sampling steps, limiting the flexibility to balance generation quality and efficiency, while one-step generation suffers from degraded visual quality and error accumulation over long sequences, leading to content drift and generation collapse. To address these issues, we propose Any Forcing, a unified framework for achieving Any-Step Generality and One-Step Stability. Specifically, we introduce a unified adversarial discriminator that jointly performs real-distribution alignment, inter-step consistency alignment, and first-frame quality enhancement, enabling flexible sampling while preserving one-step generation quality. Furthermore, we propose a training-free adaptive long-term memory selection mechanism that selects historical states based on global semantic relevance and local value contribution, while remapping their temporal positions to preserve temporal relationships within the memory cache, thereby enabling stable one-step long-video generation. Experiments demonstrate that Any Forcing achieves high-quality and stable one-step autoregressive video generation, achieving 20.9 FPS and 24.7 FPS for short and long video generation on a single H100 GPU, respectively.

Reports stable one-step generation at 20.9 FPS for short videos and 24.7 FPS for long videos on a single H100 GPU.

papers.abstract: Video generation models synthesize realistic motion, but can they respond correctly to changes in initial geometry? We introduce GeoFlip, a video generation benchmark centered on physical outcome flips induced by geometry. With shared physical settings and textual prompts held fixed, GeoFlip applies controlled interventions to support extent, object placement, and mechanism configuration, constructing paired scenes with contrasting reference events, such as remaining stable versus falling or tipping. These pairs test whether models translate geometric differences in the first frame into correct physical evolution. The benchmark comprises 482 scene pairs and 964 reference videos across six physical categories, with reference outcomes established through procedural scene construction, physics simulation, and numerical validation and verification of physical events. We evaluate 16 models for image to video generation along three dimensions: event correctness, structural integrity, and similarity to reference videos. We examine evaluation consistency with independent vision language judges. On the 442 conditions shared by all models, the highest event correctness averaged across tasks is 27.98%, revealing substantial limitations in physical generation conditioned on geometry. Model strengths vary across physical mechanisms, and the three evaluation dimensions capture distinct capabilities. Typical failures include ignoring geometric changes, generating incorrect object motion, bending rigid objects, and introducing additional components. Rank correlations between judges reach 0.906 for event correctness and 0.929 for structural integrity. By combining controlled geometric interventions, verifiable physical references, and multidimensional evaluation, GeoFlip assesses progress from visual realism toward physical consistency conditioned on geometry.

papers.abstract: High accuracy on streaming video benchmarks does not establish whether a model uses visual history. Our review of OVO-Bench and StreamingBench finds that recent frames suffice for 32% of sampled historical questions, while models also answer many questions correctly from the question and options alone. We introduce TwinPast to test whether answers correctly follow changes in history, using 350 human-reviewed video pairs spanning five historical tasks. Each pair holds the recent video context, question, and ordered options fixed while changing critical historical evidence and the correct answer. Each video is evaluated independently, and PairAcc requires correct answers for both histories. We evaluate 34 model and input configurations. For Qwen3-VL-8B and DeepSeek-Flash, historical inputs improve performance on TwinPast, reversing the recent-frame advantage on existing benchmarks. The strongest evaluated streaming system reaches 49.14% PairAcc, compared with 66.57-91.43% for the evaluated general-purpose models. This gap persists across all five tasks. Case studies further show that models select states from the wrong time or contradict recorded event order despite retaining the relevant evidence. These findings highlight the need to connect historical memory and retrieval with reasoning that uses evidence according to the question's temporal references and event relations.
authors: Haotian Yang, Yong Chen, Cheng Peng, Haobo Wang, Zhongle Xie, Xuanru Li, Gang Chen

Across 34 model/input configurations, the strongest streaming system achieved 49.14% PairAcc, below evaluated general-purpose models at 66.57–91.43%.
Failures include selecting states from the wrong time and contradicting the recorded order of events, motivating better temporal retrieval and evidence-based reasoning.

papers.abstract: Few-step flow models generate samples through a handful of large denoising transitions. Applying GRPO to such models requires introducing stochasticity into the denoising transitions, and when a single transition spans a wide range of noise levels, the choice of the resulting stochastic policy becomes a major factor in optimization. Recent constructions constrain the policy to preserve the target flow coefficients, but this constraint admits a family of policies and offers no criterion for choosing among them. We introduce Geo-FSRL (Geometry-Optimized Few-Step Reinforcement Learning), built on a selection principle: at a fixed conditioning state and timestep pair, choose the admissible policy that minimizes the conditional KL divergence induced by any given nonzero velocity-output update. Within a coefficient-preserving family of isotropic Gaussian transitions, this criterion reduces to minimizing a single scalar geometry factor that determines the conditional KL for every velocity-output update. The same factor governs velocity-space Fisher information and conditional transition log-likelihood-ratio variance. We derive the unique closed-form optimizer within this family, shared across all nonzero update magnitudes and directions, with transition coefficients determined by both the source and target noise levels. Because the minimized geometry factor still varies across timesteps, we further adopt gradient-scale matching from prior work and derive closed-form policy-gradient and KL weights that normalize explicit score scales and reference-KL curvature. Geo-FSRL trains on the original few-step schedule and retains the deterministic solver at inference. Our method achieves higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image generation and video generation models under the 4-step setting. Code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/lightx2v_rl

Geo-FSRL selects the admissible isotropic Gaussian policy minimizing conditional KL divergence under velocity-output updates.
This criterion reduces to a scalar geometry factor that also controls velocity-space Fisher information and transition log-likelihood-ratio variance.
The method derives a unique closed-form transition optimizer and timestep-dependent policy-gradient and KL weights through gradient-scale matching.
Experiments report higher final reward scores than Flow-GRPO and Flow-CPS on both image and video generation models in the 4-step setting; inference retains the deterministic solver.

papers.abstract: Flow matching depends critically on the coupling used to pair source and target samples. Optimal transport (OT) couplings can reduce velocity conflict and straighten trajectories; but, in practice, challenges remain: the source comes from a continuous distribution, only a finite number of target samples data are accessible, and the neural network has finite capacity. For these reasons, making the coupling more OT-like may not consistently improve sampling quality, in particular in the low number-of-function-evaluation (NFE) regime. Motivated by this, we introduce ReCouple, a controllable framework that constructs coarse-grained OT couplings, to better understand rollout-free OT-based post-training. We also consider extensions of this basic framework: ReCouple+ extends this toward the continuous-source setting by increasing source resolution, converging to semi-discrete OT in the appropriate limit; and ReCouple++ further adds spatial regularization, motivated by the observation that straight trajectories need not correspond to spatially simple velocity fields. Empirical validation demonstrates the effectiveness of these methods, and it reveals an NFE-dependent interplay between coupling optimality, neural realizability, and generation quality.
authors: Soon Hoe Lim, Aditi Gupta, Michael W. Mahoney, N. Benjamin Erichson
bullets: Flow matching quality depends strongly on how source and target samples are coupled.
More OT-like couplings can reduce velocity conflict and straighten trajectories, but may not help with finite data, continuous sources, limited network capacity, or low NFE.
ReCouple constructs coarse-grained OT couplings; ReCouple+ increases source resolution toward semi-discrete OT.
ReCouple++ adds spatial regularization because straight trajectories do not necessarily yield spatially simple velocity fields.
Experiments show an NFE-dependent trade-off between coupling optimality, neural realizability, and sampling quality.

papers.abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.
authors: Eadom Dessalene, Michael Maynord, Amir-Hossein Shahidzadeh, Botao He, Yasamin Tabatabaee, Ruoshi Liu, Ruohan Gao, Paul Pu Liang, Yiannis Aloimonos
bullets: Pairs egocentric video with bimanual EMG, IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation.
Uses EMG as a dense, occlusion-free alternative to costly and subjective manual action annotation.
Learns shared sensorimotor representations through video–EMG cross-modal pretraining.
Transfers the learned representations to action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction.
Also conditions video diffusion on EMG to generate fine-grained hand-manipulation videos; the approach outperforms evaluated video self-supervised baselines across four tasks and eight datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MOTORSENSE. (A) Sensorimotor Alignment. Windows 1, . . . , N of bimanual EMG (left) and egocentric video (right) are embedded by an EMG encoder and a video encoder and aligned with a symmetric contrastive objective (Section 3.2): the video and EMG embeddings of the same window (Vi, Ei) are pulled together, while embeddings from different windows are pushed apart. (B) Downstream Tasks. The learned representations are used for downstream tasks: 1) video diffusion consisting of a single reference frame as input along with EMG control signals, 2) action recognition, 3) 3D hand-object Reconstruction, 4) 3D hand contact prediction.

Figure 7: Qualitative results for video diffusion. We compare our proposed motor conditioning to a video diffusion model conditioned solely on the video history (unimodal conditioning), for a sequence involving the stirring of tofu in a pan. The video conditioning model misinterprets the action performed, generating a video of a scooping action as opposed to a stirring action, whereas our method correctly generates a video of the stirring of tofu.

Figure 8: Qualitative results for video diffusion. We compare our proposed motor conditioning to a video diffusion model conditioned solely on the video history (unimodal conditioning), for a sequence involving the spreading of mayonnaise with a spoon. The video conditioning model misinterprets the action performed, generating a rotation of the bread as opposed to a spreading action of the spoon, whereas our method correctly generates a video of the spreading of mayonnaise with a spoon.

Figure 9: Qualitative results for video diffusion. We compare our proposed motor conditioning to a video diffusion model conditioned solely on the video history (unimodal conditioning), for a bimanual manipulation sequence involving the peeling of an avocado. The video conditioning model renders the index finger as resting against the thumb, whereas our method correctly positions the index finger against the surface of the avocado for the peeling action.

A "modality gap" is observed [37] between video and EMG clusters. (b) The clips associated with each pair: the video query (left) and the clip whose EMG was retrieved (right). Each retrieved clip performs the query’s hand action—cutting, mixing in a bowl, drying—with a different object, scene, and recording. Best viewed zoomed-in and in colour.

Figure 1: EMG captures both categorical and continuous structure of hand actions. (Top) For three discrete hand configurations repeated twice—fist, point, and flat—each pose produces a distinct and reproducible EMG signature: fist is marked by a suppressed purple channel (#7) with respect to flat and a pronounced red channel (#1) with respect to point; point exhibits lower overall amplitude, with less purple than flat and less red than fist; flat is distinguished by pronounced purple and red activation. Sharp grey rectangles reflect the boundaries between hand gestures and rest states. (Bottom) A pick-and-lift sequence combines gradual and abrupt transitions: the hand moves smoothly from rest through pregrasp into grasp, changes sharply as force is applied at lift, then settles—non-instantaneously—into a steady hold. The EMG mirrors this structure, with channels quiet at rest, building subtly through pregrasp and grasp, peaking sharply as the lift begins, and stabilizing during hold.

papers.selection_reason: Egocentric video and EMG sensorimotor alignment for action understanding; learns transferable embodied knowledge from human interaction videos.
papers.title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding
papers.tldr: MotorSense introduces a large-scale synchronized video–EMG dataset and cross-modal pretraining approach that aligns visual and motor representations for improved action understanding and hand manipulation generation.

papers.abstract: The reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) can be limited by incomplete or inaccurate visual observations in the general domain. In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes, small targets, subtle attributes, and changing viewpoints further complicate perception and understanding. Therefore, we introduce Drone-PUR, a dataset and benchmark organized around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration, corresponding to the three capability dimensions of perception, understanding, and reasoning. Reasoning samples are designed to require models to combine multiple visual clues to derive visually grounded conclusions. Its 11 tasks provide 175k training and 20k test samples spanning single images, image sequences, cross-modal images, and multiple viewpoints. All test samples undergo human review. Evaluating 22 general-purpose VLMs reveals persistent limitations in spatial judgment and cross-modal and cross-view reasoning. Across models, stronger perception is associated with better reasoning, while single-task fine-tuning further reveals selective bidirectional transfer between these capabilities. To examine domain adaptation, we develop UAV-PUR from Qwen3-VL through staged fine-tuning with auxiliary supervision. Its 4B and 8B variants improve overall multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points over their pretrained counterparts, respectively. The dataset and project resources are available at https://drone-pur.github.io.
authors: Jiahe Wu, Bing Cao, Xingyue Guo, Ruipu Zhao, Beiming Yu, Jiekang Feng, Qinghua Hu, Pengfei Zhu
bullets: Targets incomplete visual observations involving small objects, subtle attributes, changing viewpoints, and multimodal inputs.
Organizes tasks around visual clue discovery, interpretation, and integration across images, sequences, cross-modal images, and viewpoints.
Contains 175k training and 20k human-reviewed test samples; evaluations cover 22 general-purpose VLMs.
Finds persistent weaknesses in spatial judgment and cross-modal/cross-view reasoning, with stronger perception linked to better reasoning.
UAV-PUR models adapted from Qwen3-VL improve multiple-choice accuracy by 18.33 and 17.52 percentage points for 4B and 8B variants, respectively.

papers.tldr: Drone-PUR benchmarks and improves VLM perception, understanding, and reasoning in challenging UAV scenes through 11 visually grounded tasks.

papers.abstract: Streaming video assistance requires models to answer asynchronous questions from an observed prefix under a fixed context budget. Existing approaches model response timing or compress history, but an online state formed before future questions are known can omit visual details before later questions reveal their relevance; the retained state alone cannot recover them. We introduce Watch-Think-Interact (WTI), a closed-loop framework for multi-question streaming video reasoning. WTI maintains compact natural-language memory entries tagged with source-video time ranges; these entries support direct reasoning when sufficient and otherwise anchor selective recall of finer visual evidence. For each question, WTI answers when current context and memory suffice, continues watching when required evidence has not appeared, or recalls a relevant past interval and decides again after incorporating the returned chunks, without replaying the full observed history. To train this behavior, we construct WTI-82K, comprising 82,335 timed questions across 4,812 causally aligned trajectories, and develop Stream-GDPO to optimize complete multi-question streaming rollouts using trajectory-level feedback for response timing, source-video recall, and memory updates. WTI achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance among the compared open-source streaming baselines, reaching 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted overall accuracy on OVO-Bench.
bullets: Addresses the problem that early online summaries may omit visual details needed by later questions under a fixed context budget.
Stores compact natural-language memories linked to source-video time ranges, enabling targeted recall without replaying the full history.
Uses a closed-loop policy that decides whether to answer, continue watching, or retrieve past visual evidence before answering.
Trains with Stream-GDPO on WTI-82K, optimizing response timing, video recall, and memory updates across complete question trajectories.
Reports 83.3% on StreamingBench and 73.6% weighted accuracy on OVO-Bench, achieving state-of-the-art performance among compared open-source baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Watch-Think-Interact. For each arriving chunk, WTI updates a short thinking state and chooses to remain silent, answer, or recall. Recall returns visual evidence and loops back to the decision at the same time step; controller-triggered memory updates separately compress elapsed observations into a bounded temporal index. Stream-GDPO optimizes the resulting complete interaction trajectories.

Figure 3: WTI-82K construction pipeline. WTI-82K converts videos into streaming-causal trajectories by standardizing clips, aligning chunk-level evidence chains, generating QAs from aligned evidence, placing query and answerable times, and checking timestamp bounds, answer availability, action grammar, and evidence-interval fields. The resulting samples cover Real-Time, Backward Tracing, and Proactive interactions under the same visibility constraints as inference.

Figure 1: Motivation for Watch-Think-Interact. In causal streaming video, asynchronous questions may require current, past, or not-yet-observed evidence. WTI uses a bounded active window for current perception, compact time-indexed memory for direct reasoning and temporal localization, and selective recall to reload a past visual interval.

Figure 4: Training-time GSPO/Stream-GDPO diagnostics. Panels report outcome accuracy, BT recall triggering, post-recall outcome accuracy, and memory quality; faint and bold curves show raw and rolling values.
Table 1: Results on OVO-Bench. Scores are grouped by Real-Time, Backward, and Forward tasks; Avg. gives the corresponding group average, and Overall gives the benchmark average.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming video reasoning with memory and RL, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: Watch-Think-Interact: Bootstrapping Long-Horizon Multi-Turn Streaming Video Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: WTI enables long-horizon streaming video assistants to answer multi-turn questions by combining compact time-tagged memory, selective visual recall, and reinforcement learning for when to watch, recall, or respond.

papers.abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to localize the spatio-temporal tube in a video corresponding to a natural language query. While recent methods achieve strong performance in fully supervised, weakly supervised, and zero-shot settings, they typically rely on computationally expensive architectures, complex training pipelines, or multimodal large language models. We present Pocket-STVG (P-STVG), a lightweight cascade architecture that addresses STVG by combining efficient pre-trained components instead of large end-to-end models. P-STVG integrates a temporal-aware video encoder based on MobileViCLIP, a spatial encoder-decoder derived from MDETR, and a shared aligned text encoder. Temporal localization is performed through either a lightweight 1D U-Net or a simple thresholding strategy, enabling the same framework to operate in both weakly supervised and zero-shot settings. Furthermore, video representations are precomputed independently of the query, yielding an indexing-friendly pipeline for efficient inference and large-scale video collections. Despite requiring fewer than 90M parameters, P-STVG performs on par with weakly supervised methods and improves on earlier zero-shot approaches at a fraction of their memory and computational cost, establishing a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off for STVG.
bullets: Targets efficient spatio-temporal video grounding without large end-to-end models or multimodal LLMs.
Combines MobileViCLIP-based temporal encoding, an MDETR-derived spatial encoder-decoder, and a shared text encoder.
Supports weakly supervised and zero-shot settings using either a lightweight 1D U-Net or thresholding for temporal localization.
Precomputes query-independent video representations to enable efficient inference over large video collections.
Uses fewer than 90M parameters, matches weakly supervised methods, and improves over earlier zero-shot approaches at lower memory and compute cost.

papers.abstract: Video captioning models are increasingly evaluated with metrics designed for single-sentence image captions. We test whether those metrics recover human judgement on dense, multi-window video description, and find that they do not. Six frontier models captioned 196 short clips. Trained annotators post-edited every caption against a failure taxonomy fixed before annotation, once as a whole-clip overview and once window by window, and a quality-control reviewer checked each annotation, yielding 1,144 overview verdicts and 4,672 window verdicts. Reference-overlap metrics do not separate the captions reviewers accepted from those they rejected: BLEU-4 reaches an AUC of 0.510 and a CIDEr-style tf-idf cosine 0.528, and restricting references to reviewer corrections leaves BLEU-4 at 0.479 (95% CI 0.431-0.529), indistinguishable from chance. Review granularity changes what is detected. The same annotators record camera and shot errors on 2.7% of captions when reading the overview and on 12.8% when reading window by window, a 4.7x gap that holds across every robustness check we ran, on the mode most likely to need a near-total rewrite. Correct-overview rates span 54.1-72.7%, but only 4 of 15 pairwise gaps survive Bonferroni correction (5 after adjusting for reviewer and clip effects), and accuracy and derived severity order the models differently. Models with statistically indistinguishable accuracy have sharply different failure profiles, which no single scalar shows. We argue that caption evaluation should record what was wrong rather than only how often, and we report the taxonomy, the per-model profiles, the corpus properties that predict difficulty, and the code that regenerates every number in the paper.
bullets: Six models captioned 196 short clips, with human corrections assessed for whole-clip overviews and window-by-window descriptions.
BLEU-4 and CIDEr-style scores were essentially chance-level at distinguishing accepted from rejected captions.
Window-by-window review detected camera and shot errors 4.7× more often than overview review.
Models with similar overall accuracy showed sharply different failure types, and accuracy and severity ranked models differently.
The study advocates reporting failure taxonomies and per-model error profiles instead of relying on a single scalar score.

papers.abstract: As robots and intelligent systems increasingly interact with humans, they must anticipate long sequences of future actions from only brief observations. While purely neural models typically require extensive observations to predict future actions and remain difficult to interpret and adjust, symbolic priors offer a structured alternative. To this end, we introduce SymAnt, a novel neuro-symbolic approach that unifies the expressiveness of neural networks with the structured reasoning of scene and knowledge graphs. Given a short video, SymAnt performs a joint-search over both graphs to construct a symbolic context, enabling unified reasoning over spatial relationships, object attributes, affordances, and associated actions. This symbolic context serves as a prior for an iterative refinement process that progressively generates and improves the sequence of future actions. By grounding predictions in symbolic context, SymAnt anticipates long-horizon actions from short observation windows in a parameter-efficient manner, while enabling users to directly edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without further training. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SymAnt, particularly when only short observation contexts are available, across five diverse datasets: Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+, and Assembly101.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual instance segmentation (AVIS) segments and tracks individual sound-producing objects in videos. Existing benchmarks predominantly use monaural audio, which lacks inter-channel cues for spatially distinguishing concurrent sound sources. We introduce AVPS-360 (Audio-Visual Person Segmentation 360), a spatial audio-visual benchmark bridging AVIS and sound event localisation and detection (SELD). Built upon STARSS23, it pairs first-order Ambisonics audio with synchronised 360{\deg} video across 230 recordings totalling 10.5 hours. Recordings average 164.0 seconds. The dataset captures intermittent sound production in real-world interactions dominated by speech, alongside laughter, clapping, and footsteps. It provides 31,678 manually reviewed instance masks linked to source identities and sound-event labels. We also present a baseline that integrates spatial audio with visual features for frame-level segmentation and identity association across frames. Experiments on AVPS-360 show that existing AVIS methods struggle with detection and identity association in long recordings with intermittent sound production, while our baseline substantially improves performance in both aspects.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly, without retraining or fine-tuning the models. We validate the method on analytic Gaussian models, where it closely matches the ground-truth targets, and on diffusion models trained on MNIST, where it samples from non-trivial combinations of the models and enables effective steering.
bullets: Naively combining diffusion-model scores produces incorrect samples, and prior corrections support only limited target families.
The method uses a generalized Feynman–Kac formulation to derive closed-form correction potentials for arbitrary functions of multiple models.
A generalized log-probability ODE tracks each model’s density along trajectories driven by another velocity field.
Corrections and reward-based steering are applied during generation in the log domain, without retraining or fine-tuning.
Experiments on analytic Gaussian targets and MNIST show close agreement with ground truth and effective sampling of non-trivial combinations.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.
authors: Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
bullets: Addresses limited generalization, motion control, and interactivity in existing video world models.
Uses skeleton and geometry representations as structured proxies to condition video generation.
Introduces adaptive masking to better align control signals with generated video rollouts.
Maintains and updates game states through an agentic framework for consistent, configurable gameplay.
Targets real-time, visually coherent world simulation with player-driven character control.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of Wizard. Our method supports diverse gameplay experiences, including world exploration, character summoning, character transformation, and scene manipulation. By combining agentic control with geometric scene proxies and articulated character skeletons, Wizard achieves fine-grained control, zero-shot generalization, and mechanics-consistent gameplay with real-time interaction at 24 FPS.

Figure 2. Dataset Overview and Processing Pipeline. We construct 50.3 hours of data spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters from four complementary sources. Scene geometry and character skeletons are jointly encoded into unified visual proxies, followed by filtering and captioning to produce aligned proxy–video training pairs.

Figure 3. Inference Pipeline of Wizard. (a) Character animation is driven by motions retrieved from a high-quality library and retargeted from compatible source skeletons to the target character’s skeleton. (b) Scene manipulation is performed by a world agent that edits 3D scene geometry and renders visual proxies using OpenGL. (c) State-aware combat control adapts boss behavior to the current game state and enforces rule-based combat mechanics. (d) Real-time video generation is conditioned on visual proxies, reference images, and previously generated frames.

Figure 4. Video Generator Architecture and Character-Aware Adaptive Masking. (a) Visual proxy latents are concatenated with noisy video latents along channels, then combined with first-frame and character-reference tokens along the sequence dimension for DiT processing. (b) Skeleton-derived spatial masks restrict reference attention to the corresponding character regions, binding appearance guidance to character locations.

papers.abstract: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.
authors: Liaoyuan Fan, Yuhao Zheng, Dongxing Mao, Hangyu Ran, Siyuan Hu, Weijia Mao, Rui Zhao, Weijia Wu, Guian Fang, Yanzhe Chen, Zeyu Zhu, Yuxin Jiang, Yiren Song, Yuchao Gu, Junchao Yi, Qi Hu, Dan Kong, Alex Jinpeng Wang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Mike Zheng Shou, Wei Liu
bullets: Agent harnesses manage context, tools, state, feedback, and budgets around video models.
Agentic video generation coordinates scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing for coherent multi-shot videos.
Agentic world models combine action-conditioned video predictions with interactive control, potentially using game engines or programs to maintain world state.
Recursive self-improvement can revise outputs, harness state, model parameters, evaluators, or the improvement process itself.
Key open challenges include long-horizon planning, memory, provenance, cost accounting, hybrid control, and evaluation tied to sustained improvement.

In a video world model, one-shot conditioning becomes sustained control, temporal context must support continuing state, and output frames become observations for the next decision. papers.abstract: Given a set of procedural steps, Video Step Grounding (VSG) aims to identify which steps occur in a video and localize when they are performed. Existing methods are either offline, requiring access to the full video before making predictions, or online, but relying on fixed-length video segments producing noisy, over-segmented outputs. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Step Decomposition (HSD), a training-free framework for online VSG that leverages the semantic understanding capabilities of Large Multimodal Models. HSD addresses two central challenges in online grounding: constructing semantically coherent temporal segments from a streaming video, and bridging the semantic gap between coarse procedural step descriptions and visual observations. To construct elementary temporal units, HSD incrementally groups incoming segments into semantically consistent events, using an anchor caption that is continuously validated against the visual stream. Based on these events, we perform zero-shot procedural step classification and selectively refine uncertain predictions by decomposing candidate steps into finegrained substeps that capture more nuanced visual evidence. By operating on semantically coherent events rather than every fixed-length segment, HSD reduces redundant computation and produces more stable predictions. Experiments on HT-Step, Ego4D Goal-Step, and CrossTask show that HSD substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, overall achieving better step recognition, more accurate temporal localization, and faster inference.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of HSD. Given an input video V , the Online Semantic Event Construction module incrementally builds each event Ej from fixed-duration segments using a frozen LMM ΦLMM. The first segment of Ej is captioned as γanc, and each arriving segment is appended to Ej if its continuity score ϵsame exceeds ϵnew ; otherwise, Ej is terminated and a new event is initialized. For each completed event Ej , the Zero-Shot Event-to-Step Grounding module predicts a probability distribution pj over procedural steps. If its entropy Hj falls below threshold η, the most likely step is predicted. Otherwise, Hierarchical Step Refinement decomposes the top-k steps into substeps, re-evaluates Ej , aggregates substep scores into psubj , and outputs the final prediction âj .

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now process hour-long videos, making extended multi-turn dialogue over a single video a natural mode of use. Sustaining such a dialogue requires more than answering each question in isolation: the model must retrieve and reuse information established earlier in the conversation, both what it has seen and what it has said, an ability we term in-context video memory. Existing video QA benchmarks leave this ability unmeasured: their questions are mutually independent, never reference one another, and each is answerable from the video alone, so nothing ever requires carrying information across turns. We introduce VideoMemBench, in which each sample pairs a single video with a long multi-turn dialogue, whose turns are connected by typed cross-turn dependencies: an Episodic Dependency refers back to a visual episode described in an earlier turn, probing memory of what the model has seen, while an Answer Dependency builds on the model's own earlier answer, probing memory of what the model has said. Every dependency is verified considering two properties: 1) necessity, meaning the question cannot be answered without its earlier turns, and 2) non-leakage, meaning the question does not restate the information from its earlier turns. To enforce these properties, we design a construction pipeline with three LLM roles: a planner, a generator, and a judger, with each dialogue reviewed by human experts. VideoMemBench comprises 326 videos with 2,476 turns, of which 1,387 depend on earlier turns, including multi-parent dependencies and long-range call-back. Among over 20 evaluated open- and closed-source MLLMs, Claude Opus 5 performs the best with an overall score of only 45.7\%, highlighting the challenge of in-context video memory. Our dataset and evaluation are released.
authors: Zhengdong Hu, Chao Wang, Kaituo Feng, Huanjin Yao, Mingfei Lu, Hehe Fan, Yi Yang

Across 20+ open- and closed-source MLLMs, the best reported overall score is only 45.7%, underscoring the difficulty.

papers.abstract: Understanding the internal routing of visual concepts is crucial for the safe and controllable adaptation of generative models. While concept localization has been widely studied in diffusion models, the emerging paradigm of next-scale visual autoregressive models remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce LoCo, the first model-agnostic framework to localize where and when specific concepts emerge within autoregressive models. Driven by the native coarse-to-fine nature of next-scale generation, our method precisely maps conceptual knowledge across three distinct dimensions: Layer, Scale, and Position. To systematically localize and evaluate concept routing without context bias, we propose LoCoBench, a comprehensive dataset spanning 10 diverse categories. Extensive probing on image and video autoregressive models like Infinity, HunyuanImage-3.0, and InfinityStar shows that the localized positions are both interpretable and causally related to concept emergence. Building on these insights, we apply our localization method to three key applications: concept erasure, model personalization, and adversarial concept injection. Experiments demonstrate that our targeted intervention achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially reducing computational overhead while preserving benign utility. Overall, our findings offer insights into how conceptual knowledge is routed during autoregressive generation, introducing a practical pathway for more interpretable, efficient, and secure adaptation.
authors: Nanxiang Jiang, Yang Liu, Yuanhao Wang, Min Xu

Probing image and video models finds localized positions that are interpretable and causally linked to concept emergence.

papers.abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation (RVOS) lacks event-stream datasets and models. We introduce Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event conversion of the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus and all additional SAMA training data: 30,650 video clips and 392,162 images. Optical-flow, FILM or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator preserves all mask, referring-expression and dialogue annotations. We also introduce Event-SAMA, adapting SAMA-4B with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialised from pretrained RGB weights and a zero-initialised event adapter. End-to-end training yields 24.37 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on the converted ReVOS valid subset, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline (RGB SAMA-4B: 55.4 on MeViS). Frozen RGB SAMA-4B with pseudo-RGB renderings or E2VID reconstructions of the same events scores 13.23 and 15.94 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$. Without retraining, Event-SAMA works on real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches their event density. A seed-controlled ablation with a measured noise floor of 0.47 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ finds gains from diverse training sources over MeViS alone (+4.99), RGB-mean event-stem initialisation (+4.33), and a trainable SAM2 mask decoder (+2.76); the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing and event polarity are within noise at this budget. An earlier, partially converted corpus snapshot trained with the identical recipe scores 1.38 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ higher on MeViS and 1.12 higher on ReVOS. Both are single runs that also differ in schedule length, so we draw no conclusion about corpus scale.

papers.abstract: Colonoscopy is inherently comparative: reliable visual assessment of polyps often depends on complementary views acquired under different viewpoints and imaging conditions. Retrieving such views requires polyp tracklet representations, which recent contrastive methods learn from temporal cues but still build from manually annotated bounding boxes. We propose an annotation-free framework that constructs tracklet views directly from raw colonoscopy videos, enabling temporal self-supervised learning on full-procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps. On REAL-Colon, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on tracklet retrieval and re-identification, outperforming both self-supervised and supervised baselines. We then introduce few-shot polyp retrieval, a task closer to clinical use, where a few observations of a target polyp are used to retrieve its remaining tracklets: with only two examples, our method surpasses most competing methods given ten. Finally, we show that a modest number of unlabeled procedures suffices for competitive performance, making on-site model development more practical. Code is available at https://github.com/lparolari/freerep.
authors: Luca Parolari, Lamberto Ballan, Carlo Biffi, Loic Le Folgoc
bullets: Addresses the need to retrieve complementary polyp views across viewpoints and imaging conditions without manual bounding-box annotations.
Builds tracklet views directly from full-procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps, for temporal self-supervised learning.
Achieves state-of-the-art tracklet retrieval and re-identification on REAL-Colon against supervised and self-supervised baselines.
In few-shot retrieval, two target-polyp examples outperform most competing methods using ten examples.
Competitive performance requires only a modest number of unlabeled procedures, supporting more practical on-site development.

papers.abstract: In segmentation-based continuous sign language recognition, an untrimmed video is first partitioned into lexical units; segmentation is therefore a means to an end---downstream recognition. However, segmenters are usually judged by local boundary detection rather than by the quality of the lexical segments and the recognition they enable. We present BEACON, a begin/end-aware segmenter that combines four-class Outside/Begin/Inside/End (BIOE) labeling, constrained Viterbi decoding over eight legal transitions, and boundary knowledge distilled from a binary teacher into a shared student. Under strict no-cut evaluation with validation-based model selection, BEACON improves segment-F1 by 14.58/14.59 points and boundary-F1 by 2.17/1.22 points, and reduces the downstream word error rate (WER) by 9.10/4.15 points relative to the state-of-the-art in the PHOENIX-14/BSL Corpus. To examine which segmentation metric better reflects downstream recognition, we evaluated five distinct architecture families. Segment-F1 aligns more consistently with lower WER than boundary-F1 in both corpora (Spearman $\rho=-1.0/-0.9$ versus $-0.9/-0.8$). These results support evaluating sign language segmentation in terms of segment quality and downstream recognition utility rather than local boundary accuracy alone.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between local boundary metrics and the quality of lexical segments used for recognition.
Uses four-class BIOE labeling, constrained Viterbi decoding with eight legal transitions, and boundary knowledge distillation from a binary teacher.
Under strict no-cut evaluation, improves segment-F1 and boundary-F1 while reducing downstream WER on PHOENIX-14 and the BSL Corpus.
Across five architecture families, segment-F1 correlates more consistently with lower WER than boundary-F1.
Supports evaluating segmentation by segment quality and downstream recognition utility, not boundary accuracy alone.

figures.caption: Figure 3. The BEACON pipeline. A frozen I3D [3] backbone supplies frame features to a shared temporal encoder (Stage 1, standard). BIOE and soft Begin/End predictions are fused and decoded over the eight legal BIOE transitions (inset), producing a preliminary segment path that satisfies the declared grammar (Stage 2, ours). A binary IO branch reads the same shared hidden states H (no extra encoder) and refines endpoints within a validation-selected radius of at most ±3 frames (Stage 3, ours). During training only, a separately trained, frozen binary teacher (shown dashed, with its own encoder, and discarded after training) distills boundary evidence into this student IO branch via a KL loss; inference uses a single 5M-parameter model with one encoder. The lower strip visualizes the per-frame BIOE labels collapsing into the final segment spans.

This design improves segment quality while retaining boundary accuracy and lowers downstream recognition WER.

papers.abstract: Compositional motion transfer requires a model to extract motions from multiple reference videos, and apply each motion to a user-specified object in one target scene. Existing methods normally struggle to reliably assign different reference motions to the correct target objects, thus a motion intended for one object may affect another. Meanwhile, some motion-specific tuning approaches are still facing another issue: they must run a new optimization whenever the reference video changes, making repeated transfers inefficient. To address these limitations, we propose RART, a framework that unifies object-wise motion extraction, target-region anchoring, and frame-aligned injection into a frozen video Diffusion Transformer for multi-object motion transfer. For each reference motion, RART extracts temporally ordered features from the masked reference video, and then conditions them on the target first-frame mask to form mask-anchored motion tokens. Frame-aligned motion cross-attention allows each generated frame to read only the motion tokens at the corresponding time slots, composing all object motions in one denoising process. During training, a motion-attention routing loss encourages each target region to attend to its corresponding motion tokens and reduces interference between objects. Therefore, RART can handle novel reference-target combinations without per-video optimization. Experiments show that RART achieves accurate motion preservation, efficient inference, and strong compositional generalization.
authors: Yuze Li, Fuchen Long, Xinlong Sun, Cheng Yan, Xinyu Zhang, Xi Chen
bullets: Addresses motion misassignment between objects and the inefficiency of per-reference-video optimization.
Extracts temporally ordered features from masked reference videos and anchors them to target first-frame masks.
Uses frame-aligned motion cross-attention so each generated frame accesses the corresponding time-specific motion tokens.
Trains with a motion-attention routing loss to improve region-specific motion assignment and reduce cross-object interference.
The abstract reports accurate motion preservation, efficient inference, and strong compositional generalization to novel reference-target combinations.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.
authors: Haitang Feng, Zhuoman Liu, Zhennan Wang, Sheng Wang, Juelin Li, Chengzhi Zhao, Hexiang Wei, Lin Shao
bullets: Addresses the need for world models that both imagine plausible futures and understand evolving geometry, semantics, and motion.
Uses a shared spatiotemporal representation and DiT backbone for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow.
Jointly trains all modalities in a unified velocity-prediction space with lightweight task modulation.
Supports multi-step future generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step perception from observed video.
Trained on embodied manipulation data across robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, it shows strong performance in generation and dense 4D perception.

Bottom right: Given an observed video, each dense modality is predicted in one step from a noisy state at its selected noise level. papers.abstract: Edited endpoint images make the target of an image-to-video transition explicit and can improve transition completion, but also preserve context in the source image's layout. Full-frame endpoint conditioning turns this preserved context into requirements on the video's final state, potentially inducing temporal artifacts. We measure discontinuity with Hard-Cut (HC), late background reversal with Background Motion Reversal (BMR), and motion suppression with Dynamic Degree (DD). These artifacts appear across five video models spanning training-free and learned endpoint conditioning, in model-specific forms. We study Partial, a selective conditioning scheme that constrains only an edit-relevant region estimated from image-editor attention and leaves the remaining terminal content to the video model. Across three backbones on TC-Bench-I2V, Partial reduces temporal artifacts relative to full-frame conditioning, with no significant difference in Transition Completion Ratio (TCR); on Wan2.2-Turbo, uniformly weakening conditioning does not reproduce these reductions. A donor-context intervention keeps full-frame conditioning and replaces only the context outside the edit-relevant region with the final frame of a Partial video. It lowers HC and BMR on HunyuanVideo-1.5 and lowers BMR while restoring DD on Wan2.2-Turbo, with no significant difference in TCR, so constraint extent alone does not account for these artifacts. Together, these findings suggest that edited endpoints should serve as partial future goals, although edit relevance does not guarantee future validity. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/wannagetacat/Edited-Endpoints-I2V.
authors: Sihyun Kim, Sanghyun Jo, Kyungsu Kim
bullets: Full-frame endpoint conditioning can force preserved source context into the video’s final state, causing discontinuities, background reversals, and motion suppression.
The study evaluates these artifacts with Hard-Cut, Background Motion Reversal, and Dynamic Degree across five video models.
The proposed Partial scheme conditions only the edit-relevant region, estimated from image-editor attention, while leaving other terminal content unconstrained.
Across three backbones on TC-Bench-I2V, Partial reduces artifacts with no significant change in Transition Completion Ratio.
Donor-context experiments suggest artifact reductions are not explained solely by weakening or shrinking the conditioning constraint; edit relevance does not always ensure future validity.

papers.abstract: 4D perception models, which classify 3D point-cloud videos, are being built into robots, assistive monitoring and AR, yet before deploying one a practitioner cannot check which cue it relies on: how a body part moves, or what shape it has. 3D attribution is single-frame, video attribution is confined to RGB pixels, gradient maps need white-box access, attention is absent from state-space backbones, and point-level perturbations assume a point correspondence across frames that real depth and LiDAR data lack. We present Kinematic Causal Attribution (KCA), a black-box, interventional attribution method that queries only the model's outputs. Its freeze operator removes a region's motion while keeping its shape, and a shape-free proxy removes the shape while keeping the motion. Together they span a motion$\times$geometry cube for every tracked region, whose order-symmetric Shapley decomposition is complete and whose interaction is measured rather than assumed away. The operators rewrite per-frame point sets, so they need no correspondences, and a context-averaged estimator handles structures that span several regions. We validate KCA on the official PSTNet, P4Transformer and Mamba4D trained on MSR-Action3D. The decisive test is an audit: two binary tasks are built from real clips whose classes differ only in the motion or only in the shape of the same arm, and the motion share of the arm's importance follows the defining cue on all three backbones (0.83 vs. 0.60 on P4Transformer, 0.86 vs. 0.30 on PSTNet, 0.92 vs. 0.61 on Mamba4D), a distinction no single attribution map can make. The split costs no faithfulness: the necessity maps have the lowest deletion AUC on P4Transformer and PSTNet, tie with the best baseline on Mamba4D, and lose their correlation with the trained model's once the weights are randomised. Skeleton ground truth, re-sampling stability and cost complete the validation.
bullets: Uses interventional operators to freeze a region’s motion while preserving shape, or remove shape while preserving motion.
Combines these interventions in a motion×geometry cube with an order-symmetric Shapley decomposition that captures interactions.
A context-averaged estimator supports structures spanning multiple tracked regions, and the operators rewrite per-frame point sets without requiring correspondences.
On MSR-Action3D audits across PSTNet, P4Transformer, and Mamba4D, motion attribution tracks whether the defining cue is motion or shape.
Necessity maps show strong faithfulness under deletion tests and lose correlation after model-weight randomization, supporting model-specific attribution.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models have increased interest in interaction paradigms for video understanding. The evolution from offline to streaming and proactive interaction has gradually shifted models from passive responders toward more proactive agents that can decide when to answer. However, existing proactive paradigms typically assume that the information required to answer a query is complete, leaving models to only wait or answer. In the real world, however, information is often incomplete due to uncertainty from either the video or the user. In proactive paradigms, such uncertainty can cause the model to wait forever or generate highly hallucinatory responses. We therefore argue that proactive interaction should be redefined with a third action: ask, allowing models to actively ask for missing information. To study when and what models should ask before answering, we introduce AskStream, the first multi-turn benchmark spanning video and user uncertainty for streaming video understanding, with four task categories and eight subtasks. It contains 438 videos with 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask, and answer. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, even the strongest model attains only 52.18% on our proposed Ask-F1 metric, highlighting substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty.
authors: Lu Wang, Zhuoran Jin, Longxiang Wang, Junhong Chen, Yupu Hao, Yao Xu, Daojian Zeng, Yubo Chen, Kang Liu, Guang Liu, Jun Zhao
bullets: Existing systems often assume complete information, risking endless waiting or hallucinated answers when video or user intent is unclear.
The benchmark evaluates multi-turn interaction across video and user uncertainty with four categories and eight subtasks.
It includes 438 videos and 2,714 manually annotated frame-level windows labeled wait, ask, or answer.
Models remain substantially challenged: the strongest reported model reaches 52.18% on the Ask-F1 metric.
The benchmark covers both multiple-choice and open-ended settings, emphasizing proactive information seeking.

papers.abstract: Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) requires localizing multiple objects and maintaining their identities over time. Recent query-propagation trackers carry target-specific representations across frames and update them with current-frame image features, yet identity association remains difficult when visually similar targets overlap or cross. During such interactions, current-frame query updates may contain components directed toward nearby active tracks, which may affect identity association in later frames. To investigate this issue, we analyze track-query updates preceding identity switches (IDSWs), where the same target is assigned a different track ID. Our analysis shows that (i) propagated track-query representations change more abruptly before IDSWs, (ii) current-frame updates have larger positive projections along directions toward other active tracks, and (iii) bounding-box intersection over union (IoU) retrieves the counterpart track involved in a subsequent IDSW with high recall when that track remains active before the switch. Motivated by these findings, we propose Test-time Track-Query Calibration (TQC), a training-free and gradient-free method for query-propagation trackers. TQC calibrates the tracker output before propagation using a bounded correction estimated from update components directed toward nearby active tracks. It requires only track-query representations and bounding boxes available during inference, without retraining or architectural modification. Across nine DanceTrack and SportsMOT test settings, TQC improves HOTA and AssA in all settings and IDF1 in eight, with an average HOTA gain of +0.38 and limited inference overhead. Controlled variants on six validation settings further show that TQC's correction direction yields more consistent HOTA improvements than alternative directions with matched correction norms.
authors: Riku Inoue, Shogo Sato, Yu Mitsuzumi, Kazuhiko Murasaki, Tomoyasu Shimada, Takashi Sano
bullets: Problem: Similar targets that overlap or cross can cause track-query updates to absorb information from neighboring tracks, leading to identity switches.

Analysis: Track-query representations change more abruptly before ID switches, with updates showing stronger directional alignment toward other active tracks; IoU often identifies the counterpart track.
Method: TQC applies a bounded, training- and gradient-free correction to tracker outputs before propagation using track-query representations and bounding boxes available at inference.
Results: Across nine DanceTrack and SportsMOT test settings, TQC improves HOTA and AssA in all settings and IDF1 in eight, with an average HOTA gain of +0.38 and limited overhead.
Scope: The method targets query-propagation trackers and relies on nearby active tracks remaining available for calibration.
