When applied to sparse, large step trajectories, they often produce frozen frames, inaccurate camera motion, and severe geometric drift. We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between the gradual viewpoint transitions seen during training and the large viewpoint changes required at inference time. To address this problem, we propose Dense Trajectory Teacher Distillation (DTTD), a post-training framework that transfers a model's generation capability from dense trajectories to large camera motions. Given a sparse trajectory, DTTD interpolates additional camera poses to construct a dense trajectory covering the same path. The frozen base model then generates reliable teacher videos along this familiar dense trajectory, and pose aligned teacher observations are used to evaluate candidate videos generated under the original sparse trajectory. In this way, the model serves as its own generation teacher, requiring neither additional video data nor a stronger external video generator. We further combine dense teacher supervision with geometry aware rewards that assess cross frame consistency and camera trajectory following, and use the resulting preferences for offline preference optimization. To stably expand the model's motion range, we introduce a cumulative curriculum that progressively incorporates larger motion steps while retaining simpler trajectories to reduce capability forgetting.
authors: Shuofeng Sun, Linqing Zhao, Haibin Yan
bullets: Existing models often fail on sparse, large-step camera trajectories, producing frozen frames, inaccurate motion, and geometric drift.
DTTD interpolates sparse camera paths into dense trajectories that the frozen base model can reliably generate.
Pose-aligned dense teacher videos supervise candidate outputs generated on the original sparse trajectory, without extra data or an external teacher.
Geometry-aware rewards measure cross-frame consistency and trajectory following for offline preference optimization.
A cumulative curriculum progressively increases motion difficulty while retaining simpler trajectories to limit capability forgetting.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training framework to extend video world models to large camera motions via dense teacher distillation.
papers.title: Distilling Dense Trajectory Teachers For Large-Motion Video World Models
papers.tldr: DTTD extends video world models from small to large camera motions by using dense-trajectory self-teaching, geometry-aware rewards, and curriculum-based preference optimization.

papers.abstract: Video spatial reasoning requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to understand how objects are arranged and related across viewpoints. While these models can recognize objects in individual frames, integrating these observations to solve complex spatial tasks remains challenging. We examine route planning as a representative task and observe that existing models become substantially less accurate as the number of required turns increases, with several models achieving accuracy close to random guessing on routes requiring three or more turns. This finding suggests that recognizing landmarks alone is insufficient: models must also connect observations across viewpoints and track how landmarks are arranged in a shared space. Motivated by this observation, we introduce GeoLift, a training-free framework that uses feed-forward 3D reconstruction to map objects detected in individual frames into a shared metric 3D scene. GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained geometry models for scene reconstruction. It then uses shared geometric regions, called superpoints, to associate observations of the same object across views without a learned matcher. The reconstructed 3D map enables explicit computation of spatial relations and multistep routes, and provides geometric evidence for estimating distances and sizes. With all model weights frozen, GeoLift improves Qwen3-VL-4B's average score on VSI-Bench from 55.4% to 64.1%, including an increase in route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, and achieves 59.8% accuracy on MindCube. These results show that connecting frame-level object grounding through a shared 3D map can improve complex spatial reasoning without task-specific training.
authors: Xinglin Li, TingTing Long, Jingzhi Zhou, Jiajing Chen, Jian Yang, Jin Xie
bullets: Existing MLLMs struggle to connect landmarks across viewpoints, with accuracy dropping sharply on routes requiring three or more turns.
GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained feed-forward geometry models for training-free 3D reconstruction.
Shared geometric regions called superpoints associate the same objects across views without a learned matcher.
The resulting 3D map supports explicit spatial-relation and multistep-route computation, plus distance and size estimation.
It raises Qwen3-VL-4B’s VSI-Bench average from 55.4% to 64.1% and route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, while reaching 59.8% on MindCube.
papers.selection_reason: Grounds video spatial reasoning in explicit 3D maps, improving MLLM spatial and route reasoning.
papers.title: GeoLift: Grounding Video Spatial Reasoning in Explicit 3D Maps
papers.tldr: GeoLift improves video spatial reasoning by mapping frame-level object detections into an explicit shared 3D scene for multiview route planning and spatial inference.

papers.abstract: Marine video understanding is crucial for a wide range of real-world applications. However, existing marine video datasets suffer from limitations, including the limited number of data samples, fine-grained text descriptions, and detailed visual attributes. To address these limitations, we introduce a large-scale, video-text dataset featuring rich, in-the-wild visual attributes tailored for complex marine environments. Our dataset comprises 2,000 video-text pairs annotated with 13 attributes covering up to four objects per scene, object visual/geometric properties, behaviors, environmental context, and camera motion, spanning diverse lighting conditions, times of day, and 7 countries. From these annotations, we generate 16,080 video-question pairs (12,080 multiple-choice, 4,000 open-ended). Furthermore, we benchmark both proprietary and open-source video-LLM models on video question answering and video captioning tasks. We find that (i) proprietary models often achieves superior performances; (ii) VLMs handle object motion well but struggle with complex camera motion; (iii) closed-source models struggle to perceive camera motion; and (iv) VLMs struggle to reason in static cameras.
authors: Quang-Trung Truong, Thanh-Nghia Nguyen, Phu-Phong Vo, Jaeyeon Kim, Cheng Chen, Jie Zhang, Binh-Son Hua, Duc Thanh Nguyen, Ivor Tsang, Sai-Kit Yeung
bullets: Addresses limited sample sizes, fine-grained descriptions, and visual attributes in existing marine video datasets.
Includes 2,000 video-text pairs with 13 attributes covering object properties, behaviors, environmental context, and camera motion.
Generates 16,080 question-answer pairs spanning multiple-choice and open-ended video question answering.
Covers diverse marine scenes across lighting conditions, times of day, and seven countries.
Benchmarks video-LLMs, revealing strengths in object-motion understanding but difficulties with complex camera motion and static-camera reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a video-text dataset and benchmarks video-LLMs for marine video understanding, fitting video understanding.
papers.title: MarineLife-16K: An Attribute-Rich Video-Text Dataset for Motion-Aware Marine Video Understanding
papers.tldr: MarineLife-16K is an attribute-rich marine video-text benchmark designed to evaluate motion-aware video understanding across objects, environments, and camera movements.

papers.abstract: Advertisers routinely create multiple duration variants of ads to meet marketing budgets and viewer preferences, a labor-intensive and costly process. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at general video understanding, their ability to perform specialized editorial tasks remains unexplored. We introduce AdShot, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on shot selection for ad clipping. It contains 823 professionally edited ad pairs (30-sec sources and 15-sec edits) across 194 brands and 17 industries, annotated with shot-level boundaries and content features (action, emotion, information, imagery). We evaluate 13 state-of-the-art video-only MLLMs and 2 audio-visual MLLMs (7B-72B parameters) on shot selection accuracy (Precision, Recall, F1), duration constraints (15s), and content preservation, including an audio ablation. We find: (1) model architecture matters more than scale, with smaller models often matching or exceeding larger ones; performance is strongest for target ads with 6-10 shots; (2) models exhibit a mean absolute duration error of 5.39s, with most tending to overshoot the 15s target, though they can still substantially reduce human editing effort; (3) all models exhibit systematic content biases, favoring information-rich and emotion-focused shots while under-selecting action and imagery. We publicly release our benchmark to facilitate research at the intersection of multimodal AI and computational advertising.
authors: Wen Xie, Om Rastogi, Sai Siddhartha Vivek Dhir Rangoju, Gijs Overgoor, Yakov Bart, Sarah Ostadabbas
bullets: Addresses the costly, labor-intensive creation of multiple ad-duration variants.
Introduces 823 professionally edited 30-to-15-second ad pairs spanning 194 brands and 17 industries, with shot-level annotations.
Evaluates 13 video-only and 2 audio-visual MLLMs on shot selection, 15-second duration compliance, and content preservation.
Architecture appears more important than model scale; performance is strongest on ads containing 6–10 shots.
Models typically overshoot the target by 5.39 seconds on average, favor information- and emotion-rich shots, and under-select action and imagery.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLMs on video shot selection, relevant to multimodal LLMs and video understanding.
papers.title: AdShot: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Video Advertisement Clipping
papers.tldr: AdShot benchmarks how well multimodal LLMs select shots to create 15-second ad edits, revealing substantial duration errors and systematic content-selection biases.

papers.abstract: Precise camera control is essential for cinematic character video generation, yet existing methods struggle to follow large-angle trajectories with combined rotation, translation, and radius variation from arbitrary initial azimuths. Such viewpoint changes also reveal character regions unseen in the initial frame, causing geometric distortions, appearance degradation, and identity drift. To systematically study these coupled challenges, we introduce CLACT, a large-scale Character-centric dataset and benchmark covering diverse Large-Angle Camera Trajectories, with accurate camera geometry and multi-view character observations for training and evaluation. We further propose WorldCast, a framework for world-consistent character video generation under diverse large-angle camera motions. Specifically, we back-project the initial frame into a 3D point cloud using estimated depth, align the point-cloud scale with the target camera trajectory, and render it along the trajectory to obtain explicit geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement the incomplete character information, we introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using relative camera poses estimated jointly from the initial frame and multi-view character anchors, we express anchor and target-view geometry in a common coordinate frame. GAMA uses this geometric alignment to guide the retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features during generation. Evaluations across diverse large-angle camera trajectories demonstrate accurate trajectory following while preserving character geometry, appearance, and identity.
authors: Lei Cao, Yu Liu, Wenhua Liao, Peng Zhang, Fei Wang, Hao Zhang, Jiajun Le, Daiguo Zhou, Jian Luan, Jiayi Ma
bullets: Addresses combined camera rotation, translation, and radius changes from arbitrary starting azimuths.
Introduces CLACT, a benchmark with large-angle trajectories, camera geometry, and multi-view character observations.
Back-projects the initial frame into a 3D point cloud and renders trajectory-aligned geometric guidance and coverage masks.
Uses Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention to retrieve and inject view-relevant character features from aligned multi-view anchors.
Experiments show accurate trajectory following with preserved character geometry, appearance, and identity across diverse motions.
papers.selection_reason: World-consistent character video generation with camera control; directly relevant to video generation.
papers.title: WorldCast: World-Consistent Character Video Generation with Large-Angle Camera Control
papers.tldr: WorldCast enables character video generation that follows large-angle, complex camera motions while preserving geometry, appearance, and identity.

papers.abstract: Active speaker detection (ASD) relies on audiovisual correspondence between speech and visible faces, yet this correspondence becomes unreliable in crowded scenes, or when visual evidence is unavailable. We introduce ROAM-ASD-C and ROAM-ASD-CR to extend ROAM-ASD with contextual and identity-aware reasoning. ROAM-ASD-C jointly reasons across simultaneously visible candidates, allowing other faces to provide complementary evidence when the target observation is ambiguous or incomplete. ROAM-ASD-CR incorporates registered-speaker representations derived from enrollment speech, allowing detection of whether a speaker is active even when that speaker is not visually observed. ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art performance across five ASD benchmarks: 96.8% mAP on AVA, 98.9% on WASD, 88.8% on UniTalk, 98.7% on Talkies, and 99.5% on ASW. It also improves ROAM-ASD by up to 13.3 mAP under 75% target-track visual removal.
bullets: Addresses unreliable audiovisual correspondence in crowded scenes and missing face observations.
ROAM-ASD-C jointly reasons over visible candidates to use complementary evidence from other faces.
ROAM-ASD-CR uses enrollment-speech representations to detect registered speakers who are not visibly observed.
ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art results across five ASD benchmarks, with mAP ranging from 88.8% to 99.5%.
It improves over ROAM-ASD by up to 13.3 mAP when 75% of the target-track visuals are removed.
papers.selection_reason: Active speaker detection is a video understanding task.
papers.title: Beyond Visible Speakers: Context-Aware Active Speaker Detection with Speaker Registration
papers.tldr: ROAM-ASD-C and ROAM-ASD-CR improve active speaker detection by using scene context and registered speaker identities when visual evidence is incomplete or absent.

papers.abstract: Short-form video combines speech, imagery, and on-screen text, creating challenges for systematic content analysis. We present a five-stage multimodal framework for measuring creators' themes and communication strategies at scale. The framework integrates platform metadata, speech transcripts, and vision-language descriptions of sampled frames, then applies large language models to generate predefined indicators and open-ended labels. An audited keyword scheme consolidates thematic labels, while creator-weighted aggregation gives each account equal weight regardless of posting volume. We demonstrate the framework on 9,852 TikTok videos from sixteen creators, retaining 7,311 videos for analysis across seven themes and seven communication indicators. Automated profiles reveal substantial differences in creators' use of education, humor, and responses to current events. Validation against two independent expert annotators yielded a mean framework-expert agreement of Cohen's $\kappa = 0.40$ across the six binary indicators, close to the $\kappa = 0.42$ the two experts achieved with each other, though agreement varied substantially across individual indicators. The framework provides a modular approach to comparative analysis of creator communication, combining scalable annotation with transparent aggregation and construct-specific validation.
authors: Julie R. Ancis, Michael Fire, Omer Tarshish
bullets: Addresses the challenge of systematically analyzing speech, imagery, and on-screen text in short-form video.
Combines platform metadata, transcripts, sampled-frame descriptions, LLM-generated indicators, and audited thematic labels.
Uses creator-weighted aggregation so accounts contribute equally regardless of posting volume.
Demonstrated on TikTok videos from 16 creators, identifying differences in education, humor, and responses to current events.
Expert validation showed moderate agreement overall, with performance varying substantially by indicator.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a multimodal framework for analyzing short-form video using LLMs, relevant to video understanding and multimodal analysis.
papers.title: A Multimodal Framework for Measuring Creator Communication on Short-Form Video
papers.tldr: A scalable multimodal framework analyzes short-form video creators’ themes and communication strategies using metadata, speech, visuals, and language models.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video question answering requires a model to continuously monitor an incoming stream and autonomously decide when to speak, what to say, and whether to emit a response. Existing streaming systems face a fundamental difficulty: retaining long visual histories is costly, whereas discarding them can lead to missed events and repeated responses. We propose \textbf{ProV-Mem}, a training-free proactive memory framework built around a frozen VLM backbone. ProV-Mem decomposes the proactive decision into three lightweight memory tiers: a temporal-trigger memory controls when to query the backbone and recovers from prolonged silence, an instructional memory guides what to say through a fixed prompting prior for concise and visually grounded generation, and an episodic memory determines whether to emit by filtering near-duplicate responses. Under an idealized conditional-sufficiency assumption, we derive a stagewise approximation bound relating the decomposed process to a full-state joint policy. We further introduce Cost-Aware Area Under the Curve (\textbf{CAUC}), which extends PAUC by explicitly discounting redundant, overly frequent, and unnecessarily long emissions. Experiments on the four scenarios of ProactiveVideoQA show that ProV-Mem achieves the best CAUC across all scenarios and the best PAUC on WEB, EGO, and TV, while maintaining low per-response inference latency.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between retaining costly long visual histories and discarding information needed for timely, non-redundant responses.
Uses temporal-trigger memory to decide when to query, instructional memory to guide concise grounded answers, and episodic memory to filter near-duplicate emissions.
Provides a stagewise approximation bound under an idealized conditional-sufficiency assumption.
Introduces CAUC, a cost-aware metric that penalizes redundant, overly frequent, and overly long responses.
On ProactiveVideoQA, achieves the best CAUC in all four scenarios and the best PAUC in three, with low per-response latency.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming video QA with proactive memory tiers; relevant to video-language understanding and efficient memory.
papers.title: ProV-Mem: Proactive Memory for Streaming Video Question Answering
papers.tldr: ProV-Mem is a training-free, three-tier memory framework that enables a frozen VLM to answer streaming video questions proactively while reducing missed events, repetition, and unnecessary response costs.

papers.abstract: Controlling the camera relative to a moving subject in an existing video is challenging: behaviors such as maintaining a frontal view require the camera to adapt to the subject's changing position and orientation, making the desired trajectory difficult to specify in advance. Existing camera-controlled video-to-video methods typically rely on explicit trajectories or reference motions, which do not directly express these dynamic camera--subject relationships. We introduce semantic camera motion control, a novel video-to-video task in which a reference video and a target motion label specify the desired subject-relative camera behavior without an explicit target trajectory. Our method, SemCam, learns to realize this behavior while preserving source content. It combines shared-basis low-rank adaptation with motion-conditioned modulation, while a background-consistency loss encourages fidelity in regions visible in both reference and target videos. We construct 661 paired videos covering eight semantic camera behaviors and evaluate on a separate 109-scene benchmark using subject-relative motion metrics, appearance measures, and a user study. SemCam achieves a semantic-motion success rate of 68.6%, compared with 45.3% for Vista4D, the strongest evaluated baseline, while maintaining comparable subject identity preservation.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying camera motion around subjects whose position and orientation change over time.
Uses a reference video plus a target motion label to express behaviors such as maintaining a frontal view.
Combines shared-basis low-rank adaptation, motion-conditioned modulation, and a background-consistency loss.
Evaluated on 661 paired videos and a separate 109-scene benchmark covering eight semantic camera behaviors.
Outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline on semantic-motion success while maintaining comparable subject identity preservation.
papers.selection_reason: Semantic camera-motion control for video generation via motion-conditioned adaptation and background consistency.
papers.title: SemCam: Semantic Camera Motion Control for Video Generation
papers.tldr: SemCam enables semantic, subject-relative camera control in video generation without requiring an explicit target trajectory, achieving a 68.6% semantic-motion success rate while preserving subject identity.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of video data has created an urgent need for efficient video understanding systems that can handle long and continuous visual inputs, posing significant challenges for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to severe memory bottlenecks. Moreover, existing compression methods often overlook the explosive accumulation of approximation errors. To address this issue, we propose Video-MemComp, a training-free and sensitivity-aware context management framework for memory-constrained streaming video understanding. Our method theoretically decomposes compression error into orthogonal local approximation error and layer-wise structural sensitivity via a first-order Taylor expansion. To minimize local approximation error, we perform token aggregation in a pre-RoPE safe zone with an attention-conserving logit bias, mitigating geometric distortions caused by RoPE rotations. To manage layer-wise structural sensitivity, we dynamically allocate the KV cache budget based on offline gradient priors and online context entropy, prioritizing high-sensitivity layers. Video-MemComp outperforms or achieves performance comparable to full-cache and state-of-the-art compression methods on benchmarks including MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema. Notably, it improves the overall accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-3B from 62.3% to 64.1% while reducing the KV cache to an equivalent of 6,000 tokens per layer, saving over 90% of KV memory.
authors: Yonghui Niu, Yuhao Ji, Chang Nie, Jiao Zhang, Yilong Li, Junlan Feng, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Chaoyou Fu
bullets: Targets memory bottlenecks and error accumulation in long-context streaming video understanding.
Uses a first-order Taylor expansion to separate local approximation error from layer-wise structural sensitivity.
Aggregates tokens in a pre-RoPE safe zone with attention-conserving logit bias to reduce geometric distortion.
Dynamically allocates KV-cache budgets using offline gradient priors and online context entropy.
Matches or exceeds full-cache and existing compression methods on MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema; Qwen2.5-VL-3B rises from 62.3% to 64.1% with over 90% KV-memory savings.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses streaming-video KV-cache and token compression for efficient MLLM inference.
papers.title: Video-MemComp: Taylor-Guided Sensitivity-Aware Memory Management for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: Video-MemComp is a training-free method that compresses streaming-video KV memory by modeling sensitivity and approximation error, achieving over 90% memory savings with improved accuracy on Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

papers.abstract: Quantitative and dense task progress feedback is essential for robotic manipulation across data curation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Existing progress annotations often rely on sparse keyframe markings derived from subjective manual judgments, limiting their scalability and cross-task consistency, particularly in long-horizon manipulation. To overcome these challenges, we propose action-aware quantification, a unified progress specification that decomposes long-horizon trajectories into object-level subtasks via a vision-language model (VLM) and assigns weighted action credits to capture fine-grained execution dynamics. Using VLM auto-labeling and human calibration, we construct an 800+ hour training video dataset and LOOM, a long-horizon progress benchmark containing 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames. To model these dense progress dynamics, we introduce NimCritic, a predictive progress critic trained via Joint Video-Progress Learning. We further incorporate Historical Progress Perturbation to mitigate sequential drift, and design a contrastive Video-Progress Alignment objective that bridges asymmetric expert streams by mutually grounding intermediate visual dynamics and denoised progress trajectories. NimCritic matches or outperforms state-of-the-art process reward models (PRMs) on the established Video Progress Benchmark (VPB) and LOOM, surpassing GVL (GPT-6-Sol) on VPB by about 65% in terminal success accuracy (TSA). On the large-scale RoboArena policy evaluation benchmark, it also retrieves human-selected successful rollouts with about 97% overall recall. These results establish action-aware quantification as a scalable foundation for dense progress feedback in robotic manipulation.
authors: Tianchi Xu, Yalin Zheng, Yangxin Zhu, Ruonan Ren, Zheng Fu, Yunlong Wang, Yuanxin Zhong
bullets: Addresses the subjectivity, sparsity, and poor scalability of keyframe-based progress annotations.
Decomposes trajectories into object-level subtasks and assigns weighted action credits using VLM auto-labeling with human calibration.
Introduces LOOM, with 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames, plus an 800+ hour training-video dataset.
NimCritic uses Joint Video-Progress Learning, Historical Progress Perturbation, and contrastive Video-Progress Alignment to predict dense progress.
Matches or exceeds leading process reward models, achieves about 65% higher terminal success accuracy than GVL on VPB, and about 97% recall on RoboArena rollout retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Predictive progress modeling for long-horizon manipulation with video-progress learning fits robot learning and video understanding.
papers.title: Predictive Long-Horizon Progress Modeling with Action-Aware Quantification
papers.tldr: The paper introduces an action-aware framework and NimCritic model for scalable, fine-grained progress estimation in long-horizon robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Deploying Vision-Language Models for video anomaly detection confronts a fundamental constraint. Their semantic reasoning demands computational budgets incompatible with the scale of real-world video streams. We present Signal-Aware Adaptive Fusion (SAAF), a framework that achieves efficient zero-shot anomaly detection through three key innovations. First, we introduce a dual-signal adaptive sampler operating in semantic embedding space: a delta signal captures sudden events via frame-to-frame cosine distance, while a drift signal detects static and gradual anomalies through deviation from rolling temporal context. Their OR-gated combination with adaptive EMA-based thresholding provides comprehensive anomaly coverage without training data. Second, we propose a threshold-gated cascaded architecture where lightweight frame-level scoring precedes expensive video-level temporal analysis, invoking it only when confidence warrants additional context. Third, we design a signal-aware weighted fusion mechanism that dynamically adapts score combination based on which signal triggered frame selection. Across four benchmarks, SAAF delivers competitive accuracy at substantially lower cost. Among training-free zero-shot methods, SAAF sets a new state of the art on XD-Violence (92.07%), MSAD (86.70%), and ShanghaiTech (80.54%) AUC-ROC, with XD-Violence and MSAD also surpassing supervised baselines. SAAF sustains 44.95, 48.61, and 41.06 FPS on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, and MSAD, a 2.43$\times$, 2.63$\times$, and 2.22$\times$ throughput improvement over the prior best zero-shot method. Code: https://github.com/kdawoud91/SAAF
authors: Khaled Waleed Dawoud, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Uses frame-to-frame semantic changes (delta) and temporal-context deviations (drift) to detect sudden, static, and gradual anomalies without training data.
Employs EMA-based adaptive thresholds and OR-gated sampling for broad anomaly coverage.
Cascades lightweight frame scoring before expensive video-level analysis, reducing unnecessary computation.
Dynamically fuses scores according to the signal that triggered frame selection.
Achieves competitive accuracy across four benchmarks and reports 2.22×–2.63× throughput gains over the prior best zero-shot method on three datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Presents an efficient zero-shot video anomaly detection framework using VLMs. It fits Video Understanding and Efficient AI (throughput improvements).
papers.title: Efficient Zero-Shot Video Anomaly Detection via Signal-Aware Adaptive Fusion (SAAF)
papers.tldr: SAAF enables efficient zero-shot video anomaly detection by adaptively sampling informative frames and selectively applying costly temporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Video reasoning requires understanding how events unfold over time, yet videos with accurate temporal annotations are expensive to collect. Self-play offers an alternative by letting a model generate and solve its own tasks without manual annotation. However, existing video self-play methods train on fixed sets of recorded videos, so they cannot alter the underlying event dynamics and rely on noisy pseudo-labels derived from the model's own outputs, such as majority voting, that risk reinforcing shared model errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Tempo-Zero, a self-improvement framework that closes a loop of executable environments, execution-verified self-play, and environment evolution, where executing a program renders a video with the ground-truth option and interval of every question. A single policy plays both Questioner and Solver, proposing questions and answering them with timestamped evidence lines, and is trained on execution-grounded rewards instead of model consensus. The Solver's performance steers a curriculum over tasks and difficulty levels, and the policy selects rule changes that enrich the event dynamics of later rounds. Despite being trained solely on simple programs, without supervised fine-tuning or external video data which prior methods typically require, Tempo-Zero outperforms the base models and recent self-play baselines on average across twelve real-world video benchmarks at different model scales, with particularly strong gains on temporal grounding tasks. Project page: https://alchemist-jo.github.io/tempo-zero/
authors: Jingmin Zhu, Yanyan Zou, Xiuyu Li, James Bailey, Dinh Phung, Tao Yu, Yunyun Hou, Jun Liu, Jun Zhou, Sirui Wang, Nan Duan, Jiachen Liu, Qiuhong Ke
bullets: Addresses the cost of collecting temporally annotated videos and the error reinforcement of consensus-based pseudo-labels.
Uses executable environments to render videos with ground-truth answers and time intervals for each generated question.
A single policy alternates between Questioner and Solver, producing timestamped evidence and receiving execution-grounded rewards.
Solver performance drives task curricula, while the policy evolves environment rules to create richer event dynamics.
Trained only on simple programs, it outperforms base models and recent self-play baselines across twelve real-world video benchmarks, especially for temporal grounding.
papers.selection_reason: Self-play in executable worlds with execution-verified rewards for video reasoning and temporal grounding; directly fits video understanding.
papers.title: Tempo-Zero: Recursive Self-Play in Executable Worlds for Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: Tempo-Zero improves video reasoning through execution-verified self-play in evolving executable worlds, without human temporal annotations or external video data.

papers.abstract: The 3rd WEAR Dataset Challenge asks for an activity label for every one-second window of four unseen participants. Each window has 15 VideoMAEv2 frame embeddings, the accelerometer signal of one random limb, and the windows are shuffled. This report is an empirical analysis of one system built after the challenge deadline. Window classifiers are stacked with features averaged over per-participant graphs of video neighbours and scored successor candidates, and a mean-field style decoder with a soft count constraint per activity labels all windows of a participant together. The setting is offline and transductive, and the count constraint relies on each activity being performed once. In a participant-wise simulation with participant-level bootstrap intervals, stacking added 0.051 macro F1 over stage-1 fusion and the count constraint 0.011 (95% interval 0.006 to 0.017). A quadratic seam distance ranks the true same-limb successor first among about 720 candidates in 83.9% of cases, but adding it to the link model changed macro F1 by -0.0001 (-0.0006 to 0.0005). With the decoder settings and the mixing weight chosen inside the folds and the mislabelled spans left out of training, the system scores 0.936 in simulation (0.940 for participants who performed each activity once); the submitted configuration scores 0.938 (0.943). Per-participant scores range from 0.80 to 0.97. These results come from a non-nested stacking protocol that uses unlabelled features transductively, so they are not a fully inductive estimate. An oracle that averages the final unary scores over the true segments reaches 0.973, and 79% of the remaining errors involve the null class. On the private leaderboard, which no choice used, the selected Kaggle submission scored 0.9231 (public 0.9254, with bounds partly tuned there), and a later one with bounds chosen in simulation scored 0.9247 (public 0.9253).
bullets: Stacking graph-based video-neighbour and successor features improved macro F1 by 0.051 over initial multimodal fusion; the count constraint added 0.011.
A mean-field-style decoder jointly labels each participant’s shuffled windows, assuming every activity occurs exactly once.
Quadratic seam matching identified the true same-limb successor first in 83.9% of cases but changed macro F1 by only -0.0001.
The simulated system scored 0.936 macro F1, while private leaderboard scores were 0.9231 and 0.9247 for two submissions.

papers.abstract: Continuous visual world simulation requires coupling evolving scene geometry with temporally persistent appearance. We present UniWorld, a unified framework that integrates depth trajectories and reference appearance within a shared video generation model. The central design maintains visual and geometric histories on a common timeline. Noise-aligned overlapping continuation places generated history at the prescribed sampling noise level and commits only newly generated latents. Rolling depth latent state preserves the corresponding geometric controls, incrementally reads newly available geometry, and keeps the conditioning fixed within each sampling window. Together, these mechanisms ensure exact preservation of latent history while bounding the active depth state by the window size. We evaluate continuous generation, paired history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scene categories. The same generator supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, while cached and incremental execution paths produce bitwise-identical outputs. Appearance changes and geometric control branches operate through the same interface without modifying committed history. The measured steady-state DiT execution path achieves real-time generation throughput, demonstrating the efficiency of UniWorld for continuous visual world simulation.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yabo Chen, Shuaiwei Wang, Zixuan Duan, Haibin Huang, Feng Xu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling temporally persistent visual appearance with changing scene geometry.
Uses noise-aligned overlapping continuation to preserve generated latent history while committing only new content.
Maintains rolling depth latents and fixed per-window conditioning to control geometry with bounded active state.
Supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, with cached and incremental execution producing identical outputs.
Evaluations cover continuous generation, history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scenes; the steady-state DiT path achieves real-time throughput.
papers.selection_reason: Continuous visual world simulation via a unified video generation model with depth and appearance histories; directly fits world models and video diffusion.
papers.title: UniWorld: A Unified World Model for Real-Time Visual World Simulation
papers.tldr: UniWorld enables real-time, continuous visual world simulation by jointly maintaining persistent appearance and evolving scene geometry in a unified video generator.

papers.abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.
authors: Yanhao Jia, Yi Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Weigao Sun, Feida Zhu, Pengkun Jiao, Sihan Yang, Ming Ma, Steven Hoi, Erik Cambria
bullets: LongVideo contains about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions spanning visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning.
4DMemoryBench evaluates reasoning across diverse context lengths, targeting persistent memory over long video streams.
The 4DMemory Harness combines four skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and model-specific retrieval-augmented generation.
Across 13 leading models, the harness improves performance by over 50%, while models perform over 10% worse than on a previous benchmark.
The benchmark targets development of agents for complex, long-horizon spatiotemporal tasks.

papers.title: 4DMemory: Benchmarking Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Memory with Harness-Augmented Agents
papers.tldr: 4DMemory introduces a long-horizon video benchmark and tool-augmented harness that substantially improves foundation-model performance on spatiotemporal reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Point-supervised Temporal Action Localization (PTAL) aims to localize action instances using only a single annotated timestamp for each instance. Such sparse supervision offers limited guidance for modeling the structural organization of an action instance. Existing PTAL methods primarily infer action regions from classification responses, leaving the structural organization of multiple action-related parts within each instance insufficiently modeled. To address this problem, we propose DeformStruct, an instance-level deformable structure modeling framework for PTAL. DeformStruct progressively constructs the structure of each action instance through three stages. First, Structural Anchor Mining discovers multiple anchors from annotated points and action-responsive regions, providing structural nodes grounded in the current instance. Second, Deformable Part Alignment associates latent structural parts with these anchors through deformation-aware matching, allowing their temporal supports to adapt to instance-dependent variations. Third, Relational Structural Organization explicitly models the relative temporal relations among the aligned parts, forming a relational representation that characterizes how different action-related parts are organized together. Extensive experiments on THUMOS14, ActivityNet-v1.3, GTEA, and BEOID demonstrate consistent improvements in point-supervised temporal localization and validate the effectiveness of deformable structural modeling.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Yonghao Dong, Jie Wang, Gang Hua
bullets: PTAL uses only one timestamp per action instance, providing limited structural supervision.
DeformStruct progressively builds instance structure through anchor mining, deformable part alignment, and relational organization.
The method adapts part temporal supports to instance-specific variations and models relations among aligned parts.
Experiments on THUMOS14, ActivityNet-v1.3, GTEA, and BEOID show consistent localization improvements.
The approach is scoped to point-supervised temporal action localization and depends on sparse point annotations.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses point-supervised temporal action localization using deformable structure modeling, providing a method to infer structural organization of actions from sparse supervision.
papers.title: DeformStruct: Deformable Structure Modeling for Point-Supervised Temporal Action Localization
papers.tldr: DeformStruct improves point-supervised temporal action localization by explicitly modeling deformable, relational structures among action parts from sparse point annotations.

papers.abstract: Video moment retrieval aims to localize a query-relevant temporal segment in an untrimmed video. Existing methods typically perform video-text alignment in Euclidean space, where representations are embedded in a flat geometry. However, accurate moment localization requires organizing query-relevant evidence across multiple grounding states, where target regions, boundary transitions, and contextual distractors exhibit distinct temporal structures and relevance patterns. Such Euclidean representations lack an explicit geometry to jointly capture these relationships, motivating us to explore structured temporal evidence organization from a geometric perspective. Specifically, we propose Hyperbolic Temporal Evidence Organization (HTEO), a geometric framework that organizes query-aware temporal memory in hyperbolic space. HTEO maps temporal representations into a Poincar\'{e} ball and organizes temporal evidence through Radial Evidence Organization (REO) and Orthogonal Angular Refinement (OAR). REO adjusts temporal tokens' radial positions to encode the structural differences among temporal evidence, while OAR enhances query-conditioned semantic alignment through orthogonal rotation. The organized representation is then projected back to the Euclidean tangent space and injected into the decoder through a lightweight residual memory update, enabling hyperbolic geometric cues to be incorporated into standard Transformer decoders while preserving the original cross-modal memory. Furthermore, we introduce radial structure regularization and angular relevance supervision to explicitly guide temporal evidence organization and query-conditioned semantic alignment, respectively. Extensive experiments and analyses across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that HTEO improves temporal localization while providing an interpretable geometric organization of temporal evidence.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Jiaxuan Lin, Gang Hua, Le Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of modeling target moments, boundary transitions, and contextual distractors with flat Euclidean representations.
Uses a Poincaré-ball memory with Radial Evidence Organization for temporal structure and Orthogonal Angular Refinement for query-conditioned alignment.
Projects the organized features back to Euclidean space and adds them through a lightweight residual memory update.
Introduces radial structure regularization and angular relevance supervision to guide the learned organization.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show improved temporal localization and interpretable evidence structure.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a geometric framework (Hyperbolic Space) to organize temporal evidence for video moment retrieval, enhancing the model's ability to reason about temporal structures and relevance.
papers.title: Organizing Temporal Evidence in Hyperbolic Space for Video Moment Retrieval
papers.tldr: HTEO organizes query-relevant temporal evidence in hyperbolic space to improve video moment localization while retaining compatibility with standard Transformer decoders.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence-based analysis of intraoperative laparoscopic videos has the potential to improve surgical decision-making and precision. However, effective surgical assistance requires models that can generalize across diverse intraoperative tasks. Here we present LapaFM, a foundation model for laparoscopic surgery trained on more than 20,000 minutes of surgical videos using a multi-stage continual learning strategy that mitigates catastrophic forgetting and inter-task interference. LapaFM learns multimodal visual representations and supports multiple tasks, including smoke removal, surgical phase recognition, instrument and polyp segmentation, and lesion identification. The model was evaluated on 13 retrospective and two prospective cohorts collected from different imaging devices. LapaFM consistently outperformed task-specific models and existing foundation models across datasets, and also generalized to gastrointestinal endoscopy tasks, including polyp detection and classification. Notably, it recovered over 90% of smoke-obscured frames and achieved clinician-level or superior performance in lymph node metastasis prediction and prospective polyp classification.
authors: Xiaobo Zhu, Shiwei Wu, Yu An, Yuechen Tao, He Sun, Song Zhang, Jianbo Wang, Xiaojing Wang, Junwei Liu, Wei Guo, Yanfei Shao, Xuan Zhao, Jiangwei Xiao, Wenbo Niu, Bo Wei, Yuhan Wang, Gang Hu, Fei Liu, Kunshan He, Chongwei Chi, Jianqiang Tang, Kang Zhang, Jie Tian, Zhenyu Liu

papers.selection_reason: Laparoscopic foundation model trained on surgical videos for phase recognition, segmentation, and lesion identification; fits video understanding.
papers.title: LapaFM: A Laparoscopic Foundation Model via Multi-Stage Continual Learning
papers.tldr: LapaFM is a multimodal laparoscopic foundation model trained with continual learning that supports diverse surgical and endoscopic tasks and performs strongly across retrospective and prospective cohorts.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires assistants to track unfolding events and respond when a user's requested condition is met. To make these decisions, assistants must accumulate relevant evidence and reassess response conditions as new observations arrive. Existing work offers complementary capabilities for this process: proactive video assistants learn when to respond, while streaming video reasoning methods generate scheduled intermediate text to organize observations and support subsequent answers. Together, these capabilities provide a foundation for proactive reasoning, but how to coordinate ongoing reasoning with timely responses remains underexplored. In a direct adaptation, fixed reasoning intervals can trigger updates when nothing relevant has changed or postpone useful updates until the next scheduled step. Sharing one generation path also couples two distinct requirements: preserving evidence for future decisions and producing only the response requested by the user. Moreover, responses generated after reasoning must wait for it to finish, even when sufficient evidence is already available. To address these challenges, we introduce SyncPro, a synchronous dual-stream framework with specialized generation paths for evidence tracking and user-facing responses. Its Inner and Response branches share causal history and activate independently, allowing relevant evidence changes to trigger internal updates and responses to proceed concurrently with ongoing reasoning. We construct 189K dual-stream examples and train SyncPro through supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. Experiments across three proactive benchmarks show improved response timing and more accurate answers to user requests.
authors: Xueyun Tian, Bingbing Xu, Jiaming Liu, Jinpeng Yu, Yang Shi, Yu Zhao, Ruihua Huang, Yuanzhuo Wang, Huawei Shen
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deciding when to update internal reasoning and when to respond as streaming video events unfold.
Uses dual Inner and Response branches that share causal history but activate independently.
Allows relevant evidence changes to trigger reasoning updates while responses proceed concurrently when enough evidence is available.
Trained on 189K dual-stream examples using supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level reinforcement learning.
Improves response timing and answer accuracy across three proactive video understanding benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Proactive streaming video understanding with synchronous reasoning and responding, fits video understanding.
papers.title: SyncPro: Synchronous Reasoning and Responding for Proactive Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: SyncPro coordinates ongoing evidence tracking with timely user responses through independently activated reasoning and response streams for proactive video understanding.

papers.abstract: Despite the promising development of deep learning for video anomaly detection (VAD), explainability (XAI) of these models remains a challenge. Explainable and privacy-protecting VAD builds transparency and trust that facilitates adoption of computer vision systems, including safety and security monitoring. However, anomaly explainability in privacy-preserving VAD systems is underexplored. In this study, we present the XAVAD approach, a unified descriptive anomaly XAI for an anonymized VAD, that integrates flexible zero-shot anonymization, anomaly type categorization, visual localization, and scene context description. We provide empirical and qualitative assessments of multifaceted explanations integrated with full-body visual anonymization for privacy protection. We adopt a multimodal CLIP embedding for videos, using improved LLM-assisted prompting and pool-scoring mechanisms for anomaly-type identification. We enhance Grad-ECLIP for spatial anomaly heatmap localization, leveraging computation and accuracy through our novel prompt-guided patching autofocus mechanism. We employ VLMs to generate context and reasoning descriptions of detected anomalies through curated prompt engineering. We have evaluated the accuracy and computational cost of XAVAD on several publicly available CCTV and video datasets. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains of our XAVAD over state-of-the-art benchmark approaches and provide insights into privacy protection trade-offs in XAI for VAD. We further present ablation studies and assessments across diverse configurations and modeling alternatives to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods. Code: https://github.com/muleina/XAVAD}{https://github.com/muleina/XAVAD .
authors: Mulugeta Weldezgina Asres, Lei Jiao, Christian Walter Omlin
bullets: Targets the limited explainability of anonymized video anomaly detection while preserving full-body visual privacy.
Combines CLIP-based multimodal video embeddings, LLM-assisted prompting, and pool scoring for anomaly categorization.
Uses prompt-guided patching with Grad-ECLIP to produce spatial anomaly heatmaps.
Employs vision-language models and curated prompts to generate contextual and reasoning descriptions.
Evaluations on multiple public CCTV and video datasets report gains over benchmark methods and examine privacy–explainability trade-offs.

papers.title: Guided Zero-Shot Anomaly Explanation for Anonymized Crowd Video Monitoring: Context, Categorization, and Spatial Localization
papers.tldr: XAVAD provides privacy-preserving, zero-shot explanations for video anomalies by identifying anomaly types, locating them spatially, and describing their scene context.

papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have been increasingly adopted in consumer smart-home camera systems to interpret recorded videos and provide insights. However, video clips captured from smart-home cameras are different from curated web videos dominating existing VLM benchmarks. Smart-home video clips often do not contain subtitles or narration and are captured from different viewing angles, under various lighting conditions, and in diverse scenarios. However, the capabilities of the model in this domain, under sparse visual signals and limited context, are not fully assessed by existing VLM benchmarks. To close this gap, we introduce OpenHome, a visual-only, four-option multiple-choice benchmark for evaluating smart-home video understanding. It contains 2,254 questions on 1,118 real-world video clips and organizes 10 tasks into three capability levels. Perception evaluates visible content, Reasoning evaluates causal, spatial, and temporal relationships, and Insight evaluates subject intent, supporting evidence and appropriate homeowner responses. Based on the dataset, we describe the task design, data pipeline and evaluation protocol, and report results for 32 closed-source and open-weight VLMs. The best model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 81.2% overall accuracy. Frontier closed-source models outperform open-weight models on every level. The best closed-source model leads the best open-weight model by 16.3% on Perception, 22.4% on Reasoning and 37.4% on Insight.
authors: Xianglong Wang, Neil Rodrigues, Pei Guo, Yiru Fang, Kevin Beussman, Shuyang Wang, Jingzhi Wang, Liangju Li, Shunyao Xu, Zhongwei Cheng, Wei Li, Lin Chen

papers.title: OpenHome: From Perception to Insight in Smart-Home Camera Videos
papers.tldr: OpenHome benchmarks how well vision-language models understand real-world smart-home camera videos, from recognizing events to inferring intent and appropriate responses.

papers.abstract: Traffic safety videos provide rich evidence for understanding interactions between pedestrians and vehicles, but synthetic-to-real evaluation makes this setting challenging because models must learn from simulated scenes and generalize to real-world traffic. In this work, we present StateBridge, a traffic video-language framework designed to operate under this synthetic-only training protocol. Our approach uses phase-aware clip construction, pedestrian and vehicle track summaries, and structured prompts to ground vision-language models in stable traffic evidence rather than appearance alone. We fine-tune public vision-language models on synthetic captioning and visual question answering examples, then combine their outputs through fact-locked caption fusion and evidence-diverse VQA consensus to improve consistency across actor roles, behavioral phases, and question types. StateBridge achieves an official S2 score of 55.4679 on AI City Challenge 2026 Track 2 using only synthetic training data. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of structured evidence transfer for traffic safety captioning and visual question answering.
authors: Blessing Agyei Kyem, Richard Dzinyela, Joshua Kofi Asamoah, Eugene Denteh, Andrews Danyo, Solomon Owusu-Ansah, Dickson Gyimah Asiedu, Armstrong Aboah
bullets: Targets synthetic-only training with generalization to real-world traffic safety videos.
Builds phase-aware clips, track summaries, and structured prompts to emphasize stable behavioral evidence over appearance.
Fine-tunes public vision-language models on synthetic captioning and VQA examples.
Uses fact-locked caption fusion and evidence-diverse VQA consensus for more consistent answers.
Achieves an official S2 score of 55.4679 on AI City Challenge 2026 Track 2.

papers.title: StateBridge: Phase- and Track-Grounded Reasoning for Synthetic-to-Real Traffic Video Captioning and VQA
papers.tldr: StateBridge improves synthetic-to-real traffic video captioning and VQA by grounding vision-language models in temporal phases and pedestrian/vehicle tracks.

papers.abstract: Generating multiple videos of a dynamic scene from a single reference video requires synthesizing both observed and unobserved content consistently across viewpoints. Existing camera-control methods for video diffusion typically rely on architectural mechanisms, including camera embeddings, cross-view attention, and geometric conditioning. Although effective for static scene content, these approaches often struggle with the fine-grained, dynamic geometry that must remain coherent across views and over time. We synchronize the diffusion process itself by sampling the Gaussian noise prior in a canonical 3D space derived from the source video and rasterizing it into target cameras, rather than sampling independently in each 2D image plane. Our method, SyncVid, lifts a monocular video into a canonical 4D representation, associates noise with scene geometry and unseen space, and rasterizes the resulting structured noise into arbitrary views. Because rendering can introduce local correlations, we further propose a cross-view-consistent whitening procedure that decorrelates neighboring pixels while preserving correspondence across views. The structured noise serves as the diffusion prior for a LoRA-adapted pretrained video diffusion model, requiring no architectural modifications. By enforcing spatiotemporal and cross-view coherence at the source of stochasticity, SyncVid generates synchronized videos and improves both perceptual quality and cross-view consistency in our experiments. Project page: https://qualcomm-ai-research.github.io/SyncVid-Webpage.
authors: Farhad G. Zanjani, Animesh Karnewar, Fatih Porikli, Amirhossein Habibian
bullets: Addresses the challenge of generating temporally and cross-view coherent videos from a single reference video, especially for dynamic geometry.
Lifts the source video into a canonical 4D representation and rasterizes geometry-aware noise into target camera views.
Introduces cross-view-consistent whitening to reduce local correlations while preserving correspondence across views.

Experiments report improved perceptual quality and cross-view consistency, though the abstract provides no quantitative results.
papers.selection_reason: World-equivariant diffusion noise for synchronized multi-view video generation; directly advances diffusion-based video generation with cross-view consistency.
papers.title: SyncVid: World-Equivariant Diffusion for Synchronized Video Generation
papers.tldr: SyncVid synchronizes multi-view video generation by coordinating diffusion noise in a canonical 3D space, improving visual quality and cross-view consistency without changing the model architecture.

papers.abstract: Existing 3D talking avatar methods mainly rely on parametric face models including 3DMM or FLAME, whose compact motion representations limit their ability to synthesize extreme expressions and to model accessories such as headwear. We introduce AudioLift, a two-stage framework that uses generated multi-view videos as the intermediate representation for audio-driven avatar generation without parametric face models or per-instance optimization. Our framework combines a synchronized multi-view video generation stage with an inconsistency-robust Gaussian reconstruction stage to recover coherent full-head geometry from a single portrait image. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AudioLift produces 3D talking avatars capable of capturing more extreme facial expressions than existing methods, with improved geometric completeness and strong multi-view consistency across the full $360^\circ$ viewing range.
authors: Zhuoyuan Jiang, Weijie Lyu, Xiaoyuan Wang, Tiancheng Shen, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the limited expression range and poor accessory modeling of 3DMM/FLAME-based avatars.
Uses a two-stage pipeline: synchronized multi-view video generation followed by inconsistency-robust Gaussian reconstruction.
Requires neither parametric face models nor per-instance optimization.
Produces more extreme facial expressions, more complete geometry, and strong consistency across 360° views.
Scope: results are reported for audio-driven single-image avatar generation; specific datasets and quantitative results are not given.

papers.title: AudioLift: Audio-Driven Single Image to Full-Head Gaussian Avatar via Multi-view Video Generation
papers.tldr: AudioLift creates full-head 3D talking avatars from one portrait and audio by generating synchronized multi-view video, enabling extreme expressions and complete, view-consistent geometry without parametric face models.

papers.abstract: A live esports broadcast needs a director who chooses which camera goes on air and a caster who talks over that choice, every second and without knowing what comes next. Streaming video language models have learned to commentate, but only over a broadcast that a human director has already produced. We study live broadcast production, in which a model receives the raw camera of every player and must both direct and commentate from the past alone. We present DirCast, a single streaming video language model that does both. Every second it scans all cameras at low resolution, decides with a hold-or-switch director whether and where to cut, and reads the chosen camera at high resolution before it speaks. Its context keeps what went on air and what was said and lets the other views expire, which bounds the cost of a stream of any length. We build a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with a camera for every hero, the human director's choices and the casters' commentary. DirCast directs better than rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, and its commentary wins 29.2 percent of comparisons against GPT-4o under the Proact-VL protocol, against 19.4 percent for the strongest of eleven streaming commentators that watch the human broadcast.
authors: Zixian Gao, Lixin Xiu, Penghao Luo, Xiangcheng Cao, Ziqi Cai, Zhen Li, Erwin Wu, Kaipeng Zhang

Scans all cameras at low resolution each second, uses a hold-or-switch policy, then views the selected camera at high resolution before speaking.
Maintains only aired visuals, commentary, and recent context while allowing other views to expire, keeping processing cost bounded over arbitrarily long streams.
Introduces a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with per-hero cameras, director choices, and caster commentary.
Outperforms rule-based and zero-shot directors, including GPT-5; its commentary wins 29.2% of Proact-VL comparisons against GPT-4o.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming video-language model for live esports directing and commentary; fits video understanding and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: DirCast: Live Esports Directing and Commentary with a Single Streaming Video-Language Model
papers.tldr: DirCast is a streaming video-language model that jointly selects live esports camera views and generates commentary using only past observations.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have enabled high-fidelity single-shot synthesis, yet practical storytelling creation requires multi-shot videos with both strong inter-shot consistency and fine-grained controllability. Existing multi-shot video generation approaches achieve strong consistency but still fall short in controllability. In this paper, we propose Mise-en-Video (MeV), a highly controllable multi-shot video generation framework that allows video creators to conduct staging the multi-shot in the 3D space and then generate the corresponding multi-shot video. To achieve this, our framework combines a hierarchical attention mechanism for multi-level narrative consistency with 3D-aware layout guidance for precise, per-shot spatial control. To support training and evaluation, we develop standardized annotation pipelines and construct a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot texts and oriented 3D bounding boxes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MeV consistently outperforms strong baselines in video quality, inter-shot consistency, and subject-level controllability.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining inter-shot consistency with fine-grained control in multi-shot video generation.
Uses hierarchical attention to maintain multi-level narrative consistency across shots.
Employs 3D-aware layout guidance for precise per-shot spatial and subject control.
Introduces annotation pipelines and a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot text and oriented 3D bounding boxes.
Experiments show improvements over strong baselines in video quality, inter-shot consistency, and subject-level controllability.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-shot video generation framework with 3D-aware layout control, directly relevant to video generation research.
papers.title: Mise-en-Video: Fine-Grained 3D Control for Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.tldr: Mise-en-Video enables controllable multi-shot video generation by planning shots in 3D space while preserving narrative consistency.

papers.abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
authors: Shengqiong Wu, Meng Luo, Bobo Li, Ziwei Liu, Shuicheng Yan, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Philip Torr, Hao Fei
bullets: Frames video as a partial, lossy, time-ordered projection of a latent temporal world.
Organizes research into reading world properties, writing videos, sharing understanding and generation, and interacting through actions and observations.
Distinguishes sequence-level temporal coherence from consistency of the underlying world state.
Highlights a shift from clip recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and decision-oriented evaluation.
Identifies open challenges in representations, models, datasets, benchmarks, and interaction-based assessment.
papers.selection_reason: Survey unifying video foundation models and world models directly fits world modeling and video understanding.
papers.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
papers.tldr: This survey unifies video foundation and world models through four operations—reading, writing, sharing, and interacting—to study how videos represent and support reasoning about evolving worlds.

papers.abstract: Video object removal and injection are reciprocal editing operations between object-present and object-absent video states, yet they differ substantially in training difficulty. Removal can be effectively bootstrapped from video inpainting and further adapted to erase object-related interaction effects. Injection, however, requires large-scale paired supervision to model object appearance, dynamics, and scene-dependent effects, while perfectly aligned real-world pairs are difficult to collect and synthetic data lacks sufficient realism and diversity. To address this challenge, we present UniVOE, a removal-driven framework for training both video object removal and injection models. We first train an effect-aware remover by transferring video inpainting priors and finetuning on object-present/object-absent pairs. The trained remover converts real object-present videos into object-absent counterparts, creating large-scale paired supervision for injection. An injection model is trained on these pairs in the reverse direction to recover objects together with their dynamics and interaction effects. Moreover, since pixel-level reconstruction alone cannot adequately capture perceptual realism, we introduce a reward-based post-training method that aligns injection results with human preferences using a proprietary reward model. Experiments against strong open-source and commercial systems demonstrate that UniVOE achieves state-of-the-art performance on both object removal and injection, particularly in challenging interaction-effect cases.
authors: Shuzhou Yang, Lanqing Guo, Lingen Li, Weiqi Li, Zhao Zhong, Liefeng Bo, Jian Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training object injection models without large, aligned real-world video pairs.
Transfers video-inpainting priors to train an effect-aware object remover, then adapts it using object-present/object-absent pairs.
Uses the remover to convert real object-present videos into paired object-absent videos for reverse-direction injection training.
Adds reward-based post-training to improve perceptual realism and align injection outputs with human preferences.
Reports state-of-the-art performance against open-source and commercial systems, especially for challenging interaction effects.
papers.selection_reason: Video object removal and injection is a video generation/editing task with a transferable training and reward post-training idea.
papers.title: UniVOE: A Removal-Driven Framework for Interaction-Aware Universal Video Object Editing
papers.tldr: UniVOE uses object removal to generate training pairs for realistic video object injection, enabling unified editing of object presence and absence.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models have learned rich 3D/4D priors, making them promising for scene generation and video re-rendering. However, their use in spatial tasks is limited by imprecise camera control, spatial and temporal inconsistencies, and entangled camera motion with scene dynamics. Existing approaches, such as task-specific fine-tuning and post-process warping, often introduce visual artifacts, generalize poorly, or incur high computational costs. We propose WorldForge V2 to achieve accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. We first develop a training-free guidance framework using warped references to iteratively refine generation along a target camera path. Optical-flow analysis identifies motion-related latent channels for selective guidance, helping separate motion control from appearance. A dual-path strategy further compares guided and unguided predictions to correct artifacts from imperfect references. Together, these components guide viewpoint changes while preserving scene appearance and object motion. To reduce refinement costs, v-cache approximates the correction using the preceding denoising prediction, avoiding an additional model evaluation. We further extend motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and introduce Trajectory LoRA, which concentrates adaptation on blocks most responsive to trajectory guidance. A two-stage training strategy teaches these adapters to denoise the states encountered during guided generation, using limited supervision effectively. This enables reliable camera control with very little training data, with a single training scene already supporting generalization to unseen scenes. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
authors: Chenxi Song, Yanming Yang, Tong Zhao, Ruibo Li, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses imprecise camera control, temporal/spatial inconsistencies, and entanglement between camera motion and scene dynamics.
Uses warped-reference guidance, optical-flow-based motion localization, and dual-path prediction to refine generation along target camera paths.
Introduces v-cache to reduce refinement cost and Trajectory LoRA to adapt only trajectory-responsive network blocks.
A two-stage training strategy enables reliable control with limited supervision; one training scene can generalize to unseen scenes.
Experiments across multiple datasets report state-of-the-art camera trajectory accuracy and generation quality.
papers.selection_reason: Camera-controlled video diffusion with trajectory guidance and efficient refinement.
papers.title: WorldForge V2: Eliciting Camera-Trajectory Alignment in Video Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: WorldForge V2 improves camera-trajectory control in video diffusion models while preserving scene appearance and object motion, using training-free guidance plus targeted lightweight adaptation.

papers.abstract: Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text-first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general-purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack-Bench, which assesses Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell-tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell-linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed-source models and 13 open-weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack-bench.
authors: Ilan Theodoro, Jord\~ao Bragantini, Lo\"ic A. Royer
bullets: Covers 15 standard cell-tracking datasets, four imaging modalities, 1,537 problems, and 9,041 cell-linking decisions.
Includes a harder subset built from failures shared by different tracking algorithms.
Evaluates environment harnesses, 9 closed-source frontier models, and 13 open-weight models.
Analyzes VLM failure modes and releases code, model outputs, and benchmark-generation tools.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for VLM spatiotemporal cell tracking; relevant to video understanding evaluation.
papers.title: CellTrack-Bench: Microscopic Cell Tracking Benchmark for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: CellTrack-Bench evaluates how well vision-language models perform cell-tracking decisions compared with specialized tracking algorithms.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong potential for video anomaly detection, but dense frame-level inference makes them impractical for real-time deployment. Existing acceleration commonly relies on uniform sampling, which ignores content dynamics and can either waste computation on static segments or miss localized anomalies. We propose MoG-VLM a motion-adaptive anomaly detection framework that leverages motion purely as a lightweight control signal to decide when VLM inference is necessary. To this end, we introduce Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) which performs content-aware sampling to concentrate computation on informative regions while avoiding redundant processing. We further introduce a hierarchical dual-stream design in which dense multi-frame VLM reasoning is activated only around frames with elevated anomaly likelihood, via anchor-triggered context-window expansion with early termination. A fusion module then reconciles these instantaneous semantic cues with temporal action dynamics. Across four benchmarks, our method achieves 91.91%, 84.30%, 87.88%, and 78.96% AUC-ROC on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, MSAD, and ShanghaiTech, respectively, establishing new state of the art on three benchmarks under the zero-shot, training-free setting. On XD-Violence, we improve over the previous best result by +0.57% while delivering a 1.31x inference speedup. These results demonstrate that content-aware allocation of VLM capacity, processing fewer frames more intelligently rather than all frames uniformly, is a more effective axis of progress than uniformly densifying VLM inference across frames. Code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kdawoud91/MoG-VLM.
authors: Khaled Waleed Dawoud, Muhammad Zaigham Zaheer, Khan Muhammad, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of dense frame-level VLM inference and the limitations of uniform sampling.
Uses Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) for motion-adaptive, content-aware frame selection.
Employs hierarchical dual-stream reasoning with anchor-triggered context expansion and early termination.
Fuses instantaneous semantic cues from the VLM with temporal action dynamics.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on three of four benchmarks and a 1.31× speedup on XD-Violence.
