papers.selection_reason: Motion-guided VLM for efficient video anomaly detection; fits video understanding and efficient inference.
papers.title: MoG-VLM: Efficient Video Anomaly Detection through Motion-Guided Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: MoG-VLM accelerates zero-shot video anomaly detection by using motion to selectively trigger expensive VLM reasoning on informative frames and nearby context.

papers.abstract: Many questions about a video concern one physical object. Where does the ball end up after the cups are shuffled? Which card is the queen? How often was the mug covered? Video-language models (Video-LMs) recognise such objects in single frames but do not keep them apart over time. On real shell-game videos, open models from 8B to 235B parameters, their thinking variants, a reinforcement-learned tool agent and three training-free tool agents all stay within ten points of chance. We separate semantic identity binding from temporal identity maintenance. An object's identity should be fixed at a moment when the evidence for it is visible, and carried afterwards by a tracker. \emph{Track, Then Bind} implements this principle without training. A promptable video tracker follows every candidate object and draws it with a track number. A frozen vision-language model answers a static question about the identifying evidence, which binds the target to a track. The answer is then derived from the tracked state in text, without asking the model to reinterpret the original video during read-out. A single configuration covers all benchmarks. With Qwen3-VL-32B it solves both VET-Bench tasks, where a fine-tuned trajectory model reaches 92\% and 90\% and the same VLM voting over 16 samples stays at 30--32\%. It answers 55.4\% of the hardest Perception Test cup games, where the best published model answers 41.5\%, and, using track-derived timelines, 48.6\% of TOC-Bench questions, against 37.1\% for the same model answering directly. Drawing the same tracks on the video and asking the question directly falls 12--19 points short of the agent on real cup games.
authors: Di Yang, Xiaochang Li, Muyang Liu, Yufei Wang, Yanhai Xiong
bullets: Video-LMs often recognize objects in individual frames but lose identity across time, especially in shell-game-style videos.
Track, Then Bind uses a promptable tracker to follow candidates and a frozen VLM to identify the target from visible evidence.
The system derives answers from track-based state and timelines rather than making the VLM reinterpret the full video during read-out.
With Qwen3-VL-32B, it reaches 55.4% on the hardest Perception Test cup games and 48.6% on TOC-Bench, outperforming the cited direct-answer baselines.
A single training-free configuration handles multiple benchmarks, though performance remains far from perfect on difficult cup games.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free object identity reasoning for video-language models, directly relevant to video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Ask About the Right Moment: Training-Free Object Identity Reasoning for Video-Language Models
papers.tldr: Track objects first, bind their identities when visible, and answer from their tracked history to improve video-language reasoning without training.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses $\sim$10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.
authors: Ruicong Liu, Liangyang Ouyang, Fengbo Lan, Zhixiang Wang, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses programmer-art visuals produced by AI-built games.
Uses video-to-video generation from plain footage, without G-buffers, object labels, or 3D proxies.
LoRA-fine-tunes a reference-video-conditioned video model on paired game-rendering clips and gameplay recordings.
Introduces an entity-level benchmark with 59 held-out cases and 753 entities.
Improves temporal entity matching from 50.9% to 62.9% and reduces missed count changes from 34.7% to 21.3% versus the base model.
papers.selection_reason: Entity-consistent video-to-video generative rendering, relevant to video generation and editing.
papers.title: AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark
papers.tldr: AnyGameRenderer converts simple game footage into detailed visuals while preserving each entity’s position, timing, appearance, and count across diverse game genres.

papers.abstract: World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible-impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.
authors: Taekoan Yoo, Wonkyung Jung, Kyunghun Kim, Kyeongbo Kong
bullets: Addresses the lack of evaluations that identify which physical expectations conflict with video observations.
Uses MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations aligned with video windows to detect and describe violations without task-specific probes or classifiers.
Introduces IntPhys2-Timing, an extension of IntPhys2 with annotated violation intervals.
Achieves up to 70.7% hit rate across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and improves overall possible–impossible discrimination accuracy over compared methods on IntPhys2.
Reveals attribute- and noise-dependent violation-localization patterns across timesteps in reconstructed diffusion- and flow-based video trajectories.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free temporal localization and interpretable evaluation of physical consistency in video generative models.
papers.title: PhysTrace: Interpretable Temporal Evaluation of Physical Consistency in Video Generative Models
papers.tldr: PhysTrace is a training-free framework that temporally localizes and explains physical inconsistencies in generated videos by comparing history-conditioned expectations with observed events.

papers.abstract: Real-time polyp segmentation in computer-assisted colonoscopy is hampered by the difficulty of deploying high-accuracy models under strict latency budgets. Frame skipping, which performs inference every K frames and reuses or interpolates the rest, improves throughput but introduces motion blur and lesion misalignment that degrade temporal consistency. To close this gap, we propose the Lightweight Frame Compensator (LFC), a 77K-parameter plug-and-play module inserted before a frozen segmentation backbone. Operating on a three-frame window, LFC fuses consecutive frames via spatio-temporal attention into a single compensated frame, and is trained only on pseudo-labels generated by a differently seeded model, without any expert annotation. Experiments on three polyp video benchmarks show that LFC recovers most of the accuracy degraded by direct frame skipping and, in several settings, reaches the accuracy of frame-by-frame inference, while retaining a 2.05X--2.55X throughput gain. We further evaluate the temporal stability of three backbones spanning CNN, pyramid Transformer, and global-attention Transformer architectures, revealing a spectrum of sensitivity to frame skipping that arises from how locally or globally each architecture aggregates misaligned input. The compensation gain of LFC follows this spectrum: it is largest for high-capacity Transformer backbones, which achieve the best static accuracy but suffer the most under skip-frame inference. LFC thus offers a lightweight, pluggable, and deployment-friendly route to real-time polyp segmentation.
bullets: Addresses motion blur and lesion misalignment caused by skipping frames during real-time colonoscopy segmentation.
Uses a 77K-parameter, plug-and-play module before a frozen backbone to fuse a three-frame window with spatio-temporal attention.
Trains solely on pseudo-labels from a differently seeded model, requiring no expert annotations.
Across three polyp-video benchmarks, often matches frame-by-frame accuracy and recovers most skipping-related degradation.
Benefits high-capacity Transformer backbones most, as they are more sensitive to misaligned skipped-frame inputs.
papers.selection_reason: Lightweight temporal frame compensator enabling accurate real-time polyp segmentation under frame skipping.
papers.title: Lightweight Frame Compensation for Real-Time Polyp Segmentation under Frame Skipping
papers.tldr: LFC is a lightweight, annotation-free frame-compensation module that largely restores polyp-segmentation accuracy lost from frame skipping while preserving a 2.05×–2.55× throughput gain.

papers.abstract: Moving object segmentation is conventionally formulated at the sequence and object level, marking an entire instance as moving once it moves anywhere in a video. Recent instantaneous formulations distinguish moving from stationary intervals, but still generate masks at the object level through frozen segmentation foundation models. Because the mask is derived from an instance-level proposal, motion is typically attributed to the entire instance rather than localized to the regions that actually move. Moreover, such instance-level predictions can produce masks even when no part of the instance is actually moving, revealing a more fundamental issue: motion is not an intrinsic property of an instance; it can only be determined by comparing at least two frames. Building on this premise, we introduce MoRSe, which jointly interprets two frames to predict a moving-region mask, distinguishing actual scene motion from apparent motion induced by the camera. A single RGB encoder replaces multi-stage foundation stacks, so no optical flow, point tracks, or separate mask generator is needed at inference. We release MoRSe-5K, a benchmark of 42 sequences with Static, Dynamic-Static, and Dynamic settings designed to evaluate the model's ability to distinguish and localize moving and stationary regions under different camera and scene motion conditions. MoRSe outperforms both specialized moving object segmentation methods and dense 4D reconstruction methods with motion-thresholded predictions, while producing the fewest false positives on sequences where nothing moves.
authors: Wenhua Jin, Tiancheng Chen, Sheng Tang, Jiahao Li, Yupeng Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
bullets: Existing instance-level methods label an entire object as moving even when only part moves—or when nothing moves.
MoRSe treats motion as a relational property requiring comparison between frames.
A single RGB encoder predicts moving-region masks without optical flow, point tracks, or separate mask-generation stages.
MoRSe-5K contains 42 sequences spanning Static, Dynamic-Static, and Dynamic motion settings.
It outperforms specialized and motion-thresholded reconstruction baselines, with the fewest false positives on static sequences.
papers.selection_reason: Two-frame moving-region segmentation separating true motion from camera-induced apparent motion.
papers.title: Moving Regions, Not Moving Objects: Segmenting What Actually Moves under Camera Motion
papers.tldr: MoRSe jointly analyzes two frames to localize only the regions that truly move, separating scene motion from camera-induced apparent motion.

papers.abstract: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.
authors: Jiahao Meng, Qize Yang, Yuxuan Wang, Yunfei Chu, Wensi Dai, Jin Xu, Yunhai Tong
bullets: Targets video-centered research, where agents must identify questions, retrieve multimodal web evidence, and link report claims to relevant video moments.
Proposes a skill-based workflow, OmniDR-Bench, and Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs) covering audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation.
Uses Audited Rubric Construction to create reliable, task-specific evaluation criteria across 50 Chinese and English tasks in 19 real-world categories.
Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3/100, indicating substantial room for improvement.
Remaining weaknesses include limited content coverage, weak cross-modal causal and logical analysis, and inaccurate citation support.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks video-centered deep research agents with audiovisual grounding and multimodal evidence use.
papers.title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports
papers.tldr: Introduces a benchmark and rubric framework for evaluating agents that turn videos plus external evidence into interactive, well-grounded deep-research reports.

papers.abstract: Generated robot videos can look convincing while depicting the wrong interac- tion: a different object is moved, a grasp disappears, or a placement ends out- side its destination. We introduce RGraph-Eval, a reference-based framework that makes these discrepancies explicit through task-grounded temporal scene graphs. Unlike approaches that construct separate evidence representations for different evaluation dimensions, we organize task entities, interactions, and motion within a unified, interpretable scene graph representation. A foundation-model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, grounds persistent object masks, infers and verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs manipulated- object motion in three dimensions. Applying this representation to a generated video and a reference demonstration supports an interpretable RGraph-Eval score with visible-object, relation-change, and 3D path-shape components. We also introduce ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources annotated with the multimodal representation. Our eval- uation separates graph-generation quality from agreement with human video judgments, and includes comparisons with adapted SVG2 and SG-Ego, a bench- mark of three video generators. The framework connects robot-video assessment to the observable entities and interactions underlying a task, while making the graph annotations reusable beyond evaluation. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/SashaDance/rgraph-eval.
authors: Aleksandr Lazarev, Sofia Zimina, Roman Kuznetsov, Tatiana Zemskova, Iaroslav Koshelev, Dmitry Yudin
bullets: Targets visually convincing but task-incorrect robot videos, such as wrong objects, lost grasps, or incorrect placements.
Uses a unified scene graph covering entities, interactions, motion, state transitions, action intervals, and reconstructed 3D object paths.
Produces interpretable scores based on visible objects, relation changes, and 3D path shape.
Introduces ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 annotated manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources.
Separately evaluates graph-generation quality and alignment with human judgments, and benchmarks three video generators.
papers.selection_reason: Temporal scene-graph framework for evaluating robot videos; fits video understanding and task-grounded video reasoning.
papers.title: RGraph-Eval: Task-Grounded Scene Graphs for Evaluating Robot Video Generation
papers.tldr: RGraph-Eval evaluates robot video generation by comparing task-grounded temporal scene graphs of generated videos and reference demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.
authors: Songlin Yang, Zhe Wang, Xiaotong Zhao, Xi Wang, Ran Zhang, Shuai Li, Taiyi Wu, Songlian Li, Eric Liu, Alan Zhao, Anyi Rao
bullets: Addresses the gap between useful MLLM representations and their reliable use by video diffusion transformers.
Uses latent-only generator grounding to make the DiT depend on frozen MLLM latents.
Learns factor-aware editing through paired videos with target-factor changes and non-target preservation.
Trains temporal inference from text or incomplete video by optimizing the MLLM and connector through a frozen DiT.
Reports consistently better performance than baselines across sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Cinematic video generation with MLLM latent grounding and factor-aware control fits diffusion video generation interests.
papers.title: Making MLLM Latents Matter: Factor-Aware Predictive Learning for Cinematic Video Generation
papers.tldr: FAPL trains MLLM latents to become actionable for cinematic video generation with sparse temporal guidance and factor-aware control.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, placing greater demands on reliable AI-generated video detection. Existing artifact-based detectors typically identify generation artifacts as evidence for source prediction, yet they may either fail to recognize subtle artifacts or reach the correct source decision without faithfully identifying the evidence underlying it. In this work, we systematically investigate how to design and train effective artifact detectors and formulate artifact detection as a structured process comprising three complementary capabilities: Inspection Planning, which determines what should be examined; Evidence Verification, which verifies whether the inspected content exhibits genuine generation artifacts; and Evidence Aggregation, which integrates the verified evidence into the final source decision. Building on this formulation, we introduce Verus-Insight, trained with human-anchored full-process supervision and progressive capability training to strengthen both fine-grained artifact detection and video-level detection. We further introduce Verus-Bench, a benchmark with fine-grained human annotations of perceptible artifacts for evaluating artifact detection. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that Verus-Insight achieves strong performance in both fine-grained artifact analysis and AI-generated video detection, with substantial gains in recovering human-perceived artifacts. Further analyses reveal that the three capabilities are complementary yet distinct, and that Verus-Insight more reliably converts relevant inspection targets into supported artifact evidence without increasing spurious artifact claims.
authors: Zhuoran Zhang, Yang Shi, Qixun Wang, Tengfei Liu, Yuqi Tang, Xuanyu Zhu, Yizhuo Jia, Jingyun Hua, Shixuan Liu, Xianghua Ying, Haotian Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Wenjing Yang
bullets: Existing artifact-based detectors can miss subtle evidence or make correct source decisions without identifying why.
The framework separates detection into Inspection Planning, Evidence Verification, and Evidence Aggregation.
Verus-Insight uses human-anchored full-process supervision and progressive capability training.
Verus-Bench provides fine-grained human annotations of perceptible video artifacts for evaluation.
Experiments show strong fine-grained artifact analysis and video-level detection, with better recovery of human-perceived artifacts without more spurious claims.
papers.selection_reason: AI-generated video artifact detection with structured explanation fits video understanding interests.
papers.title: Verus-Insight: Towards Explainable Artifact Detection in AI-Generated Videos
papers.tldr: Verus-Insight makes AI-generated video detection more explainable by systematically finding, verifying, and aggregating human-perceived visual artifacts.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generation enables low-latency streaming, yet prevailing training pipelines separate causal adaptation from distribution matching. Recent representation-based text-to-video methods retain this separation by starting from ODE-initialized checkpoints, even when the target distribution is defined directly by reference videos. We introduce Direct Forcing, a single-stage framework that uses reference videos both as paired examples of how a history continues and as a target population for self-generated rollouts. Causal Continuation Alignment learns paired spatiotemporal correspondence under reference histories, while Rollout Distribution Matching uses maximum mean discrepancy to align the representation distributions of self-generated and reference videos. Together, these complementary signals allow a pretrained video model to learn causal continuation and the target video distribution in a single training stage. Dynamic Gradient Balancing adapts the relative gradient contributions of continuation alignment and distribution matching during training. Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, Direct Forcing learns a four-step autoregressive generator in 250 updates without a separate initialization stage or online diffusion-score supervision, achieving 84.63 VBench Total and 86.01 Quality. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of dynamic gradient balancing and reveal distinct representation preferences: deeper features benefit continuation alignment, whereas intermediate features yield better performance for rollout distribution matching.
authors: Haojun Xu, Jie Huang, Xin Lu, Mingchen Zhong, Zihao Fan, Linjiang Huang, Si Liu
bullets: Addresses the separation between causal adaptation and distribution matching in few-step autoregressive video generation.
Combines Causal Continuation Alignment on reference histories with Rollout Distribution Matching via maximum mean discrepancy.
Uses Dynamic Gradient Balancing to adapt the contributions of the two training objectives.
Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, it trains a four-step generator in 250 updates without separate initialization or online diffusion-score supervision.
Reports 84.63 VBench Total and 86.01 Quality; ablations show different feature depths favor continuation alignment versus distribution matching.
papers.selection_reason: Autoregressive text-to-video generation with single-stage training.
papers.title: Direct Forcing: A Single-Stage Training Recipe for Few-Step Autoregressive Text-to-Video Generation
papers.tldr: Direct Forcing trains a pretrained video model in one stage to generate high-quality text-to-video clips autoregressively in just four steps.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based audio-visual generation methods typically perform joint denoising of audio and video latents throughout the entire sampling trajectory, repeatedly executing modality-specific denoising branches and cross-modal attention at every timestep. However, we observe that such uniform joint computation is not always necessary. The key is a modality-asymmetric recoverability: audio-side drift introduced by mid-stage caching can be substantially reduced by only a few terminal joint denoising steps, whereas video-side degradation caused by caching leads to persistent loss of motion and temporal details. This asymmetry suggests that inference acceleration should selectively cache recoverable audio-side computation while preserving full video refinement. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache (CAVC)}, a training-free modality-asymmetric caching framework. CAVC adopts a sandwich-structured computation allocation: after detecting that audio denoiser outputs enter a cache-tolerant regime, it caches and reuses the audio denoiser output to bypass audio denoising and cross-modal attention in the middle stage, while the video branch continues independent spatio-temporal refinement; a few joint steps are then restored at the end to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and improve synchronization. Experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that CAVC achieves 1.10--1.35x wall-clock acceleration, improves several visual dynamics and temporal statistics, and maintains competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yibo Zhao, Senlin cheng, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses unnecessary joint audio-video denoising and cross-modal attention at every sampling step.
Uses a training-free, convergence-adaptive cache with sandwich-structured computation allocation.
Caches audio denoiser outputs in a cache-tolerant middle regime while video undergoes full spatio-temporal refinement.
Restores a few terminal joint denoising steps to reduce cross-modal drift and improve synchronization.

Across public benchmarks, achieves 1.10–1.35× wall-clock acceleration while maintaining competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment and improving several visual dynamics and temporal statistics.
papers.selection_reason: Accelerates audio-visual diffusion generation via modality-asymmetric caching, relevant to video diffusion and inference efficiency.
papers.title: CAVC: Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache for Modality-Asymmetric Diffusion Generation
papers.tldr: CAVC accelerates audio-visual diffusion generation by caching recoverable audio computation mid-sampling while preserving video refinement and restoring joint denoising at the end.

papers.abstract: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.
authors: Yifeng Yao, Jinghan Li, Zhihao Zhang, Yajiao Xiong, Yang Jin, Kun Xu, Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao
bullets: Motivation: Existing masked and autoregressive video methods do not fully capture future dynamics or match joint-embedding representation quality.
Method: A causal encoder summarizes past observations, while a state predictor infers the next frame in a fixed space from a frozen semantic tokenizer.
Detail: An auxiliary lightweight decoder reconstructs future-frame patches to preserve spatial detail alongside semantic content.
Unification: Still images are converted into local-to-global crop sequences so the same prediction objective applies to images and videos.

Results: VANE improves with model and data scaling, reaches state-of-the-art on most evaluated unified-encoder benchmarks, and exceeds V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 mean-class recall@5 points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation.
papers.selection_reason: Next-frame prediction in embedding space for scalable visual world modeling and video representation learning.
papers.title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual Representation Learning
papers.tldr: VANE learns scalable visual representations by predicting entire future-frame embeddings, combining semantic next-frame prediction with fine-grained spatial reconstruction across images and videos.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have substantially improved visual fidelity, yet existing models still struggle to understand the physical evolution implicit in user prompts, making it difficult to generate videos with continuous physical state evolution. Here, we propose PhyEvolve, a multi-agent framework that enhances natural-language prompts through structured state-evolution planning. PhyEvolve consists of three agents: a Director, a Physical Evolver, and a Composer. Given a user prompt and an optional first frame, the Director grounds the scene and disentangles physical events from observation changes. The Physical Evolver uses scene evidence to identify physical mechanisms then constructs causally linked state transitions that unfold throughout the video, whether visible or not. The Composer utilizes these transitions to enhance the original prompts. Without retraining or model modification, PhyEvolve works directly with existing generators through prompt replacement. Extensive experiments on four major benchmarks show that PhyEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the cutting-edge prior agentic baseline by 7.9 percentage points on average. These results demonstrate that explicit causal state-evolution planning improves physical consistency and state continuity in generated videos through natural-language prompt enhancement.
authors: Yang-Hao Zhou, Lixing Tan, Zhiqi Li, Guang Yang, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses poor modeling of continuous physical evolution in text-to-video generation.
Uses three agents: Director, Physical Evolver, and Composer.
Plans causally linked physical state transitions, including changes that may not be directly visible.
Works with existing video generators through prompt replacement and optional first-frame input.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results and a 7.9-point average gain over a prior agentic baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic prompt planning for physics-aware text-to-video generation improves video diffusion outputs.
papers.title: PhyEvolve: Multi-Agent State-Evolution Planning for Physics-Aware Video Generation
papers.tldr: PhyEvolve improves physics-aware video generation by using multi-agent causal state-evolution planning to enhance prompts without modifying or retraining the video generator.

papers.abstract: Adding control to video generation often requires training, which demands additional computational resources, data, or architectural changes. We propose a training-free approach that utilizes pretrained video diffusion models to control object layout and motion using coarse layouts. Our method operates in two passes: first, it steers spatiotemporal placement through prompt-guided cross-attention to produce a coarse visual guide; second, this guide conditions the same model to generate a high-quality, layoutconsistent video. The approach enables coordinated motion with strong temporal consistency, supporting diverse trajectories and object interactions without additional training. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms prior work in overlap and trajectory accuracy, as well as visual quality across static, dynamic, and multi-object scene settings.
authors: Asaf Joseph, Moshe Mandel, Ohad Fried
bullets: Addresses the computational and architectural costs of training-based video-generation control.
Uses prompt-guided cross-attention to create a coarse spatiotemporal visual guide.
Conditions the same pretrained model on this guide to generate layout-consistent videos.
Supports diverse trajectories, coordinated motion, and multi-object interactions without additional training.
Experiments report improved overlap, trajectory accuracy, and visual quality across static and dynamic scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free layout-guided control of pretrained video diffusion models for temporally consistent video synthesis; fits video generation interests.
papers.title: Latent Space Jam: Layout Guided Video Synthesis
papers.tldr: A training-free two-pass method controls object layouts and motion in pretrained video diffusion models while preserving temporal consistency and visual quality.

papers.abstract: We study mountain-bike action quality assessment (AQA) with weak labels and candidate feedback. The training corpus comprises 95 field-recorded jump clips with binary labels denoting good or poor technique. These are coarse categorical labels, not continuous expert quality scores; phase-boundary and aspect-level annotations are unavailable. Our pipeline summarizes four heuristic phases using frozen V-JEPA 2 video features and two-dimensional pose and motion measurements. A small transformer predicts a binary-label score. A separate reference layer compares phase-specific measurements with those of clips labelled as good technique to propose phase, body-parameter, and direction cues. We detail the measurements, network, and evaluation so that the limits of each output are explicit. In five-fold clip-level cross-validation, the full scorer obtained pooled out-of-fold AUROC 0.768 and average precision 0.812. These are exploratory figures because the reporting fold also selected the neural training epoch and riders were not separated between folds. Removing biomechanical scoring inputs raised AUROC to 0.809. A separate inner-selection run obtained AUROC 0.678, but used about 57 rather than 76 training clips per outer fold, so its difference from the test-selected run does not quantify selection bias. The unsupervised aspect head did not learn distinct factors. On a 17-clip external probe, an earlier checkpoint obtained binary accuracy 0.412 and Spearman association -0.135 with expert scores. Candidate cues had precision 0.118 and recall 1.0 against each of two coaches, with substantial disagreement about direction. These findings do not establish rider-independent scoring or reliable corrective feedback; they identify the empirical work needed to evaluate either use.
bullets: Uses 95 field-recorded jump clips with coarse good/poor technique labels, rather than continuous expert scores or phase/aspect annotations.
Summarizes four heuristic phases with frozen V-JEPA 2 features and 2D pose/motion measurements; a small transformer predicts binary quality.
A separate reference layer compares phase-specific measurements with good-technique clips to generate body-parameter and directional feedback cues.
Five-fold clip-level cross-validation yielded pooled AUROC 0.768 and average precision 0.812, but epoch selection used the reporting folds and riders were not separated.

The external probe showed weak performance and feedback agreement: binary accuracy 0.412, Spearman association −0.135, and cue precision 0.118 with recall 1.0; the aspect head found no distinct factors.
papers.selection_reason: Action quality assessment from video using temporal representations and pose/motion measurements; fits video understanding.
papers.title: V-JEPA 2 Meets AQA: Phase-Based Scoring and Reference-Based Feedback for Mountain Biking
papers.tldr: An exploratory mountain-bike AQA pipeline using frozen video features, pose/motion measurements, and reference-based cues shows moderate binary-label discrimination but does not yet support reliable rider-independent scoring or feedback.

papers.abstract: Cinematic multi-shot video generation requires both narrative planning and iterative refinement. Existing methods either lack narrative reasoning or rely on feed-forward workflows without policy updates. In this paper, we propose CineEvolve, an agentic self-evolution framework for cinematic multi-shot video generation that unifies a Director and a Critic within a single vision-language policy. Emulating real-world filmmaking that couples iterative direction with critical feedback, we train CineEvolve via alternating reinforcement learning, where the Director surfaces flaws to sharpen the Critic, and the updated Critic guides the Director's targeted revisions. To stabilize co-evolution, we introduce Evolutionary GRPO (E-GRPO), leveraging historical anchoring and revision safeguarding to mitigate advantage inflation. Additionally, we contribute CineTraj, a 40K cinematic trajectory dataset spanning creation, critique, and revision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CineEvolve outperforms existing approaches. Our code will be available at https://github.com/JingZhe-8/CineEvolve.
bullets: Addresses the need for both narrative planning and iterative refinement in multi-shot video generation.
Unifies a Director and Critic in one vision-language policy trained through alternating reinforcement learning.
Introduces Evolutionary GRPO (E-GRPO) with historical anchoring and revision safeguarding to stabilize co-evolution.
Provides CineTraj, a 40K trajectory dataset covering video creation, critique, and revision.
Experiments report improved performance over existing approaches, though specific metrics are not given.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic self-evolution framework for cinematic multi-shot video generation directly targets video generation research.
papers.title: CineEvolve: An Agentic Self-Evolution Framework for Cinematic Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.tldr: CineEvolve uses an evolving Director–Critic agent pair to iteratively plan, critique, and refine cinematic multi-shot videos.

papers.abstract: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.
authors: Ruotong Liao, Meikel Kokowski, Xiaoxiao Sun, Yongqin Xian, Laura Bravo S\'anchez, Shiye Su, Federico Tombari, Serena Yeung-Levy, Volker Tresp
bullets: Evaluates Information Capture, State Tracking, and Location Tracking for ambient memory needs.
Tests two levels of proactiveness: timely notifications and active start-to-stop memory-maintenance interventions.
Includes Daily and Scientific tracks with associated question-answering evaluations.
Finds that even strong proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines struggle to be both timely and accurate.
Supports evaluation of proactive multimodal assistants and video agents operating alongside users.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for proactive memory in streaming egocentric video; directly targets embodied memory and video-language understanding.
papers.title: ProactEgoMem: Benchmarking Proactive Memory in Streaming Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: ProactEgoMem benchmarks whether video agents can proactively capture, update, and maintain useful memories from streaming egocentric video.

papers.abstract: Increasing the attention context length significantly improves streaming video generation quality, while incurring prohibitive memory and computational costs as the context grows. Existing methods attempt to capture this contextual information through attention selection or compression, but remain limited by bounded representations and lack explicit attention-level supervision to retain historical contributions to current queries. To address this, we introduce Attn-Forcing, a novel framework that preserves full-context attention contributions for streaming video generation under bounded memory and computation. We achieve this by introducing attention proxies that continuously approximate the attention responses induced by the historical context. Specifically, we implement the proxies as learnable visual latents and employ a Proxy Update Module to incorporate visual context from historical latents. Moreover, we propose an Attention Matching Loss to explicitly constrain the attention behavior of the learned proxies using full-context attention supervision. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that Attn-Forcing consistently improves streaming video generation quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance over existing baseline methods.
authors: Junyao Gao, Sibo Liu, Jiaxing Li, Yanan Sun, Hanxin Zhu, Weidong Zhang, Jun Zhang, Cairong Zhao
bullets: Longer attention contexts improve quality but create prohibitive memory and computational costs.
The method uses learnable visual latents as attention proxies for historical context.
A Proxy Update Module continuously incorporates context from historical latents.
An Attention Matching Loss provides explicit supervision from full-context attention behavior.
Experiments report consistent quality improvements and state-of-the-art performance over existing baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Learns full-context attention proxies for streaming video generation under bounded memory/compute; relevant to efficient attention and video generation.
papers.title: Attn-Forcing: Learning Full-Context Attention Proxies for Streaming Video Generation
papers.tldr: Attn-Forcing enables higher-quality streaming video generation by approximating full-history attention with learned visual proxies under bounded memory and computation.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.
authors: Chenxu Zhou, Zhiyuan Yu, Yudong Jin, Yinji Shentu, Yu Zhang, Jiaming Sun, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Targets costly dense multi-view capture requirements and the limited resolution and 4D consistency of prior generative methods.
Builds auxiliary data from capture videos and combines latent representations with layout-aware positional embeddings.
Adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to model relationships across viewpoints and time.
Uses latent frequency-domain supervision to reduce the gap between generated videos and real captures.
Experiments on DNA-Rendering and the self-captured RealVV dataset show improved visual fidelity and 4D consistency over existing methods.
papers.selection_reason: Unified video diffusion framework for enhancing sparse multi-view captures into 4D-consistent volumetric video; directly relevant to video diffusion and 3D video generation.
papers.title: RealMe: Immersive Volumetric Video from Minimal Captures
papers.tldr: RealMe uses a high-resolution video diffusion model to turn sparse, low-resolution captures into immersive, temporally and multi-view consistent volumetric videos.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve. Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution. We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context. Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged. Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution. Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.
authors: Ruopeng Gao, Yukun Huang, Jiarui Hu, Shuai Wang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Limin Wang
bullets: Teacher forcing can exploit temporal redundancy, favoring local continuity over genuine modeling of visual evolution.
FCP adds an auxiliary future-chunk prediction objective alongside teacher-forced denoising.
The method uses training videos directly, requires no pretrained visual encoder, and does not alter inference.
It improves physical plausibility while using less overall training compute than standard teacher-forced training.
Visualizations suggest FCP produces a more structured representation space, potentially benefiting autoregressive world models.
papers.selection_reason: Future-chunk supervision for autoregressive video diffusion; fits autoregressive video generation.
papers.title: Looking Ahead: Modeling Future Evolution in Autoregressive Video Generation
papers.tldr: Future Chunk Prediction improves autoregressive video models’ understanding of scene evolution by training them to predict temporally separated video chunks without intervening context.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can produce visually plausible videos, yet their camera ego-motion often drifts over long horizons. Camera ego-motion determines how the viewpoint changes between frames and is essential for maintaining consistent geometry and trajectories. To address this problem, we propose CausalAlign, a causal alignment framework with two components. First, we diagnose how precise ego motion is represented, used, and retained within VGMs using linear probes and causal interventions, revealing a rise-and-fall pattern during denoising. Second, we strengthen ego-motion state in VGM by aligning the representations at the identified layers to a 3D foundation model through delta-token space. This space encodes the changes between consecutive frames, allowing the alignment to focus on ego-motion dynamics rather than static scene content. With Wan2.2 fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, CausalAlign can largely improve motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness, while preserving visual quality. For example, it improves geometric consistency by more than 20% relative to the base model. Moreover, with the fine-tuned VGM, CausalAlign improves the success rate of world action models (WAMs) by 10 points on mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365 benchmark. Overall, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency in diffusion-based VGMs and yields noticeable gains in embodied models.
authors: Kai Zhu, Yintianrun Zhang, Shuwei Jiang, Ruolin Zuo, Yixin Chen, Duomin Wang, Miao Liu, Yin Li, Daquan Zhou, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Targets ego-motion drift, which harms geometric and trajectory consistency in generated videos.
Uses linear probes and causal interventions to locate where ego-motion is represented, used, and retained during denoising.
Aligns representations at identified layers in delta-token space, emphasizing frame-to-frame motion changes over static scene content.
Fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K with Wan2.2, it improves motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness while preserving visual quality.
The improved video model also raises world action model success rates on RoboCasa365 mobile-manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Causal alignment of diffusion video generators for consistent ego-motion; fits video diffusion.
papers.title: CausalAlign: Causal Alignment of Video Generation Models for Consistent Ego-Motion
papers.tldr: CausalAlign improves long-horizon camera ego-motion consistency in diffusion video generation models by causally aligning motion representations with a 3D foundation model.

papers.abstract: Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.
authors: Marcos Junca (Senecta Inc.), Mauro Junca (Senecta Inc.)
bullets: Evaluated Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.7 Flash as deployed decision stages using one request per short thermal clip, with audio when available.
On staged laboratory data, Gemini 3.8 Flash detected 69% of held-out-subject falls and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying down and rising.
In 76 hours of occupied-home footage, it produced no false calls and detected 4 of 9 visible staged falls; the reported upper bound was 1.2 false alarms per day.
Removing a prompt warning about people leaving view substantially increased sensitivity, but caused deliberate lie-downs to be labeled as falls.
Performance fell to 34% sensitivity at 8×6 pixels; identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows, while detected falls were temporally localized accurately.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates a multimodal LLM for zero-shot event/action understanding in thermal video, fitting video understanding and multimodal LLM application.
papers.title: Asking a Multimodal LLM Whether Someone Fell: Zero-Shot Screening of Low-Resolution Thermal Video in a Laboratory and an Occupied Home
papers.tldr: A zero-shot multimodal LLM screened low-resolution thermal clips with no false alarms in tested ordinary home activity, but its fall sensitivity depended strongly on prompt wording, resolution, and whether falls went out of view.

papers.abstract: How do diffusion transformers (DiTs) represent image content and learn rules for reusing it to generalize? We develop an aggregator--predictor view of DiTs as input-adaptive local denoisers, in which context aggregation and patch prediction provide functional roles for interpreting attention and MLPs. We first establish that, for Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) priors, the global Bayes denoiser can be approximated using only a subset of context patches, with error decaying exponentially in context radius. We further show that patchwise linear denoisers, often invoked to explain diffusion generalization, recover the empirical local denoiser with sufficiently informative aggregation. Within this view, AdaLN-modulated attention naturally parameterizes an input- and noise-dependent aggregator, while the MLP admits a learned key--value representation for tokenwise patch prediction. Our experiments support this view. DiTs trained on real images exhibit noise-dependent denoising contexts resembling those in the analytic GMRF setting, while attention mass exhibits a qualitatively corresponding broadening pattern. In a controlled CelebA64 study, shared-memory patch predictors used in place of DiT MLPs achieve competitive denoising and generative performance. Finally, cross-dataset component transplantation reveals compatibility patterns consistent with the proposed roles of QK in spatial weighting, VO in feature transport, and MLPs in patch prediction. Together, these results provide a component-level account of DiT denoising and motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled intervention.
authors: Gyeonghun Kang, William Xingxu Chen, Xiang Cheng
bullets: Models DiTs as local denoisers that aggregate relevant context patches and predict clean patches.
Shows that, for GMRF priors, near-optimal denoising can use a limited context whose approximation error decreases exponentially with context radius.
Interprets AdaLN-modulated attention as a noise- and input-dependent aggregator, and MLPs as learned key–value patch predictors.
Experiments on real images, CelebA64, and component transplantation support these functional roles and identify QK with spatial weighting and VO with feature transport.
The findings motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled component interventions.
papers.selection_reason: Component-level analysis of DiT denoising is transferable to video diffusion and world model architectures.
papers.title: How Do DiTs Denoise? An Aggregator-Predictor View of Attention and MLPs
papers.tldr: The paper explains DiT denoising as input- and noise-adaptive context aggregation followed by patch prediction, assigning complementary roles to attention and MLPs.

papers.abstract: Understanding and modeling light transport in human-centric scenes is a longstanding challenge. While recent progress in diffusion models has boosted research in relighting, precise illumination control still lags, primarily due to the scarcity of diverse, high-quality, precisely labeled video relighting datasets. Existing end-to-end relighting approaches model light transport implicitly through neural networks, which substantially complicates controllability. In contrast, some works resort to path-traced irradiance cues as an explicit blueprint for light transport. However, such constructed irradiance cues are prone to artifacts and hinder generative quality when directly used as control signals. With the key observation that noise corruption removes high-frequency artifacts and preserves low-frequency light transport, we introduce an asynchronous joint-modeling paradigm that facilitates fine-grained illumination control. During two-stage training, we force the model to jointly denoise RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames with separate timesteps scheduling. A domain matching strategy is applied to the second stage to bridge the domain gap between irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps. At inference time, we introduce an asynchronous hijacked generation pipeline that facilitates flexible illumination control. For training data, we develop a multi-illumination high-quality synthetic video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model exhibits robust generalization to real- world scenarios and outperforms prior approaches in both lighting fidelity and generative quality. The code and dataset will be publicly released.
authors: Henglei Lv, Bailin Deng, Xiaoqiang Liu, Yichen Wang, Haoxian Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Lin Gao
bullets: Addresses limited high-quality, precisely labeled video-relighting data and poor controllability in implicit light-transport models.
Jointly denoises RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames using separate timestep schedules across two training stages.
Uses domain matching to reduce the gap between constructed irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps.
Introduces an asynchronous inference pipeline for flexible illumination control.
Trains on a synthetic multi-illumination video dataset and reportedly generalizes to real scenes, improving lighting fidelity and generative quality over prior methods.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based video relighting with joint RGB-irradiance modeling, fitting video diffusion and generation interests.
papers.title: JointLight: Human-Centric Video Relighting with Asynchronous RGB-Irradiance Joint Modeling
papers.tldr: JointLight enables controllable human-centric video relighting by asynchronously modeling RGB frames and irradiance cues to preserve illumination structure while reducing cue artifacts.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) is a challenging task for surveillance systems due to the scarcity and diversity of anomalous events. While semi-supervised VAD approaches have advanced the field, many rely on computationally intensive optical flow networks to capture motion dynamics. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are also widely used for spatial encoding, but their effective receptive field is highly local. To address these limitations, we introduce MS2CAST, an end-to-end semi-supervised predictive VAD framework. For spatial encoding, we employ a multi-scale cross-attention encoder that fuses the hierarchical feature representations from a vision transformer (MViTv2-S) and a CNN (ConvNeXt-T) to exploit their distinct receptive fields. To model spatiotemporal dynamics without optical flow estimation, we integrate two interchangeable spatiotemporal modules in the latent space. One module (SwinLSTM) incorporates a Swin Transformer, while the other (VMRNN) integrates Vision Mamba blocks. Our objective function combines L1 loss, Gradient Difference Loss (GDL), and Multi-Scale Structural Similarity Index Measure (MS-SSIM) to ensure pixel-wise accuracy, sharpness, and structural integrity. Evaluations across the UCSD Ped2, CUHK Avenue, and ShanghaiTech datasets demonstrate frame-level Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Area Under the Curve (AUC) scores that are competitive with top-tier techniques while maintaining a peak GPU memory usage of under 1 GB.
bullets: Addresses scarce and diverse anomalies while reducing reliance on computationally intensive optical flow.
Fuses hierarchical features from MViTv2-S and ConvNeXt-T to capture complementary spatial receptive fields.
Uses either SwinLSTM or VMRNN to model latent spatiotemporal dynamics.
Combines L1, Gradient Difference, and MS-SSIM losses for accurate, sharp, and structurally consistent predictions.
Shows competitive frame-level ROC-AUC performance on UCSD Ped2, CUHK Avenue, and ShanghaiTech, with peak GPU memory below 1 GB.
papers.selection_reason: Video anomaly detection framework with spatiotemporal modeling fits video understanding.
papers.title: MS2CAST: A Video Anomaly Detection Framework via Multi-Scale Spatial Cross-Attention and Efficient Spatiotemporal Networks
papers.tldr: MS2CAST is a memory-efficient semi-supervised video anomaly detection framework that combines multi-scale spatial cross-attention with optical-flow-free spatiotemporal modeling.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative models have enabled highly realistic face forgeries, yet generalizing deepfake detectors to unseen manipulation pipelines remains a major challenge. One critical yet underexplored issue is that the learned forensic representation itself may fail to remain stable across different manipulation sources. In this paper, we provide new evidence that naively fine-tuned vision models suffer from severe \textit{forensic representation collapse}: their extracted cues are often entangled with unstable, dataset-specific artifacts, resulting in structurally fragile representations and poor cross-domain generalization. Leveraging this insight, we propose \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{S}patial \textbf{P}rototype (\textbf{HSP}) regularization, which explicitly models the forgery manifold by learning a structured prototype subspace over spatial features. We further introduce prototype orthogonality and second-order assignment balance, which jointly preserve the geometric independence of latent forgery factors and promote high-effective-rank utilization of the forensic representation, thereby reducing reliance on dataset-specific shortcuts. Empirical results demonstrate that our method substantially improves generalizability, yielding average frame-level AUC gains of 5.6\% and 5.3\% in the cross-dataset and cross-manipulation settings, respectively. Moreover, when used as a plug-in module, HSP boosts the average video-level AUC of existing state-of-the-art detectors to 95.3\% (+1.8\%). These results demonstrate the practical value of HSP as an easy-to-adopt regularization module for enhancing deepfake detectors.
authors: Chao Shuai, Shaojing Fan, Kun Pan, Jinwu Hu, Weichen Lian, Ziqi Yang, Zhongjie Ba, Zhenguang Liu
bullets: Identifies forensic representation collapse as a key cause of poor cross-domain generalization in naively fine-tuned vision models.
Learns a structured prototype subspace over spatial features to model the forgery manifold.
Uses prototype orthogonality and second-order assignment balance to preserve distinct latent forgery factors and encourage broader representation usage.
Improves average frame-level AUC by 5.6% cross-dataset and 5.3% cross-manipulation; as a plug-in, raises video-level AUC to 95.3% (+1.8%).
Designed as an easy-to-adopt regularization module for existing deepfake detectors.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses deepfake detection by proposing Hierarchical Spatial Prototype regularization to improve cross-domain generalization, fitting Video Understanding.
papers.title: Beyond Shortcut Learning: Hierarchical Spatial Prototype Regularization for Face Forgery Detection
papers.tldr: HSP regularization improves deepfake detection across unseen datasets and manipulation types by preventing forensic representations from collapsing onto dataset-specific shortcuts.

papers.abstract: Full 3D attention is costly in video Diffusion Transformers. Block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only selected attention blocks. However, existing methods either overlook the potential to optimize sparsity allocation or rely on heuristic rules or local metrics to guide it. In this work, we observe that sparsifying attention in different layers and at different denoising steps affects final-video fidelity to substantially different degrees. Yet the identities of the most sensitive layer-step pairs remain nearly unchanged across inputs. Building on these findings, we propose Allocating Layer-step Latency by Output Tests (ALLOT), a training-free sparsity allocation method. Treating each layer-step pair as a cell, ALLOT estimates each cell's contribution to final-video error through (i) cell probing and (ii) trajectory calibration, then jointly optimizes cell densities under a measured-latency budget. It preserves existing selection strategies and kernels, replacing only the allocation component. At equal or shorter wall-clock time, ALLOT outperforms every compared allocation strategy with XAttention, with an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo. Extensive experiments across four additional published pipelines on Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and HunyuanVideo show that ALLOT outperforms or ties the default in all nine settings.
authors: Tianze Xia, Xiaoling Zhou, Ruya Lan, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song, Shiming Xiang
bullets: Full 3D attention is expensive, and different layer–step pairs have unequal effects on final-video fidelity.
ALLOT estimates each pair’s error contribution using cell probing and trajectory calibration.
It jointly optimizes sparsity densities under a measured-latency budget while retaining existing block-selection strategies and kernels.

Across five video diffusion pipelines and nine settings, ALLOT outperforms or matches the default allocation; with XAttention, it achieves an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo at equal or lower runtime.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes ALLOT, a training-free method to optimize block-sparse attention allocation in Video Diffusion Transformers, directly addressing efficiency and video generation.
papers.title: Sparsity Should Be ALLOTted by Output: Training-Free Allocation of Block-Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: ALLOT is a training-free method that allocates block-sparse attention across layer–denoising-step pairs to improve video diffusion quality under a latency budget.

papers.abstract: Unlike question answering, where a query specifies a perceptual target, open-ended detailed captioning must determine what evidence to acquire and how to integrate it into a coherent global description. We propose Observation-Adaptive Video Captioner (OACap), a caption-centered agent that turns unsupported or missing information into targeted observation requests, uses spatiotemporal tools to acquire evidence, and iteratively verifies and revises the caption. OACap captions consistently improve performance across general video-understanding benchmarks using a fixed text-only reader. To better diagnose the information they preserve, we introduce Factual-Semantic Captioning Bench (FSCap-Bench). Its Core-Support Factuality Score (CSFS) combines claim precision with importance-aware fact coverage and responds as expected to four controlled perturbation types on 93.0-98.3% of valid caption pairs. Its Cross-Modal Semantic Round-Trip Score (CSRS) measures semantic preservation through a video-caption-video-caption round trip by matching atomic facts from source and recovered captions. Together, they connect downstream textual-memory utility with factual and semantic preservation.
authors: Hao Shi, Hong Yan, Xiaoyang Zhang, Qing Cui, Chao Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deciding what evidence to observe for open-ended, detailed video captioning.
Uses a caption-centered agent that identifies missing or unsupported information, gathers targeted spatiotemporal evidence, and revises captions iteratively.
Improves captioning performance across general video-understanding benchmarks with a fixed text-only reader.
Introduces FSCap-Bench with CSFS for importance-aware factual coverage and CSRS for cross-modal semantic preservation.
CSFS responds appropriately to four controlled perturbations in 93.0–98.3% of valid caption pairs.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an active observation agent for detailed video captioning, relevant to video understanding and multimodal agents.
papers.title: OACap: Caption-Guided Active Observation for Detailed Video Captioning
papers.tldr: OACap actively requests and verifies visual evidence to produce more detailed, factually supported video captions, while FSCap-Bench evaluates their factual and semantic preservation.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy. Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Sangyoon Lee, Jaeho Lee
bullets: Problem: Idle-time KV prefill must use restricted context, causing a mismatch because relevant query information is unavailable and irrelevant context may be included.
Method: At query time, re-prefill selected video tokens with query-relevant context and replace their cached KVs; no additional training is required.
Contribution: Enables shorter idle-time attention windows, lowering prefill computation while preserving or improving contextualization.
Results: Across three SVU frameworks and five benchmarks, accuracy improves by up to 3.9 percentage points.
Efficiency: On RVS-Ego, per-frame prefill FLOPs decrease by over 20%, while total processing time drops by 14–59% for retrieval-based frameworks.
papers.selection_reason: Selective KV recomputation for streaming video LLMs; directly combines video understanding with cache-efficiency and memory reduction.
papers.title: Cache Locally, Recompute Selectively for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FrameBlend improves streaming video understanding by selectively recomputing cached video-token representations with query-relevant context, reducing preprocessing cost while increasing accuracy.

papers.abstract: Autonomous industrial inspection requires strictly deterministic real-time inference under tight memory and computational constraints. However, existing Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) models suffer from prohibitive scaling: dense temporal memory grows with spatial resolution and sequence length, while fixed-capacity decoders fail to exploit the inherent sparsity of industrial scenes, creating a practical memory wall on resource-constrained edge platforms. We present DetM-Tracker, a streamlined VIS framework for autonomous industrial inspection, where target objects often exhibit highly similar appearance under constrained "micro" fields of view. DetM-Tracker eliminates architectural redundancy through three synergistic components: (1) Compact Scalar Memory, which condenses high-dimensional instance features into four-scalar descriptors, reducing temporal memory complexity from $O(T \cdot N \cdot R)$ to $O(T \cdot \hat{N})$. This mechanism effectively compresses frame-level representations into a bank of active instances, where $R$ denotes resolution, $N$ and $\hat{N}$ represent global and window-specific instance counts, respectively and $T$ the temporal window size; and (2) Dynamic Instance Channels, which adaptively allocate query capacity according to the actual number of visible objects; and (3) Entropy-Gated Skip Connection, which concentrates computational budget on high-uncertainty spatial regions to refine object boundaries in a single forward pass without auxiliary refinement heads. Our approach effectively bridges the gap between modern VIS models and the practical demands of industrial edge deployment, reducing inference latency by approximately 20$\times$ and VRAM consumption by 6$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art dense-feature baselines.
authors: You-Rui Lin, Jen-Chieh Wu, Tzu-Ti Wei, Jen-Jee Chen, Yu-Chee Tseng
bullets: Targets the memory and compute limits of edge platforms running autonomous industrial inspection.
Uses Compact Scalar Memory to reduce temporal memory complexity from O(T·N·R) to O(T·N̂) with four-scalar instance descriptors.
Dynamically allocates instance channels based on the number of visible objects.
